title: Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction set for Los Angeles, with many big names skipping the stage
summary: The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony on Saturday may feel like an '80s night
story: The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony on Saturday may feel like an '80s night

LOS ANGELES -- It may feel like '80s night at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony, with the new members including Billy Idol, Phil Collins, Sade, Queen Latifah, New Order, Luther Vandross and Iron Maiden.

But it's hard to say exactly what the vibe will be on Saturday at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, with many of the inductees opting out of performing or appearing, and the Hall of Fame revealing next-to-nothing about the show during the run-up.
After streaming the ceremony live the past few years, the Rock Hall is returning to its previous model, where the public won’t see it until an edited version airs on ABC and Disney+ on Dec. 9.
Here's what we do know about the show:
Oasis, youngest of the inductees, won’t be coming. Guitarist Noel Gallagher is playing a gig back home in Britain, and his little brother, Liam Gallagher, just doesn't want to come.
“It’s too far to be going for the night,” he said in a post on the social platform X. He added in another, “I dont like award ceremonies they freak me out I dont know why I just get weird vibes."

Iron Maiden will be on tour in Australia. Sade is opting to sit it out, too. Collins is likely to appear, but he said he has to decline from playing his songs for health reasons. Key members of New Order, getting a joint induction with their previous incarnation Joy Division, will also be out for health reasons. Vandross died in 2005.
But the show will go on, and hip-hop could be the highlight. Wu-Tang Clan will be inducted along with Queen Latifah and MC Lyte, and all are expected to appear and probably perform.
And Idol, being inducted with his longtime guitarist Steve Stevens, will take the stage ready to rock.
Latifah and Lyte enter the hall as recipients of the Early Influence Award along with posthumous nominees Gram Parsons, Fela Kuti  and Celia Cruz.

Parsons, an essential figure at the crossroads of country and rock in the 1960s and '70s, got his own separate tribute Wednesday night at the legendary Troubadour club in West Hollywood, where his duet partner Emmylou Harris along with Rock Hall-of-Famers Elvis Costello and Sheryl Crow sang his songs and saluted his legacy.
Kuti will become the first African-born artist in the hall, and Cruz will become the first member who sang primarily in Spanish.

A group of producers will be inducted via the Musical Excellence Award: Rick Rubin, Linda Creed, Arif Mardin and Jimmy Miller. And TV host Ed Sullivan will get in as the winner of the Ahmet Ertugun award, which goes to nonmusicians who've made rock history.

Many other major stars are likely to appear to induct the new members or to play the absentees' songs in tribute. The past few years, the hall has announced several special guests, though not their roles, the week of the show, but with no live airing this year it has returned to a model of keeping nearly everything secret until it happens.
The show is in Los Angeles for the second straight year, and organizers have said it will be here more often while still rotating to New York and Cleveland, where the actual hall resides.

title: 'The Sun Also Rises' at 100: Women are now leaders in Hemingway scholarship
summary: Hilary K
story: Hilary K

NEW YORK -- Hilary K. Justice, an Ernest Hemingway scholar at Boston's John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum, remembers having to defend her chosen field of expertise as a graduate student some 30 years ago.

“I was told that studying Hemingway amounted to committing professional suicide — ‘Haven’t we killed him yet?’ was the comment of one professor in my PhD program,” she said in a recent interview. Justice oversees the Hemingway collection at the JFK library, where the author's papers are stored.
“I used to be able to count on being asked ‘How do you, as a woman, justify studying Hemingway?’ at every Q&A session at every public speaking event.”

This year marks the centennial of Hemingway's classic breakout novel, “The Sun Also Rises,” an occasion for scholars and fans to celebrate his work — and express relief that his outsized legend has receded enough that his books can stand or fall on their own. Hemingway died more than 60 years ago, and at least a generation of students has come of age knowing little about the man who for countless predecessors embodied the very ideal — or anti-ideal — of the writing life: the macho adventurer, drinker and womanizer who once famously defined courage as “grace under pressure.”

At a centennial event last month at the 92nd Street Y Unterberg Poetry Center in Manhattan, Maya Hawke, Will Harrison, Sarah Pidgeon and other actors read from “The Sun Also Rises,” and a panel discussion featured “Bright Lights, Big City” novelist Jay McInerney and a handful of Hemingway descendants. Grandson Brendan Hemingway, a teenager during the rise of second-wave feminism in the 1970s, spoke of female classmates approaching him in high school hallways just to tell him how much they despised the author.

“People decided that they'd project on to me whatever they liked or didn't like about Ernest Hemingway and were surprised that wasn't a great experience for me,” said Brendan Hemingway, now 65. “And the big thing for me at 100 (years of “The Sun Also Rises”) is for my daughter's generation that's all gone. We've outlasted the baggage. We've outrun the backlash. For my daughter's generation, you read him or you don't."

Justice and other Hemingway scholars say they generally encounter little resistance these days. Verna Kale, an associate research professor at Penn State, says she recently asked a group of students if they had ever read Hemingway and was told that none of them had. Ross K. Tangedal, an associate professor of English at the University of Wisconsin-Stevens Point and a member of the Hemingway Letters Project editorial team, said his students usually were “exposed to his work in small doses in high school.”
“So when they come to my college classroom they encounter the work before the myth,” he added.

Hemingway's 1926 novel follows British and American expatriates adrift in Europe, sustaining themselves on sex, alcohol, boxing and bullfights. It was a foundational text for the so-called “Lost Generation” of the post World War I era, and for many aspiring writers after. McInerney, 71, told the audience gathered at the Poetry Center that he first read “The Sun Also Rises” while in college and remembered how the novel “blew me away.”

“I couldn't believe how fresh it was and how it seemed really cool, to me” he said. "When the book was published, it essentially revolutionized English prose. It was a really radical new voice that somehow still spoke directly to me."

“The Sun Also Rises” is still popular, although its numbers fall well short of the book's famous contemporary, F. Scott Fitzgerald's “The Great Gatsby.” According to Circana, which tracks around 85% of the print market, “The Sun Also Rises” has sold just under 40,000 copies this year so far, down from a peak of more than 60,000 for each of several years in the 2010s. Over the past 20 years, sales in the U.S. have topped 1 million copies ("Gatsby" sales over the same time period approached 8 million).

Debra Moddelmog, who serves on the editorial board of The Hemingway Review, acknowledges that many readers familiar with Hemingway's image regard the women in his books as stereotyped and marginalized. But she thinks of Hemingway as a “deceptive” writer whose famously terse prose holds unexpected dimensions. She cites the libertine Lady Brett Ashley of “The Sun Also Rises" as someone whom close reading reveals to be a “complex character rather than the typical femme fatale.”

Justice notes that women hold many of the leading roles in Hemingway scholarship, including Moddelmog; Sandra Spanier, general editor of the Hemingway Letters Project; and Suzanne del Gizzo, editor of The Hemingway Review.

Kale, an associate editor for the Hemingway letters project and the editor of a Norton Library edition of “The Sun Also Rises,” is a self-identified Gen-Xer who started out as a student of medieval literature. She changed her focus after experiencing a Hemingway-esque epiphany as she read “The Sun Also Rises” — on a night train to Spain during a trip to Europe.

“I was just the right age to read it, and I became very interested in the expatriate modernists,” she said. “I’ve never had any misgivings about studying Hemingway whatsoever. I find his writing captivating, and documenting his life through his letters has become my life’s work.”

title: Incoming congressman Bobby Pulido was just one political moment at the Latin Grammys
summary: Bobby Pulido is a member-elect for the U.S. House of Representatives who has also recently won the Latin Grammy for best Tejano album
story: Bobby Pulido is a member-elect for the U.S. House of Representatives who has also recently won the Latin Grammy for best Tejano album

Shielded by the shadow of his signature cowboy hat, Bobby Pulido took to the stage of the Latin Grammys to accept the award for best Tejano album. It was his third time accepting a win in the category, but it was his first as a member-elect in the U.S. House of Representatives.

One week earlier, the Democrat won a competitive race to flip Texas’ Republican-held 15th Congressional district. Onstage, he confirmed his retirement from a monumental music career, but underscored his gratitude in representing both the politics and music of the Lone Star State.
“I have so much pride to be from Texas, to be Tejano, and to represent this music,” Pulido told the audience Thursday.

The appearance from the future congressman was one of several long-dormant political references during this year’s ceremony in Las Vegas. From red carpet interviews to main stage performances, emboldened artists called for international unity and representation across the diaspora.

Ten years ago, the Latin Grammys made headlines for restricting journalists for asking political questions on the red carpet. In past performances, artists proudly denounced racism in American politics and brought attention to human rights crises in Mexico. A 2016 policy quieted this advocacy in the years that followed.

After historic milestones for representation in the recent midterm elections, propelled in no small part by Latino voters, Pulido’s double victory matched similar messages championing change across music and politics.
“We have to represent,” Pulido said in his speech. “We have to get to work, to use our voice for something different.”
The Latin Grammys did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Associated Press on Friday.

Daddy Yankee opened his crowning performance as the Person of the Year honoree draped in a flowing cape of the Puerto Rican flag. Building on a landmark year of advocacy from Boricua artists, Yankee proclaimed: “Puerto Rico isn’t small. The map is small.”

“Years ago the government even thought that we were criminals, that we had no future,” said Yankee in his acceptance speech. “Once I dreamed of being a baseball player. So I’m grateful that I’m getting hits here in the big leagues, at the Grammys.”
Silvana Estrada, a Mexican folk musician with a legacy of advocating against femicide in her home country, told the AP that the role of a musician today is “super important.”

“Artists should step forward without fear and say what we think, because that’s how we encourage the people who follow us to find that confidence in themselves,” said Estrada, who’s single “Dime” was awarded best singer-songwriter song.

In the most overtly political moment of the night, Brazilian artist Anitta 's victory for best pop contemporary Portuguese album marked the first time an award in the language was handed out during the televised ceremony. Anitta used her platform to call for unity across the different communities of Latin America and in her home country.
“For many years Black culture was erased in Brazil,” Anitta said. “This album comes to help with that, so that Black culture in Brazil is strong forever.”
Getting ready for the red carpet, Anamaria Sayre of NPR’s “Alt.Latino” had one major question on her mind. She asked online: “Are the Latin Grammys going to get political tonight?”

Sayre is a producer of El Tiny, the Latino version of NPR’s Tiny Desk, where she’s followed the shift in alternative musicians being recognized by the Latin Recording Academy, especially ones who, she said, “overtly” center their advocacy in their art.

Sayre attributes this wave of genre-bending creativity to the very reason the Latin Grammys were founded. “We needed a whole other Grammys to fit all of the different types of music that come out of Latin America,” she told the AP.

Political turnover took place across the Western Hemisphere this year, with broader right-wing movements across Latin America matched by progressive shifts in the U.S. and Brazil. “It doesn’t split that cleanly,” Sayre added, which, to her, underscored the correlation between musical and political change-making even more.
“I don’t think you can ever look at music, or how we value music, as independent from a political landscape,” Sayre said.
Associated Press journalist Leslie Ambriz in Los Angeles contributed reporting.

title: After 8 nominations without a win, Glenn Close is 'overwhelmed' by honorary Oscar
summary: Glenn Close is receiving an honorary Oscar on Sunday at the Governors Awards
story: Glenn Close is receiving an honorary Oscar on Sunday at the Governors Awards
When Glenn Close got the call that she’d been chosen to receive an honorary Oscar, the 79-year-old actor had two somewhat unconventional thoughts.
“My first reaction was I don’t need a consolation prize,” Close told The Associated Press in a recent interview. “And my second reaction was, I don’t know … do I want to end my loss record?”

Close does indeed have an Oscars record going: Over the course of her career, she’s been nominated for acting prizes eight times and never won. It’s a distinction she has worn with grace and humor over the years, and she’s in good company: Peter O’Toole was similarly nominated eight times without a win.

The honorary Oscar, also known as the Academy Honorary Award, is indeed different from a competitive Oscar. Although the golden statuettes are the same, the award is not given for a specific film, but for a body of work and contributions to the motion picture industry. The voters, or rather selection committee, is also much smaller: The film academy’s Board of Governors as opposed to the entire Academy membership. There are no “losers.” And, since 2009, the prizes have been presented not during the Academy Awards but in a separate event in Los Angeles known as the Governors Awards.

Perhaps most importantly, however, with no broadcast television cameras, the Governors Awards have the luxury of time, for touching montages and thoughtful speeches by friends and collaborators, and the honorees themselves. There is space to reflect without the pressure of a ticking clock, or an orchestra ready to play you off.

“I’m still processing it and it means it means a lot, you know, at this point in my life,” Close said. “I’ve been a working actor for over 50 years, I got my first Oscar nomination 43 years ago. So it’s been a life, you know? And it’s overwhelming.”

The occasion has Close thinking about her own history with the Oscars, and how much things have changed over the years. Her first nomination came for her first film role, in George Roy Hill’s “The World According to Garp.” She remembers receiving the news while shooting “The Big Chill,” where her performance as Sarah Cooper, the woman hosting the gathering after the death of their friend, would earn her a second nomination.
“It was the furthest thing from my mind,” Close said. “I never even thought about the possibility of being nominated for an Oscar. I still can remember my absolute astonishment.”

The thing that she remembers most about that first ceremony, held at the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion in 1983, was what she wore: “The most beautiful little velvet dress,” she said, designed by her friend, costumer Ann Roth.

Some of her memories are about what other people wore, like the one time she sat behind Madonna and marveled at her “fabulous” white fur. Then there was the year she was nominated for “Fatal Attraction,” when there was a whole section of the crowd outside that had styled their hair in tight curls like her character, Alex Forrest.
“That was fabulous,” she said.

What was a little confusing, however, was when she walked out to present an award with her co-star Michael Douglas and the audience laughed. She was eight months pregnant at the time and had to fly to Los Angeles on a private plane, with her OB-GYN as chaperone, because she wasn’t allowed to fly commercial.

“At first, I thought, why are they laughing?” Close said. “And we realized it was because in the movie, I say I’m pregnant with this child and he doesn’t want to have anything to do with it, denies it, and there was always a question whether she really was telling the truth or not. And there I was, hugely pregnant, walking out with Michael. So it was very funny.”

Douglas recently made headlines for saying on The Graham Norton Show that Close deserved to win that year. When asked if she was surprised that he’d said that, Close paused and said: “Publicly, yeah.”
While the phrase “it’s an honor to be nominated” has become a bit of a cliché, it’s also a kind of mantra for Close, who has never done a role thinking that it would lead to awards.

“I have the DNA of an outsider,” Close said. “So because of that, I’ve always felt the greatest honor was to actually be in the room … the winner loser thing — especially in the temperature of our country now — for me, does not apply. The fact that you are in the room with some of the most creative people on the planet is what counts.”

She hasn’t decided where she might put her statuette in her home, but she is already thinking about how she can share it with the people of Bozeman, Montana. Close has been grateful to be able to continue working as much as she does (just this year she’s appeared in the Spanish language epic and presumed Oscar nominee“La Bola Negra,” the latest season of “All's Fair” and a new Hunger Games movie ). But her ability to leave, to go home to a place away from Hollywood, is the thing that allows her to recharge between performances.

“In some ways, I want to share it with the community here,” she said. She wants to find a place where, “for a day, people can go and see what a real Oscar looks like.” And she has an idea for where: A “fantastic bakery called the Wild Crumb.” But, she added, she hasn’t talked to them about it yet.
At the Governors Awards on Sunday, Close will be accompanied by her daughter and son-in-law, and wearing a custom Armani gown, which she’s very excited about.

The honorary Oscar doesn’t negate Close’s competitive Oscars record either. O’Toole also received one, in 2003, after all. Now, she’s just feeling grateful and putting the finishing touches on her speech.
“It’s incredibly special and it’s a huge honor,” Close said. “I don’t know how I’m going to get through it because it’s very emotional for me. But I will somehow.”

title: US visa restrictions force some African contestants out of Miss Universe competition
summary: Two African contestants will miss this year’s Miss Universe competition in Puerto Rico due to visa restrictions imposed by President Donald Trump’s administration
story: Two African contestants will miss this year’s Miss Universe competition in Puerto Rico due to visa restrictions imposed by President Donald Trump’s administration

HARARE, Zimbabwe -- Two African contestants will miss this year’s Miss Universe competition in Puerto Rico because of visa restrictions imposed by President Donald Trump’s administration, while two others are struggling to obtain visas.

Representatives from Zambia and the Republic of Congo have withdrawn from the pageant, which takes place this month in the U.S. territory, after failing to secure visas. Contestants from South Sudan and Zimbabwe are still awaiting theirs.
The United States has imposed sweeping travel restrictions affecting dozens of countries, many of them in Africa, under proclamations issued during Trump’s second administration.

Last December, the administration expanded restrictions to additional countries, including Zambia and Zimbabwe, while maintaining a full suspension of entry for nationals of the Republic of Congo and South Sudan.

“She earned her crown, she earned her title, and she deserves the opportunity to represent the nation she proudly serves,” Miss Universe Zambia organizers said in a statement this week announcing the withdrawal of their representative, Mubanga Pamela Hatyoka.

In the Republic of Congo, Georgina Kambongo made history when she was crowned the Central African country’s first Miss Universe representative. National organizers say her inability to travel to Puerto Rico is linked solely to Trump’s travel restrictions.

“American visa challenges have delayed that journey, but the fight is not over,” Zimbabwe’s representative, Roseanna Hall, said in a social media post. “After months of preparation, I am not giving up. I remain confident that God who began a good work in me will bring it to completion.”
In South Sudan, organizers said contestant Adut Deng’s participation remained uncertain despite months of efforts to secure the necessary travel documents and approvals.
“South Sudan deserves to be seen, heard, and represented. Our queen carries the hopes, dreams, beauty, and resilience of a nation,” organizers said in a statement.
The competition’s 75th edition is expected to attract up to 120 contestants. Delegates began arriving in Puerto Rico on Sunday for rehearsals and other preliminary activities.
A national costume competition is scheduled for Nov. 21, followed by swimsuit and evening gown segments the following day. The winner will be crowned on Nov. 24.

title: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade 100th edition: Which stars are in the lineup?
summary: The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade promises a spectacular celebration with Megan Moroney, Teddy Swims, Queen Latifah, Keke Palmer, Jimmy Fallon & The Roots and JoJo among the performers
story: The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade promises a spectacular celebration with Megan Moroney, Teddy Swims, Queen Latifah, Keke Palmer, Jimmy Fallon & The Roots and JoJo among the performers

NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — Megan Moroney,Teddy Swims, Queen Latifah, Keke Palmer, Jimmy Fallon & The Roots and JoJo will help celebrate the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade this year, a lineup that includes a record-breaking, very appropriate 100 inflatables in the sky, including Bluey, Mickey Mouse and Hello Kitty.

The parade will begin at 8:30 a.m. on Thanksgiving Day in all time zones and will feature a tribute to Dolly Parton led by Megan Hilty, and special appearances by Melissa Joan Hart, Jack McBrayer, Janet McTeer, Holly Robinson Peete and Rodney Peete, all leading the way for Santa Claus.

Performances will also include EJAE, Indigo Girls, Natalie Merchant, Baha Men, Natasha Bedingfield, Blues Traveler, DEVO, Feid, Mckenna Grace, Icona Pop, Il Volo, Wyclef Jean, Jamie Miller, Ryan Peter Murphy, Leslie Odom Jr., Anthony Ramos, RIIZE and Smash Mouth.

The familiar TV hosts — Savannah Guthrie, Hoda Kotb and Al Roker from the “Today” show — will return on NBC and Peacock. A Spanish-language simulcast on Telemundo will be hosted by the network’s Andrea Meza, Aleyda Ortiz and Clovis Nienow.

“For our 100th parade, we’re creating a celebration of unprecedented scale and will deliver an unforgettable Thanksgiving for millions across the country,” said Sharon Otterman, Macy’s chief marketing officer, in a statement.

New balloons and inflatable elements include Bluey, Buckaroo Bob the Minion, Earl the Squirrel, Hello Kitty Big Apple, Joe Cool & Woodstock from “Peanuts,” Sorcerer’s Apprentice Mickey, Underdog and a new balloonicle, Fuzzyeti’s Fur Wheel Drive by Levi’s. Macy’s Studios also created Billie Brightpaw for the centennial lineup, described as a cheerful and curious bear.

New floats in the 2026 parade lineup include Dashing All the Way with DoorDash; Hogwarts Holiday with HBO; Mr. Peanut Power Plant with Planters; Purina Dog Chow Salute to Service Dogs with Purina Dog Chow; Road Trip to Parade with GEICO; and Macy’s Tony Sarg’s Amazing Marionettes.

There also will be iconic characters from past parades, including Angry Birds’ Red, Arthur, Bugs Bunny, Bullwinkle J. Moose, Curious George, Adventure Time’s Finn & Jake, Jimmy Neutron, Popeye & Olive Oyl & Swee’Pea, Pink Panther, Poppy from “Trolls,” Scooby-Doo, Sonic the Hedgehog, the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles and Wild Thing.
“Few holiday traditions capture the excitement of Thanksgiving morning quite like Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade,” said Jen Neal, executive vice president at NBC & Peacock, in a statement.

The parade will be preceded by a new documentary, “America’s Parade: 100 Years of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade,” set to air Nov. 20 on NBC and begin streaming the next day on Peacock. The film will be “celebrating the people, artistry and imagination behind the tradition,” blending archival moments with a look at preparations for the milestone march. It will include interviews with previous performers like Billy Porter and Andrew Rannells.

This year’s marching bands will represent schools from Indiana, Tennessee, South Carolina, Hawaii, Texas, Alabama, Connecticut, Illinois, as well as the New York Police Department Marching Band and Macy’s Great American Marching Band, which represents students from all 50 states.
There will also be performances from Maria Verdeja School of the Arts, The Divine Nine Unity Step Team, Native Pride Productions, Spirit of America Cheer and Spirit of America Dance.
Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade made its debut in 1924 and has become an annual tradition and hallmark of the holiday season, with the exception of a three-year break during World War II.

title: At Sing Sing prison, incarcerated men get preview of new PBS documentary on nation's justice system
summary: Incarcerated men at the Sing Sing Correctional Facility have previewed a new docuseries on the history of the nation's criminal justice system
story: Incarcerated men at the Sing Sing Correctional Facility have previewed a new docuseries on the history of the nation's criminal justice system

OSSINING, New York -- As the lights dimmed inside the chapel at the Sing Sing Correctional Facility in New York, around 30 incarcerated men sat scattered across the pews, waiting to preview a new docuseries on the history of the nation’s criminal justice system.
Our Lady of Hope chapel was soon abuzz with discussion, as some learned new things about an American institution with which they already have a great deal of personal experience.

The four-part series, “Crime and Punishment in America,” is set to premiere Monday on PBS. It spends eight hours tracing how the justice system evolved, from the colonial period to present day, and viewers get to hear from legal scholars, formerly incarcerated people, victims’ families and corrections officers.

The U.S. maintains the world's largest incarcerated population, with nearly two million people behind bars in prisons and jails. In 2024, each state incarcerated more people per capita than most countries, according to the Prison Policy Initiative.

“What are we hoping to accomplish with this?” film director Lynn Novick said in an interview with The Associated Press. “Digging into the history and revealing it will help us to have a different conversation about what justice means in this country.”

Novick developed the series with frequent collaborator Ken Burns, an acclaimed filmmaker with numerous PBS documentaries to his name. In 2019, the two partnered on “College Behind Bars,” which followed a Bard College program to provide a liberal arts education to incarcerated people.

Sing Sing was Novick’s sixth screening for prison populations in correctional facilities: Maine, Connecticut, California and Washington state prisons, as well as New York City’s Rikers’ jail, have hosted previews of “Crime and Punishment in America.”
Sing Sing prisoners were shown a 47-minute reel from the full series.

“I hope that as people see this documentary, that they are challenged to think about what we have to do differently,” said Michael Shane Hale, 54 and from Kentucky, who has served 32 years of a 50-to-life prison sentence.

Hale said the viewing public should no longer question whether it's possible for prisoners to turn their lives around. The question, he added, should instead be “what do we do with transformed people?”

The conversation at Sing Sing was more animated than Novick had anticipated. Some of the prisoners gathered in the chapel were invigorated by news of California Gov. Gavin Newsom saying he would commute hundreds of death sentences before leaving office, which experts say would be the largest mass clemency in American history.

Several prisoners inundated a panel of speakers with concerns about what rehabilitation through incarceration looks like for their families and for victims. Others drew connections between their crimes, mental illness and economic circumstances.

“Nobody is the sum of their worst mistake, right?” said José Colon, 44 and from the Bronx, who entered prison at age 17 and has been incarcerated for nearly 28 years. “No matter where you are in life, there’s always room for growth.”
John Rizzo, another Sing Sing prisoner, asked the panel what “rehabilitation” means to society.
“When we come in here, we’re tainted,” Rizzo said later in an interview with the AP. “When we go back out into society, when is the incarcerated individual going to be acceptable again?”

Rizzo has served 16 years so far on a conviction for conspiracy and attempted murder. He said he spends his time helping peers apply for prison jobs and studying for a bachelor’s degree in behavioral science that he intends to earn while incarcerated.

Reginald Dwayne Betts, a panelist and poet who served eight years for a carjacking at 16, agreed with Rizzo. He said people seemed to focus on his past when he returned to life after prison. “It was always, ‘Can you tell me more about your crime?’” he said.
Betts has created a documentary following his life and became known for his work installing libraries in the nation’s prisons.

Daniel F. Martuscello III, the first former correction officer appointed commissioner of the New York State Department of Correction, said he agreed to screen Novick's film because he sees it as an extension of the prison’s Rehabilitation Through the Arts workshops.

“It’s our obligation, not only as commissioners, but as people running the system, lawmakers, to make sure that we’re telling that story,” Martuscello said. “Because to not do so, it takes away from that transformation, and really, it degrades public safety.”

John J. Lennon is an incarcerated Sing Sing prison journalist and a recipient of a 2026 Guggenheim Fellowship, a prestigious and competitive grant to support scholars, artists and scientists for work “under the freest possible conditions.” In-prison programs, he says, are what allowed him to build a writing career after entering prison with a ninth-grade education.
He said New York, and the nation as a whole, has much more reform work to do.
“If you want accountability in America, then there has to be forgiveness on the table,” Lennon said. “There has to be mercy on the table.”

title: Rosalía’s ‘Lux’ wins album of the year at the 2026 Latin Grammy Awards
summary: Spanish singer Rosalía has taken home the top prize of album of the year at the 2026 Latin Grammys on Thursday night for her 2025 album “Lux.”
story: Spanish singer Rosalía has taken home the top prize of album of the year at the 2026 Latin Grammys on Thursday night for her 2025 album “Lux.”
LAS VEGAS -- Spanish singer Rosalía took home the top prize of album of the year at the 2026 Latin Grammys on Thursday night for her 2025 album “Lux.”

She opened the 27th annual Latin Grammy Awards, live from Sin City, with an emotive medley of her “Lux” tracks “La Rumba Del Perdón,” “La Perla” and “Dios Es Un Stalker,” joined by angelic dancers ornamented with halos atop a stage meant to look like heavenly clouds.
It was a reminder of the expansiveness of her album: an offbeat, full-hearted embrace of her classical training through huge orchestral movements, inspired by the lives of female saints.

Her “La Perla” also won song of the year, and during her speech, she thanked Mexico and invited her collaborators on the song, the American urban sierreño trio Yahritza Y Su Esencia, to join her on stage.

Daddy Yankee, the 2026 Latin Grammy Awards' person of the year and first Latin urbano artist to receive the honor, ripped through his biggest hits an hour into Thursday's award show, treating the stage like a stadium floor.

It was one for the history books: There were outfit changes, set changes and his native Puerto Rico always at the forefront as he ran through “Ella Me Levantó,” “Con Calma,” “BOTZ,” “Despacito,” “Lo Que Pasó, Pasó,” “Sonríele,” “Rompe,” “Pokito” and, of course, “Gasolina” — joined by Bizarrap, Bad Gyal, Feid, Jay Wheeler, French Montana, LL Cool J and Diljit Dosanjh.

When it came time for Daddy Yankee to receive his honor, it was delivered to him by Janet Jackson “with admiration and respect,” as she said in her speech. When he accepted the award, he concluded by saying “Puerto Rico, recuerda. ... Puerto Rico no es pequeño. Pequeño el mapa." In English: “Puerto Rico, remember. ... Puerto Rico is not small. The map is small.”
The award show is taking place live from Las Vegas’ MGM Grand Garden Arena. It's being aired live on Univision, UniMás, Galavisión and ViX and hosted by actor, producer and musician Roselyn Sánchez.
For the first award of the night, Pablo Alboran and Backstreet Boys’ Howie D presented Juanes with best pop/rock album for “Juanesteban.”

Performances were at a high level: Karol G was joined by a full orchestra and 12 Mariachis for her música mexicana ballad “Ese Hombre es Malo.” Mon Laferte broke hearts with her soulful “Femme Fatale.” Silvana Estrada’s “Dime” bridged culture and heritage with her signature Venezuelan cuatro, a four-stringed instrument similar in structure to a ukulele.

Kany García stunned with her acoustic, aflamencado single “La Niña Que Fui.” The Uruguayan-born Jorge Drexler’s rendition of “Las Palabras” felt like theater. And Argentine rapper Milo J performed “Solifican12” and “Gil,” joined by the Latin American folk icon Gustavo Santaolalla.
Carín León brought the house down with “Desde Que Te Tengo,” as did Juanes and Vivir Quintana with “Humano.” Elena Rose was joined by sword-wielding dancers for “Alma."

Brazilian superstar Anitta did a medley of her “Equilibrium” hits — “Desgraça,” “Choka Choka” and “Meia Noite” among them — an eclectic mix of Brazilian funk, samba, bossa nova, semba, reggae, electronic pop performed in Portuguese, Spanish and English.
Soon after, she was back on stage accepting the trophy for Portuguese language contemporary pop album. She used her speech to shine a light on the Black culture of her native Brazil.

There was a touching tribute to the late ranchera icon, Mexican singer-songwriter José Alfredo Jiménez, produced by Edgar Barrera: The Warning covered “Te Solté la Rienda,” Reik did “La Media Vuelta,” Sofía Reyes and Yami Safdie dueted “Si Nos Dejan” and Camila Fernández brought it home with a big belting “El Rey.” Not soon afterward, she headed back to the stage to perform a full-throated “Serpiente De Cascabel.”

It was the first of two tributes: The second was for Willie Colón, the social activist and Grammy-nominated architect of urban salsa music, who died in February of this year. His son, Miguel Colón, as well as Nathy Peluso and Luis Figueroa and others performed.

Awards were handed out quickly, too. Karol G took home the trophy for urban music album for “Tropicoqueta.” Xavi won contemporary Mexican album for “Dosis,” his first Latin Grammy. Fonseca was presented the trophy for contemporary tropical album shortly thereafter for his album, “Antes Que El Tiempo Se Vaya.”

Best new artist went to Colombian singer Aria Vega, who gave her acceptance speech through tears. This year, the Latin Recording Academy made changes to the category so that only artists with fewer than three albums or 25 singles released were eligible to win.

Most of the evening’s awards were handed out during a pre-televised Premiere Ceremony. That included Bobby Pulido winning the Latin Grammy for best Tejano album for his release “Bobby Pulido & Friends: Una Tuya y Una Mía (Vol. 2/En Vivo)." Just days earlier, Pulido made history in the U.S. midterm elections by securing a seat in the House of Representatives for the Democrats by flipping a Texas district seat.
“I want to tell you that I’m retiring from music, and I’m leaving with so much gratitude,” he said in his acceptance speech.

title: 'Malcolm in the Middle' star, race car driver Frankie Muniz hospitalized after Daytona crash
summary: Actor and race car driver Frankie Muniz was hospitalized Wednesday following a practice-lap crash at Daytona International Speedway, according to his racing team
story: Actor and race car driver Frankie Muniz was hospitalized Wednesday following a practice-lap crash at Daytona International Speedway, according to his racing team
Actor and race car driver Frankie Muniz was hospitalized Wednesday following a practice-lap crash at Daytona International Speedway, according to his racing team.
Team Reaume said the “Malcolm in the Middle” star was “awake and alert.”
The 40-year-old Muniz was practicing for a Proud to Honor Veterans Day Classic event, a benefit race set for Wednesday night at Daytona's road course.
“We’ll share updates as they become available,” Team Reaume posted on X that it would provide updates when available while thanking followers for "respecting Frankie’s privacy at this time.”

Muniz and NASCAR driver Austin Cindric were set to represent Team Air Force in an exhibition race that benefits six nonprofits that support military and veteran communities through the Proud to Honor Fund, according to a NASCAR release.
A dozen Ford Racing drivers were split into six teams to race head-to-head in Mustang Dark Horse cars in honor of a branch of the U.S. military.
Musical performances by the Zac Brown Band, Russell Dickerson, Jo Dee Messina, Brittney Spencer, and Warren Zeiders were also part of the event.

Muniz was nominated for an Emmy and two Golden Glove Awards for his work in “Malcolm in the Middle” and was one of the best known child actors of his time. He has also appeared in films such as “Big Fat Liar,” “Deuces Wild," "Agent Cody Banks" and “Racing Stripes.”
According to his website, Muniz took a hiatus from the entertainment world in 2006 to pursue professional racecar driving.

He began competing in the Formula BMW USA Championship and later went on to race in the Champ Car Atlantic Championship from 2007-09. Muniz was fourth in the 2009 championship standings with two races to go before a season-ending injury resulted in multiple surgeries, the website said.
In 2024, Muniz ran 38 races each on the NASCAR O'Reilly Auto Parts and trucks series.
He's participated in 117 trucks series races over the last three years, with one top-10 finish at Daytona in 2025.
See AP’s full auto racing coverage here

title: Rapper Yella Beezy convicted of hiring gunman who fatally shot rapper MO3 in Dallas
summary: A Dallas County jury has unanimously convicted rapper Yella Beezy of capital murder in a brazen daylight attack on rapper MO3 on a busy Dallas interstate in 2020
story: A Dallas County jury has unanimously convicted rapper Yella Beezy of capital murder in a brazen daylight attack on rapper MO3 on a busy Dallas interstate in 2020
DALLAS -- Rapper Yella Beezy was found guilty on Wednesday of hiring the gunman who fatally shot rapper MO3 in a brazen daylight attack on a busy Dallas interstate in 2020.

Yella Beezy, 35, whose real name is Markies Conway, was unanimously convicted of capital murder by a Dallas County jury in the death of MO3, whose real name was Melvin Noble. He was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
In September, a jury found Kewon White guilty of capital murder for fatally shooting Noble. He was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
Prosecutors said the killing was the result of an escalating feud between Conway and Noble that had lasted years. Both men lived in Dallas.
Prosecutors said Conway paid White $40,000 for the shooting.

Noble, 28, was driving on Interstate 35 in south Dallas around noon on Nov. 11, 2020, when White pulled alongside him, authorities said. White stepped out of his vehicle holding a gun. Noble got out of his own vehicle and began running on the freeway as White shot at him, authorities said.
Prosecutor Tommy Adams said White wore a mask and fired over 40 rounds from an AK-47-style pistol while chasing Noble.
White shot Noble and a bystander who was inside a car, police said. The bystander survived, but Noble died at a hospital.

During closing arguments, prosecutors showed jurors a video clip of Conway talking about revenge in an interview, saying he would “get his lick back.” Prosecutor Krystal Biggins drew a comparison between Noble’s killing and a roadway shooting that injured Conway in 2018.
In October 2018, Conway survived being shot while driving on a tollway in the Dallas suburb of Lewisville when someone pulled up next to him and opened fire, hitting him three times.
“This was for the world to see,” Biggins said. “Over a rap beef, we are here for capital murder.”
The defense argued prosecutors hadn’t proven their case. “This is capital murder and the state has brought you a lot of speculation," defense attorney John Gussio said.
Noble had more than 800,000 Instagram followers and was best known for a 2019 remix of “Errybody,” with Baton Rouge, Louisiana, rapper Boosie Badazz.
Conway is best known for his 2017 single, “That’s On Me,” and the 2019 song “Bacc At It Again” with Quavo and Gucci Mane.

title: Irma P. Hall, 'Soul Food' and 'The Ladykillers' actor, dies at 91
summary: Irma P
story: Irma P

Irma P. Hall, the veteran actor who brought warmth and authority to matriarchal roles in “Soul Food” and “The Ladykillers,” and whose acting career took off after decades as a teacher, died Tuesday in Dallas. She was 91.
Her family announced her death Wednesday. No cause was given.

Hall was best known to many viewers as Big Mama, the family’s steadying force in the 1997 film “Soul Food.” The role earned her an NAACP Image Award and led to a return as the character in the television series based on the film.

She received a Cannes Film Festival Jury Prize for her performance as Marva Munson, a Bible-reading landlady opposite Tom Hanks in the Coen brothers’ 2004 comedy “The Ladykillers.” Hall also appeared in “A Family Thing,” “Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil,” “Beloved,” “Patch Adams,” “Collateral” and Tyler Perry’s “Meet the Browns.”

Hall was 60 when “A Family Thing” brought her a major film role. She played Aunt T., a blind woman whose counsel helps guide two half brothers, played by James Earl Jones and Robert Duvall. The part drew attention to an actor who had spent years developing her craft onstage and in smaller screen roles.

“I was just concentrating on developing this craft,” Hall said in a 1996 interview with The Associated Press. “I guess you really never know where you are, you probably think you are on a lower rung than you really are.”

Hall had not set out to become an actor. Born Irma Dolores Player on June 3, 1935, in Beaumont, Texas, she was raised in Chicago and later returned to Texas for college. She taught English and foreign languages in Dallas public schools for more than two decades.

Her path to the screen began when actor and director Raymond St. Jacques heard her recite poetry in Dallas and cast her in his 1973 film “Book of Numbers.” Hall continued teaching as she took acting roles, then made performance her full-time work in the 1980s. She also helped establish the Dallas Minority Repertory Theatre and remained involved in developing young artists.

Hall’s career included theater, television and film. Her credits ranged from the 1997 Clint Eastwood drama “Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil” to the 1998 films “Beloved” and “Patch Adams.” She also voiced Great Aunt T. in the 2001 “Rugrats” Kwanzaa special.

In 2004, Hall was recovering from serious injuries suffered in a car crash, including open-heart surgery, a broken arm and a crushed ankle, when she traveled from a Chicago convalescent center to attend a private screening of “The Ladykillers.”
“I loved the whole thing,” she told The Associated Press. “You never really know until you see it on the screen.”
Hall said she had heard from Hanks and the Coen brothers while recuperating. They had signed her pillow, she said. “Whenever I miss them, I hug it.”

In Dallas, Hall was also a longtime member and Church Mother at Inspiring Body of Christ Church. Her family remembered her as a woman of faith who read to children at the church’s school and stayed active in its theater ministry.
“She started as a teacher in the classroom but ended up being a teacher to the world,” her daughter, Irma Hall Crayton, said in the family’s announcement.

title: Movie Review: James Gray delivers a milestone crime drama in ‘Paper Tiger’
summary: Miles Teller and Adam Driver play brothers trying to work on a deal in 1986 New York in James Gray's “Paper Tiger.”
story: Miles Teller and Adam Driver play brothers trying to work on a deal in 1986 New York in James Gray's “Paper Tiger.”

The American Dream has seldom looked so bleak as in “Paper Tiger,” James Gray’s beautifully punishing tragedy about a middle class family in Queens. With operatic grace and 35 mm grit, “Paper Tiger” shrewdly and authentically explores ideas about wealth, worth, the cost of family and the price of wanting more.

In 1986 New York, Wall Street might be booming in its “greed is good” era, but across the East River — where the grass still grows tall and the twin towers look small and distant on the skyline — Irwin Pearl (Miles Teller) is up early making storm windows for the winter. This is being done very much against the wishes of one of his teenage sons, who is trying to sleep in. Winter is three months away anyway, he complains.

Irwin is an ordinary dad, kind and a little goofy, resplendent in a constant stream of neatly but not stylishly tucked-in plaid shirts and windbreakers. He seems older than his years, though he’s probably barely 40. Part of that might be due to the choices Teller has made for his voice and accent, sounding a little like Peter Falk in “The Princess Bride,” but it’s also spiritually true that every generation gets to believe that all the ones prior were always “old.”

Irwin is married to Hester ( Scarlett Johansson ), a practical but spirited woman who has started to fantasize about life in the suburbs. They live in a modest house where you can practically feel the texture of real life. It's a home of laughter, love and schoolwork — both parents dream of their boys going to Ivy League schools and doing better than they did. The boys also have their eyes on a fancier life, whining, “Why do we always have to buy crappy stuff and live crappy?”

They wouldn’t be the first ungrateful teens who fail to recognize just how good they have it. But they get glimpses of the rich life in their uncle Gary (Adam Driver), a former police officer who now does quite well as a security consultant. He has the suit and car, and the grand gestures he makes seem casual. When we meet him, he’s dropped by Irwin and Hester’s with a steak dinner for five from “Luger's.”

Gary proposes an idea to his brother, an engineer with a specialty in risk assessment: There’s a project in the works to clean up the Gowanus Canal, and they might be able to help. The businesses, once controlled by the mafia, are being taken over by Russian immigrants. Gary has spotted an opportunity to help them navigate the ins and outs of regulations.

The offer of a windfall comes as a relief for Irwin, stressed by the looming cost of college for two kids. Gary, too, is going through an expensive divorce. Irwin wonders if there is something shady beneath it all, but Gary reminds him that “we’ve never played in the dirt.” Still, there’s a foreboding feeling that this is not going to be as simple, clean and easy as Gary is promising. The movie, after all, began with a quote from Aeschylus: “Let there be wealth without tears; enough for the wise man who will ask no further.”

It’s only a matter of time before things start going very wrong: One night, Irwin takes his boys out for a “nighttime risk assessment,” and they soon find themselves swarmed by paranoid Russian goons with guns.

Gray, who finds new notes in a genre he’s already put his mark on with films like “Little Odessa,” “The Yards” and “We Own the Night,” is masterful at slowly, methodically building tension and dread to an almost unbearable crescendo. The decisions these brothers make, first together, then separately, take on the grandeur and weight of a classic tragedy.

Hester, meanwhile, becomes a physical manifestation of the polluted canal as she endures her own secret health crisis. Like many mothers before and after her, she feels it is her duty to bear the weight of a death sentence in private. There are louder, uglier, bigger things happening all around and she doesn’t want to worry anyone. It’s a beautiful performance from an actor who often gets lost in franchise and spectacle.

But it’s Driver who really steals the show as a man doomed by the responsibility he feels for his brother. Beneath Gary's easy smile, charm and flash festers a different kind of heartbreak and loneliness. He can also be shockingly violent. And, when it comes down to it, the brotherly loyalty and desire to protect at any cost might only go one way.

It builds to one of the more thrilling and inventive showdowns in recent film history — a rare movie that embraces, rather than tries to disguise, the omnipresent sound of planes taking off and landing at a nearby airport.

The whole grimy affair is agonizing, as everyone tries in vain to do the right thing. The morbid joke is that it was rigged from the beginning — not just the job, but the entire system, the false promises of capitalism, the ways in which corruption is enabled, and the paradox of honest wealth.
“Paper Tiger” may be set 40 years ago, but in the most fundamental way, it’s not a movie about our past.

“Paper Tiger,” a Neon release in select theaters Friday and nationwide on Nov. 20, is rated R by the Motion Picture Association for “language and some violence.” Running time: 115 minutes. Three and a half stars out of four.

title: The 2027 Coachella lineup is here: Dua Lipa, Tame Impala and SZA to headline
summary: The 2027 Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival lineup is finally here
story: The 2027 Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival lineup is finally here
INDIO, Calif. -- Three acts who are no strangers to Coachella will headline the annual festival in the California desert next April, the organizers announced Wednesday.

Dua Lipa, Tame Impala and SZA, who have all previously performed at the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival, will each headline one of the evenings of the event, which is held on consecutive three-day weekends.
Tame Impala, the musical project of Kevin Parker, claimed one of the top spots back in 2019, when he became the festival's first Australian headliner.

Both Lipa and SZA have Coachella experience, too. SZA joined Justin Bieber on stage as a surprise guest during his headlining set earlier this year. And Lipa joined Martin Garrix on stage back in 2017.

And Daddy Yankee, who will become the first Latin urbano artist named artist of the year at the 2026 Latin Grammys Thursday night, is a featured act making his Coachella debut. Last month, he released “La Postal,” his first concept album.

Also in next spring's Coachella lineup: Madonna, Phoebe Bridgers, Weezer, Dom Dolla, Don Toliver, Robyn, Zara Larsson, Steve Lacy, Kelela, Kehlani, Jisoo, Diljit Dosanjh, Tiësto, Kygo, Adéla, Måneskin, Four Tet, Underworld, Giorgio Moroder, Peggy Gou, Angine de Poitrine, Social Distortion and many other acts.
The festival will be held at the Empire Polo Club in Indio, California, on April 9-11 and April 16-18, 2027.
Tickets go on sale Friday at 3 p.m. EST.

title: Ted Turner's son says his Western art collection reflects the media mogul's passion for 'big'
summary: A collection of paintings depicting the American West from Ted Turner's Montana ranch are due to be auctioned by Christie’s in New York
story: A collection of paintings depicting the American West from Ted Turner's Montana ranch are due to be auctioned by Christie’s in New York
BILLINGS, Mont. -- Ted Turner didn't do small.

Whether racing sailboats, building CNN into a global news organization or buying up ranches across the U.S. West to become one of the largest landowners in the nation, the media mogul turned conservationist had a passion for big, his son, Teddy Turner, said in an interview.

And so it was with the art lining the log walls of Turner's sprawling Flying D Ranch in south central Montana: Paintings by American masters Thomas Moran and Albert Bierstadt capture the grandeur and beauty of the early Western landscape when it was still largely untouched by European settlers.

Over Turner's imposing stone fireplace was a painting of Yosemite Valley. Elsewhere in his home were images of the Grand Canyon, Oregon's Mount Jefferson and a Bierstadt work titled “Buffalo at Sunset,” depicting a group of bison near a pool of water that reflects a glaring sun.

Turner died in May and a collection of the paintings from his Montana ranch are due to be auctioned on Jan. 20 by Christie's in New York. The proceeds will go to the Turner Foundation to further its work preserving natural habitats across large landscapes and helping restore species like the bison that graze on the 178-square-mile (460-square-kilometer) Montana ranch.

What Turner saw in the pieces being auctioned, his son said, was perfection — versions of a bygone West not yet marred by human industry. Turner had similar aspirations for his ranch, where he sought to turn back the clock to an era when bison roamed freely and in immense herds that were hounded by packs of wild wolves.
Turner’s son described him as a person of action — not one to “just sit around staring at his paintings.”

“He loved a professional and if he didn't deem you an expert, he had no time for you,” Teddy Turner said. “Everything that he wanted to surround himself with was perfection. And he saw perfection in these paintings.”

Ted Turner was born in Cincinnati and made his fortune in cities including Atlanta, where he founded CNN. But the West captivated him, and in the 1980s, Turner started buying up properties in Montana and elsewhere, Teddy Turner said. He restored the sites including with bison herds that now number some 45,000 across his properties, according to Ted Turner Enterprises, which manages his holdings.
Teddy Turner said he would have liked to continue looking at the art for the rest of his life “but that was not his plan.”

“They were always in the great rooms, in the center of our lives for so long,” Teddy Turner said. “So they will definitely be sorely missed. It's hard to replace a Bierstadt over the mantel. I think maybe some Pulp Fiction posters? Probably not going to get it done.”

title: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore to release book ‘Repair’ on healing a divided nation
summary: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore is releasing a new book next year
story: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore is releasing a new book next year
NEW YORK -- One of many potential Democratic candidates for the 2028 presidential election, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, is releasing a book next year.

Henry Holt & Company told The Associated Press that Moore's “Repair: Healing a Divided Nation” will be published March 9. The publisher is calling his book an “honest assessment” of the country that offers a “path forward that leaves no one behind.”

The 48-year-old Moore, Maryland's first Black governor, was reelected in a landslide last week. In a statement released Wednesday through Holt, Moore said he hoped his experiences in his home state would lead to a larger conversation.

“In Maryland, I’ve seen what happens when good people do hard things, even in the face of unimaginable odds. This book documents those stories, as well as other memories of service from my life inside and outside of politics,” his statement reads in part.

“My goal was never to produce a personal political memoir. It was to pose hard questions and spark honest dialogue. This book is about how we can rediscover our common humanity and relearn our common purpose. I offer my thoughts, with an invitation for readers to lend theirs. In the work of repair, every fingerprint matters,” he wrote.

Moore has said he won't be running in 2028, but book releases are standard for White House candidates. Other possible contenders such as Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg have already released books or have them in the works.

Moore was an established author before he ran for public office; his books include the memoirs “The Work” and “The Other Wes Moore,” in which he reflected on his unexpected bond with a convicted murderer also named Wes Moore.

title: Jordan Firstman has been a lot of things, but 'Club Kid' confirms he's a filmmaker
summary: It’s taken some time but Jordan Firstman, with “Club Kid,” feels like he’s finally made it
story: It’s taken some time but Jordan Firstman, with “Club Kid,” feels like he’s finally made it
NEW YORK -- When Jordan Firstman arrives for lunch at a Manhattan bar, he sees a burger on one side of the table, and a salad on his.
“What are you guys trying to tell me?” he asks with mock offense.

Firstman isn’t on a diet but he is trying to keep himself in line. His directorial debut, “Club Kid,” is one of the year’s biggest breakthroughs. In it, Firstman stars as a gay New York party promoter named Peter who’s blindsided by a hard-to-fathom revelation: He has a 10-year-old son (Reggie Absolom).

Since its debut at the Cannes Film Festival, “Club Kid” — vivid with downtown nightlife that Firstman knows firsthand — has been a sensation. After a bidding war, A24 picked it up for $17 million and is releasing the film in the heart of awards season. Minutes before sitting down for a recent interview, “Club Kid” was nominated for best feature and Firstman for breakthrough director by the Gotham Awards.

Beginning with the Cannes premiere — where Firstman reveled in puns of the theater’s name, Debussy — it’s been a surreal ride for the Los Angeles-based viral comic turned filmmaker. His movie dreams have come true, but there are perils in being famous for “Club Kid.”

“When you make a movie like this and have a culture surrounding it, people are shoveling drugs in your face. It’s a big exercise in saying no,” Firstman says. “I messed up once and I didn’t again. You could see it in my eyes in press the next day. But I want to be on my game.”

Firstman, 35, has been a viral video star (you might remember his pandemic bit as the publicist for banana bread), a consultant on “Big Mouth” and a writer for HBO’s “Search Party.” He’s released a comedy-music album (based on secrets shared by Instagram followers) and been an increasingly accomplished actor, on the series “I Love LA” and the 2023 film “Rotting in the Sun.”

But with “Club Kid,” Firstman has finally arrived at the role he always most wanted: filmmaker. Eleven years ago, Firstman made the short “Sold.” about a needy screenwriter celebrating a breakthrough that may be imagined. Now that he has arrived, he intends to stay.

“This is the first time of my career I’ve actually had the mind to be like: There’s something more important than what I’m saying. I’ve said the wrong thing in the past and I’ve gotten punished for it,” says Firstman, who last year was slammed online for criticizing the authenticity of gay sex on “Heated Rivalry.” “My movie is so important to me that if I have an opinion, I’m telling my friends or I’m keeping it to myself. You could ask me about my least favorite movie right now, and I’d be like: ‘I really liked it, actually.’”

“Club Kid” stands out for its unique duality. It’s a crowd-pleaser with a plot not unlike Adam Sandler’s “Big Daddy,” but it’s also a moving and faithful depiction of gay life. It’s an edgy, ketamine-covered movie about club life, but it’s also a tender movie about growing up.
Those dichotomies — sweet and childlike, provocative and satirical — Firstman believes are his superpower.

“I’ve gone so back and forth on the subject of: Am I mainstream?” Firstman says. “There’s something maybe about my look that feels familiar to people. I think I feel like people’s cousin, or something. But then my insides are very specific and broken and transgressive and subversive. I have perversions. I have issues that are unsavory. My gift, and this is going to sound sexual, is making hard things soft.”
Firstman smiles. “And I’ve done it before. I’ve made a lot of hard things soft.”

The story of “Club Kid” may sound contrived, but it comes from a more personal place than its narrative twist suggests. Even that has some truth. Firstman, just after finishing the script, was a sperm donor for his older sister's wife.

Firstman's screenplay attracted Alex Coco, producer of Sean Baker's best picture-winning “Anora.” “Club Kid,” shot on 35 mm, similarly became an authentic portrait of New York, shooting in real, underground parties. The colorful ensemble includes Miss Benny, Alaska Riley and Saturn Risin9 as Peter’s hard-partying friends.

“A lot of it was similar to how we approach Sean’s movies: casting people from the community, whether they’re first-time actors or seasoned actors,” Coco says. “Shooting in real locations, embracing the chaos of shooting in a living, breathing world.”
For Coco, Firstman may have played around with different personas, but “Club Kid” represents his true self.

“He’s becoming who he always was. He started off with shorts early in his career wanting to tell meaningful, personal stories about the queer experience,” Coco says. “He’s so talented that he’s able to succeed creatively in almost everything he does. But I think the most natural state of who he is is this version, which is a more serious, big-hearted filmmaker.”

In one memorable scene in “Club Kid,” Peter and a love interest played by Diego Calva exchange sincere reflections on their earliest sexual encounters. Firstman, the son of journalists for Newsday, grew up in Northport, Long Island, making weekend trips into Manhattan as a teen. For Firstman, that scene reflects his own coming of age.

“It’s a very New York gay thing to not take your own trauma seriously, or think it’s not worth it,” he says. “I had that happen to me when I was a kid by a couple people — some consensual, some less so. I think throughout my whole 20s, I was just like, ‘Haha!’ Then I got into my 30s and started going to therapy and taking it more seriously.”
Firstman shrugs and smiles. “Damaged goods,” he says.
Yet Firstman usually projects uber-confidence, which he acknowledges has shaped perceptions of him.

“I have my moments, for sure,” he says. “I do think to be gay is to be broken. But I think there’s something very beautiful about brokenness. I think that’s why all my characters have that shield around them or a harder edge. Deep down, they’re very sensitive and sad. Peter is the first time I got to really just show my heart. I think there’s been this perception of me that I’m, like, a b----”
“I have some unsavory qualities like anyone else,” adds Firstman. “But I did just want to show the world a little bit who I am.”

Meanwhile, Firstman is getting used to his new life as an acclaimed, Cannes-approved auteur and — maybe more surprisingly — a monogamist. He's now “in some form of a relationship,” he says. Acting on an instinct, Firstman invited someone he had met only once to Cannes. Just as his movie launched, he was falling in love. “A lot,” he sighs, “was happening at once.”

The arrival of so much maturity, Firstman grants, has been head-spinning. Yet his mischievousness is far from gone. When it comes time for Firstman to leave for a photo shoot uptown, he stands and makes one request: “Give me a good headline,” he says. “All people read is the headline.”
Any suggestions?
Firstman hardly pauses. “Jordan Firstman is a talented, childlike genius,” he says, grinning. “And hot.”

title: Actor Stacy Keach, star of stage and ‘Mike Hammer’ series, dies at 85
summary: Stacy Keach, known for his role as Mike Hammer on TV and work onstage, has died at 85
story: Stacy Keach, known for his role as Mike Hammer on TV and work onstage, has died at 85

Stacy Keach, one of America's finest stage actors who became best known for playing scruffy private eye Mike Hammer on TV and whose career was nearly derailed after he was imprisoned in 1984 for trying to smuggle cocaine into Britain, died Tuesday. He was 85.

Keach died at home in Magdalenka, Poland, “after a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure,” his wife, Malgosia Tomassi Keach, said in a statement. Keach had previously suffered a heart attack onstage in Chicago in June 2017.

Though he was considered a preeminent interpreter of Shakespeare and a favorite of such legendary directors as John Huston, Keach was indelibly linked with his take on the hard-boiled Hammer, the fictitious TV private detective created by crime novelist Mickey Spillane.

Unwilling to do the same thing over and over, Keach left behind a crazy quilt of roles, playing a stoner cop on film, King Lear onstage and also narrating “World's Most Amazing Videos” on TV. He played a deranged colonel in “The Ninth Configuration” (also known as “Twinkle, Twinkle Killer Kane”), led the TV show “Titus," had a role in Alexander Payne’s Oscar-nominated drama “Nebraska,” and played a New York archbishop in a recurring role on the CBS police drama “Blue Bloods.” Last year, he had an excellent turn as George Clooney's bitter father in “Jay Kelly.”

“My objective was to have as varied a selection of roles as possible. It probably did hurt my career,” he told New York magazine in 2012. “My choices have had a cost attached to it. But I’ve gotten to play Hamlet, and Richard III, and King Lear, and I would not give that up for anything.”

Actor Lou Diamond Phillips, who played Keach's son in the 2008 TV movie “Lone Rider,” said in a post on X that Keach was a “consummate actor, gracious, giving and incredibly kind even while he had the presence of a smoldering volcano. One of the greats. Proud to have shared some frames with him.”

He played French painter Julien Mistral in the CBS miniseries “Mistral's Daughter,” a Russian prince in the miniseries version of Judith Krantz's novel “Princess Daisy,” Barabbas in Franco Zeffirelli's “Jesus of Nazareth” and Maj. Jonas Steele in “The Blue and the Gray.” He won a Golden Globe playing Ernest Hemingway in a six-hour miniseries, for which he gained 35 pounds (16 kilograms).

Keach earned a Tony Award nomination for his portrayal of Buffalo Bill in the Broadway play “Indians,” played Edmund opposite Lee J. Cobb in “King Lear” on Broadway and had other onstage roles there in “The Kentucky Cycle” in 1993, “The Country Wife” in 1965 and “Other Desert Cities” in 2011.

He also headed the national touring company cast of “Frost/Nixon,” portraying the fallen president, and went on tour with “Sleuth” with Maxwell Caulfield as his co-star. He starred in a 2006 production of “King Lear” at the Goodman Theatre in Chicago and returned in 2017 for “Pamplona,” a one-man show about Hemingway, where he collapsed onstage, leading to the run's cancellation.

While he was still doing “Mickey Spillane’s Mike Hammer” (later titled “The New Mike Hammer”), Keach was arrested in 1984 at London's Heathrow Airport after trying to smuggle 1.3 ounces of cocaine concealed in an aerosol shaving cream can and elsewhere in his luggage. Also arrested was his secretary.

“As my sentence was read — nine months in prison — I felt like someone had kicked me in the groin with lead cleats,” he wrote in his 2013 book, “All in All: An Actor’s Life On and Off the Stage.” He added: “It was the lowest moment of my life.”

He was handcuffed and taken to prison, a cell the size of a closet and where an orange plastic bucket would serve as his toilet. Before he went inside, an officer asked him to autograph a copy of the book “The Blue and the Gray.”

The then-44-year-old actor was sent to Reading Prison, a medium-security lockup, because authorities felt a minimum-security jail would have provided too easy access for reporters. He was released after six months.

In his book, Keach wrote that while in prison he got warm letters from Gregory Peck, Burt Reynolds, Roger Moore and Al Pacino. He was put in charge of showing a movie one Sunday per month and recalls once picking his own, “The Long Riders.” He said the experience was “very lonely, very depressing, very sad. I spent a lot of my time trying to re-evaluate my own stupidity.”

After prison, he narrated the TV documentary “High on the Job,” and testified before Congress, telling a House panel how he first became hooked on cocaine in the mid-1970s. “There is no greater imprisonment than that of being dependent on a chemical substance for one's existence,” he testified.

Keach took his warnings to college campuses and rehab centers. He also married Polish actor Malgosia Tomassi, whom he met when she appeared in the “Hammer” series. He said he treasured her photos and letters behind bars.
Keach, who was married four times, is survived by Malgosia, and his children, Shannon and Karolina.

His first role after his release was in the CBS movie, “Intimate Strangers” with Teri Garr, and it became the third-highest rated TV movie of the 1985-86 season. His next film, “The Return of Mickey Spillane's Mike Hammer,” also played well, and then the “Mike Hammer” series, which had been on the production shelf since his arrest, was given a slot on CBS' 1986-87 schedule.

Many years later, in the TV series “Prison Break” that aired from 2005-2007, Keach played a prison warden and said he tried to model his character after his real-life warden in England, whom he said had great compassion and wanted to help inmates rehabilitate themselves.
Born in Savannah, Georgia, Keach was the son of actors who met at Northwestern University. Keach attended the University of California, Berkeley, where he earned degrees in English and dramatic art.

In the summer of 1963, he worked with the Oregon Shakespeare Festival and played Henry V, Mercutio and Lord Berowne. He attended the Yale School of Drama and, in the summer of 1964, played several roles at New York’s Public Theater in “Hamlet” with Julie Harris. He went to study at the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art as a Fulbright scholar and returned to New York to do various stage roles.

Keach made his film debut in 1968 in “The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter” and played stoner cop Sergeant Stedenko from the Cheech and Chong movies. He worked for director John Huston twice, in “Fat City” and “The Life and Times of Judge Roy Bean” and had roles in “American History X” with Edward Norton and “The Bourne Legacy.” He played a tough trucker in “Roadgames,” was electrocuted in “Children of the Corn” and a robot removed his heart in “Class of 1999.”
His biggest break, though, came with the role of Hammer, whom he played as a modern-day knight, a champion of the underdog.

“Keach makes a dashing, dapper Hammer. He looks almost jaunty in his tilted gray fedora,” said Fred Rothenberg, a TV writer for The Associated Press, in 1983. “He knows how to speak lust with his eyes, and talk dirty with his fists.”
AP Entertainment Writer Andrew Dalton contributed reporting from Los Angeles.

title: British comedian and children's author David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct
summary: British children's author and comedian David Walliams is facing allegations of using his fame to groom girls and young women for sex
story: British children's author and comedian David Walliams is facing allegations of using his fame to groom girls and young women for sex
LONDON -- British children’s author and comedian David Walliams used his fame to groom girls and young women for sex, two British news outlets reported on Tuesday.

ITV News and the Guardian newspaper said their joint investigation featured interviews with multiple women who gave first-hand accounts of Walliams' conduct. One woman alleged he sexually assaulted her at his house when she was 15, while others accused him of grooming them when they were teens.

Walliams, 55, denied the allegations. He had sought a court injunction to bar ITV News and the Guardian from identifying him in their reporting. His lawyers claimed that publication of sexual misconduct allegations would lead him to take his own life.
A judge rejected his injunction request last week, but protected his identity until late Monday.

“I am not a sexual predator,” Walliams said, according to ITV. “I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.”
“Whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did,” he added.

Walliams’ lawyer, Sara Mansoori, earlier told the High Court that he had made a suicide attempt when he received letters from ITN and Guardian News and Media seeking his response to the allegations. He later made another attempt, she said, and he was recently admitted to the hospital for psychiatric care.
The case drew widespread attention in Britain because it highlighted questions over public figures’ right to privacy and what media can report on the basis of public interest.

Gavin Millar, representing the media companies, has said that the allegations were gathered after “a wide-ranging and rigorous investigation” and that there was a strong public interest in publishing them.

He told the court that the investigation involved speaking to more than 100 people, and alleged that over a period of years Walliams "used his status and influence as a well-known public figure to establish contact with young women, some considerably younger than him, and that he engaged or sought to engage in seriously inappropriate conduct,” according to a summary of the court judgment.
Some of the alleged conduct could amount to criminal offenses if proven, it said.

Walliams was dropped last year by publisher HarperCollins after allegations were made of inappropriate behavior. Few details were published at the time, but the Guardian reported Tuesday that there were concerns about his behavior for years, including an allegation that he had an inappropriate sexual relationship with a junior female employee.

Walliams is best known for comedy sketches on “Little Britain," a hugely popular British TV show in the 2000s, but he's also a celebrated children's book author with some 40 published titles that sold more than 60 million copies worldwide, according to his website.
Several of them, including “Gangsta Granny,” have been adapted into BBC comedy dramas and stage productions.
He was also a judge for years on “Britain’s Got Talent," though in 2022 he stepped down after apologizing for making “disrespectful comments” about auditioning contestants.
The BBC said Tuesday it was removing some programmes, including “Little Britain,” while it carried out a review of “all material featuring and written by David Walliams on our platforms."
The literary agency Independent Talent Group also said it was dropping Walliams following the new allegations.
In dismissing the injunction bid by Walliams, Justice Matthew Nicklin said such a legal measure would mean “an exceptionally serious interference” with the rights of the media companies.

He noted that Walliams had a “serious and longstanding psychiatric vulnerability” which must be taken seriously, and said a decision allowing the allegations to be published will substantially increase his risk of suicide. However, he added that the evidence did not “establish that suicide is inevitable.”

title: Oprah Winfrey names Mary Lawson's 'Solace in Winter' as her new book club pick
summary: Oprah Winfrey has selected Mary Lawson's novel "Solace in Winter" for her book club
story: Oprah Winfrey has selected Mary Lawson's novel "Solace in Winter" for her book club

NEW YORK -- NEW YORK (AP) — Oprah Winfrey's new book club pick is an acclaimed Canadian author's novel about a small community in the late 1960s that's upended by a young American who has crossed the border to flee the Vietnam War draft.
Winfrey praised Mary Lawson's “Solace in Winter,” which came out Tuesday, as “beautifully written and deeply moving.”

“'Solace in Winter' reminds us that even in our loneliest moments, unexpected connections can open our hearts, heal old wounds, and change our lives in ways we never imagined,” Winfrey said in a statement. Her discussion with Lawson can be seen on Winfrey's YouTube channel and other video podcast outlets.

The 80-year-old Lawson is known for her prize-winning debut novel, “Crow Lake,” and for two books longlisted for the Booker Prize: “The Other Side of the Bridge” and “A Town Called Solace.” Winfrey, as she has done with previous choices, phoned the author without warning to give her the news. Lawson said in a statement that she thought at first she was being scammed.
“Is this for real?” she remembered asking.
Yes, Oprah told her. It's real.
“Oh goodness. Oprah,” Lawson responded, recognizing her voice. “Hello.”

title: Broadway finds its Prince: Jordan Fisher cast as 'The Boy' in 'Purple Rain' musical
summary: Jordan Fisher will star in the Broadway adaptation of “Purple Rain” as “The Boy.”
story: Jordan Fisher will star in the Broadway adaptation of “Purple Rain” as “The Boy.”
NEW YORK -- Broadway has found its Prince — Jordan Fisher.
The actor, whose Broadway credits include “Hadestown,” “Dear Evan Hansen,” “Sweeney Todd” and “Hamilton," will play Prince's leading role of “The Boy” in a musical adaptation of “Purple Rain.”
The musical will premiere at the Majestic Theatre next spring, beginning previews in March. Additional casting will be announced at a later date.

“Purple Rain” tells the vaguely autobiographical story of an up-and-coming rock musician in the Minneapolis club scene who is juggling a tumultuous home life and a budding romance. The film, which won an Oscar for its song score, includes the hits “Let’s Go Crazy,” “When Doves Cry” and “Take Me With U.” The soundtrack won two Grammys.
