title: Ukraine fires nearly 1,200 drones at Russia as US-led talks consider Europe security
summary: Ukraine has launched nearly 1,200 drones at Russian targets in one of its largest aerial attacks since the invasion began almost five years ago
story: Ukraine has launched nearly 1,200 drones at Russian targets in one of its largest aerial attacks since the invasion began almost five years ago
KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukraine fired almost 1,200 drones at Russian targets overnight in one of its biggest aerial attacks since Moscow’s invasion nearly five years ago.

Meanwhile, U.S. and Russian negotiators raised the stakes in talks to stop the fighting by including for discussion wider European security arrangements that have been in place since the end of the Cold War. That change, long sought by Moscow, has alarmed European leaders and placed a question mark over NATO’s future role.

“Russia wants to talk about questions of European security architecture. We don’t need to talk about that. There is one,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said, referring to the NATO military alliance.

After two days of talks with Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi this week, U.S. envoys went in person to brief Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who was meeting with European leaders in Dublin, Ireland.
Further talks are planned as negotiators seek a breakthrough in peace efforts, according to U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.

Kushner said Russia has agreed to include Europe in upcoming talks, after Moscow's long insistence that the continent’s governments should be excluded because they were part of the problem by supporting Ukraine.

Europe’s presence at the negotiating table will allow negotiators “to address the broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia,” Kushner said on X.
As European leaders scrambled to find an envoy to the talks, they were also wary of Russian maneuvering as well as Trump’s praise for Putin and his administration’s sharp criticism of Europe.
The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said Friday that Europe must insist on a ceasefire before taking the negotiations further — the opposite of what Putin demands.
“If we start to talk about what Russia is asking regarding the security architecture, we actually walk into the traps that Russia is setting us,” she said in Dublin.
Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden insisted that Europe must take its fate into its own hands. “We cannot let neither the Americans nor the Russians decide about our future,” Frieden said.
Moscow is aiming “to dismantle NATO and the post-Cold War European security architecture,” the Institute for the Study of War said in an assessment late Thursday.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov reaffirmed that Russia is open for contacts with the Europeans.

“Once we understand (Europe’s) true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to make a decision on holding a dialogue regarding a settlement in Ukraine in an expanded format,” Peskov said.

Zelenskyy on Friday repeated his complaints about drone speed limits on the U.S. Starshield system — SpaceX’s military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service — that Ukraine needs for its defense.

The speed restrictions are limiting Ukrainian drones to 161 kph (100 mph) on the entire front line and in Russian-occupied territory, he said, making it impossible for Ukraine to deploy its interceptors effectively against Russia's fast-moving jet-powered drones.
“We still have no clear explanations,” he said of the unannounced restrictions, after first raising the issue on Thursday.
Ukrainian officials are asking the U.S. Department of State, the Pentagon and SpaceX to clarify and resolve the situation, he said.
Last month, similar SpaceX limits on Ukrainian drone speeds severely disrupted operations, alarming Kyiv officials who fear a drop in U.S. support.

Elon Musk acknowledged in October that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink internet service in Ukraine for about a week, saying the system couldn’t be used for offensive strikes against Russia.

Russia’s Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 1,198 Ukrainian long-range drones between late Thursday and early Friday. However, strikes on three Russian regions killed seven people, including a 12-year-old, and wounded 17, local officials said.
The massive Ukrainian barrage appeared designed to show that Kyiv is holding its own in the war, countering Moscow’s insistence that a Russian victory is inevitable.
Kyiv’s forces are using drones and ground robots to help defend against Russia’s army along the about 1,200-kilometer (750-mile) front line snaking down eastern and southeastern Ukraine.
With its troops largely bogged down on the battlefield, Moscow has used strategic bombardment of civilian areas to hurt Ukraine.
Russia launched 117 drones against Ukraine overnight, killing at least two people, including a 17-year-old, authorities said.
A single Russian attack on southern Zaporizhzhia on Friday hit two five-story apartment blocks and wounded 25 people, including six children, officials said.
The war has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians, analysts and humanitarian organizations say.
Russian attacks against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure caused widespread power outages across about half of the country's regions Friday, First Deputy Minister of Energy Artem Nekrasov said.
Moscow has battered Ukraine’s power grid each winter since the war began, hoping to weaken public morale.
AP reporters Sam McNeil in Dublin, Susie Blann in Kyiv, Ukraine and Barry Hatton in Lisbon, Portugal contributed to this story.
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: Hundreds of roaming cows wreak havoc in North Macedonian town, frustrating farmers
summary: Residents of Kriva Palanka in North Macedonia are dealing with a herd of over 1,000 roaming cattle
story: Residents of Kriva Palanka in North Macedonia are dealing with a herd of over 1,000 roaming cattle
KRIVA PALANKA, North Macedonia -- They descend from the surrounding hills, mostly at night, chomping their way through gardens and crops to satiate their hunger.

For years, residents of Kriva Palanka, a farming town of about 19,000 people in northeastern North Macedonia, have struggled with a herd of roaming cattle that has grown to more than 1,000 animals, destroying property and threatening their livelihood.
It's not just crops. The wandering cows pose a serious risk to the town's water supply and to drivers on a road that leads to neighboring Bulgaria, residents say.
Many fault the country's bureaucratic maze for failing to enforce a 2024 Food and Veterinary Agency order to seize the herd from their three owners.
And even when authorities took legal action against one of the owners, bureaucratic failures derailed the case and allowed the owner to walk free, Kriva Palanka Mayor Sashko Mitovski said.
Mitovski said residents have had enough and are staging protests to urge authorities to take action.

He is asking the conservative government of Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski to declare a 30-day state of emergency in the municipality for authorities to resolve the bovine problem once and for all.
“The number of cattle has increased from 400 four years ago to more than 1,000 today,” Mitovski told The Associated Press.

“We convened a crisis management headquarters because we concluded that, for years, none of the responsible institutions had shown either the willingness, commitment or capacity and resources to resolve the problem.”
Pensioner Lazo Stamenkovski, 71, who lives on the town's outskirts, said the cattle have destroyed more than 150 trees in his orchard.
“They constantly destroy the produce in my garden, wander onto the highway and endanger traffic safety on the road leading to Bulgaria," Stamenkovski told the AP.

Several residents of a neighborhood on the town's outskirts said the animals were not to blame, but the system was. They said some angry residents have beaten the cows and in some cases even slaughtered them.

“The government is responsible for everything that is happening to us. Not just this government, but all previous governments as well,” Venka Nikolovska, 59, a housewife from Kriva Palanka, told the AP. “We are all suffering — both people and animals.”
Despite their frustration, residents haven’t lost their sense of humor.
One man standing on the bridge over the Kriva Reka river that runs through the town said that the cows had gorged on the flowers in his backyard.
“Next time, I’ll prepare a flower salad and invite the cows to a party,” he said.
Mitovski said the cows roam freely through 34 surrounding villages and he blamed the Food and Veterinary Agency for not enforcing its own order to seize the cattle from its three owners.

"Since 2024, the herd has been the property of the Food and Veterinary Agency. The absurdity is that the agency issued the seizure order but has failed to enforce it,” he said, adding that the municipality has no legal authority to intervene.
The mayor said some cattle died near the town's main water sources last year, potentially poisoning the supply. He again faulted the Food and Veterinary Agency for failing to take action.
A government spokesperson did not immediately respond to an AP request for comment Friday evening.

One of the cattle owners was charged and detained last year for obstructing an agency operation to seize the animals. But Mitovski said the owner was released from custody after an agency inspector testified in court that he hadn't obstructed the attempted seizure.
“What I am saying is that this is an interconnected system involving serious wrongdoing by numerous people, and it is difficult to determine where it ends,” Mitovski said.
He said a government declaration of a temporary state of emergency would provide authorities with the money and resources needed to resolve the problem permanently.
Based on current livestock market prices, the value of the herd is estimated at between 360,000 and 570,000 euros ($385,000 to $610,000).
Some residents point out that the government could put the cattle up for sale at an affordable price so people could buy them and take care of them.
That could help many in the country of 1.8 million people, at least one-third of whom live in poverty.
“North Macedonia imports meat, milk, vegetables and fruit, while 1,000 cows roam unchecked across the country and destroy the farms,” Nikolovska said. “It makes no sense.”

title: South Sudan postpones first national elections again, to February 2027
summary: South Sudan has again postponed its first national elections since independence in 2011, moving polling from December to February
story: South Sudan has again postponed its first national elections since independence in 2011, moving polling from December to February

JUBA, South Sudan -- South Sudan has again postponed its first national elections since independence in 2011, moving polling from December to February amid concerns about insecurity, funding shortages and the country’s readiness to vote.
A revised timetable published Saturday by the National Election Commission sets Feb. 11, 2027, as polling day, replacing Dec. 22. The document did not give a reason for the postponement.
The polls have been repeatedly delayed, including in 2022 and 2024. The latest announcement follows warnings that elections could further unravel the country’s fragile peace.
The commission published the timetable on social media on the day voter registration was scheduled to begin. It also sets dates for candidate nominations and campaigning.

A day earlier, commission chairperson Gabriel Bol Deng told journalists in Juba that registration would run from Nov. 14 to Nov. 28 at 3,161 registration centers across the country’s 10 states and three administrative areas.
Deng urged eligible citizens to register and called on political parties, civil society groups, community leaders and the media to help raise public awareness.

South Sudan became independent from Sudan in 2011 after decades of civil war. A new conflict broke out in 2013 between forces loyal to President Salva Kiir and followers of his rival, Riek Machar. A peace deal was signed in 2018 and a transitional government of national unity was formed in 2020.

Fighting between government and opposition forces escalated in early 2025, and Machar was placed under house arrest in Juba that March. He and seven co-defendants are on trial on charges including treason, murder and crimes against humanity linked to an attack on an army garrison in Nasir, in the northeast. They deny the charges.
The transitional unity government was dissolved in September and replaced by a caretaker administration.

The South Sudan Civil Society Forum said in a statement issued in late October that conditions did not support fair, credible, peaceful and inclusive elections within the remaining time. It called for an inclusive dialogue on electoral preparations and the country’s transition.

Kiir’s ruling Sudan People’s Liberation Movement, or SPLM, has been holding primaries across the country. But there has been little electoral activity among other registered parties, Anita Kiki Gbeho, head of the United Nations Mission in South Sudan, told the U.N. Security Council on Nov. 10.

“Elections must be a milestone in the transition, not its conclusion. Elections cannot substitute for political dialogue, confidence-building and continued implementation of the Peace Agreement,” she said.

On Thursday, two SPLM delegates were killed in an attack in Miri Loko village, in Western Equatoria state, while returning from party primaries and congresses, officials said. It was the third security incident affecting the party’s primaries and congresses in the state, according to Deng Dau Deng, who chairs the SPLM’s high-level committee there.
One of those killed was Veronica Lucy Gordon, a former South Sudan Broadcasting Corporation journalist who had recently been nominated to contest a women’s seat in the National Legislative Assembly.
Edmund Yakani, director of the Community Empowerment for Progress Organization, condemned the attack, urging those opposed to the delegates’ political views to pursue dialogue rather than violence.

Following news of the postponement, Yakani called for transparency in the commission’s decisions. He also said the locations of registration centers remained unpublished on the day registration was scheduled to begin, leaving citizens without clear information about where to register.

title: International Criminal Court limits Afghanistan investigation to Taliban crimes
summary: Judges at the International Criminal Court have ended the part of the global tribunal’s investigation into Afghanistan that could have involved U.S. military personnel
story: Judges at the International Criminal Court have ended the part of the global tribunal’s investigation into Afghanistan that could have involved U.S. military personnel

THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- Judges at the International Criminal Court have ended the part of the global tribunal’s investigation into Afghanistan that could have involved U.S. military personnel, instead limiting the probe to crimes committed by the Taliban, according to court filings released Friday.

The ruling comes as the court and 13 current and former staff members are under sanctions by the Trump administration, which is opposed to any investigation into American citizens or U.S. allies, such as Israel.

The decision, which was issued Thursday but only made public on Friday, cites “significant limitations to the Prosecution’s ability to conduct its investigations and secure evidence” in the case. It does not elaborate.
The court's prosecutor's office told The Associated Press it has already appealed the decision.

It is not clear if the decision will mitigate Washington's attacks on the court. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has threatened to “dismantle the ICC — brick by brick, if necessary." The United States is not a member of the court and does not recognize its jurisdiction.

But the U.S. has also taken issue with the ICC's investigation into Israeli officials. The court has outstanding arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as well as his former defense minister, over allegations of crimes against humanity in Gaza. They have strongly rejected the accusations. Judges at the global court authorized an investigation in 2020 covering offenses allegedly committed by Afghan government forces, the Taliban, American troops and U.S. foreign intelligence operatives dating back to 2002. Two years later, then-chief prosecutor Karim Khan chose to “deprioritize” aspects of the investigation that could have involved Americans, citing challenges in obtaining evidence. Khan was ousted over sexual misconduct allegations earlier this year.
The part of the investigation involving the Taliban will be split off into a separate inquiry.

Last month, the court unsealed arrest warrants against four senior Taliban leaders, accusing them of the crime against humanity of gender persecution against women, girls and members of the LGBTQI+ community in Afghanistan since the Taliban seized power in 2021.

title: Spain's Sánchez faces political test as train crash casts shadow over election
summary: Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez had hoped to leverage widespread discontent over unaffordable housing when he called snap elections
story: Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez had hoped to leverage widespread discontent over unaffordable housing when he called snap elections

MADRID -- Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez hoped to leverage widespread discontent over unaffordable housing when he called snap elections in October. Then a high-speed train rammed into another, killing 69 people and casting a pall over the nation.
It was Spain's second deadly rail collision this year and couldn't have come at a worse time for Sánchez.

With the campaign officially underway, the 54-year-old progressive is working to keep the tragedy from derailing his message to voters. Instead, he has projected his administration as willing to assume responsibility for errors on its watch. More than that, he has folded the disaster into his campaign's main message: that a right-wing government would be worse for Spaniards, who need government help for housing, healthcare, infrastructure and more.
“If there is one lesson to be drawn from the Urda rail tragedy, it is that public services matter,” Sánchez wrote on X after the collision. “This is what is at stake.”

It may be a tough sell. Until this year, there had never been a fatal crash on Spain’s dedicated high-speed lines, and analysts told The Associated Press that the lethal crashes won't be so easy to downplay.
On the morning of Oct. 28, Sánchez was putting a message of positivity onto social media:
“There are so many reasons to be optimistic in this country. We respond to the haters with data, intelligence and humor.”
Minutes earlier, as he would soon learn, a high-speed train south of Madrid slammed into a stationary one, leaving authorities searching for dozens of bodies in the wreckage.

Even so, in recent weeks he has kept an uplifting tone, especially in his speeches while sporting red T-shirts emblazoned with aspirational slogans: “The Strength of Love,” “The Strength of the People,” and “Vote with Strength.” He spoke at his campaign kick-off event Thursday night in Seville, hours before the official midnight start.

The Spanish leader has also tried to invigorate his campaign by pointing to recent elections in Brazil, where leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured reelection with a come-from-behind victory in a runoff, and in the U.S. where Democrats seized control of the Senate and the House.
“It has happened in Brazil, it has happened in the United States, and it will happen in Spain too. The key is mobilization,” he said in an interview with newspaper La Vanguardia this week.

A Spanish prime minister is elected by Parliament, needing an absolute majority in the first vote or a simple majority in the second, often relying on coalition agreements or support from other parties.

Sánchez’s strategy is to “instill a sense of hope, the idea that things can be reversed, that change is possible — and, by doing so, to launch a campaign of optimism and foster a positive outlook,” said Alejandro Quiroga, a professor of political science at Madrid’s Complutense University.

On Monday, the Brazilian president will visit Spain and lend his support to the Socialist’s campaign. It’s unclear how much the Spanish leader will benefit from basking in the reflected glory of a foreign leader; analysts including Quiroga and Sánchez’s party officials themselves acknowledge that the 2 1/2-week campaign will be dominated by domestic concerns, such as housing, immigration and corruption — and last month’s deadly crash.

Six days after the rail accident, Sánchez’s transport minister Óscar Puente stepped down. He did so at the tail-end of a parliamentary grilling about his administration of the country's high-speed rail network, the second largest in the world after China's.
At every turn since, Sánchez and his top officials have pointed to the minister's resignation as proof that the government is accountable.
“We have stepped forward with absolute transparency,” Sánchez wrote soon after on X, calling the minister's move an “act of dignity.”

Sánchez himself was notably absent at a state funeral held this week in central Spain for the crash's victims, perhaps due to the potential for volatile scenes at the service attended by mourning family members of the dead.

But ordinary Spanish voters have shorter memories, and Sánchez appears to be counting on that, according to Quiroga. Still, his right-wing opponents are sure to make the two crashes a central topic of their campaigns and debates, as they undercut Sánchez's arguments about his record.

“There is a sense of public shock, compounded by the nature of these accidents,” said Montserrat Nebrera, former conservative politician and political analyst. “It points to a failure in management over the last eight years.”
Several opinion polls conducted before and after the Oct. 28 train crash showed Sánchez’s Socialist Party behind the combined support of the conservative Popular Party and far-right Vox.

On Wednesday, a nationwide protest over soaring rents and home costs drew over 100,000 people to the streets of Spain's major cities. It was well-timed for Sánchez, bringing the national conversation back to Spain’s housing woes on the eve of the campaign.
The demonstration was part of a general strike — the first in 14 years in Spain — and the first whose main driver was born from frustrations over housing.

While Sánchez’s Socialist Party did not organize or participate in the strike, his government praised the effort. Affordability issues are traditionally more favorable to left-wing politics and he has sought to appease housing activists who, since the dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman, have been protesting regularly.

Right-wing parties' rejection of Sánchez's two proposed emergency housing decrees served as the trigger for him to call the early general election, on Nov. 29. His government on Thursday passed one of them through a smaller interim parliament.
Sánchez and his allies hope the move shows Spanish people that he's working on their behalf, and that the Popular Party's promise to repeal the decree if it takes power will help motivate voters.
“Yesterday, the right to housing won on the street and in workplaces, and I hope it will win again at the ballot box,” Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez told lawmakers after its passage.

title: French-speaking nations hold a summit in Cambodia but an African conflict threatens a rift
summary: France's President Emmanuel Macron and other leaders are attending a biennial meeting of French-speaking countries and territories in Cambodia
story: France's President Emmanuel Macron and other leaders are attending a biennial meeting of French-speaking countries and territories in Cambodia

PHNOM PENH, Cambodia -- PHNOM PENH, Cambodia (AP) — Emmanuel Macron is set to attend a biennial meeting of French-speaking territories beginning Saturday in Cambodia, where the French president contending with public unrest at home will face international political challenges as an African conflict hangs over the proceedings.

The Organisation internationale de la Francophonie is holding the three-day meeting through Monday in the Cambodian capital Phnom Penh. Macron is expected to engage in bilateral discussions and join the summit meeting of the loose confederation of 90 member states and governments comprising 53 full members, five associate members and 32 observers where French is spoken.
Cambodia will take over the summit's chairmanship from Macron, who served as chair in 2024 when France was the host nation.

Before departing for Malaysia on Monday, Macron is scheduled to visit the Angkor World Heritage Site near the city of Siem Reap, where he and King Norodom Sihamoni will mark the completion of a French-supported restoration of the West Mebon temple.

The French leader's trip comes at a time of widespread domestic protests. France’s Interior Ministry said more than 600,000 people took to the streets earlier this month in a demonstration to demand higher wages and support the country’s student protest movement, which has resulted in thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries and schools set on fire.

The summit's sticky diplomacy for Macron and other leaders will take place when participants decide on Monday who will serve for the next four years as the group’s leader and chief executive in the role of secretary-general.

The choices include candidates from two bitterly feuding African members, Rwanda's Louise Mushikiwabo, who is seeking reelection to a third four-year term, and the Democratic Republic of Congo's Juliana Lumumba, the 71-year-old daughter of the country’s martyred independence hero, Patrice Lumumba.

Congo, the United States and experts from the United Nations accuse Rwanda of backing the M23, one of about 100 armed groups that have been vying for a foothold in mineral-rich eastern Congo, along the border with Rwanda. Rwanda’s government consistently denies backing armed groups in Congo.

Congo has threatened to leave the OIF if Mushikiwabo is reelected. With a population exceeding 110 million people, over 40 million more than France, Congo is the most populous nation where French is the official language and its withdrawal would mark a significant blow to the Francophonie organization.
Two other candidates, from Romania and Mauritania, are poised to serve as compromise picks.
France is influential in the decision as the largest contributor to the OIF 2026 budget of €71.7 million ($79 million).

The outcome also could be delicate because the challenge comes on the heels of the withdrawals of Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso from the OIF announced in March 2025, following their membership suspensions over military coups.

Mali said the suspensions infringed on sovereignty, but the withdrawals also came in the context of Francophone African countries in recent decades shedding French political, military and cultural influence that they regarded as overbearing.

The summit's slogan, “Reinvest in Peace for Shared Prosperity and Lasting Stability,” is seen as a reflection of Cambodia’s recovery from years of war and unrest in the last quarter of the 20th century.

About 20 government leaders, including Canada’s Mark Carney, Vietnam’s To Lam, Rwanda’s Paul Kagame and the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s Félix Tshisekedi, are expected to attend the summit and likely will meet with Cambodia's king as well as Prime Minister Hun Manet.

Most of the summit’s agenda is uncontroversial. Documents set to be approved concern political commitment to peaceful coexistence, social, cultural and economic cooperation, resolution of crisis situations and peace-building, and the protection of cultural heritage and the promotion of cultural diversity.

Host Cambodia, which has an opportunity to showcase tourism potential and business opportunities, is holding side events highlighting commercial partnerships, cultural exchanges, science and technology.

Local political activists see the meeting as an occasion to press for more democratic freedoms in a de facto one-party state. U.N. Special Rapporteur Tom Andrews issued a statement pleading with summit delegates to uphold OIF values and pressure the Cambodian government for the release of detained rights activists.
“No one should be detained for defending human rights, reporting on matters of public concern, or voicing critical opinions,” he said.

Cambodia can lay claim to helping birth the OIF, as its late king and mercurial independence leader, Norodom Sihanouk, was one of four founders in 1970 of the Agency for Cultural and Technical Cooperation. Sihanouk was overthrown and his immediate successors did not join, as Cambodia subsequently endured civil war and the brutal rule of the communist Khmer Rouge from 1975 to 1979. Cambodia joined the Francophonie as an observer in 1991 and became a full member in 1993.
Peck reported from Bangkok.

title: Nauru's president has no political opponents after all lawmakers joined the government side
summary: Nauru’s president, David Adeang, has announced that all opposition lawmakers in parliament have joined his government
story: Nauru’s president, David Adeang, has announced that all opposition lawmakers in parliament have joined his government

WELLINGTON, New Zealand -- Nauru’s president, David Adeang, has said all opposition lawmakers in parliament have joined his government, a move he said reflected “unity, stability and shared purpose” in the Pacific Island country’s politics.

The unusual move leaves the 19-member parliament without any political opposition. While it’s common for island countries in the South Pacific Ocean to take fluid approaches to forming government and opposition blocs or for lawmakers to switch between them, political debate is habitually robust and Nauru is rare in having no opposing politicians at all.

In a Facebook post Tuesday, Adeang didn’t explain what had prompted the change beyond a “shared commitment” to put Nauru's interests first. He also didn’t suggest who would supply the scrutiny usually provided by opponents in a country with a single house of parliament.
“There will still be a diversity of views and robust debate as in any strong and healthy democracy,” Adeang wrote.

The appointment of two lawmakers, Pyon Deiye and Jason Bingham Agir, as deputy cabinet ministers meant that Nauru’s parliament was in total support of the government for the first time since the country’s independence in 1968, Adeang said.

Government Facebook posts announcing the change were the sole source of information about it; all news outlets in the country of 12,000 people are government-owned. Foreign reporters are discouraged from traveling there, with journalist visa applications priced at 8,000 Australian dollars ($5,445).

Adeang made global news headlines in August when he said his country would officially become known as Naoero, making it the latest state to formally adopt the local spelling of its name. It brought international attention to a country visited by few.

Nauru, a constitutional republic and United Nations member, is one of the world’s smallest countries by both population and size. Limited infrastructure, a remote location and the environmental damage wrought by phosphate mining mean it attracts few visitors, unlike many other Pacific islands where foreign tourism is the main economic driver.

But it's among the South Pacific countries where domestic politics have drawn keener outside interest in recent years as the sprawling ocean where Nauru is located has become the site of geopolitical contest between major powers.

The potentially wealthy exclusive economic zones surrounding some of the poorest Pacific nations and the strategic importance of their locations in times of global volatility have provoked a race between China and Western countries with interests in the region to win influence with governments there.

Nauru is no exception. In 2024, it was one of a dwindling number of countries to hold diplomatic relations with Taipei, but severed them in order to resume ties with Beijing, which holds that Taiwan is part of China. It’s become one of Beijing’s warmest allies in the region since.
Australia in turn signed a lucrative pact with Adeang later in 2024 in which Nauru promised Canberra veto power over any security deals with Beijing.
Adeang’s government said Friday that the president had arrived in China for meetings with officials, accompanied by other lawmakers including newly appointed cabinet members Deiye and Agir.
The president has led the country since 2023 when a no-confidence motion ousted his predecessor. He was chosen unopposed to continue in the job among lawmakers sworn in after the 2025 election.

In 2014, then Justice Minister Adeang suspended opposition lawmakers from Parliament for remarks they made to international news outlets. Most lawmakers in Nauru run as independents and don’t belong to political parties, which is common in Pacific Island countries.

Freedom House, a Washington-based organization that promotes democracy, said in its 2026 report that Nauru’s people “generally enjoy political rights and civil liberties” but that corruption was “an ongoing challenge.” The country was one of the world’s richest per capita at the height of phosphate exports but the economy plummeted when the industry collapsed.

Nauru experimented with a golden passport scheme and became a tax haven for a period. It now subsists on foreign aid, sales of tuna fisheries licenses in its waters and funding from Australia first to host that country's offshore detention facilities for asylum seekers and later to accommodate foreign criminals Australia wanted to deport.

title: Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it destroyed a US radar in Bahrain, and other Mideast news
summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it destroyed a U.S. early warning radar in Bahrain, marking the first such claim in months
story: Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it destroyed a U.S. early warning radar in Bahrain, marking the first such claim in months

Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it destroyed a U.S. early warning radar in Bahrain, the first such claim in months. The Guard also said a tanker struck a mine while trying to sail through the Strait of Hormuz, causing an explosion.
Neither claim could be independently verified.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Friday. Read our full coverage here.

A report by Iran's official IRNA news agency quoted a statement by the Guard as saying the attack on the U.S. radar system followed a U.S. strike on a telecommunications pole in the southern Iranian port of Sirik.
Bahrain has been one of the strongest critics of Iran and is home to the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet.
The statement said the attack on the radar was a serious warning to the U.S. to cease its strikes. It was the first report by Iran on targeting a facility in Bahrain since September.

During an air war that began in February, Iran targeted U.S. bases in neighboring Arab nations including Bahrain in retaliation for U.S. strikes. Since then, Iran routinely targets oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, the critical waterway for international oil shipments.
U.S. Central Command and Bahrain's Ministry of Information did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard said Friday that a liquefied petroleum gas tanker struck a mine, causing an explosion, while trying to sail through the Strait of Hormuz, according to state-run IRNA news agency.

The Guard said the vessel ignored repeated warnings while transiting the eastern part of the strait. The claim could not be independently verified, and there was no immediate report of the incident from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, a British military agency that monitors incidents at sea.
Iran continues to warn ships not to pass through the strategic shipping lane without its approval.
This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.

title: Gold smuggled from war zones entered the UAE despite new regulations, report says
summary: A new report says that the United Arab Emirates remains a key destination for gold smuggled from conflict zones despite new regulations on the trade
story: A new report says that the United Arab Emirates remains a key destination for gold smuggled from conflict zones despite new regulations on the trade

CAIRO -- The United Arab Emirates remains a key destination for gold smuggled from war zones despite new regulations on the trade imposed by the government after facing international pressure, a new report says.

Many gold refiners and traders in the UAE are not following the rules and enforcement is lax, according to the report by Swissaid, a Switzerland-based aid and development group. The report recommended that the UAE be added to an international watchlist for possible financial wrongdoing.

The Emirates, which refines and processes the precious metal to send to major markets like Switzerland, India and China, was the second-biggest gold exporter in the world after Switzerland in 2024, a year after the new rules took effect. Smuggled gold from Russia, Yemen and Sudan continues to flow into the UAE, the report says.

The UAE introduced the new guidelines to regulate the gold trade, including responsible sourcing and vetting supply chains, after a global anti-money laundering body raised concerns that the UAE was not doing enough to stop criminals and militants from hiding wealth there.

Despite the new rules, the UAE imported at least 591 tons of illicit gold, valued at $74 billion, the report says. Gold smuggled out of conflict zones, Russia or African countries accounted for 42% of the UAE's total imports of the precious metal in 2024, the report says.

Imports of the precious metal mined and smuggled out of Africa made up nearly half the gold coming into the UAE from the continent, the report said. Some of that gold entered the UAE officially, through third countries. That trade showed a slight increase in 2024, according to the report.

“The UAE remains by far the main destination for gold linked to armed conflicts in Africa. And it continues to be a major destination for gold exports from countries subject to international sanctions,” the report said.
The UAE did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the report’s findings.

Swissaid said most of the smuggled gold in 2024 — some 453 tons valued at over $56 billion — reached Dubai refineries from African gold-producing countries, including Guinea, Mali and Sudan, a country that faces international sanctions. Nearly 29 tons of gold originated in Sudan, according to Swissaid, whose findings were based on data from the U.N., official trade statistics and civil and international organizations. Authors of the report said 2025 data was incomplete, but partial recent data showed the rising trend continuing.
“We had hoped that with the new regulations, conflict gold from countries subject to international sanctions would be stopped,” Marc Ummel at Swissaid told The Associated Press.

The illicit gold trade has been a key component of Sudan's war between the country's military and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. Since the war began in 2023, large quantities of gold have been smuggled out of Sudan to finance the RSF, who control gold-producing areas in Darfur and Kordofan regions, according to U.N. experts.
The RSF carried out mass killings, sexual violence and destruction in northern Darfur, in a “campaign of destruction” that U.N. experts said bears the “hallmarks of genocide.”
“From our point of view, since April 2023, all gold from (Sudan) should be considered as conflict gold,” Ummel said.
The Swissaid report found that in 2024 an additional 137.7 tons, valued at nearly $17 billion, were imported into the UAE from Russia and Yemen, which are also subjected to international sanctions.

Despite the risks associated with sourcing gold from the UAE, Switzerland was the top importer of gold from the UAE. The report said gold imports from the UAE increased drastically between 2024 and 2025 — going from 155 tons to 420 tons.
The Swiss government did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The report’s authors recommended that the UAE again be placed on the “gray list” of the Paris-based Financial Action Task Force, an international body that combats money laundering and terrorist financing. The gray list calls for increased monitoring, while its “black list” recommends countermeasures against countries with the most serious deficiencies.
The FATF placed the UAE in 2022 on the gray list. It removed it in 2024 after the new gold supply chain regulations.

title: Violent attacks on critics of China in Taiwan raise concern over transnational repression
summary: Comedian Huang Yi-hao was involved in a car accident in September, but it turned out to be a deliberate attack
story: Comedian Huang Yi-hao was involved in a car accident in September, but it turned out to be a deliberate attack

TAIPEI, Taiwan -- In September, comedian Huang Yi-hao was involved in a car accident, something that could happen to anyone. But one thing stood out: the men in the other car were unusually polite, and even offered to cover his medical bills and the damage to his car.
Huang later received a call from Taiwanese police telling him it wasn't an ordinary accident.

Taipei prosecutors in October charged five men for deliberately attempting to injure Huang in a case that has drawn attention across Taiwan. Authorities say it is part of a growing trend where operatives paid by China harass or attack people on the self-ruled island who are seen as critical of the government in Beijing.

“In the beginning, it was verbal harassment, then it morphed to pouring paint and property damage ... to the level of causing a fake car accident," Chiu Shao-Chou, the commissioner of Taiwan's Criminal investigation Bureau, said. "There's a trend of increasing severity, and that's something we have to take seriously.”

Taiwan is a democratic island claimed by Beijing, which hasn't ruled out using force to annex it. Taiwanese authorities have long worried about Chinese infiltration attempts, including spy plots targeting senior military officials and the president's bodyguards, disinformation schemes during elections or the use of cultural exchanges as a way to spread Communist Party ideology.

China's tactics to harass, spy on or even harm dissidents abroad have come to light in recent years. In 2023, authorities in New York made arrests in connection with secret police stations set up on behalf of the Chinese government to surveil Chinese dissidents.

Huang said the car attack might have been linked to his performance at the end of last year, in which he criticized Chinese President Xi Jinping and compared him to Winnie the Pooh. Huang is a comedian trained in the xiangsheng tradition, a form of Chinese comedic dialogue that relies heavily on wordplay and rhymes.

Prosecutors say the five men accepted about 450,000 New Taiwan dollars ($13,900) from someone from China who went by the alias “K” and wanted them to injure Huang seriously enough that he could no longer perform.

Huang said he had stopped collaborating with other comedians and believes his criticism of Xi is the reason. He said he knows of other comedians who had performances canceled in China and Taiwan because they had collaborated with him. He has no plans of taking his shows to China.
His solo shows, however, have sold out since the attack.
“The Communist Party is very childish. Your country’s leader was criticized by a comedian and as a result, you give such an aggressive response?” Huang said.
Hong Kong gangsters have been accused of plotting to assault Japanese political commentator Akio Yaita in what Taiwanese prosecutors called another instance of “transnational repression."

According to an October statement from prosecutors, five Hong Kong triad members, paid by a fellow gangster, entered Taiwan in early July and inspected the area around the hotel where Yaita was expected to give a speech. But before the attack, two withdrew, and the pair, alongside another member, left Taiwan, the statement said.

One of the men was offered 100,000 Hong Kong dollars ($12,750) to assault Yaita, the prosecutors said. He punched the commentator in the face and was later arrested, while another, who acted as a lookout, fled Taiwan.
Yaita, a former reporter in Beijing who now leads a think tank in Taiwan, believes the assault was linked to his remarks, including his criticism of the Chinese government’s policies.
“By violently attacking me, they hope to silence others who criticize China, including myself,” he said, adding that he wouldn't change his views.
The man who was arrested pleaded guilty on Tuesday and will be sentenced later, Taiwan's Central News Agency reported.

Matt Brazil, a fellow at The Jamestown Foundation in Washington, D.C., said the recent attacks represented a “big step beyond" sending navy ships and warplanes around the island. He said anyone in Taiwan who speaks out against Xi and the Chinese Communist Party could be a target.
“(It) shows that Beijing may be turning toward a more militant stance in acting against its critics (in Taiwan). If successful, the party may expand such tactics elsewhere,” he said.

Taiwan's police say the threat of transnational repression isn't limited to Taiwan. They said they are in close coordination with U.S. authorities about similar cases that involve Taiwanese nationals overseas.
In October, U.S. authorities arrested a woman in Los Angeles for allegedly conducting surveillance on the son of Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te on behalf of the Chinese government.

“Taiwan is a democratic and pluralistic society, but with these types of actions which harm our national security, the investigation of this is of the highest importance,” Chiu, the police commissioner, said. He added that police treat the cases as national-level threats and coordinate with immigration authorities, the coast guard and other government agencies.
Catching the criminals before they leave Taiwan is a top priority, he said, adding that police would also investigate Taiwanese collaborators.
The island's Mainland Affairs Council, which handles relations with China, said it would seek to strengthen the Anti-Infiltration Act — a law designed to punish such acts.

In response to the attack on Yaita, China’s Taiwan Affairs Office said in July that the Hong Kong man who punched Yaita had acted out of “righteous indignation” and that it was an ordinary public security incident.

China denied any involvement in the attack on Huang. The Taiwan Affairs Office said Wednesday that “transnational repression” was a lie by Taiwan’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party. It said that the party had created the Anti-Infiltration Act to suppress political dissidents and restrict cross-strait exchanges.
But for Huang, who now travels with a police escort to every performance, the intended message was clear.

“They want to tell everyone that there's a cost to criticizing the Chinese government and its leader. They want to tell people, clearly, ‘If you do something abroad, we will come deal with you, so shut your mouth and accept reunification.'”
Wu reported from Bangkok. Leung reported from Hong Kong.

title: Judo star Teddy Riner is taking on what may be his toughest battle in the French presidential race
summary: Judo star Teddy Riner is taking on what may be his toughest battle in the French presidential race
story: Judo star Teddy Riner is taking on what may be his toughest battle in the French presidential race

PARIS -- In a contest of who has the firmer handshake, it's not a stretch to suggest, as he does, that French judo great Teddy Riner would get the better of Donald Trump if ever they were to meet as presidents of their respective countries.
But that's a big “if.”

Even with five Olympic gold medals under his black belt and more than 3.3 million followers on his socials, Riner's newly announced bid for the presidency of France is likely to be a harder contest than many of the judokas he crushed.

The list of celebrities who successfully campaigned for elected office is shorter in France than in the United States, where Trump, Ronald Reagan, Arnold Schwarzenegger, Jesse Ventura, two-time NBA champion Bill Bradley, former Buffalo Bills quarterback Jack Kemp and others turned small-screen, big-screen and sporting stardom into political power.

Two-time Olympic champions David Douillet, in judo, and Jean-François Lamour, in fencing, and Guy Drut, the 110-meter hurdles champion at the Montreal Olympics in 1976, won seats in France's parliament in retirement and served as sports ministers. But Riner is aiming to be the first celebrity to hold France's top office since World War II hero Gen. Charles de Gaulle.
To appear on the ballot for the first round of voting in April, Riner needs a minimum of 500 elected officials to sponsor his candidacy, a requirement designed to not be easy.

The measure, intended to limit the size of the field and filter out fanciful candidacies, is an indication of how France has traditionally regarded running the country as a serious business. It has been in place since the 1981 election and was one of the barriers that foiled a presidential bid by comedian and actor Coluche that year.

“In France, there are complex hurdles to entry for people who don’t come from the establishment,” said François Hourmant, a professor of political science at Angers University who has studied celebrity culture in French and North American politics.
“Moving from the tatamis to the political arena isn’t that simple, and isn’t something everyone can do,” he said in a phone interview with The Associated Press.

A thicket of cameras that greeted the 37-year-old on Friday, when he made his first campaign stop at a hospital in the northern suburbs of Paris, testified to the star power that Riner brings to the race.

Looking fighting fit in a dark suit and open-neck shirt, he towers over everyone from the height of his 2.04-meter (6-foot, 8-inch) frame. His imposing physicality and easy charisma translate readily to television.

But the policy proposals Riner plans to bring to the campaign remain unclear. He describes himself as neither left nor right on the political spectrum and says France “needs common sense” and not “a professional politician who recites lessons and squabbles all day long.”

In a two-minute, 37-second video that launched his campaign Monday and in an interview with the newspaper Le Parisien, Riner spoke of problems that he sees in France, among them “fear,” “anger,” a “social divide” and people unable “to envisage a future.” But he offered few solutions or blueprints for building what he called “the France that we want.”

Outside the hospital after meeting staff members, Riner said he is still working on his campaign platform and didn't answer questions, responding with a “have a good rest of the day, au revoir” before heading back to his car.

Far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, widely seen for now as the favorite to succeed President Emmanuel Macron in May, took a gentle swipe during a campaign stop of her own on Friday, saying she couldn't form an opinion about Riner's bid without knowing anything about his platform.

As a dominant judoka whose mantra was “Never let anyone steal your beefsteak,” Riner told the AP in 2013 that he would sometimes wrestle up to five people at once in training to make it more challenging. As a fledgling politician, he says he is steeled for more rough-and-tumble.
“When you know how to take punches, you also know how to throw them,” he told Le Parisien.
The rise of Le Pen and the challenge she faces from the other end of French politics from far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon together suggest a swath of French voters want deep and disruptive change.

But analysts believe many also want a seasoned hand to deal with the multitude of domestic and international challenges that France faces, including its record public debt and the threat to European security posed by Russian President Vladimir Putin and his war in Ukraine.

“Teddy Riner certainly embodies renewal, but he doesn’t necessarily embody experience. So that is probably one of his main disadvantages,” said Mathieu Gallard, research director at the Ipsos polling institute.

Riner, who is Black, was born on the French Caribbean island of Guadeloupe and grew up in Paris. Both Gallard and Hourmant said the potential that Riner is more likely to understand and combat discrimination could attract people of color in an election where Le Pen's party and others on the far right are again seeking to focus on immigration.
“But again, is that enough to translate into votes,” Gallard asked.

“Teddy Riner’s skin color will be a political issue for some people,” Hourmant said. For some, “it may be a reason to support him, seeing a racialized candidate from the overseas territories. For others, it will be a deterrent.”

title: Pope's visit to hub of Afro-Peruvian community casts spotlight on African slave trade to Peru
summary: Pope Leo XIV is putting the spotlight on Afro-Peruvians during a visit to a hub of their community
story: Pope Leo XIV is putting the spotlight on Afro-Peruvians during a visit to a hub of their community

ZAÑA, Peru -- When Susana Baca, the Latin Grammy-winning Afro-Peruvian singer, serenaded Pope Leo XIV upon his arrival in Peru, it was a sign that the visit would provide an unparalleled spotlight on the culture that grew out of the African slave trade in this country.

Baca was also Peru’s first Black Cabinet minister, and she became a leading figure in the campaign to end the discrimination that has long made second-class citizens of Black Peruvians and Peru’s Indigenous peoples.

The U.S.-born Leo, whose own family tree includes enslaved people and slave owners, is expected to highlight Peru’s African-descended community when he visits the hub of Afro-Peruvian culture on Saturday in the city of Zaña.
Leo will lead a prayer meeting at the sanctuary of St. Turibius of Mogrovejo in Zaña, where he often visited to pray while he was bishop of nearby Chiclayo.

In the 16th century, Mogrovejo was the first archbishop of Lima. He defended the rights of Indigenous and enslaved people and was known for having confirmed St. Martin de Porres, the first Black saint of the Americas and the patron saint of racial harmony, social justice and people of multiracial backgrounds.

In his first encyclical, “Magnificent Humanity,” Leo made a sweeping apology for the role of past popes in legitimizing slavery and failing to condemn it for centuries. It was a reference to the series of 15th-century directives from the Vatican that authorized European sovereigns to conquer Africa and the Americas and enslave non-Christians.

“It is impossible not to feel deep sorrow when contemplating the immense suffering and humiliation endured by so many in stark contrast to their immeasurable dignity as persons infinitely loved by the Lord,” Leo wrote. “For this, in the name of the church, I sincerely ask for pardon.”

The estimated 100,000 African slaves brought to Peru after the arrival of Spanish conquistadores toiled in sugar plantations and silver mines, with some becoming urban artisans. At one point, they and their descendants were more than 40% of Lima’s population.
Blacks now are a small fraction of Peru's 35 million people. But they have struggled to advance in the more than 170 years since emancipation.
The national census in 2017 reported that 1,311 people residing in Zaña identify as Afro-Peruvian, while in the entire Lambayeque region, the figure was 78,639.
Baca told The Associated Press that she felt connected to the pope because of the importance he has placed in asking forgiveness for injustices.

“I believe that one of the most important things in the history of Afro-Peruvians is that we did not remain submerged despite our history of suffering," she said. “We are an Afro-Peruvian people who have learned to forgive.”

“And perhaps this is what connects me, in my conscience, to the pope. I feel that in all his homilies and teachings, the pope emphasizes the importance of asking for forgiveness and forgiving — that the injustices of many moments in history are less painful if we have the capacity to forgive and to be forgiven."

She said she chose to sing “Canción de Fe” (“Song of Faith”) and “Si me quitaran totalmente todo” (“If Everything Were Taken From Me”) to the pope because they embody the same notion of faith that Leo shares.

Zaña, a historic town of northern Peru located in the Chiclayo province, was recognized by UNESCO in 2017 as a “site of memory of slavery and African cultural heritage.” Peru's government says the recognition is the first of its kind granted to a Peruvian Afro-descendant community or comparable communities along South America's Pacific Coast.

“There are communities capable of withstanding any blow — even seven ‘El Niño’ weather phenomena, or the even harsher, more perverse blows dealt by the darkest side of humanity, such as slavery,” former Culture Minister Salvador del Solar said during a ceremony in Zaña’s main square.
“Communities like Zaña can truly say that no blow has ever been strong enough to break them completely; they continue to reaffirm their Afro-descendant identity with pride.”
The Afro-descendant community is celebrating the return of Leo, their former bishop, and is particularly proud of Baca’s performance before the first pope with Black roots.
“I’m so proud to see an Afro-Peruvian person singing to the pope, and to know that Black blood courses through his veins,” said Felipe Gutierrez, a local chef and a poet known as Frontado.

“That the pope has Afro-descendant blood is also a source of pride for Zaña because Zaña identifies with the Afros,” said Gutierrez, who writes and improvises the Peruvian art form known as “decimas.”

All four of Leo’s maternal great-grandparents were “free people of color” in Louisiana based on 19th-century census records. As part of the melting pot of French, Spanish, African and Native American cultures in Louisiana, the pope’s maternal ancestors would be considered Creole.

Zaña is home to an Afro-Peruvian museum, which features a rich collection of historical photographs, plantation carts and percussion musical instruments of African origin from Peru, Cuba and Brazil. It also stores documents of enslaved people and some of the shackles used to restrain them.

One of its walls has photos of Leo during visits to the town when he was bishop. There are also large framed photographs of Barack Obama, the first Black president of the United States, as well as South African anti-apartheid leader Nelson Mandela.

“We pay homage to them here in Zaña,” Gutierrez said during a recent visit to the museum, wearing a Chicago Bulls shirt with Michael Jordan’s iconic number 23 on the back. Chicago is where Leo was born.

“They show us how someone who is Black as we are in Zaña became a president and we’re proud because we all deserve the same rights," Gutierrez said. “Black, Indigenous, all of us are equal in the eyes of God.”
Winfield contributed from Chiclayo, Peru.
