title: Southeast Asian leaders, with US and Chinese counterparts, will renew alarm over online scams
summary: Southeast Asian leaders and key counterparts, including from the U.S. and China, are raising alarms over online scams
story: Southeast Asian leaders and key counterparts, including from the U.S. and China, are raising alarms over online scams

MANILA, Philippines -- Southeast Asian leaders and their key counterparts, including from the United States and China, will renew their alarm over the escalating threat of online scams, according to a draft statement seen by The Associated Press on Friday.

Such transnational crimes, which have swindled billions of dollars from people in Asia to the United States and elsewhere, will be high in the agenda when leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations gather in an annual summit with their Asian and Western counterparts on Tuesday in the Philippine capital.

The Philippines currently holds the rotating leadership of ASEAN, an 11-nation bloc in a poverty-stricken region where criminal groups have used technology and resorted to human trafficking to expand their illicit and lucrative operations to other parts of the world.

The leaders of the expanded ASEAN bloc, called the East Asia Summit, will express their “grave concern over the escalating threat posed by transnational criminal organizations inflicting harm through online scams, including those originating from scam center operations and associated criminal conduct such as human trafficking,” according to a draft of their joint statement to be issued after their summit.

They acknowledged “the exploitation of digital and other advanced technologies and digital financial platforms, by increasingly sophisticated criminal actors and the need to strengthen financial and digital systems, as well as the severe human consequences associated with scam centers.”

Authorities in Southeast Asia have reported in recent years how large numbers of workers, who were lured by recruitment syndicates into working in online scam centers, including in the Philippines and Cambodia, have been subjected to threats and even torture when they tried to escape or defy orders.

Aside from sharing of information and strengthening law enforcement coordination, the leaders will encourage “the sharing of threat assessments and best practices" as well as strengthening cooperation between relevant authorities in dismantling scam centers, the leaders said in their draft statement, without elaborating.

In July, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime reported how Southeast Asia-based criminal groups have increasingly used integrated networks and technology to expand to other regions. The scams caused estimated combined losses of $88.3 billion to $114.1 billion in 2025, according to the report.
Criminals are using new technologies to launder money through global financial systems and using artificial intelligence to steal from victims worldwide, the U.N. report said.

East Asian crime syndicates are running businesses that use malware, generative AI and deepfakes for sexual extortion and exploitation in a trend that increases the risks of in-person as well as livestreamed abuse. Apart from outright trafficking for the sex industry, victims can be sold into domestic servitude, forced begging and forced labor, among other forms of exploitation, the report said.

The East Asia Summit leaders meeting in Manila will underscore “the need to address underlying drivers and other related factors of online scams," such as poverty, lack of social protection interventions, outdated domestic laws, private and public coordination gaps, corruption and limited economic opportunities.
They will stress that government responses to online scams must be consistent with international law and respect human rights.

title: An iconic puzzle comes home as production of the Rubik's Cube returns to Hungary
summary: The Rubik's Cube, invented by Hungarian architect Ernő Rubik in 1974, has become one of the world's most beloved puzzles
story: The Rubik's Cube, invented by Hungarian architect Ernő Rubik in 1974, has become one of the world's most beloved puzzles

BUDAPEST, Hungary -- More than half a century ago, a Hungarian architect, sculptor and professor invented what would become one of the world's most popular and beloved puzzles whose appeal has spanned generations: the colorful, mind-bending, six-sided Rubik's Cube.

Now, after selling more than half a billion units and becoming a worldwide cultural touchstone, production of the cube is returning to Hungary, where its inventor, Ernő Rubik, first conceived of the iconic object that bears his name.
Hungary “is the home of the cube. The cube was born here,” Rubik, 82, said on Tuesday at the opening of a new, fully automated Rubik's Cube production line in the Hungarian city of Jászberény.

The journey of the Rubik's Cube began in 1974, when Rubik was teaching design at the Academy of Applied Arts and Design in Budapest. Seeking to create a three-dimensional object that was “infinite,” he said, he completed a prototype — then made of wood — of a cube that could rotate on multiple axes and was made up of 27 blocks.

Recognizing its consumer value, Rubik soon began producing more of the puzzles. Beginning in 1977, an initial 5,000 units of what was then called the “Magic Cube” were sold at specialty shops in the Hungarian capital.

The invention — or what Rubik prefers to describe as a “discovery” — gained popularity, and after having difficulties procuring materials for the cubes in then-socialist Hungary, he realized: “We were not prepared for that size of production ... We can’t fulfill the needs of the market worldwide.”

The cube was licensed to a British and then a U.S. toy company, and its production was moved abroad. By the early 1980s, its popularity had exploded in what Rubik called “the first big wave,” in which he said 200 million units were sold between 1980 and 1983.
While sales of the cube dipped after its initial success, it still attracts plenty of users eager to try their hand at solving the puzzle. Millions are sold every year.

At the new production line in Hungary, a series of robotic arms assembles the cubes and tests them for functionality and durability — a level of automation Rubik said was “very different” than in the early days when the cubes were assembled by hand.
The new line in Jászberény plans to produce 1 million cubes annually.

Steve Radewych, a senior vice president with Canadian toy company Spin Master, which owns the Rubik's Cube trademark, said at Tuesday's opening that the theme of the day was: “Back to its roots: The cube comes home.”
“Ernő, your discovery is more than a toy,” Radewych told Rubik. “It's a global social phenomenon.”
Radewych noted the “incredible staying power” of the Rubik's Cube, and the fact that the puzzle continues to hold the fascination of young people even today.
“The cube represents an intellectual journey, a symbol of intelligence, problem-solving and cognitive discipline,” he added, which “has brought joy — and frustration — to many generations.”
The cube has enjoyed another surge in popularity in recent years as global competitions have proliferated, measuring who can solve the puzzle the fastest.
The current record, set only last month in China by nine-year-old Xuanyi Geng, is 2.51 seconds, according to the World Cube Association, which organizes and certifies competitions across the world.

Rubik, who does not consider himself a speed competitor, said that for him, the cube represents a “transformable sculpture,” the place where art and engineering meet and users can manipulate and change the cube in nearly endless variations.
“If you are doing something, creating something, you have the chance to do something that is meaningful — that’s one part — and beautiful,” he said.

title: US has seized $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency stolen from Binance, FBI says
summary: The FBI says it has seized or restrained more than $1.2 billion of cryptocurrency reported stolen last month from Binance
story: The FBI says it has seized or restrained more than $1.2 billion of cryptocurrency reported stolen last month from Binance
WASHINGTON -- The FBI said Thursday that it had seized more than $1.2 billion of cryptocurrency reported stolen last month from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange.

The theft of about $6.3 billion from Binance is regarded as the biggest crypto heist in history, and the FBI has previously attributed it to a North Korean hacking group known as TraderTraitor. The U.S. government and private sector have so far combined to freeze more than $2.7 billion of the stolen funds, and the Justice Department said Thursday that it has now obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of that total.
Typically in those situations, the U.S. government will file a claim of forfeiture with a judge, who will then determine who has a legitimate claim to the recovered funds.

Also Thursday, the FBI blamed North Korea for a separate social engineering scheme that officials say resulted in the theft of $400 million worth of cryptocurrency over the last 18 months. That scheme, known as FaceStealer, involves a complicated chain of events combining the hijacking of popular messaging apps and the recording of deepfake videos.
U.S. officials have repeatedly accused North Korea of using cyber schemes to generate funds for its regime, including its illicit weapons program.

title: Advocacy groups sue AI giants to freeze new models, warning of 'catastrophic' risks
summary: A coalition of online safety and consumer advocacy groups has sued five leading AI companies to halt further development
story: A coalition of online safety and consumer advocacy groups has sued five leading AI companies to halt further development

NEW YORK -- A coalition of online safety and consumer advocacy groups on Thursday sued five of the world’s leading artificial intelligence companies to halt further development, alleging the tech giants can’t prevent their own creations from causing “catastrophic” harm.

The lawsuit in San Francisco Superior Court follows a midterm election that could bring a moment of reckoning for the fast-moving AI industry, as Democrats who won back control of Congress stress the need to regulate the technology.

The filing, first reported on by The Associated Press, asks a judge to stop Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceXSI from developing or deploying new AI models, pointing to documented examples of cyberattacks and other harmful actions by AI systems and the companies’ own alarming acknowledgments that their technology has the potential to someday destroy humanity.

“No other industry is allowed to treat its own development of unsafe products — much less ones that could kill us all — as inevitable,” reads the complaint from the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative and the Alliance for Secure AI. “Plaintiffs bring this suit to stop Defendants from continuing their unlawful path to disaster.”

The AI industry has generated excitement and stock market gains, but also deep fears that the technology could go rogue and escape human control. Recent incidents of AI agents hacking government websites and companies — including when OpenAI's ChatGPT hacked into another AI company on its own in July — have accelerated those concerns.

President Donald Trump, a proponent of rapid AI development to keep the U.S. ahead of foreign competitors like China, has so far encouraged the companies to police themselves on matters of safety, though he has expressed openness to more guardrails. Congress also has stopped short of regulating the technology, but that may change with its Democratic takeover.

Some CEOs of major AI companies, meanwhile, have voiced support for slowing development of the technology to give safety measures a chance to catch up. They also haven't held back in recognizing the risks. Anthropic's Dario Amodei, for example, last year said he thinks there’s a 1 in 4 chance AI’s future goes “really, really badly,” compared with a 3 in 4 chance it goes well. Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, told Fox News in 2023 that AI could lead to “civilization destruction.”

The plaintiffs, all nonprofits, allege that the companies named in the lawsuit have violated a California unfair competition law by endangering public health and interfering with the use of property such as computer systems. They claim they’ve had to divert resources away from other planned work to address the acute harms threatened by each of the companies’ advancing AI models.

They also warn that the companies' goals of creating AI systems that are broadly as smart as humans and can increasingly manage tasks and learn things autonomously could result in a permanent loss of control of the technology and heighten existential risks to humanity.
The companies named in Thursday's lawsuit didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

title: Europe's Hera spacecraft begins close inspections of asteroid rammed by NASA
summary: A European spacecraft has begun close inspections of a harmless asteroid rammed by NASA four years ago in a planetary defense test
story: A European spacecraft has begun close inspections of a harmless asteroid rammed by NASA four years ago in a planetary defense test
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. -- A European spacecraft has begun close inspections of an asteroid rammed by NASA four years ago in a planetary defense test.
The European Space Agency announced Wednesday that the Hera spacecraft is now studying Didymos and its moonlet Dimorphos from just 15 miles to 18 miles (25 kilometers to 30 kilometers) away.
NASA’s Dart spacecraft deliberately slammed into little Dimorphos in 2022 to see whether such a defensive move might help save Earth from a killer space rock one day.
The impact shortened the moonlet's orbit around Didymos. More importantly, it nudged the moonlet into a slightly different path around the sun.
Next month, the small car-sized Hera, launched in 2024, will venture even closer — just 12 miles (20 kilometers) away.

ESA officials consider this a "crash site investigation" worthy of its finest robotic detective. Hera is carrying 25 science instruments as well as a pair of shoebox-sized Cubesats to survey Dimorphos even more closely and attempt to land on it.

The Dart spacecraft — short for Double Asteroid Redirection Test — sent rubble and even boulders flying off Dimorphos, providing an extra kick to the impact’s momentum. The debris trail extended thousands of miles (more than 10,000 kilometers) into space for months.
Some of that debris could still be in the vicinity, according to scientists.
Dimorphos is an estimated 500 feet (151 meters) in diameter. Didymos is roughly 2,560 feet (780 meters) in diameter.

title: How Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital affair could cause collateral damage in Washington
summary: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, is under scrutiny after revelations of an affair with a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, who is suspected of spying
story: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, is under scrutiny after revelations of an affair with a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, who is suspected of spying
WASHINGTON -- Extramarital affairs are usually private matters. Jensen Huang’s has global implications.

The 63-year-old is the leading face of the artificial intelligence revolution with his black leather jackets and fluff of grey hair. He runs the company Nvidia, which produces highly coveted computer chips. That's landed him on a late-night-phone-call basis with President Donald Trump, a promoter of the industry.

But Huang was also liaising with a Chinese businesswoman who has allegedly fed intelligence — as well as advanced chips — to China. The woman, Alice Huang, is a former executive at the Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed.

It's a saga of personal betrayal, corporate espionage and high-tech development, and the fallout is spreading across Washington. There are bipartisan calls for investigations on Capitol Hill. The U.S. Department of Justice has opened its own probe. Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, is conducting an internal review.

Some expect the technology to reshape human civilization by imbuing computers with the vast powers of creation and analysis, and Trump has repeated that “whoever wins AI, wins." Nvidia is the backbone of America's plans for dominating the field.
When asked about Huang's affair, Trump said this week that he had spoken to the tech executive as the scandal grew.
“I think he’ll be in good shape," Trump said, adding that "he said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”
As for when the president first learned about the concerns involving Alice Huang, Trump brushed off the question.
“They could have been mentioned," he said. "Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me.”
With the AI race between the U.S. and China often framed as a fierce and consequential rivalry, the Justice Department has persistently warned of the espionage threat posed by Beijing.
That includes efforts to cultivate well-placed relationships in government and private industry, as well as to acquire sensitive technology such as AI chips developed in the U.S.

Last year, Megaspeed faced scrutiny from the U.S. Commerce Department over its alleged skirting of U.S. export laws and routing of a large amount of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese users. The company denied those allegations. U.S. intelligence officials eventually concluded that Alice Huang had spied for China, according to The New York Times.

The Commerce Department's probe was handed off to the Justice Department, and its National Security Division is investigating whether Megaspeed violated export control laws in an inquiry that will also include scrutiny of Alice Huang, according to a person familiar with the matter who insisted on anonymity to discuss an ongoing law enforcement probe.
Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday, and The Associated Press was unable to reach Alice Huang.

Jensen Huang has apologized to his company about the affair, saying he hurt his wife and their children, but he didn’t address reports that Alice Huang was a suspected spy. Nvidia’s board said that it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, and that Huang would remain in charge while cooperating with the investigation.
Beijing has said the “Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated" and called it “nothing but smears.”
After their first dinner together at Mar-a-Lago in early 2025, Trump latched onto Huang as a tech titan positioned to deliver on the president’s own promises of an economic renaissance.

The computer chips produced by Nvidia would essentially turn data centers into factories that made raw intelligence, which could then be applied across the economy to produce cars, new pharmaceutical drugs, advanced weapons and seemingly unparalleled wealth.
Trump would regularly phone Huang to discuss this future.

“From the moment that I met him, the only thing that he’s ever talked to me about is creating more jobs, re-industrializing the United States, of protection, of national security,” Huang told AP in an interview this summer. "He knows that if America is wealthy, we have a lot of tax revenues. We can fund the military, we can fund our economy, we fund our communities, create more jobs.”

Trump saw his political fortunes — and that of the country — in Huang's Nvidia. Huang joined Trump on Air Force One for a state visit to Beijing earlier this year. Just last month, Trump awarded Huang with a National Medal of Science.
The president called him “a man whose determination laid the foundations for the explosion of super intelligence and put America at the front of the race, an amazing man, gotten to know him so well.”
Nvidia also donated $25 million to help fund the construction of Trump’s White House ballroom.
Multiple estimates suggest that more than half of the stock market gains during Trump's second term came from the growth of the AI industry and the construction of data centers.

Without that growth, consumer spending could slump, delivering another economic setback to a president who has already failed to deliver on his campaign promise of stopping inflation. Rising prices were among the reasons that voters delivered a harsh rebuke to Republicans in last week's midterm elections, returning control of Congress to the Democrats.

While Huang said his interests were in helping America succeed, he also expressed a strong view that Nvidia should be able to sell some of its less advanced chips such as the H200 to China. Nvidia long argued that the sales would help ensure that the broader AI ecosystem was tied to America, boxing out Chinese chipmakers that are developing semiconductors and systems to compete with his company.

Those arguments previously came under scrutiny, including from Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who wanted him to appear before the Senate Banking Committee to answer questions about his desire to loosen export restrictions.

Huang has so far refused to appear, and Democrats responded angrily when his infidelity came to light, raising concerns that a bulwark of American technology may have been compromised by the Chinese government.
Warren said in a statement Monday that Nvidia had reportedly gotten approvals to export “hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips to China, including to companies tied to China’s military.”
And Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, Warren continued, “raises important questions NVIDIA must answer about the extent to which these activities were related."

Chan reported from Hong Kong and Ng from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Associated Press journalists Wu Jia in Beijing, Didi Tang in Washington and Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia, contributed to this report.

title: Tech consultant sentenced to 16 years to life in stabbing death of Cash App founder
summary: The tech consultant convicted in the stabbing death of Cash App founder Bob Lee has been sentenced in San Francisco to 16 years to life to prison
story: The tech consultant convicted in the stabbing death of Cash App founder Bob Lee has been sentenced in San Francisco to 16 years to life to prison
SAN FRANCISCO -- The tech consultant convicted in the stabbing death of Cash App founder Bob Lee was sentenced in San Francisco on Tuesday to 16 years to life to prison.

A jury in December 2024 found Nima Momeni guilty of second-degree murder, rejecting the defendant's claim that he had acted in self-defense. He has remained in custody since his arrest nine days after the April 4, 2023, killing.
Before imposing the sentence, San Francisco Superior Court Judge Alexandra Gordon rejected Momeni’s request for a new trial. His attorneys have said they plan to appeal.
Members of Lee’s family addressed the court on Tuesday, including his 18-year-old daughter, Scout Lee, who spoke directly to Momeni.
“You did not just end his life, you ended an entire future built around a man,” she told Momeni, according to media reports.
Momeni, wearing an orange jail jumpsuit, maintained that he acted in self-defense. He told Lee’s family that he understood their loss.
“Unfortunately, we have completely different understandings of what transpired,” Momeni said.
Lee, a renowned tech mogul, was found staggering on a deserted downtown street, dripping a trail of blood and calling for help. Lee, 43, later died at a hospital.

Prosecutors said Momeni planned the attack on Lee, driving him to an isolated spot under the Bay Bridge and stabbing him three times, including once to the heart, with a knife he took from his sister's kitchen. They said Momeni was angry with Lee for introducing his younger sister to a drug dealer she says gave her GHB and other drugs and then sexually assaulted her.

But Momeni testified on the stand that Lee was the one who attacked him with a knife, angry after the tech consultant chided him about spending more time with his family instead of searching for a strip club that night. Momeni, who studies martial arts, said he didn't realize he had fatally wounded Lee or that Lee was even hurt.

Lee had created mobile payment service Cash App and was the chief product officer of the cryptocurrency MobileCoin when he died. He had recently moved to Miami from the San Francisco Bay Area, where his ex-wife Krista Lee lives with their two children, and had returned to California for a visit.

Jurors in the end rejected a charge of murder in the first degree, which required prosecutors prove that Momeni acted deliberately, willfully and with premeditation. Murder in the second degree does not require premeditation.

title: Appeals court limits order for LinkedIn to disclose journalists' communications in leak probe
summary: A federal judge must narrow an order requiring LinkedIn to divulge journalists’ communications on the social media platform to the Trump administration for a leak investigation
story: A federal judge must narrow an order requiring LinkedIn to divulge journalists’ communications on the social media platform to the Trump administration for a leak investigation

WASHINGTON -- A judge must narrow an order requiring LinkedIn to divulge journalists' communications on the social media platform to the Trump administration as part of a leak investigation, a federal appeals court ruled Tuesday in a case with profound free-speech implications.

A three-judge panel from the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said the government isn't entitled to a “blanket” order for LinkedIn to disclose a broad array of user records belonging to the journalists, whose employer isn't identified in court records.

“A request by the government to scoop up reporters’ records wholesale and ascertain the identity of their sources would tip the balance against informed discourse in a manner inimical to democratic health,” Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson III wrote in the court's unanimous opinion.

But the panel also rejected LinkedIn's request to entirely quash the district court's "substantially overbroad” disclosure order. The panel recognized that the journalists' First Amendment rights must be balanced against the administration's duty to protect national security information.
“Serious security and speech claims are in tension in this case. There is space under law for both," wrote Wilkinson, who was nominated to the court by Ronald Reagan, a Republican.
The panel also included Judge James Andrew Wynn, who was nominated by Democratic President Barack Obama, and Judge Nicole G. Berner, who was nominated by Democratic President Joe Biden.
U.S. District Judge Elizabeth Hanes, a Biden nominee based in Newport News, Virginia, issued the order that LinkedIn challenged in the case.

Republican President Donald Trump's administration opened its leak investigation when an unidentified news organization published an article about a top-secret U.S. military operation in a foreign country, revealing classified information.

The journalists targeted by the leak investigation had reported on nearly 1,000 stories on many topics over the 18-month period covered by the judge's order. The order would unmask every confidential source that the targeted journalists communicated with on LinkedIn over that span.

“While that order may catch sources relevant to the government’s investigation, it will also inevitably sweep in every other confidential source with whom the targeted journalists spoke," Wilkinson wrote.
The panel returned the case to Hanes with an instruction to narrow the disclosure order.

“That court was right to accord the government considerable latitude in pursuing and maintaining the integrity of its investigation,” Wilkinson wrote. “Even so, that latitude is not infinite. It is not appropriate for district courts to approve requests purely because the records requested are logistically feasible to compile.”

title: Anthropic seeks valuation of about $1.3 trillion when it becomes a publicly traded company
summary: Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic is looking for an approximately $1.3 trillion valuation in its initial public offering
story: Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic is looking for an approximately $1.3 trillion valuation in its initial public offering

Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic is looking for an approximately $1.3 trillion valuation in an initial public offering despite new questions about the massive amounts of money flowing into the sector.

The company behind the Claude chatbot said in a regulatory filing on Tuesday that it will sell 825 million shares priced between $70 and $78 a share. That would give Anthropic the ability to raise more than $61 billion, if the IPO is priced at the midpoint.

The initial pricing of a company's shares is a complex process. If they are priced too high, it can send shares skidding on the first day. If shares are seen as cheap, the company and the banks running the IPO can leave money on the table.
The San Francisco company is anticipated to make its Wall Street debut this month.

Anthropic could be among the biggest initial public offerings of stock ever, but now seems like it will fall short of eclipsing the record $86 billion raised by SpaceX in its IPO in June. An Anthropic IPO would also put the company ahead of OpenAI in going public, setting the stage for a pair of blockbuster stock debuts by rival AI developers.

“For tech and AI, this is the first time a U.S. frontier lab carries a standalone public market price, uncluttered by an ad business or a rocket business,” Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., wrote in an analyst note.
The IPO could give Anthropic enormous resources to accelerate its expansion and potentially add billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela Amodei.

A regulatory filing last month showed that Anthropic’s revenue is growing rapidly, reaching more than $16 billion in the first half of the year — 14 times its revenue from the same period last year. But like many other tech companies going public, the company has yet to turn a profit.

Formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company. But both companies have plenty of other competitors, including Google, newer startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business. Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI division have all been losing more money than they make because of the huge costs of resources in building AI, fueling concerns of a bubble.

There was also a brutal sell-off on Wall Street late last week, led by stocks tied to the buildout of AI data centers. Stock markets around the world felt pressure from continued drops for companies that had benefited from the boom in the artificial-intelligence technology industry. Shares in AI companies have been swinging for months on worries that the construction of further AI data centers may slow because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money. Critics also believe that an AI bubble may be forming.

Dario Amodei cautioned in September that the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the entire internet within six to 12 months.

He offered a plan in a post on his website to increase checks on the industry, noting that Anthropic is already undertaking part of this on its own. As for other steps, though, he said that would require coordination across the industry and with governments around the world, including authoritarian ones.
The shares are expected to list on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the “ANT” ticker symbol.

title: Australia to launch AI safety regulator after OpenAI's breach of a government portal
summary: Australia plans to create an artificial intelligence safety regulator in response to a breach of an Australian health department website by an OpenAI agent in June
story: Australia plans to create an artificial intelligence safety regulator in response to a breach of an Australian health department website by an OpenAI agent in June

MELBOURNE, Australia -- Australia plans to create an artificial intelligence safety regulator in response to a breach of an Australian health department website by a rogue OpenAI agent in June, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Tuesday.

The regulator would enforce world-leading legislated AI standards that would apply to all frontier AI companies that want to operate in Australia, Albanese said. Financial penalties would apply, although the government has yet to detail those penalties.

“When it comes to the generational opportunity that artificial intelligence offers Australia, I’ve been very clear: our task is to make sure we shape AI rather than AI shape us,” Albanese told reporters. “Australia is the first mover in this space and we want to make sure that we continue to work so that we can reap the potential benefits from AI.”

The standards would include companies maintaining security controls across all stages of models’ development and deployment, as well as identifying and managing serious risks. The standards also would mandate rapid notification to the government of incidents such as “misaligned behavior” conflicting with developers' intentions.
Australian government documents define frontier AI as the most sophisticated models at the cutting edge of current technological capability.

Albanese told OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman that the U.S. company took too long to inform the government in September that a rogue agent had infiltrated government websites three months earlier, which was the first occurrence of such a breach with the technology.

Information taken without authorization from the public-facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal on June 18 has since been made public. It is not clear whether the portal breach broke any Australian laws.
OpenAI apologized in September for the breach and its slow response.
“We are sorry and working to do better in the future,” OpenAI said in a statement. “We also should have handled our response better.”
A government inquiry into the June breach made several recommendations including that the government consider changing the law.
Albanese said his government had accepted all the inquiry’s recommendations, including for potential criminal law reform.

“The point is law needs to get ahead of and in some cases make sure that it catches up with what is a very fast-changing world. And to be clear, Australia is a first-mover in these areas,” Albanese said.

The proposed AI regulator would follow Australia appointing an eSafety Commissioner in 2015. The office describes itself as the world’s first government agency dedicated to keeping people safer online.
Since December last year, the commissioner has been enforcing a world-first ban on Australian children younger than 16 holding accounts on popular social media platforms.

title: Trump says FBI is looking at Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with alleged Chinese agent
summary: President Donald Trump says the FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese government agent
story: President Donald Trump says the FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese government agent

WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump said Monday that the FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese government agent, but said he doesn’t think the executive who has helped to develop artificial intelligence has a reason to worry.
“I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape,” Trump said at a White House briefing.

The sudden emergence of Huang's infidelity has rocked the political class and America's tech sector, creating new concerns about whether China has been able to access the cutting-edge chips designed by Nvidia that are powering the development of artificial intelligence.
Trump suggested the extraordinary step of directly involving himself in a counterintelligence investigation, a sign of his friendly relationship with Huang and the possible geopolitical stakes.
“I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling all right, how you’re doing," Trump said. "He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”

Huang — a singular figure in the technology landscape and one of the world’s wealthiest people — has acknowledged he had an affair, issuing an apology to his wife and to the company in an open letter posted on Nvidia’s website. The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence determined that the woman was gathering information for Beijing.
“I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security,” Huang said in his letter.
Nvidia announced Sunday it was conducting an independent investigation into reports that Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

The episode also is attracting congressional scrutiny, with top Democrats Sen. Mark Warner and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries saying Monday they are interested in investigating it further. Jeffries said the Nvidia issue came up during a closed-door session with the CIA director and the Director of National Intelligence that was primarily about Iran.

“We’re going to need a full briefing, specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue, so we can all get to the bottom of what has happened,” he said, “and what the implications are in terms of America’s national security.”
Trump is slated to meet next week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, but he was noncommittal about bringing up the situation with Xi.
“No, I don’t think so,” Trump said. “I mean, maybe. I’m sure President Xi will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he’s a very honorable man.”

FBI counterintelligence investigations often examine efforts by foreign powers to spy on the United States, whether by surreptitiously stealing technology designed by American companies, covertly waging foreign influence campaigns aimed at shaping public opinion or cultivating relationships with powerful political and industry figures. Such investigations can take years and do not necessarily culminate in criminal charges. China has been regarded across presidential administrations of both political parties as a persistent counterintelligence threat.

China denied Monday that it engaged in an attempt to ensnare Huang. “The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China,” Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

Beijing earlier had dismissed The New York Times report saying Huang had developed a close relationship with a Chinese citizen named Alice Huang, who ran a company that last year faced claims it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China.

Huang and Nvidia play a critical role in the artificial intelligence industry as many of the world’s leading AI developers rely on the company’s specialized chips to power their systems. Huang has also helped persuade Trump to take a lighter touch on regulating AI, arguing that existing laws could cover any security issues stemming from the technology and that individual companies should behave responsibly with the products they develop and release.

Huang also has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China in recent years, winning Trump’s approval for selling its H200 chips this year. It’s unclear if Beijing would allow Chinese companies to buy those chips in large quantities. Nvidia said in a regulatory filing in August that it has sold only a small amount to China as such sales are restricted by the Chinese government.

The H200 chips are not Nvidia’s most cutting-edge models, but they are still advanced. Previously, Huang also lobbied Trump to be allowed to sell Nvidia’s less-advanced H20 chips, which were designed to comply with U.S. export restrictions on China.

In an exclusive interview with The Associated Press in June, Huang said: “National security should always be the top concern of all technologies. But having said that, you know, you have to be very specific about the risk that you’re concerned about, before setting up policies for export controls.”
Nvidia shares dropped more than 4% in trading Monday. Nvidia stock has shed roughly 11% of its value since last Wednesday.
The New York Times said Alice Huang was a former executive of a Singapore-based data center company called Megaspeed International, whose website prominently touts its partnership with Nvidia.
Many offices in Singapore were closed Monday for a holiday. Megaspeed and the Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs did not immediately reply to requests for comment.

Nvidia is one of the world’s most valuable publicly traded companies, alongside Apple and Microsoft. Its sales of computer chips to China have at times been targeted by U.S. regulators seeking to limit Beijing's access to such technology.

“The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised,” said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, a Washington-based consultancy.
“Those questions require evidence rather than speculation,” he added in a text message to reporters.

Chinese media have largely focused on Huang admitting to the affair and state media outlets have mainly echoed the official government line. Some have said the New York Times report was aimed at destabilizing U.S.-China relations.
“Whenever China-US relations begin to improve, there are often those firing shots from the shadows,” the state-owned Global Times said.

Associated Press writers Chan Ho-him in Hong Kong, Huizhong Wu in Bangkok, Barbara Ortutay in San Francisco and Eric Tucker and Lisa Mascaro in Washington contributed to this report. Huamani reported from Los Angeles.

title: What to Stream: U2, 'Misty Green,' 'The Chosen' and Randy Travis
summary: U2's new album and a Proud Family Christmas special are among the new streaming releases this week
story: U2's new album and a Proud Family Christmas special are among the new streaming releases this week
U2's new album and Chris Rock’s latest film are some of the new television, films, music and games headed to a device near you.

Also among the streaming offerings worth your time this week, as selected by The Associated Press’ entertainment journalists: a “Proud Family” Christmas special, a new season of “The Chosen” and an album of unreleased Randy Travis music.

— It’s been 11 years since Chris Rock directed a feature. In “Misty Green” (Nov. 9 on Netflix), Rock returns as writer and director of a Hollywood character study. Rosalind Eleazar (“Slow Horses”), in a breakthrough performance, stars as a talented but self-sabotaging Los Angeles actor whose once bright future in the industry is fading. In his review, AP’s Mark Kennedy called it “one of Rock’s best projects, boosted by the ferocious abilities of Rosalind Eleazar as Misty.”

— “Being Heumann” (Nov. 13 on Apple TV), Siân Heder’s follow-up to the best picture-winning family drama “CODA,” is about disability rights pioneer Judy Heumann and the 1977 San Francisco sit-in that helped lead to making federal spaces accessible. Ruth Madeley stars as Heumann in a film richly detailed with the day-to-day challenges of a 28-day demonstration by people with disabilities. Co-starring Mark Ruffalo.

— “Avedon” (Nov. 11 on Netflix) chronicles the life and work of photographer Richard Avedon. Directed by Ron Howard, the documentary draws on extensive access to Avedon’s personal archives to explore how his eye for fashion, people and more shaped the imagery of the 20th century.
— AP Film Writer Jake Coyle

— U2 is back. Did you miss them? “Carnaval De Luz” is the Irish rock band’s first full-length release since 2017’s “Songs of Experience.” “Carnaval De Luz” — which translates from Spanish and Portuguese to “Carnival of Light” — is produced by Jacknife Lee, who has been working with U2 since 2004’s “How to Dismantle an Atomic Bomb.” There’s a lot to be excited about in that last sentence alone, and then there’s this: The last track on the album is “Torn,” a duet with Dolly Parton that turned out to be her last recorded vocal performance.

— In July 2013, country star Randy Travis was hospitalized with viral cardiomyopathy, a virus that attacks the heart, and later suffered a stroke. The Country Music Hall of Famer had to relearn how to walk, spell and read in the years that followed. A condition called aphasia limits his ability to speak — it’s why it felt like a miracle when he released a new acoustic ballad in 2024, “Where That Came From,” utilizing artificial intelligence to get his voice back. Now, on Friday, he’ll release “Same Old Way,” his first album of original music in over 18 years featuring previously unreleased tracks. No AI here, but all Travis.

— The hyperpop hero 2hollis returns with “Pirouette” on Friday, a post-internet, post-Skrillex discordant release — 16 tracks of EDM-indebted future-seeking dance music. He’s a rapper (“Warhorse”) except when he’s not (“Sex”) and something else entirely (“Hurt.”) This one's for his dedicated fans and those unafraid to join him.
— AP Music Writer Maria Sherman

— Chris Harrison is back to matchmaking with Fox Nation’s first original dating show called “Chris Harrison’s The Vow.” It debuts Wednesday with two episodes, then goes weekly. Jace Cates, 30, courts 10 women looking to get married. Harrison hosted “The Bachelor” franchise for nearly two decades before exiting in 2021 after racial comments about a contestant. The show centers on faith and shared values, and the women are urged to leave if the match isn't working. Former “Bachelor” Sean Lowe and his wife, Catherine, drop in with advice.

— Hulu’s “Rivals” returns Wednesday for the second half of Season 2 with three episodes dropping at once, and the last three arriving weekly. The Emmy- and BAFTA-winning series is adapted from the novel “Rivals” by Jilly Cooper. It’s about two men (played by David Tennant and Aidan Turner) feuding over a British TV franchise.

— Peacock releases all six episodes of the limited series “The Good Daughter” on Thursday. It’s based on Karin Slaughter’s 2017 novel. Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy play Samantha and Charlotte Quinn, sisters who are still grappling with a brutal crime that struck their family decades earlier. Slaughter wrote all the episodes. Brendan Gleeson co-stars.

— Anthony Mackie and Jamie Dornan star in and executive-produce the eight-episode series “12 12 12,” debuting Friday. Mackie plays a disgraced FBI agent on the trail of Dornan's character, a thief who robs a Zurich bank vault. The story shifts between three timelines: 12 months of planning, 12 hours of execution and 12 days on the run.

— “The Proud Family” has a Christmas special called “A Proud Family Wizmas,” a stop-motion musical coming to Disney+ on Saturday. Penny Proud's rant about the commercialization of Christmas causes Santa to quit on Christmas Eve, so she reluctantly steps into his suit to deliver presents.

— The first three episodes of Prime Video's “The Chosen” Season 6 drop Sunday. Jonathan Roumie returns as Jesus in a season about his last day, building to the crucifixion. The finale is headed to theaters next spring.
— AP Writer Alicia Rancilio

— The title character of “Hope in the City” is a teenager living a comfortable life in Shenyang, China — until her parents disappear. Fortunately, Hope is fearless and has a good eye for evidence, and as she puts together the pieces of a conspiracy, “every clue reveals more of the city’s darkest secrets.” Canada’s Lofty Sky Games presents the mystery with stylized polygonal graphics that evoke the classic point-and-click adventures of the 1990s. The investigation begins Tuesday on Xbox X/S and PC.

— Worried about artificial intelligence? Stardock Entertainment is giving you a chance to fight back with “Ashes of the Singularity II,” the latest epic from the masters of real-time strategy. Three factions are battling for control of the galaxy: the human United Earth Forces, the hyper-efficient Post-Human Coalition and the relentless AI Substrate. The solo campaign puts you in charge of humans trying to undo the damage left after years of expansion by the other two groups. Multiplayer skirmishes let you control any faction to fight against or alongside your friends. Plug in Tuesday on PC.
— Lou Kesten

title: FAA ground stop live updates: Duffy blames 'overloaded' routers after stop lifted
summary: The DHS secretary said there were no indications of a cyberattack.
story: The DHS secretary said there were no indications of a cyberattack.

The Federal Aviation Administration ordered a rare nationwide ground stop for all airports Friday -- a more than four-hour disruption that snarled travel from coast to coast with canceled flights and stranded passengers.

At a White House news conference Friday night, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed old technology that became overloaded and called on Congress to provide billions more in funding to modernize critical equipment, calling the situation an "emergency."
Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters there was no indication the incident stemmed from a cyberattack, but that officials were still investigating.
Thousands of flights were canceled amid the ground stop.
"I believe that it's going to take us some time to get back to capacity," Duffy said when asked how long air travelers should expect delays and cancellations to continue.

'You will have more of these' unless system upgraded, Duffy says of outage that led to ground stop

At a White House news conference, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy insisted that the U.S. has the "safest airspace in the world" but also suggested an incident like Friday's ground stop would happen again and that flying will continue being “less safe” unless Congress provides funding for flight system advancement.

"We didn't think we would have this kind of outage," Duffy said. "The systems that were deployed kept everybody safe -- everyone landed. We're able to review what went wrong and then reboot the system and go. But you will have more of these. You will have more of them unless the American people and the Congress tell us to build."
Duffy called on Congress to provide $50 billion for a "complete overhaul" of the system.
United says it's resuming operations
Following the lifting of the ground stop, United Airlines said it is "resuming operations, including some planned Friday night flights."
Duffy makes plea for funding: 'This is an emergency'
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called for funding from Congress to upgrade what he called an "incredibly old air traffic control system" in the wake of Friday's nationwide ground stop.
"This is an emergency," he told reporters. "I want Congress to give us emergency funding. This is bipartisan. This is American. I want $50 billion."
In describing Friday's issue, Duffy pointed to "old switches, old routers."
"We use 1980s little copper lines. It's an old system that went down and went down everywhere. It got overloaded," he said.

"I think our fix gives us a pretty good indication that it was a legacy network problem that went down," he continued, adding, "By the way, all of the new equipment that we put in, none of that went down."
Will 'take time' to make up for disruptions: Duffy
On how long to expect delays and cancellations due to the ground stop, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters, "I believe that it's going to take us some time to get back to capacity."
He said, "it's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened this afternoon," adding that "hopefully tomorrow we are going to start to see far better movement."
Duffy said he believes things will be "back up and operational" heading into Thanksgiving travel.

title: Trump to meet with Putin and Xi in China next week, US officials say
summary: Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China, and Russia on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in China next week.
story: The meeting will be the first between the three leaders.

President Donald Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in China next week, senior U.S. officials told reporters Friday evening.

Trump is expected to discuss Iran with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the officials said, but he does not intend to discuss Russia's war with Ukraine during the trilateral meeting.

Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.

Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying, "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will meet ahead of their meeting with Putin but Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.

Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels, the officials said, but did not specify Musk's reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to his business interests in China.
An official said some additional U.S. business leaders are expected to attend the APEC CEO Summit but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.

Trump's trip to Shenzhen, China, for the APEC Summit will be his second trip to China this year, as well and his third meeting with Xi. Before the China leg of the trip, Trump will be in Manila for the ASEAN Summit.
There are no plans for a meeting with North Korea's Kim Jung Un while Trump is in Asia, an official added.

The senior U.S. officials said they do not expect the Nvidia controversy of this week to have any impact on the president's trip or his planned meetings after former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the tech company over concerns that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Officials said they don't expect Trump to raise with Xi the allegations against Alice Huang, a Chinese national and tech executive at Megaspeed who is accused of being a Chinese spy, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.

"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.

Trump will depart from the White House on Monday morning en route to Manila, where he will participate in a series of multilateral meetings about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region, the officials said. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand, they added.

While in the Philippines, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony and state visit with Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. Trump is expected to secure "commercial deals and strategic investments" during his two-day visit to the Philippines, officials said.

Trump will then travel to Shenzhen, where he will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Xi.
The Trump-Xi-Putin meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia trip.

title: 2 Americans die in suspected drowning incident in the Bahamas
summary: Two Americans died in a suspected drowning incident in the Bahamas on Friday afternoon after a group of swimmers was swept away by strong currents, police said.
story: "Several individuals were reportedly swept away by the strong currents."
Two Americans died in a suspected drowning incident in the Bahamas on Friday afternoon after a group of swimmers was swept away by strong currents, police said.

The victims, a 38-year-old man and a 40-year-old woman, were among a group of people swimming beyond an area marked with a warning sign cautioning against strong currents, according to the Royal Bahamas Police Force.
Police said they received a report shortly before 3 p.m. and responded to the southern point of North Bimini, near the entrance to Bimini Harbour.

"Upon arrival, officers were informed that the victims were among a group of individuals swimming beyond an area marked with a warning sign cautioning against strong currents," according to a statement from the Royal Bahamas Police Force. "While swimming, several individuals were reportedly swept away by the strong currents."
A nearby ferry boat helped rescue some of the swimmers, but the two Americans became unresponsive and were pulled from the water.

CPR was administered before the victims were taken to a local clinic, where medical personnel continued life-saving efforts. Both were pronounced dead by an attending physician shortly before 4 p.m., police said.
Foul play is not suspected, according to police. An autopsy will be conducted to help determine the exact cause of death.
The investigation into the circumstances surrounding the incident is ongoing.

title: Sarah Huckabee Sanders receives 2028 presidential encouragement
summary: Supporters and donors have been encouraging GOP Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders to run for president in the 2028 cycle, sources told ABC News.
story: Georgia GOP Gov. Brian Kemp is also said to be getting encouragement to run.

Supporters and donors have been encouraging Republican Arkansas governor and former White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders to run for president in the 2028 cycle, according to multiple sources with direct knowledge of the situation.

​When asked about the outreach Sanders has been receiving, her communications director Sam Dubke told ABC News that “Governor Sanders looks forward to serving the people of Arkansas for the next four years.”

​Sanders, the daughter of Mike Huckabee, himself a former Arkansas governor, Repubican presidential candidate and current U.S. ambassador to Israel, won re-election as governor last week. She became the first woman ever elected Arkansas governor in 2022.

Before becoming governor, Sanders served as President Donald Trump's press secretary in his first term from July 2017 to June 2019 after having served as deputy press secretary. She was also a senior adviser to Trump's 2016 presidential campaign.

​While Sanders formally briefed the White House press corps less than her predecessors, she became one of Trump’s closest and most trusted advisers and has maintained a close relationship with him, having worked for Trump in the White House for 3 1/2 years.
Sanders has long been viewed as a rising star in the Republican Party.

In 2023, a few months after winning the gubernatorial race in Arkansas, Sanders delivered the Republican response to former President Joe Biden’s State of the Union address -- remarks usually reserved for individuals seen as on their way up in the party.

Georgia's retiring popular two-term Republican Gov. Brian Kemp is also considering a presidential bid after he leaves office in January and has been encouraged by donors and other Republican officials to run, a source familiar with his thinking told ABC News.
​In the days leading up to the midterm elections, Kemp traveled to South Carolina, one of the early nominating states for Republicans, to campaign for Gov.-elect Alan Wilson.
ABC News has reached out to Kemp's political operation for comment.
​After Republicans' midterm losses, the party is reflecting on what went wrong and how to move forward, with some of those conversations happening publicly.
​Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, who has not ruled out a 2028 presidential run, called Republicans' performance in the midterm elections a "Watergate-level repudiation" of the party.
​Outgoing Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis described the election results as a "meteor strike," arguing that even a "wave" fails to capture the scale of the Republican losses.

​DeSantis is keeping his options open for another presidential run, two people familiar with his thinking told ABC News, after the governor said Florida fended off a blue wave in this year's midterm elections.

title: Schumer and Van Hollen face off for Senate majority leader. What do Democrats think?
summary: Within moments of Chris Van Hollen announcing his intent to challenge Chuck Schumer in a race to lead next year’s Senate Democratic majority, endorsements began flying.
story: Van Hollen says he has support, Schumer says he has the votes to remain leader.

Within moments of Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen announcing his intention to challenge Minority Leader Chuck Schumer in a race to lead next year’s Senate Democratic majority, endorsements began flying in favor of both candidates.

Van Hollen branded himself as an “underdog” while announcing his candidacy during an interview on MS Now Thursday night. But he also said he’d garnered the support of at least 10 senators -- enough to raise eyebrows about his potential to shake up caucus dynamics.

"We should not be preserving our institutions if they are not delivering for the American people, and we should be making delivering for the American people the single mission of our government, even when that means shaking things up, and that is why I'm running for the majority leader in the United States Senate,” Van Hollen said during a summit event in Denver, Colorado on Friday.
Already, Van Hollen has garnered critical support among some members of the incoming freshmen class.

“The American public spoke clearly last week. They rejected Trumpism. But we have yet to earn our mandate. That will require bold leadership. I called on Sen. @ChrisVanHollen to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience. We need both right now. Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority,” Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed posted on X Thursday night.
Minnesota Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan also threw her support behind Van Hollen.

“Minnesotans are demanding change. Democrats need to deliver. That starts with new voices in our leadership. I believe @ChrisVanHollen is the leader and fighter we need to bring about real change, so no American is left behind,” Flanagan posted on X on Friday morning.
It’s not just new members backing Van Hollen. Sen. Bernie Sanders, a longtime face of the progressive movement, called for a change in leadership before backing Van Hollen.

“This election was about CHANGE. The Democratic Party must CHANGE. Now is the time to take on the oligarchs and fight for working families,” Sanders posted on X. “That is why I will be supporting Chris Van Hollen for Majority Leader.”

Sanders’ endorsement went further than a handful of other Democrats, who have called for a change in the party leadership without endorsing any particular candidate. Sen. Elissa Slotkin along with a number of other incoming Democrats, fall into this category.
But Schumer, who led Senate Democrats for nearly 10 years, doesn’t seem to be sweating it.

In a post on social media Thursday night that came within seconds of Van Hollen announcing his intent to challenge him, Schumer said he’d already clinched the necessary votes to be re-elected as leader for what would be a sixth two-year term.

Democrats picked up a whopping eight seats during the midterm elections, something Schumer claims partial credit for. When the new Senate is sworn in in January, Democrats will go from being the minority party to holding at least a 55-45 seat majority. The Senate race in Alaska has yet to be projected, but a Democratic victory there could secure Democrats an even larger share of seats.

“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together -- 55 seats and counting is an amazing result -- and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader,” Schumer said.
Endorsements for Schumer followed almost immediately after.

“Chuck Schumer is one of the principal architects of the most successful election in modern history, and I see no reason to change the leadership that helped make that success possible,” Sen. Angus King, a Maine independent who caucuses with Democrats, said in a statement. “Why would you fire the manager when you just won the World Series?”
Sen. Jacky Rosen of Nevada joined King and a number of her colleagues in highlighting Schumer’s role in helping Democrats to secure their resounding majority in the midterms.

“I’ve seen up close how hard @SenSchumer works for our entire caucus. He did the work to deliver what will soon be a 56-seat Senate majority against all odds, and I know he has the experience and the fight to continue leading our diverse caucus at this crucial moment. I’m proud to support him to be our Majority Leader,” Rosen posted on X.
Her fellow Nevada senator echoed that.

“Leader Schumer was instrumental in Democrats flipping 8 -- soon to be 9 -- Senate seats and securing a historic majority. I will be supporting him as our Democratic leader,” Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto said in a post.

To clench the majority leader title, a candidate will need to amass a simple majority of conference votes during a closed-door leadership election. Though no date for the election has officially been announced, Democrats are expected to hold it in early December.
The leadership election is held by secret ballot. Newly elected senators will get a chance to vote in that election but outgoing senators will not cast ballots.
Depending on the results in Alaska, either 55 or 56 Democrats will vote in the election. The winner of the election will need either 28 or 29 supporters, depending on the Alaska results.

Senate Republicans elected their new leadership following a lengthy closed-door discussion on Tuesday. Current Majority Leader John Thune will remain the top Republican in the Senate leading the GOP minority for the next two years.
ABC News' Lalee Ibssa and Hannah Demissie contributed to this report.

title: Iran live updates: Bessent blasts Iranian threats
summary: President Donald Trump announced "major combat operations" against Iran on Feb. 28.
story: The secretary attacked Iranian leadership after moving to a military base.

Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February. The opening strikes killed a host of top Iranian officials and commanders, among them Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though have not returned to the intense fighting seen in the early stages of the conflict. The U.S. says it is enforcing a naval blockade of the country's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway.

Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military, oil infrastructure and transport facilities.
See the most recent developments below.
Key Headlines

Nov 13, 2026, 1:01 PM ESTIranian foreign minister calls US attacks violation of international lawNov 13, 2026, 11:47 AM ESTBessent says economic campaign against Iran is working, he moved to military base due to Iranian threatsNov 13, 2026, 9:23 AM ESTUS denies Iran's claim that it destroyed US radar in BahrainNov 12, 2026, 11:34 AM ESTWhite House won't say if talks with Iran have stopped
Nov 13, 2026, 1:01 PM ESTIranian foreign minister calls US attacks violation of international law
Nov 13, 2026, 11:47 AM ESTBessent says economic campaign against Iran is working, he moved to military base due to Iranian threats
Nov 13, 2026, 9:23 AM ESTUS denies Iran's claim that it destroyed US radar in Bahrain
Nov 12, 2026, 11:34 AM ESTWhite House won't say if talks with Iran have stopped
Iranian foreign minister calls US attacks violation of international law

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi criticized the U.S. attack on Iran saying if states were free to attack one another "based on their own assessments of possible future threats, what would be left of the international legal order?" in an opinion piece released in Japanese Outlet Kyodo News.
"Use of force is governed by law, and no state, however powerful, is entitled to place its own judgment above binding rules of international law," Araghchi wrote.

"The military attacks launched by the United States and the Zionist regime against Iran constitute a clear violation of the prohibition on the use of force and an infringement of Iran's sovereignty. Their legality must be assessed against the U.N. Charter and established principles of international law, not against political arguments or justifications advanced after military operations have begun," Araghchi wrote.
Bessent says economic campaign against Iran is working, he moved to military base due to Iranian threats
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent sharply attacked Iranian leadership on Friday in response to his recent move to a military base because of Iranian threats.
"'F' the Iranian leadership," Bessent said on CNBC this morning, when asked about the recent news and his current safety.
"I'm not going to be cowered that they have initiated death threats against me. The other members of the cabinet were not going to be cowered," he said.
Bessent claimed that these threats against him mean the economic campaign Treasury launched in August against countries and entities that do business with Iran is "working."
"The IRGC, they're like a dangerous, cornered animal. So I follow the Secret Service instructions and have moved from my home to a military base," Bessent said.
Bessent touted U.S. strength during the war through economic restrictions on Iran.

"We are squeezing the regime. I think that they are panicked. In what they're seeing for the first time since they began producing oil, they have no oil on the water. They have no revenues, and we have cut them off," Bessent said.
Asked about next steps in settling the war and if there is concern that Iran will ramp up aggression because they’re "cornered," Bessent claimed Iranians will "eventually want to make a deal."
-ABC News' Isabella Murray
US denies Iran's claim that it destroyed US radar in Bahrain
The U.S. denied Iran's claim that it destroyed an American early warning radar in Bahrain.
"The IRGC launched two one-way attack drones toward Bahrain and both were shot down by U.S. forces. There were no injuries or damage," U.S. Central Command said Friday.

The IRGC claimed its the attack was carried out in response to a U.S. strike on a telecommunications tower in the southern Iranian port of Sirik, warning the U.S. to cease its hostilities, according to Iran's state-owned Press TV.
The IRGC also claimed a tanker caught fire after striking a naval mine while trying to sail through the Strait of Hormuz, Press TV reported.
White House won't say if talks with Iran have stopped

A White House official would not say whether U.S. talks with Iran have ended, after President Donald Trump posted on social media Thursday morning that "We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed."

When asked whether the president meant there are no more negotiations happening with the Iranians, the official provided a statement highlighting what Trump said this morning -- the U.S. naval blockade and economic pressure against Iran -- adding, "President Trump holds all the cards, will do what is best for the United States, and will make sure that Iran never has a nuclear weapon."

"The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. The President has been clear that the greatest naval blockade in history, Operation Economic Outcast, and the new Operation Iron Gate will continue with full effect. President Trump holds all the cards, will do what is best for the United States, and will make sure that Iran never has a nuclear weapon," a White House official said in a statement.
The president's post came after he said the war with Iran would end "soon" on Wednesday during his Veteran's Day remarks at Arlington National Cemetery.

title: Republicans push for Jensen Huang's testimony following Nvidia CEO's resignation
summary: "I don't think he's got anything to hide now. Let it fly," Rep. Burchett said.
story: "I don't think he's got anything to hide now. Let it fly," Rep. Burchett said.
Republican lawmakers are continuing to call for testimony from Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned Thursday morning following reports that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

GOP Rep. Tim Burchett said it was a "good move" for Huang to resign, adding that the former Nvidia executive should testify as lawmakers have raised concerns about the national security implications of Huang's reported relationship given that he ran the world's largest computer chip manufacturer.
"I don't think he's got anything to hide now. Let it fly," Burchett said to reporters at the Capitol Thursday morning.
Rep. John Moolenaar, the chairman of the China Select Committee, told ABC News that lawmakers have growing concerns as details of Huang's affair continue to come to light.

"The concerns are our national security, whether he was being influenced by a Chinese spy, and the Chinese intelligence was gathering information about our crown jewels of American technology, and also this issue of chip diversion," said Moolenaar, who added that he would support a congressional subpoena to compel Huang's testimony.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Rep. Brian Mast and Moolenaar both say that they're still in active conversations with Huang to schedule testimony after the former Nvidia CEO had previously signaled a willingness to testify.

"We are in discussions with him right now on a date to come and meet with us. If for some reason that were not to happen, all three committees, all three chairs have said we will use our subpoena power," Moolenaar said.
Republican Rep. Jay Obernolte said he believes that Huang's affair is a distraction.

"I hope we can keep the conversation centered around the pros and cons of our export policy regarding our most advanced chips, and you know, not talk about, you know, personal peccadillos,” Obernolte said.

Before Huang's resignation, lawmakers had called for him to testify. Last week, GOP Reps. Mast as well as Rick Crawford, the chair of the House Intelligence Committee, and Moolenaar sent Huang a letter requesting he appear for a "joint, closed-door briefing." Moolenaar said Huang responded to that letter and they are discussing a "date that works."

Congressional Republicans on the Select Committee on China also sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear for a closed-door briefing Nov. 18 concerning his relationship with Alice Huang. Jensen Huang admitted to an affair, but he didn't say with whom.
Jensen Huang has not responded to ABC News' previous requests for comment about testifying on Capitol Hill. ABC News is working to contact Huang on Thursday -- after he left Nvidia.

On the Democratic side, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer posted on social media on Thursday morning that despite Huang's resignation, Congress needs more answers from Huang, Nvidia and the administration.
"Despite Jensen Huang’s resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk," Schumer wrote.

Democratic Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons are asking the White House and the Departments of Commerce and State to preserve all documents related to the export of NVIDIA's advanced AI chips to China following reports that some senior officials were aware that Huang may have been the target of a Chinese spying operation. The two senators wrote a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller on Wednesday.
Coons and Warren are also requesting preservation of all materials related to the reported intelligence operation and for a briefing to members of Congress.

Some Republicans have brushed aside concerns, however, when asked whether Huang's access to President Donald Trump at state dinners and flying on Air Force One was problematic given his affair with an alleged Chinese spy was purportedly known to the intelligence community.
"I'm not concerned about -- about Jensen's access to the president. I'm sure the president can take care of that," Obernolte said.
Republicans have said they are hoping to bring in Huang before handing over majority control to Democrats in January.

"You know, it's obviously -- with him resigning -- that does change the dynamic," Moolenaar said. "He has stated he's a patriot. He has questioned people who viewed export controls as a sound policy. I would hope he would want to come in and have that discussion with us."
ABC News' Allison Pecorin contributed to this report.

title: Republicans dazed by midterm election defeats grapple with what went wrong
summary: Republicans are grappling with unexpected losses after the midterm elections
story: Republicans are grappling with unexpected losses after the midterm elections

WASHINGTON -- Rep. Richard Hudson wanted a triumphant return to Capitol Hill this week after steering Republicans to another majority. Instead, the North Carolina Republican is facing the reality that he and dozens of colleagues will soon clear out their offices.

“It was really people coming out to send a message,” Hudson, the chair of the House GOP's campaign arm, said in a brief interview. “They, rightly so, felt gas was too high, things were too expensive.”
“The mistake Republicans made,” he said, “is we didn't convey to them that we cared about that and cared about them.”

Back in Washington this week for the first time since the GOP’s sweeping midterm losses, Republicans were in something of a daze. Even as they acknowledged the depth of their defeat, there was little appetite for a wholesale break from President Donald Trump.

Instead, they met behind closed doors to talk about what went wrong. And they scrutinized the calendar to figure out how to push through as much of their agenda as possible before Democrats assume control of the House and the Senate in January.
There was widespread frustration that Republicans who were awarded full control of the White House and Congress just two years earlier had lost touch with voters.
