“You cut rural healthcare spending, when you abandon pro-lifers, when you abandon the poor, when you abandon the needy, when you abandon working people, you’re gonna get your butt kicked,” said Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., who unsuccessfully sought to delay his party’s leadership elections in the Senate. “And you’re gonna deserve it.”
“We collectively failed,” said Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., who is trailing her Democratic challenger in a district that Republicans carried by more than 18 percentage points in 2024.
“It’s very clear,” she said. “The American people let us know we have failed in this governing experience for this Congress.”

The anger is sharp in part because of the rosy predictions from top Republicans ahead of the election. Rep. Virginia Foxx, R-N.C., who is also trailing a Democratic rival, said people kept telling her she couldn't lose. But she knew otherwise.
“I couldn’t get anybody to listen to me,” she said. “People just didn't think it could happen, but we knew it could.”

House Speaker Mike Johnson spent the final stretch of the campaign rejecting the historic headwinds that often befall a president's party during a midterm. He toured the country, insisting the polls were wrong and Republicans would retain their majority even as some incumbents were skeptical.

Back on Capitol Hill this week, Johnson said voters made the “wrong choice” as Democrats flipped more than 40 Republican-held seats. That puts the Democrats on track to hold the most robust majority since the early years of Barack Obama's presidency.

Republicans, meanwhile, are weighing how to proceed, balancing calls for moderation against an impulse for hard-line positions that might reenergize the party's base. Each chamber took different tracks, previewing divisions that may lie ahead.

In the House, the Republicans who will remain in Washington next year largely represent staunchly conservative districts where Trump remains popular. Their decision to elect Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan as their next leader reflected a fighting stance.

Jordan is a co-founder of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, currently chairs the Judiciary Committee and has previously chaired the Oversight Committee. From those positions, he's waged heated fights against Democrats and become a top Trump ally.
“The way that Jim fights says a lot about where this conference is,” said Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla.
In the Senate, the desire for combat was less intense.

The question for Republicans there was less about whether they would stick with John Thune of South Dakota as their leader than when they would make that decision. Hawley and a small group of conservatives spent hours huddled with Republicans in the Old Senate Chamber arguing for a delay in leadership elections to allow the party to consider alternative candidates.

But the problem was that no one would come forward to offer themselves as an alternative to Thune, who has faced criticism from Trump at times for his refusal to abandon Senate rules to make it easier to pass conservative legislation.
“It's a bad job,” Hawley said.
After hours of deliberation, Republicans ultimately backed Thune without so much as a voice vote.
“We're going to let our leader be the leader,” said Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, who was also elected to lead the party's effort to regain seats in the 2028 election.

Perhaps the biggest question for Republicans going forward is how to manage their relationship with Trump, whose policies on trade and the war in Iran helped contribute to their losses. He's in the last two years of his second term, and the election defeats have raised stark questions about the durability of his Make America Great Again movement.

But there was no rush to distance themselves from the president as House Republicans, even those who have been critical of his administration, overwhelmingly blocked an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Only Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie, who led the push alongside Democrats, broke ranks.
“What I found out tonight is they still haven’t broken from the spell of Donald Trump,” Massie said after the vote. “He still controls this conference.”

When asked whether the election was a referendum on Trump, Thune said the results stemmed from “a combination of things,” refusing to directly blame the president for contributing to the party's challenges.
But there were signs that Trump's influence had limits.

Few echoed his argument in a social media post this week that there were problems with the election. In conceding a closely fought Senate contest in Mississippi, Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith said she would “respect the decision” of voters.

Several Republicans, including Sens. Joni Ernst of Iowa, Tim Scott of South Carolina and John Cornyn of Texas and Rep. Mike Lawler of New York, posted pictures of Democrats who will either succeed them or soon represent their states, harkening to an earlier era of postelection unity.

Rep. James Comer of Kentucky pushed back against White House warnings to congressional Democrats that planned probes of the Trump administration could amount to “blatant criminality.” Comer, who oversaw extensive investigations of Democratic President Joe Biden and his family as chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said lawmakers have a role in holding any White House accountable.

“Regardless of who is in the White House, there’s always going to be a strong desire for the Oversight Committee to be a check and balance on the executive branch, regardless of the political scenario,” Comer said.
Associated Press writer Kevin Freking contributed.

title: Maryland Sen. Van Hollen says he will challenge Sen. Schumer for Democratic leader
summary: Maryland Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen says he will challenge New York Sen. Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader in the new Congress.
story: Van Hollen said the party needs "new leadership."
Maryland Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen says he will challenge New York Sen. Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader in the new Congress.
In a social media post, Van Hollen said the party needs "new leadership" following the midterm elections in which Democrats won enough seats to take control of the chamber.
"This isn't about any one person -- it's about answering that call," Van Hollen said in the post.

In an appearance on MSNOW on Thursday announcing his bid, Van Hollen, a two-term senator, said: "This is a generational opportunity for the Senate to respond to the call of the American people for change ... They've given us a chance. We have to earn their trust, and my view is that you can't earn that trust with old leadership. You need to move on to new leadership."

Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since 2017, quickly responded to the news of the challenge, saying he welcomes "discussion about the future of our caucus" while also confidently adding "I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader."

"I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead. I'm proud of what we've accomplished together--55 seats and counting is an amazing result--and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader. I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people," he posted on X.
The Senate Democratic leadership elections are expected to be held in December. A leader is selected based on a majority vote of the caucus.
Van Hollen acknowledged he was the underdog in the leadership elections but remained optimistic that he could garner support from his Senate colleagues.
"Now people will have to make a decision, one way or the other, and they have to decide whether they want to vote for change or whether they want to vote for the status quo."
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

title: US soldier accused of spying for Russia identified: Source
summary: US officer who was arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia is 41-year-old Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, according to a source familiar with the investigation.
story: Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner was entrusted with sensitive information, a source said.

The U.S. soldier who officials say was entrusted with sensitive information and was arrested in the United Kingdom on suspicion of spying for Russia is 41-year-old Lt. Col. Brandon Tyner, according to a source familiar with the investigation.

Tyner, 41, was taken into custody Tuesday near Gloucester, England, as part of a British counterterrorism investigation, according to U.S. and British officials. U.S. Army officials said the officer had been entrusted with sensitive information.
ABC News has not been able to reach Tyner. It is unclear if he has retained a lawyer.

Tyner was assigned to Imjin Barracks in the United Kingdom, a military garrison that is home to the headquarters of NATO's Allied Rapid Response Corps, which manages plans for ground troops in case of a crisis.
Tyner's identity was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

Tyner, an Afghanistan war veteran, has held numerous high-profile personnel assignments throughout his more than two-decade Army career, according to a LinkedIn account matching his name. British law enforcement officials said the investigation involves suspected violations of the National Security Act of 2023, a law aimed at combating espionage and foreign interference.

It remains unclear exactly what Tyner is accused of doing. He is expected to be formally charged by British authorities in the coming days and subsequently face separate charges from the U.S. Army, according to a source familiar with the matter.

U.S. troops convicted of crimes in allied countries can serve prison sentences abroad before facing separate prosecution in the American military justice system, according to Army court records, which, could mean a second trial and, if convicted, an additional sentence in a U.S. military prison.

U.S. troops convicted of espionage-related crimes have often been junior or mid-level service members, according to Army data, with financial gain a common motive. Cases involving senior officers are less common, and those ranks typically have greater access to sensitive military information that could be particularly valuable to foreign adversaries, though it's unclear what specific information Tyner had access to.

Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, who leads U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, said in a statement following the arrest that the case is, "a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent."

title: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has finalized his divorce
summary: An attorney for Republican Ken Paxton says Texas' outgoing attorney general has finalized his divorce
story: An attorney for Republican Ken Paxton says Texas' outgoing attorney general has finalized his divorce
AUSTIN, Texas -- AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has finalized his divorce from his wife, Angela, one of his lawyers said Thursday.

It comes nearly a week after Paxton, a Republican, lost his U.S. Senate race by double digits to Democrat James Talarico in one of the most expensive contests of the midterm elections that saw a wave of victories for Democrats across the country.

Angela Paxton, a state senator, cited allegations of adultery when she sought to end their 38-year-marriage. She filed the divorce after her husband had launched his run for Senate, posting on social media that she was doing so on “biblical grounds.”
Jared Julian, a lawyer for Ken Paxton, said the terms would remain private.
“From my observation, however, they share a mutual respect for one another,” Julian said. He added that both appeared to be looking forward “to the next chapters of their lives.”
An attorney for Angela Paxton did not immediately respond to phone and email messages Thursday. The finalized divorce was first reported by The New York Times.
After Paxton entered the race, some Republicans considered Paxton a potential drain on GOP resources because of legal, ethical and personal questions he has faced for years.

Angela Paxton had stuck by her husband through a decade of legal troubles that included state and federal corruption investigations and a 2023 state impeachment trial that publicly exposed an extramarital affair.

The Senate race that seemed like a longshot for Democrats when the year began became partly a referendum on Paxton’s history. Despite beating the long-seated incumbent, Sen. John Cornyn, in a primary and gaining President Donald Trump's endorsement, Paxton struggled to find traction in the general election against Talarico.
In October, less than a month before the election, Angela Paxton urged voters to back the Republican ticket but did not mention her estranged husband by name.
“It’s not as much about the individual players on the team. It’s about getting the whole team across the finish line,” she said in a campaign advertisement.
Democrat Nathan Johnson was elected attorney general and will take office in January.

title: Colom’s historic Senate win could reshape Mississippi’s political future: Analysis
summary: The question is whether his victory can establish a lasting realignment.
story: The question is whether his victory can establish a lasting realignment.
Scott Colom’s victory is more than a Democrat winning in a ruby-red state. It is a breakthrough in who can represent Mississippi and could reshape expectations about who can win there next.

Mississippi sent the nation’s first two Black U.S. senators -- Hiram Rhodes Revels and Blanche Kelso Bruce -- to Washington during Reconstruction. Both were elected by the state legislature. After Bruce left office in 1881, Mississippi went nearly a century and a half without another Black senator.

That gap cannot be separated from the violent dismantling of Reconstruction, the rise of Jim Crow and generations of deliberate suppression of Black voters. Mississippi’s 1890 constitution turned racial exclusion into governing policy through poll taxes and literacy requirements.
Now, Mississippi voters have directly elected a Black person to the U.S. Senate for the first time.
“I had the courage to believe in Mississippi,” Colom told supporters at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday night.

His slim victory over incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith challenges the assumption that Mississippi’s statewide political outcomes are predetermined. Future candidates, party officials, donors and organizers will have to consider whether an electorate that has long been treated as predictable deserves another look.

For Black Mississippians, whose right to vote was obstructed for generations, this victory puts a Black man in a position to help shape the state’s future. Colom will exercise the same authority as every other senator, from voting on legislation to weighing judicial nominations.

But one victory does not establish a lasting realignment. The ultimate test is whether the coalition that elected Colom can outlast him and this political moment. The question becomes whether that coalition will support other candidates, sustain voter participation and make future elections competitive.

Colom campaigned on raising wages, protecting rural hospitals and addressing the cost of living. Those promises now become the standards against which voters will judge him. Delivering will require legislative allies and translating national debates into benefits for Mississippi communities, including those that did not support him.
“My commitment is to be someone that continues to stay in prayer, continues to have faith, and continues to work to make every Mississippian’s life better,” Colom told the audience at Tougaloo.

That promise connects the historic achievement to the work ahead. His victory gives future candidates evidence that a path to statewide office exists. His performance will help determine whether voters see that path as worth taking again.
A state that once systematically denied Black citizens political power has chosen a Black man to represent everyone. The next test is what that representation delivers for Mississippians.

title: Trump administration blames ‘overloaded’ systems for ground stop after FAA lets flights resume
summary: The Federal Aviation Administration says airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by communications problems
story: The Federal Aviation Administration says airplane departures can resume after the agency lifted a nationwide ground stop caused by communications problems

WASHINGTON -- Trump administration officials said Friday that new technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated parts of it and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years.
It was lifted in the evening after a five-hour stretch when most flights were not allowed to take off from airports in the U.S.

Thousands of flights and potentially over a million travelers were affected. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that no one was in any danger as more than 3,000 flights were safely landed. But Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said he could not guarantee it wouldn’t happen again.
Mullin said the FAA was installing “new equipment, new technology” and “it was overwhelming the older system.” There appeared to be no indication of a cyberattack, he said.

A limited number of domestic flights began departing late Friday after the ground stop was lifted, but it will likely take days for airlines to fully recover because so many planes and crews were out of position. Officials said they think the system will be back to normal in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.

The nationwide ground stop was the first since January 2023, when another key FAA computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the aftermath of the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

Asked whether he could rule out a cyberattack or rogue artificial intelligence incident, Mullin said there are no “footprints” showing an attack and that the problem appears to be “mechanically driven.” He said officials were still looking for the cause.

At least 827 flights had been diverted. By 7:05 p.m. EST, 670 flights were sent back to the airport from where they originally took off, while 157 were redirected to a different airport, according to Cirium, an aviation analytics company.

Duffy was defensive, blaming Congress for failing to approve more funding for new technology, while downplaying the fact that trying to implement new fixes overtaxed the system. He implored lawmakers to act.
“By doing nothing, you inject way more risk into the system,” he said.

Duffy said he expected flights around the country to be “back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel” next weekend ahead of Thanksgiving, but he also suggested more disruptions might occur.
“We didn’t think we would have this kind of outage. We did,” he said, while also noting, “We were able to review what went wrong, and then reboot the system and go. But, you will have more of these.”
Duffy said the problems were not linked to the FAA’s new AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky because that isn’t connected to what failed on Friday.
“This is all the old legacy equipment. All of the new equipment that’s been deployed did not go down,” Duffy said.

The FAA has already replaced thousands of old copper wires with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.
Many flights ended up being diverted to places including Washington Dulles International Airport, Los Angeles International Airport and Nashville International Airport.
Some 11,000 flights carrying more than 1.5 million passengers had been scheduled to take off from airports in the U.S. after 4 p.m. EST.
At the time of the ground stoppage, more than 3,500 airplanes were in the sky, Duffy said.

At Chicago O’Hare Airport on Friday, travelers passing through security learned about the ground stop when they looked up at screens that showed flight delays across the board. Some called friends or family members, debating whether to stay the night in Chicago or find another way to their destinations.
Amber McQuilkin, 27, sat on a bench, disappointed that she might miss a trip with friends to New York for the League of Legends world finals.

“There’s not really any information being passed to me,” said the Seattle software engineer. “I contemplated just abandoning the flight and driving, but then the more I thought about it, the more I’m like, that would be miserable.”

Ruth Coles was still stuck on her plane five hours after it landed at the Los Angeles International Airport from Newark even after the ground stop was lifted. She said they were told they were waiting for a gate to open up.
“The pilot keeps saying they are telling him we are next in line,” Coles said, but that was several hours ago.

NBA, NHL and college teams were left stranded as they tried to reach their destinations. Meanwhile, NFL teams were left to wonder whether the issue would be resolved in time to travel to their games this weekend.
Duffy said NCAA teams will be prioritized ahead of football games on Saturday.
“I would encourage those football teams to reach out to the FAA, to schedule their flight times and make sure they can move” to make their kickoff, he said.
Cargo flights were also delayed by the ground stop.
FedEx, the world’s largest cargo airline, said it was prepared to activate contingency plans to keep any possible disruptions at a minimum.

U.S. airlines move about 61,000 tons (55,340 metric tonnes) of goods — from letters to packages — to and from more than 220 countries daily, according to the industry trade group Airlines for America.

The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, although that disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fiber optic line. Aging equipment was also blamed for the brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference this time is that it happened on a nationwide scale that left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.

“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them,” said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.

Friday’s ground stop was also different than the one after 9/11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.

Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska. AP writers Mead Gruver in Fort Collins, Colorado; Ali Swenson in Chicago; Alex Veiga and Jaimie Ding in Los Angeles; Seung Min Kim and Aamer Madhani in Washington; Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City; and Hallie Golden in Seattle contributed to this report.
This story has been corrected to show the Sept. 11 attacks were in 2001.

title: Memorial opens honoring victims of the 2015 Charleston church massacre
summary: Eleven years after a white gunman killed nine Black parishioners inside the South’s oldest African Methodist Episcopal Church, a long planned memorial is opening to honor their lives
story: Eleven years after a white gunman killed nine Black parishioners inside the South’s oldest African Methodist Episcopal Church, a long planned memorial is opening to honor their lives

It took Alana Grant years to find the strength to set foot in the basement of Mother Emanuel AME Church in Charleston, where her grandfather, the Rev. Daniel Lee Simmons, attended his final Bible study.

Her fears have been replaced by gratitude and hope now that there is a completed memorial in a courtyard by the front door for the “Emanuel Nine,” the Black churchgoers killed by an avowed white supremacist in 2015.
The memorial provides a public space where “people can go and remember really what happened here,” Alana Grant said as she and her husband, state Rep. Hamilton Grant, got their first look.
On Saturday, the long-planned memorial at the South's oldest African Methodist Episcopal Church opens to the public.

Emphasizing remembrance and reflection, the marble memorial is anchored by a Fountain of Grace, symbolizing God's eternal love and mercy. Water flows from a shallow basin etched with the names of the six women and three men slain. Two Fellowship Benches with curved backs, sheltering anyone seated, flank the fountain. There is also a Cross of Hope, signifying redemption in the wake of suffering. A garden honoring the five survivors will come next.
The Rev. Eric Manning, co-chair of the Mother Emanuel Memorial Foundation board, hopes it will mean something to everyone.
“I was actually standing out there the other day,” said Manning, who took over after pastor and state Sen. Clementa Pinckney was among those killed. “Just for a moment, a peace came over me.”

Grant sees the memorial as a place to inspire conversations with her three small children about their great-grandfather. Because the facts of the shooting have been so public, she doesn't want them to hear more from someone else.
“I spent a lot of time thinking about it and praying about it,” she said. “I do want them to go so that they can kind of see what even brought me to South Carolina.”

Former North Carolina state senator and Charlotte City Councilman Malcolm Graham, whose sister Cynthia Graham Hurd died huddled under a desk in the fellowship hall, attended the 2023 groundbreaking. He has anticipated visiting the memorial to reflect on “all the good times Cindy and I had as kids growing up, and being at the church and going to Sunday school.”
A library, scholarship and other awards now carry the name of the accomplished librarian. Now she'll live on in the memorial, too.
“She said before she died that I was the most famous person in the family,” Graham said. “She is the most famous person in our family and I still look up to her.”
As for the survivors to be honored with a garden, Grant says their living with memories of the shooting is “nothing short of heroism.”
“There are not a lot of spaces where you get to see the survivors. We as Black people have survived so much,” Grant said.

When a committee sought an architect in 2017, they heard from designers all over the world, said John Darby, another memorial foundation co-chair who runs a Charleston real estate development firm. The final candidates were not asked to submit design proposals, but instead give written responses to deep questions on topics like forgiveness.

That unconventional request was very prescient, said Michael Arad, an architect on the 9/11 Memorial whose design was ultimately chosen. He wrote about his admiration for the victims' families who offered forgiveness to the shooter.

A white, Jewish New Yorker who had never visited South Carolina, Arad did a deep-dive into the community for more than a year after he was selected. Having lengthy conversations with members of the congregation and researching the church's 200-year history was essential, he said, and while the 9/11 memorial was a bigger endeavor, this design wasn't any less complex.

“My job as a designer was to allow people who visit the site to see and hear what was here all along,” he said. “We understand who we are as Americans through stories like this, through our response.”
Arad said he embraces emotionally weighted projects as “a tremendous privilege” and he “could not imagine turning down a project like this.”
The foundation has raised around $25 million over the last decade for the memorial, garden and other costs, much of it from foundations, endowments and corporations, Darby said.
“It was one of those things that people wanted to be a part of,” Darby said. “We don't want it to be an expense to the church.”

Established in 1818, Mother Emanuel was built by free and enslaved people. In the 20th century, the church became a place of resistance where the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. and other civil rights figures spoke.

The Emanuel Nine's families applauded in 2015 when Gov. Nikki Haley removed the Confederate battle flag from state buildings. But with Republicans stirring an angry backlash against diversity and equity efforts, Graham said “racism, hatred and discrimination continue to be this country's Achilles' heel.”

Alana Grant has tried over the years to gather support for a hate crimes statute, and her husband is among the lawmakers who pushed legislation named for Pinckney that would add enhanced penalties for hate crimes to South Carolina's criminal code. It failed to pass, even though a senator was among the Emanuel Nine.

She sees this memorial as an opportunity to raise “generational awareness” so younger people will campaign against hate. Tourists still come to the church daily out of curiosity or sympathy, and could leave the memorial feeling inspired.
“We want more than your thoughts and prayers. We want your advocacy,” she said.

title: Thousands of flights canceled as airlines work to dig out from nationwide ground stop
summary: Airlines across the U.S. are working to dig out from the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years
story: Airlines across the U.S. are working to dig out from the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years

WASHINGTON -- More than 2,000 flights were canceled Saturday as airlines across the U.S. worked to dig out from the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years, which stranded passengers and forced professional and college sports teams to scramble for alternate transportation.

Trump administration officials said new technology being added to the nation’s air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps, leading to the flight shutdown of more than four hours.

A limited number of domestic flights departed after the stop was lifted around 8:15 p.m. ET. But the effects could be felt for days, with officials saying the system is likely to be operating normally in time to handle the Thanksgiving travel rush.
The nationwide stop was the first since January 2023, when another key FAA computer system that sends notices to pilots malfunctioned, and the second since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

Emily Brown and her 14-year-old daughter waited more than four hours Friday at the Dallas airport for their flight to Columbus, Ohio, before giving up. They were traveling to surprise her daughter’s best friend. Instead, she had to settle for phoning the friend through tears in the airport, Brown said.
“She saved up her money to buy her own ticket, and she’s planned this whole weekend,” Brown said. “Now we’re not sure when we’re gonna be able to go.”

Ruth Coles was stuck on her plane for more than five hours after landing at Los Angeles International Airport from Newark, New Jersey. She said the passengers were told they were waiting for a gate to open.
“The pilot keeps saying they are telling him we are next in line,” Coles said.
At airports across the U.S., passengers stared at screens showing delays or rushed to find buses or trains to their destinations. Some passed the time by breaking out in song.
Sports teams scheduled to play this weekend adjusted game start times, searched for hotel rooms, rescheduled flights and chartered buses.

Auburn University's football team opted to take a bus to Mississippi State and the Saturday start time was pushed from noon ET to 4:15 p.m. Other universities affected by the stoppage included Baylor, Washington, Kansas State, Minnesota and No. 19 Ole Miss, which did not plan to fly until Saturday morning for its game against Oklahoma.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy encouraged NCAA football teams to reach out to the FAA so the agency can prioritize flights for Saturday games.
More than 2,500 flights were canceled in the U.S. Saturday and hundreds more were delayed, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions.

Corbyn Wascher's flight was on the tarmac at the Charlotte Douglas International Airport for four hours Friday on his way home to Moline, Illinois, from a conference in Miami. Everyone was cordial on the American Airlines plane as they talked and stretched their legs and the flight attendants handed out water, pretzels and biscotti snacks, he said.

“The stewardesses were amazing. You could tell that they were pretty stressed out,” said the 37-year-old high school teacher, who took a $100 uber to a hotel 25 minutes from the airport after he was unable to find new flights. He was scheduled for a Saturday afternoon flight to Chicago O’Hare International Airport.
Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House that no one was in any danger as more than 3,000 flights were safely landed Friday.

Duffy blamed Congress for failing to approve more funding for new technology, while downplaying the fact that trying to implement new fixes overtaxed the system. He suggested more disruptions might occur.
“We didn’t think we would have this kind of outage. We did,” he said. “We were able to review what went wrong, and then reboot the system and go. But, you will have more of these.”
Duffy said the problems were not linked to the FAA’s new AI-powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky because that isn’t connected to Friday's failure.
“This is all the old legacy equipment. All of the new equipment that’s been deployed did not go down,” Duffy said.

The FAA has already replaced thousands of old copper wires with fiber optic lines and upgraded hundreds of radio systems as part of the overhaul that began last year after Congress approved $12.5 billion of funding. Duffy and the White House are pushing for $30 billion more to complete the work.

The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, although that disruption was linked to a construction crew cutting a fiber optic line. Aging equipment was also blamed for the brief radar outages last year that disrupted Newark airport.
Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said the difference this time is it happened on a nationwide scale that left controllers unable to reliably talk to pilots.

“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground and not put them in the air, where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them,” said Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot.

Friday’s ground stop also was different from the one after 9/11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.

Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska, and Golden from Seattle. Associated Press journalists Mead Gruver in Fort Collins, Colorado; Jessica Hill in Las Vegas; Ali Swenson in Chicago; Alex Veiga and Jaimie Ding in Los Angeles; Seung Min Kim and Aamer Madhani in Washington; and Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City contributed to this report.

title: Canada’s Carney reports progress in trade talks with Trump as he expands ties with Asia
summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada and the U.S. are making progress on a trade deal after talks collapsed in August
story: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada and the U.S. are making progress on a trade deal after talks collapsed in August

TORONTO -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Saturday that he had a lengthy conversation with U.S. President Donald Trump and senior administration officials before leaving for Europe and Asia and that the two countries are making progress toward a trade deal after negotiations collapsed in August.

The comments came as Carney announced that Canada had substantially concluded free-trade negotiations with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, a bloc of nearly 700 million people, and completed separate negotiations with the Philippines. Both agreements are part of Canada’s efforts to reduce its dependence on the United States during Trump’s trade war.
Carney was in the Philippine capital ahead of a key three-day summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and their Asian and Western counterparts that starts Sunday.

“I had quite a long, substantive conversation with President Trump just before leaving for this trip,” Carney told reporters in Manila. “We are making progress. There is the possibility of a deal, a bilateral deal. But we’re not yet there.”
Carney said U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and Trump’s new White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, also participated in the call.
Carney said Canada would not accept a deal that undermines its auto industry, which has been battered by Trump’s tariffs.

Canada suspended trade negotiations in August after last-minute U.S. demands that Ottawa considered unacceptable. Washington subsequently imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion in Canadian goods, prompting retaliatory Canadian tariffs in September. The countries have since resumed discussions.
Canada and the United States have one of the world’s largest trading relationships. A trade deal could reduce some tariffs on key sectors, including steel and aluminum.

Trump said before the midterms that the countries were “very close” to an agreement, while Carney said Washington had backed away from demands involving Canada’s culture, French-language protections and ability to negotiate other trade agreements.
U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods became an issue in the midterms, with Democrats blaming them for higher prices and pledging to challenge them.
The Democratic victories have left Canada with a dilemma: Accept a deal that reduces Trump’s tariffs but leaves some in place, or hold out for free trade as Congress prepares to challenge them.

The Canadian government estimates the ASEAN agreement could add nearly 2 billion Canadian dollars (US$1.4 billion) to Canada’s economy and create almost 14,000 jobs, particularly in agriculture and manufacturing. Officials hope to sign it next year.

The Philippines agreement, expected to be signed next year, covers more than 90% of tariff lines, Carney said. The Canadian government said the agreement could help triple Canadian exports to the Philippines by 2035.

Carney attended the European Political Community summit in Ireland before traveling to Manila for the ASEAN summit. He will also attend the Francophonie summit in Cambodia and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, where he is scheduled to meet President Xi Jinping.
Carney has made doubling Canadian exports to countries other than the United States by 2035 a central goal.

title: With shifting Iran rhetoric following US elections, Trump leaves Mideast in limbo about path ahead
summary: President Donald Trump has been all over the map as he's articulated his thinking about the Iran war since last week's midterm elections
story: President Donald Trump has been all over the map as he's articulated his thinking about the Iran war since last week's midterm elections
WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump has had a lot to say about his thinking on the way ahead in the Iran war since Republicans were trounced in last week's midterm elections.

In exchanges with reporters, broadcast interviews and social media posts since Election Day, he's somehow managed to back away from carrying out additional strikes while also backing away from the prospect of additional talks with the Islamic Republic's negotiators on ending the 8-month-old conflict.

The president acknowledged on the day after the midterms that the war and the global economic tumult it's caused were partly to blame for Republicans' electoral losses, while maintaining it was the right thing to do.

Then, at the start of this week, he huddled with Qatar's prime minister at the White House and afterward told reporters that he believed it was highly unlikely he'd need to order new major strikes on Iran, declaring that the war “militarily is effectively over.”

But by Thursday, he was again raising questions about whether he needed to rush to find an endgame. He declared that the U.S. no longer needs a deal with Tehran and brusquely directed Vice President JD Vance — who served as his chief negotiator in earlier peace talks with Iran — to shift his attention to the administration's domestic anti-fraud campaign.
All the while, Trump warned Iran that the U.S. military is “locked and loaded” and keeping an eye on Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to Iran’s nuclear program, for signs of activity.
“If something does not work out, I would not hesitate" to act, Trump told conservative broadcaster Hugh Hewitt on Thursday.

Trump's tonal shifts have only added to the uncertainty about what comes next in a war in which America's allies were not consulted before it was started but nonetheless struggle to deal with its economic ramifications.

“President Trump is now acting like an arsonist who has set ablaze our foreign policy,” Democratic Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey said in an interview Friday on the sidelines of the Democrats’ postelection gathering in Denver. “And now he just wants to walk away.”

The president's ambiguous positioning on the war is expected to loom large during a visit next week to the Philippines and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings in the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen.

While in Shenzhen, Trump will hold an unprecedented three-way summit with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin. Trump is expected to discuss Iran and the three powers' nuclear stockpiles with Xi and Putin.

The White House declined to comment directly to queries on Trump's postelection rhetoric on Iran. But Secretary of State Marco Rubio underscored that Trump's approach is leading to the Iranian economy collapsing.

“The economic pain that we are inflicting on that regime is so great that there’s no need for military action because we’ve weakened them so much,” Rubio said in a Friday evening speech to the Federalist Society.

Chief mediator Qatar continues to try to negotiate an interim agreement that would restore traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital passageway for the flow of oil and natural gas from the Persian Gulf to global markets, while leaving open options for further discussions between the U.S. and Iran.
But those efforts are now clouded by uncertainty following Trump’s shifting — and sometimes contradictory — comments, according to two Middle East diplomats familiar with the process.

The diplomats, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter, said the situation had appeared to be on the right track earlier this week after Qatar’s prime minister met with Trump.

But Trump's social media post Thursday declaring that the U.S. doesn't need a deal with Iran and directing Vance “to focus his complete and total attention” on his anti-fraud campaign has created a sense of limbo.
One of the diplomats said the post raised questions about why Trump appeared to be sidelining Vance, who was skeptical about launching the war but ultimately supported Trump.

Trump's post came as Vance had been weighing a possible reengagement with senior Iranian negotiators, according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The president posted his message calling on Vance to steer away from Iran negotiations the morning after The Wall Street Journal reported Vance was thinking about resuming talks. Trump — who had been aware of Vance's deliberations — believed the Iranians weren't acting in good faith, the person added.
Trump is also increasingly confident that he can credibly declare that he's achieved his military objectives in the war.
But traversing the Strait of Hormuz remains treacherous. The United Nations reports October had the highest number of incidents against commercial ships in the contested waters since February.

Still, Trump believes with oil shipments through the strait reaching near-prewar levels, he could potentially leave it to Gulf countries to negotiate a deal with the Iranians on governing the critical waterway, the person said.
The other regional diplomat described the push for peace as falling into a holding pattern as people await clarification from the White House on Trump’s intentions.

That diplomat added it was not entirely clear to mediators or the Iranians if Trump’s comments meant he was abandoning a negotiated agreement or was just posturing after the congressional midterm elections that cost his Republican Party control of Congress.
Iran remains unwilling to engage in negotiations over its nuclear program until the U.S. agrees to several core conditions that Iran has been demanding be part of any ceasefire agreement.
Differences with Iran over its nuclear activities remain the thorniest issue and one that Trump insists must be resolved as part of any deal meant to end the war.

Tehran's rhetoric has hardly cooled. Iran’s deputy U.N. ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi told the United Nations Security Council on Friday that Iran “has never closed the door to diplomacy.” But he warned that should the U.S. or Israel return to bombing, his country would offer “an immediate and decisive response.”
Rubio earlier this week stressed that the U.S. is not opposed to mediators continuing their efforts.
“If there’s a deal to be done, the president will be the first one to be in favor of it," Rubio said. "But it’s not going to be a stupid deal. It’s not going to be a bad deal.”

Michael Singh, managing director at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, said he expects the status quo to persist for some time, with the U.S. and Iran locked in a stalemate over the Strait of Hormuz and the U.S. continuing its monthslong naval blockade that's curbing the flow of Iranian crude to the global market.
Singh said the American strategy of squeezing Iran economically is a far more attractive option for Trump than military escalation or making concessions to Tehran.
He also suggested Trump could always reverse his position on Vance engaging with Iranians if the president finds the Iranians are ready to seriously negotiate.

“It’s probably the most sensible path as well to sort of be patient, keep the pressure on, allow the mediators to keep doing their work,” said Singh, who worked on Middle East issues in former President George W. Bush's White House. “And when the time is right, but not before then, is when you want to engage senior officials like the vice president and so forth.”
Associated Press writers Nicholas Riccardi in Denver and Edith M. Lederer at the United Nations contributed reporting.

title: The Nvidia scandal is heightening America's AI rivalry with China ahead of Trump's visit
summary: The scandal that led to Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO of Nvidia is threatening to intensify the rivalry between the U.S. and China on artificial intelligence
story: The scandal that led to Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO of Nvidia is threatening to intensify the rivalry between the U.S. and China on artificial intelligence

HONG KONG -- Well before reports emerged that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, the advanced chips made by his company were at the center of the race between the U.S. and China to dominate artificial intelligence.
The scandal now threatens to intensify that rivalry.

As President Donald Trump prepares to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping next week in China, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle in Congress are seizing on the affair to press for tighter restrictions on technology exports to protect America's edge.

“The scandal, in many ways, encapsulates the rivalry, where concerns around national security, export control, and foreign policy get intertwined,” said Lian Jye Su, a chief analyst at London-based technology research and advisory group Omdia.

At the heart of the competition to build the most advanced artificial intelligence is the race to access the most powerful AI chips. U.S.-led restrictions have barred China from getting the world’s most advanced AI chips, a strategy that has led Beijing to accuse the U.S. of pursuing an AI monopoly.

Once commanding some 95% of market share in China, Nvidia’s sales to China have plummeted due to the export restrictions, first applied during the Biden administration. After Huang lobbied Washington to loosen the limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China, Trump earlier this year greenlighted the export of its highly-advanced, though not the most powerful, H200 chips.

Trump has spoken admiringly of Huang — a man at the center of the AI boom Trump has been keen to promote — and the two have talked regularly during his second term, including at least twice this week as the scandal grew around the tech executive.

The strategy in Washington has been largely focused on hardware, with officials believing if they controlled where California-based Nvidia’s best chips go, they’d be in control of the race for the most capable AI, said Shaoyu Yuan, an assistant professor at New York University’s Center for Global Affairs.
That strategy was effective in slowing down Chinese companies, Yuan said, but it assumed the primary threat was the physical hardware, not access to leaders like Huang.

Yuan said what he called “China hawks” in Congress — who have been bullish on oversight and stronger export controls long before this incident — will now have “a story with a name and a face” to support their argument.
“I don’t think anybody in Washington wants to be seen as loosening the controls on chip exports to China right now,” he added.

This week several congressional Democrats wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to ask what officials knew of Huang's affair with a reported Chinese spy — and to demand an immediate halt to exports of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China.

Lawmakers from both parties have become more outspoken in their calls for tougher legislation to prevent China from accessing advanced U.S. chip and AI technologies. The Senate version of a defense policy bill includes authorizing Congress to review licenses to sell advanced AI chips to China, authorizing the Commerce Department to track AI chips to ensure they aren't diverted to unauthorized regions, and compelling U.S. allies to match U.S. restrictions on exports to Chinese chipmakers.

Beijing has warned the U.S. against using the episode as a reason to impose new restrictions, with Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning telling reporters on Thursday: “The U.S. should stop fabricating the ‘Chinese spy’ narratives as a pretext for imposing technology restrictions.”

The woman in the relationship with the Nvidia chief is reported to be Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed. According to reporting by The New York Times, U.S. officials suspect she was a Chinese spy recruited to potentially influence Nvidia to make its cutting-edge chips more available to China.
Beijing has refuted claims she was a Chinese spy and called the allegation “unsubstantiated.”

Trump doe s not plan to confront Xi on the Nvidia issue, according to senior U.S. officials who briefed reporters Friday on the condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the White House. The officials also said they do not expect Chinese retaliation if they close loopholes to existing measures that prohibit China from smuggling or using advanced computer chips.

Huang has been a frequent visitor to the White House, and in May, he jumped onto Air Force One in Alaska, joining Trump at the last minute for a state visit to Beijing, where he captivated locals by sampling street food. He and his wife, Lori, were seated at the head table with the two leaders when Trump hosted Xi in September in Washington. At a tech summit that month, Huang took a phone call from the president while he was in a live appearance.
Meanwhile, the U.S. and China have committed to the idea of a hotline for AI national security-related incidents.

Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Washington-based think tank Brookings Institution, said the Nvidia scandal — and the possibility of new U.S. export control measures — could throw a wrench in the AI talks. “The question is whether Beijing can separate export controls from the AI safety discussion or will view them as connected issues,” Chan said.

The U.S. and China have been moving AI technology forward in different ways. U.S. companies are chasing AI frontiers supported by cutting-edge chips and the country’s rapidly expanding data center infrastructure. China is pursuing wider global adoption of its open-source, more affordable models.

Increasingly, experts say, China is emerging as an AI counterweight to the U.S. and closing the gap in its lead on the technology. But advanced chips and other technology from Nvidia are still crucial for many Chinese AI companies and research, analysts say.

Chinese chipmakers, including Huawei, have been making rapid progress to narrow the gap by finding ways to work around the U.S. restrictions, including by clustering large numbers of less advanced domestic chips. But Nvidia's cutting-edge chips still lead in single-chip capability and outperform Chinese alternatives in training advanced AI models, analysts say.

China's push for technological self-reliance may have contributed to a reluctance to buy larger amounts of American chips. Despite the U.S. approval to sell some H200 chips to China, Nvidia said earlier this year it had shipped only a small amount to China.
The Huang episode could ultimately add momentum to China's domestic chip industry, said Rui Ma, founder of Tech Buzz China and a China tech expert.

“For Beijing, the fallout only adds urgency to its efforts to build a domestic semiconductor supply chain. That was already a strategic priority, but if access to Nvidia computing power becomes even more restricted, Chinese companies will have increasingly few alternatives,” Ma said.
AP journalists Kaitlyn Huamani in Los Angeles, and Didi Tang, Seung Min Kim and Kevin Freking in Washington contributed.

title: Democrats try out a strange new emotion at post-midterms What's Next conference — hope
summary: Democrats met for two days in Denver to pore over the results of the midterm elections and emerged feeling pretty good about themselves
story: Democrats met for two days in Denver to pore over the results of the midterm elections and emerged feeling pretty good about themselves

DENVER -- When Democrats started planning a post-midterms conference in Denver months ago, political consultant Stephanie Valencia figured it would be more of the same — a bunch of strategists poring over the latest results and plotting a path forward in a country dominated by President Donald Trump.

She never expected that her party would still be celebrating what they consider a dream election, where they won virtually every contested race, flipped U.S. Senate seats in Mississippi and South Carolina, turned Texas blue and won big majorities in Congress.
"I did not expect to be coming here with so much hope,” said Valencia, the co-founder of Equis, which researches Latino voters. “For the first time we can see the outlines of a post-Trump era.”

Democrats spent two days chewing over their future at the What's Next conference and trying to deal with the fact that it looks, for a moment at least, quite bright. Suddenly, anything seemed possible for a party that's become more accustomed to hand-wringing than fist-pumping. Speakers tossed around the word “supermajority.” One data analyst casually discussed pushing for 60 seats in the Senate and displayed a slide suggesting there were winnable races in places like Missouri and Utah.

“Everybody's happy about the results, but everybody's looking over their shoulder saying, ‘Can we really be happy about this?’” quipped former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg, one of several potential presidential candidates who attended. He urged the party to celebrate while not taking future wins for granted.

Some warned that voters hadn't fallen back in love with Democrats, they were just turning to them out of frustration over high prices, the Iran war and concerns about government corruption. No clear recipe emerged from the conference to address widespread dismay about affordability and the economy. But there was hope among attendees that they had the power to figure it out.
Jason Delattre and several friends came to Denver from the Rio Grande Valley after working on Democratic campaigns in Texas. They were still stunned at the opportunities now open to them.
“We have to figure out what we're going to do next,” said Delattre, wearing a cowboy hat and pin for winning U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico.
“We have so much power we didn't have before,” said his friend, Jose Robbie Juarez.
Some even had hope that statehood for Puerto Rico was finally possible.
“It finally feels we're going to get it done,” said Luis Davila, the Democratic chair on the island.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, a possible White House contender, suggested that his party should aim for a landslide win in the next presidential race. Instead of “going out and scrapping for 270,” the minimum electoral votes for victory, they should be "fighting hard to swing for 370.”
That would be five more Electoral College votes than Barack Obama won in his historic 2008 presidential campaign, which was Democrats’ previous high-water mark this century.

The setting was tailor-made for good vibes — a well-known music venue in one of Denver’s hippest neighborhoods, with concert-style posters of politicians and operatives plastered on the walls. Distant snow-capped peaks framed the horizon outside.

Some old divisions reared their heads. A handful of protesters from the leftist Sunrise Movement protested outside the gathering Friday, complaining that it was sponsored by a group, Majority Democrats, that's more centrist and funded by wealthy businesspeople.

A couple of protesters interrupted what was supposed to be a triumphant appearance by the likely new House speaker, Hakeem Jeffries. They demanded a Green New Deal and an arms embargo against Israel. One man shouted profanities at Jeffries and called him a “traitor” while being led from the auditorium.
Jeffries brushed it off.
“I’m from Brooklyn," he said. "This is light work.”

Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who is challenging New York Sen. Chuck Schumer for caucus leadership, appeared at the conference Friday. He's allied himself with Democrats' liberal wing, and he argued that voters have demanded change.
But many were not worried about those signs of discord.
New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker, who may run for president again, said the leadership fight was a “family conversation” the party would have in Washington, and he welcomed signs of dissent.

“I think this is a wonderful thing that we have right now, that we're having a real discussion,” Booker said in an interview. “At a conference like this you're seeing the future," he added, returning to the party's optimism. "A new day is dawning in America.”
Rep. Joe Neguse of Colorado said Democrats were “the big tent party.”
“We have an ideological spectrum that covers virtually every element of Democratic thought," he said in an interview. "And I think that’s exciting.”

title: Trump is taking Elon Musk on his Asia trip, but he plans to avoid talking about Nvidia scandal
summary: President Donald Trump plans to take the world’s wealthiest man, Elon Musk, with him next week when he travels to the Philippines and China
story: President Donald Trump plans to take the world’s wealthiest man, Elon Musk, with him next week when he travels to the Philippines and China
WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump plans to take the world's wealthiest man, Elon Musk, with him next week when he travels to the Philippines and China.

As the head of SpaceX and Tesla, Musk has economic and national security interests that make him a valuable adviser to Trump, according to administration officials who insisted on anonymity as a condition for previewing the president's plans on a Friday call with reporters.

The journey comes as the fallout spreads from Jensen Huang being ousted as the CEO of Nvidia for having an extramarital affair with an alleged agent of the Chinese government. Beijing denies that Alice Huang is a spy. Her company Megaspeed was accused last year of shipping Nvidia's advanced computer chips into China.

But Trump does not plan to confront Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the matter and administration officials do not expect Chinese retaliation for any follow-up actions to prohibit China from smuggling or using advanced computer chips, officials told reporters.

The administration believes the situation with Nvidia should not have any bearing on the trip, as the U.S. does not make its use of export controls subject to negotiations with foreign countries. Trump's aides are discussing the possibility of closing loopholes in existing trade measures, including the use of export licensing and preventing the ability of Chinese firms to use advanced chips over the internet through remote access.

The trip will be capped with a historic trilateral meeting with Xi and Russian leader Vladimir Putin, where efforts to limit nuclear weapons will be a chief topic. Still, there are no plans for Trump to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, whose nuclear arsenal has been a source of consternation to the U.S. and its allies.

Trump is set to arrive Tuesday in the Philippines to meet with his counterparts in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. While in Manila, he intends to sign a trade deal with Thailand and meet with the Quad, an alliance composed of the U.S., India, Australia and Japan.

On Wednesday, Trump will leave for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he’ll have his third in-person meeting this year with Xi. Afterward, Trump and Xi will hold their joint meeting with Putin.

The leaders are expected to talk about the Iran war, but Russia's war in Ukraine is not expected to be part of the agenda, officials said — and Musk, whose Starlink system has been integral to Ukraine's ability to fight back against Russia's invasion, will not be part of the trilateral meeting.

title: Savannah Guthrie, popular and enduring face of morning TV, renews NBC contract after 15 years
summary: Savannah Guthrie has extended her contract with NBC News, ensuring she continues as co-anchor on "Today."
story: Savannah Guthrie has extended her contract with NBC News, ensuring she continues as co-anchor on "Today."
NEW YORK -- Savannah Guthrie has extended her contract at NBC News, ensuring she will continue to greet viewers each morning on “Today” after more than 15 years at the network.

The move by one of morning television's most enduring and popular personalities was confirmed to The Associated Press by a person close to the situation, speaking on condition of anonymity because the news has not been made public. It was not clear for how long the contract was extended.

The extension also came during a year of personal pain and turmoil for Guthrie. Her mother, Nancy Guthrie, 84, was last seen at her home just outside Tucson on Jan. 31 and was reported missing the following day. Authorities believe she was kidnapped, abducted or otherwise taken against her will. The case remains dogged by questions; no suspects have been arrested.

In July, authorities released two ransom notes initially sent to a Tucson television station days after Guthrie went missing. The first note, sent Feb. 2, said she was safe but scared and would be released unharmed once her captors received $4 million in cryptocurrency. The second note, sent Feb. 6, said Guthrie died shortly after she was kidnapped.

Guthrie and her family have shared their pain and pleaded for information in videos posted to social media. Most recently, Guthrie addressed the tragic situation on Instagram, posting an old drawing from her daughter, Vale, which she said “says so much about how I feel.”
The drawing depicted an umbrella amid falling raindrops, with an accompanying message: "I know it might not seem like it but I really need my mommy.”
“The world goes on, things appear 'normal,' ” Guthrie wrote in her post, “as we try to keep going and be strong, especially for our young kids — but it’s not and it never will be.”

“We ache for her, we cry out for answers, we cannot move forward,” she wrote in the post, to which she also attached a smiling photo of her mother. “We need someone to help us, tell us what you know. Our mom was a light in this world. We want to celebrate her and give her the dignity she deserves. The reward is still available. Please. We are begging you. Please help us.”

Guthrie, 54, became a main co-anchor of “Today” in 2012, after joining the show the previous year. She now co-hosts with Craig Melvin. She is also a primary anchor for NBC's election coverage, most recently for last week's midterm elections.

title: Rubio acknowledges 'people are struggling' economically in speech after GOP midterm wipeout
summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio has acknowledged that Americans are struggling in the current economy
story: Secretary of State Marco Rubio has acknowledged that Americans are struggling in the current economy

WASHINGTON -- Secretary of State Marco Rubio gave a sweeping speech to fellow conservatives on Friday evening acknowledging that Americans are struggling in the current economy, while also railing against what he called the “weaponization” of international law to constrain the U.S. from acting in its own interests.
His comments to the conservative Federalist Society touched on a core issue of the midterm elections — economic pain — that U.S. voters cited in delivering massive losses to Rubio's Republican Party.

“I think we have to recognize that people are struggling. There’s no doubt about it,” he said. “The health of our economy has nothing to do with the stock market. The health of their economy is whether they have enough money to be able to afford the things they need.”

President Donald Trump often points to the stock market as evidence that the economy is doing well. But voters angry over higher costs gave Democrats control of Congress after blaming Trump for his tariffs, his war in Iran and his unfulfilled campaign promise two years ago to bring down prices.

Rubio's remarks had the overtones of campaign speech, though the former Florida senator has consistently refused to discuss whether he would seek the presidency in 2028 in a race that could pit him against Vice President JD Vance. Rubio gave another wide-ranging speech last month in Greece that focused on Western values and also appeared to reflect his political aspirations beyond being America’s top diplomat.

Rubio on Friday defended the Iran war, arguing that it was necessary to stop the threat of the Islamic Republic obtaining a nuclear weapon. But he acknowledged that the unpopular conflict has driven up gasoline prices for Americans and other connected costs.

“It’s not easy to address these things because it’s not popular to address them," Rubio said. “It’s difficult. And oftentimes it inflicts, you know, pain, economic pain and otherwise. So we recognize that.”

He also pointed to the need for American leaders to continue a tradition of ensuring the next generation is better off than those before them. Economic prosperity is “not self-perpetuating,” he said, but an enormous undertaking that requires years and decades and is not accomplished “election cycle to election cycle."

“That’s the challenge before us now, because I do think there’s a legitimate fear that we will be the first generation to leave the next worse off, and that can’t happen. That’s un-American,” he said.

Rubio also hit back hard on critics of Trump administration policies such as deadly strikes on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America, the January capture of then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and strict immigration policies.
He accused other countries and international organizations of trying to stymie the U.S. from acting in its own best interests by accusing the Trump administration of violations of international law.

“We’ve heard the concept international law invoked against nearly every major foreign policy decision or action of this administration,” he said, describing it as “the weaponization of international law.”

Rubio also condemned the United Nations, the International Criminal Court, the “global elite” and organizations staffed by “international activists and bureaucrats,” all of which he said want to weaken the United States.

“They lecture us on the importance of sovereignty, even as they demand that nations surrender control of their borders and outsource their immigration laws to unelected international courts,” Rubio said. "They oppose, they say, all forms of imperialism, of conquest, of domination, but they seek to exercise authority over every country and every government on earth.”
AP Diplomatic Writer Matthew Lee in Washington contributed.

title: Investigation says understaffing and unexpected fire behavior led to firefighter deaths
summary: Unexpected fire behavior, chronic understaffing, a lack of trained employees and a new policy to quash fires quickly were among the factors that contributed to the deaths of four helitack firefighters as they battled a blaze in western Colorado in June
story: Unexpected fire behavior, chronic understaffing, a lack of trained employees and a new policy to quash fires quickly were among the factors that contributed to the deaths of four helitack firefighters as they battled a blaze in western Colorado in June

Unexpected fire behavior, chronic understaffing, a lack of highly trained employees and a new policy to quash fires quickly were among the factors that contributed to the deaths of four helitack firefighters as they battled a blaze in western Colorado in June, according to a report released by the U.S. Department of the Interior.

The firefighters, working for the U.S. Forest Service and the newly created U.S. Wildland Fire Service, were part of an interagency response to the Knowles fire that merged with others to form the Snyder Fire on the Colorado/Utah border. The Rifle Helitack crew had been dropped in a remote area to work on a fire line, but became trapped when strong winds blew the fires in their direction and overtook them.

Their deaths came after the Trump administration revived a previously discredited policy to stomp out all wildfires quickly. Decisions on how to fight the Knowles fire were driven by the desire to prevent the spread of cheatgrass and protect sage-grouse habitat and a downwind community, the report said.

These factors “established an organizational posture to aggressively suppress new starts while small,” the report said. “This policy framing drove the decision to insert helitack firefighters onto small wilderness starts on a day with extreme fire weather conditions forecast.”

Emily Barker, Nick Hutcherson, and Sydney Watson were killed at the scene while Nathan Matthews sustained burn injuries and died on July 24. A fifth firefighter on the team sustained burn injuries but survived.

Ron and Lisa Hutcherson, Nick's parents, said the crew should not have been sent out ahead of the fire because dangerous winds were in the forecast. After meeting with investigators and visiting the site, they said they believe the deaths were preventable and were caused by a failure of leadership and oversight.

“Telling us how the fire reached our son does not answer why he was still there,” Ron Hutcherson said in an email to The Associated Press. “Who was watching the bigger picture? Who was responsible for bringing those firefighters home while there was still time?”
Lisa Hutcherson added: "My son depended on the people responsible for tracking the fire threatening him and making the decisions needed to keep him safe. We want answers, and we want accountability.”
The Serious Accident Investigation report detailed the circumstances that led to the decision to send out the helitack team and the many problems that led to their deaths.
Multiple lightning fires ignited on June 27 in Colorado's Black Ridge Canyon Wilderness. The region was experiencing extreme drought conditions, and the winds were picking up.

An incident team orchestrated coverage of the various fires by calling in aircraft and crews. At one point, the official in charge ordered all aircraft to the Jones fire, but constant high winds challenged all pilots that day, with many saying it was the most difficult flying of their careers, the report said.
By the early afternoon, communication systems broke down, with many trainee dispatchers trying to coordinate operations. There was also confusion over who would track aircraft.

“Dispatchers simultaneously tracked up to 16 active aircraft, three emerging incidents, multiple new starts, county river evacuations, and non-stop media inquiries, leading to severe cognitive task saturation,” the report said. “Due to constant radio congestion and workload strain, dispatchers felt they were unable to transmit the mandatory scheduled 1000 Fire Weather Forecast broadcast across the zone.”
The incident commanders on the Snyder and Jones fires did not have clear information about the location of the firefighters on the Knowles and Gore fires to the east, the report said.

“Because no operational role was assigned to continuously map personnel location against the emerging fires’ trajectories, overhead did not recognize that firefighters were positioned directly in the fire’s line of advance,” the report said.

A large fire about eight miles to the west of the helitack crew was observed three and a half hours before the entrapment, the report said. In less than three hours, the fire ran over complex terrain and reached the five firefighters, who were forced to deploy fire shelters, because a helicopter was unable to reach them in time.

The Hutcherson family met with fire investigators in Grand Junction on Oct. 26 for a three-hour official readout of the report, they said. The review described a failure of lookouts, communications, escape routes and safety zones, they said.

An aging mobile radio system and software crashes compromised official channels during critical operations, the family was told. Overlapping transmissions and confused radio traffic forced firefighters to use cellphones to communicate.

The Knowles fire was in a remote location, the family said, so the central question remains: “What justified keeping this crew exposed as communications, observation, and extraction options deteriorated?”

Timothy Ingalsbee, executive director of the nonprofit Firefighters United for Safety, Ethics and Ecology, said the problem can be traced back to the Trump administration's full-suppression policy, which has prompted crews across the country to take unreasonable risks.

“It was outrageous to have a full-suppression policy on a lightning-caused fire in the wilderness to prevent the spread of cheatgrass,” Ingalsbee said. “The policy driving this aggressive attack of all fires is an obsolete paradigm that is just humanly or ecologically unsustainable. And unfortunately this crew paid the ultimate price, ultimate sacrifice.”

title: Trump administration cancels mandatory pay hike for Head Start teachers
summary: The Trump administration said it would cancel a rule mandating pay increases for teachers in the Head Start preschool program
story: The Trump administration said it would cancel a rule mandating pay increases for teachers in the Head Start preschool program

WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration on Friday said it would cancel a rule mandating pay increases for teachers in Head Start, the federally funded early education program that serves more than 700,000 of the nation's neediest preschoolers every year.

The move will undo a requirement that large Head Start programs gradually increase pay for teachers, so they would reach parity with their local public preschool teachers. The rule, created under Democratic President Joe Biden, also called for expanding employee benefits and would have cost around $2.1 billion annually by 2031.
The Trump administration announced Friday that it was finalizing the repeal of the pay-hike mandate. The new rule will take effect in January.

The money saved could allow Head Start programs to serve more children with the same amount of federal funding, President Donald Trump's administration said. The administration has pushed to scrap many of Head Start's quality regulations, saying programs can enroll more kids if they have more flexibility on spending.

“The Trump Administration is working hard to ensure that the promise of Head Start reaches as many children as possible with the funds Congress has appropriated,” said Alex J. Adams, an assistant secretary at Health and Human Services who oversees Head Start.

Advocates for Head Start educators say eliminating pay hikes could actually hurt enrollment. Some programs have been unable to recruit enough staff to operate at capacity and have had to shutter classrooms and preschool centers. Teacher turnover was particularly acute during the pandemic. More than 20% of Head Start teachers left in 2022, some fleeing for higher-paying jobs in public schools or in other sectors, such as retail or food service.

A majority of Head Start teachers hold bachelor’s degrees. But according to data reported by programs in 2026, Head Start teachers with master’s degrees earned less than $60,000 a year on average, while those with only a bachelor’s degree earned less than $50,000. Meanwhile, public schoolteachers earn an average of $75,000 a year, according to the National Education Association union.

The Trump administration “asks Head Start educators to keep doing more for less,” the National Association for the Education of Young Children said in a statement. If teachers move on to other jobs, kids cannot enroll, the group said. “A funded slot without a qualified teacher serves no one.”

The change had also been condemned by congressional Democrats, who take control of Congress in the new year. This past June, they authored a letter urging the Trump administration to change course and leave the Biden-era pay requirements in place.

Head Start was started in the 1960s as an antipoverty initiative. It targets children in low-income households, plus those who are homeless or in foster care or have disabilities. The program, which provides training and job opportunities for parents along with education for preschoolers, has long had bipartisan support.

But it has faced threats under the Trump administration. A White House budget draft last year proposed scrapping the program altogether. More recently, Adams proposed scrapping many of Head Start's regulations, which form the basis for many of its signature offerings, such as medical screenings and family supports. His proposal would also do away with federal student-to-teacher ratios, deferring to state childcare regulations, which tend to be looser.
