title: DOC NYC documentary film festival returns. Check out this year's lineup.
summary: America's largest festival for nonfiction cinema, with more than 115 feature-length documentaries plus short film programs, opens in NYC theaters and streams online.
story: DOC NYC, America's largest festival for documentary films, returns to New York City and streaming for the 17th year, with screenings in Manhattan beginning Wednesday through Nov. 19, and continuing online through Nov. 29.

The festival includes more than 115 feature-length documentaries — many making their world, U.S. or New York City premieres — as well as short film programs, while the DOC NYC Pro Conference offers panel discussions and workshops in a variety of areas of nonfiction filmmaking and distribution.

The festival's opening-night feature is the American premiere of "The Hummingbird Paints Fragrant Songs," about an Indigenous artist in the Peruvian Amazon who uses her art to advocate for her people and their land. The film won best international documentary at the São Paulo International Film Festival.

Barbara Kopple's "Union Town," the festival's centerpiece, tells three stories of workers fighting for better conditions in the U.S. Kopple won two Academy Awards for her films "Harlan County, U.S.A." and "American Dream."
The closing-night feature explores our fascination with solar eclipses. In "Totality," 21 film crews across the U.S. captured how the public embraced the 2024 total eclipse of the Sun.

See below for more highlights of some of the films screening at DOC NYC. There are also screenings of some of 2026's most notable nonfiction releases, including "You Can See Everything," "Once Upon a Time in Harlem," "NAZA," "Musk," "American Doctor," "Everybody to Kenmure Street," "Nuisance Bear," and "One In a Million."
Check out the festival's website for more program details, schedules, ticket and day pass information, and online screening availability.
Profiles
Among the personalities who are profiled in documentaries at the festival are:

Singer Darlene Love ("Darlene Love: I Know Where I've Been")Film director David Cronenberg ("The Flesh And The Soul")Rock star Chrissie Hynde ("Pretenders")Women's soccer star Megan Rapinoe ("Rapinoe") Veteran music critic Robert Christgau ("The Last Critic")Cconcert pianist Emanuel Ax ("All the Music In the World")The Chicano rock group Los Lobos ("Los Lobos Native Sons")Oscar-winning cinematographer Robert Richardson ("Robert Richardson: The White Devil")The creator of Mad Magazine ("The Mad World of Harvey Kurtzman")
Singer Darlene Love ("Darlene Love: I Know Where I've Been")
Film director David Cronenberg ("The Flesh And The Soul")
Rock star Chrissie Hynde ("Pretenders")
Women's soccer star Megan Rapinoe ("Rapinoe")
Veteran music critic Robert Christgau ("The Last Critic")
Cconcert pianist Emanuel Ax ("All the Music In the World")
The Chicano rock group Los Lobos ("Los Lobos Native Sons")
Oscar-winning cinematographer Robert Richardson ("Robert Richardson: The White Devil")
The creator of Mad Magazine ("The Mad World of Harvey Kurtzman")
Environment

Using archival footage and interviews, "Whiddy" recounts how the community on a small Irish island was affected by the construction of a Gulf Oil terminal for supertankers in the 1960s, leading to numerous oil spills and an oil tanker explosion in 1979 that killed 50 people.
Aided by archival footage and photos, Icelandic poet Andri Snær Magnason creates a time capsule of Iceland's melting glaciers and their importance to his family in "Time and Water."

In England, two neighboring farmers are each determined to use their land differently – while one farms with traditional methods, the other turns to rewilding – in "Derek vs. Derek." "Neighbours of the Beast" examines the impact of the inhabitants of the Indian city of Panna on the tiger population of nearby forests.

"Understory" uses macro imagery, animation and time-lapse photography to study the extraordinary intelligence of plants. In "Materia Prima," Bolivia's vast lithium reserves draw the interest of outside developers, augering yet another form of colonialism in South America.
Art and music

Jazz trumpeter Marcus Belgrave (1936-2015) was a force in music for more than six decades, supporting stars and mentoring gifted young talent along the way. Multitudes of musician-fans offer their praise in "...And Damn, He Could Play: The Marcus Belgrave Story."

Photographer Ethan Russell always seemed to be in the right place at the right time, which allowed a young American in England to obtain unique access to The Beatles, The Rolling Stones and The Who, as well as myriad other rock stars. He tries to explain his great luck in "Let It Be, Let It Bleed: The Unlikely Rock n' Roll Journey of Ethan Russell."

In 2021 singer-songwriter Beldina Odenyo died tragically at age 31. "Bel" explores the traumas that affected Odenyo, her family's grief, and the determination of her sister, Leah, to complete the unfinished album that Odenyo left behind.

"Make Work" delves into the creative process of dance, following choreographers at the New York City Ballet's Choreographic Institute. Experimental filmmakers Nathaniel Dorsky and Jerome Hiler explain their hands-on approach to capturing the ephemeral nature of life on celluloid in "Illuminations."
"Frida: The Girl Just Doesn't Go Away" asks, how did painter Frida Kahlo become a global brand? Cuban artists resist censorship and state repression in "#SOSCUBA."
Addiction helped derail a promising opera career for singer Tim Blevins. "Figaro Up, Figaro Down" follows Blevins as he uses his talent to survive on the streets.
Social activism

Puerto Ricans in small fishing boats mount resistance against the U.S. Navy's occupation of Vieques in "Zenón and the Rebel Boats." In 1970s and '80s Los Angeles, feminist artists challenged the art world. How they fared is covered in "Acting Like Women."

"A Better Way: James Lawson, Architect of Nonviolence" tells the story of The Rev. James Lawson, a colleague of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., who preached faith and nonviolence in fighting racism, police violence and Apartheid. Crusading lawyer Lee Merritt dedicates his life to advocating for the families of Black Americans killed by the police in "Enough."

Following the 1968 assassination of Martin Luther King Jr., Iowa schoolteacher Jane Elliott devised the "Blue Eyes/Brown Eyes" exercise to help her students see the cruelty of racism. That lesson earned Elliott much blowback, and stiffened her resolve to combat racism, as shown in "Jane Elliott Against The World."

In the 1960s, a group of filmmakers and journalists came together to document the counterculture movement as a counterpoint to mainstream media. Their work is chronicled in "The Newsreel: Characterization of Subversive Organization."
Health and Medicine

Emma Fogarty, who lives with a rare and painful genetic disorder called epidermolysis bullosa, teams up with a friend, actor Colin Farrell (who is battling personal demons of his own), to run the Dublin Marathon together, in "The Slightest Touch." An advocate fights for women's healthcare in Venezuela in "The Cord."

In "The Sickling," a man undertakes an experimental stem cell treatment for his pain-inducing sickle cell disease. In "Under Fire," an Idaho fire captain treats the PTSD of the mental strain from his harrowing job with experimental ketamine therapy.
Technology

"MySpace" makes a nostalgic trip back to 2003, when MySpace was the prototypical social media platform before Facebook, Youtube, Instagram and TikTok, and at one point drew more internet traffic than Google's home page. How far has social media come since? Where did MySpace go? And is it coming back?
"The Sandbox" examines how ubiquitous surveillance systems and military technology are used to control the global refugee crisis, with life-or-death consequences.
Exposés

Historical and archival investigations of challenging stories include "Primetime Preacher$," about how Jim Bakker, Jerry Falwell and Jimmy Swaggart turned their evangelical ministries into media giants and founts of political power.
"The New Extinction" digs into the dinosaur fossil industry, where paleontology confronts commercial bone hunters and wealthy buyers.
How do flat-earthers and alien truthers come to their versions of reality? "Gimme Truth" introduces us to some colorful conspiracy theorists.
Justice
DOC NYC will debut the first two episodes of the Amazon Prime miniseries "The Boy Who Stole Billions?," about cryptocurrency fraudster Sam Bankman-Fried.

"An Eye For an Eye" examines the legal system in Iran, where a woman convicted of killing her abusive husband must make a blood money payment to her husband's family to avoid execution. But will they accept?

In 2020 in Hungary, under pressure from Viktor Orbán's far-right government, 80 journalists from the independent newsroom Index.hu resigned in protest — and then picked up their cameras. "80 Angry Journalists" is the result.

The weaponization of non-disclosure agreements is examined through the stories of three people who face retaliation after breaking their NDAs meant to silence them about accusations of rape, racial discrimination and corporate crimes, in "My NDA."

Following his death in 1994, singer, songwriter and holy teacher Rabbi Shlomo Carlebach was posthumously accused of sexual abuse, shaking the Jewish community in New York City. "The Darkest Light" follows the path of survivors seeking healing.
Lawyer and first-time filmmaker Suja A. Thomas takes a humorous look at failures in the nation's justice system, and pop culture's caricature of it, in "The Best Justice System In the World."
Food
Go inside the kitchen of the Budapest Michelin-starred Onyx, where the personalities of owner and staff clash during a reinvention of the restaurant, in "The Taste of Democracy."

Traditional family winegrowers in Italy's Piedmont region face pressure from deep-pocketed foreign buyers to sell off their land, as climate change creates even greater stressors on their annual harvest, in "Low Lies the Land."
War and Conflict

Ukrainian women bear witness after surviving sexual assault by Russian soldiers in "Traces" (Ukraine's submission in the best international feature film category for this year's Oscars). In "Black Sunflowers," 10 young Ukrainians grapple with the effects of the Russian invasion.

In "For Life," a Palestinian woman wants a child with her husband, who has been setenced to life in an Israeli prison. "From Gaza With Love" tells the story of a friendhip between a French journalist and a Palestinian photographer.
Following the 1980 U.S. election, thousands of women assembled at the Pentagon to protest policies of war, in "With Love and Rage."
Sports and Endurance
In "The Ascent," Mandy Horvath climbs Mount Kilimanjaro after having lost both her legs. Young sumo wrestlers train at Tokyo's Sakaigawa Stable in "Sumo: Spirit Weighs Nothing."

"Kick" follows American trans nonbinary runner Nikki Hiltz on their road to the Olympics. In rural Turkey, women bond while defying traditional boundaries through their training for a shooting competition in "32 Meters." The sport of car spinning in Cape Town is captured in "From Dust We Spin."
Americana

"Ashland" is a meditative look at the people and landscapes of Montana. In a small Maine town, artisans construct a 56-foot sailboat on commission in "Boatbuilders."  Maine lobstermen are the subjects of the cinema vérité  "Bucks Harbor."
"Love Apptually" explores how dating apps have changed the way we find love. In "Baby/Girls," three teenagers from the Bible Belt face unexpected pregnancies and motherhood.
An Albanian immigrant buys a failing shopping mall in Johnstown, Pennsylvania, and tries to turn it around in "Mall Country."

Fifty years ago, Native Hawaiian Nainoa Thompson sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti without the aid of modern instruments, the first to do so in 600 years. Now he mentors young navigators to repeat the perilous 2,400-mile journey in "The Navigator."

In-person screenings will be held at the IFC Center, SVA Theatre, and Village East by Angelika. For information about more entries in their year's festival, as well as breakdowns of their short film programs, visit the website of DOC NYC.

title: Judge dismisses Dolly Parton's estate's lawsuit against her nephew
summary: The details of the resolution between Dolly Parton's estate and her nephew, Bryan Seaver, were not immediately known.
story: Update: A Tennessee judge on Monday dismissed the lawsuit filed by Dolly Parton's estate against her nephew and former head of security, Bryan Seaver. The judge dismissed it without prejudice, meaning it can be filed again.

The estate of the late country music icon Dolly Parton has filed to dismiss its lawsuit against her nephew and former head of security, Bryan Seaver, following accusations he threatened to commit acts of violence and destroy Parton's brand.
The details of the resolution were not immediately known.

"Mr. Seaver is grateful to put this misunderstanding behind him so that the entire family can continue to grieve peacefully and ensure that the bright light of Dolly's legacy remains completely untouched," attorneys for Seaver told CBS News in a statement.
Attorneys for Parton's estate did not respond to a request for comment.

Seaver, who heads the private security firm Squadron Augmented Protection Services, had been tasked with announcing Parton's death in August. But in September, Seaver and SAPS were fired by She's Alive, which manages Parton's estate and business interests. Parton's longtime manager, Danny Nozell, who runs She's Alive, then filed for a restraining order against Seaver and SAPS.

Parton died of cancer at the age of 80. Seaver rose to national prominence when he announced Parton's death in a prerecorded video, in which he said it was "something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality."

She's Alive, or SAL, had alleged in its request for a restraining order that Seaver "made repeated, written threats to Ms. Parton's staff, partners, legal and business advisors, and others" and that he "sought to extract money from SAL and trusts through an obscene, deliberate, and escalating campaign of threats."

In one instance prior to Parton's death, SAL alleged that Seaver threatened to "destroy the entire brand" over a disagreement involving Dollywood, the theme park and resort opened by Parton in 1986. The lawsuit also alleged that Seaver repeatedly referenced his security business, which it described as a "heavily armed, paramilitary-style force capable of projecting threat and coercion against SAL's personnel and business partners."
Seaver made many of these alleged threats via text, according to the lawsuit.

Seaver, in a response to SAL's request to extend its restraining order last month, denied "each and every allegation." He said he and Nozell had been close friends for many years and that, until his firing, the two had never had an argument "apart from a minor disagreement years ago over a company logo."

While he admitted to using coarse and blunt language, he denied threatening anybody, including Parton or her estate's business partners, saying the text messages were "private messages" between himself and Nozell.

"They were sent in the course of private conversations between two friends who were both frustrated, grieving, and discussing strategy following Ms. Parton's illness and death," the court filing states.

He insisted the messages about the Dollywood disagreement were not threats of violence but that he was "privately warning" Nozell that he thought certain associates were "harming [Parton's] brand and imploring him to help."

Seaver also said in his response that Nozell didn't respond to the various texts cited in the lawsuit with any sort of pushback or alarm. In fact, Seaver claimed Nozell urged him to publicly play up his military and security history before trying to use those ties as evidence that Seaver was dangerous and threatening.

"I have declined to speak with the media about this case and have asked my attorneys to handle all media communications," Seaver wrote at the end of his affidavit. "I care about Ms. Parton, her music, her legacy, and her family. I do not want this dispute to harm her legacy."
This story published first on CBS News at 6:19 p.m. on Nov. 5, 2026.

title: "The Altruists" actor Julia Garner on surprising herself
summary: In "The Altruists," the Emmy-winning star of "Ozark" plays Caroline Ellison, girlfriend of Sam Bankman-Fried and business partner in a multi-billion-dollar cryptocurrency fraud. Julia Garner talks about how, for her, the eyes truly are the windows to the soul.
story: Julia Garner has become known for her remarkable transformations. In the new Netflix series "The Altruists," she plays Caroline Ellison, the business partner and girlfriend of Sam Bankman-Fried, his accomplice in a multi-billion dollar fraud that led to the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX.

Her performance as Ellison has many mannerisms. Asked how she puts them together, Garner replied, "I notice everything. I do! I might look like I'm a little [whistling and gesturing like birds are fluttering overhead], but I'm not!

"You know, you can tell a lot with somebody's eyes," she said. "I look at photos, I obsess over photos. This sounds so crazy, but I'll cover half of their face and I'll just focus on their eyes. And I'm like, I want those eyes for that person that I am about to become."
Asked if she chooses characters based on complexity, she laughed, "Yes, but I feel like they also choose me!"
To watch a trailer for "The Altruists," click on the video player below:

Garner grew up in the Riverdale section of the Bronx, taking arts and crafts classes at the Wave Hill Cultural Center near her parents' home. Her father teaches art; her mother was an actress-turned-therapist ("Which is probably why I'm an actor," Garner said).

Describing herself as "deathly shy" growing up, Garner took her first acting class at 14. "Now when I look at my childhood, I think I was acting my whole life," she said. "Because I had lot of problems as a kid. I had a lot of, like, learning problems, and I always felt like such an outcast. And acting always protected me."

At 16, she landed her first film role in 2011's "Martha Marcy May Marlene." Garner's breakout would come in 2017 in the Netflix crime series "Ozark." Her performance as Ruth Langmore, a whip-smart hustler who runs a crime ring from a trailer park, would win her a Golden Globe and three Emmys.
"My life was so different before 'Ozark,'" she said.

Asked what playing Ruth taught her, Garner replied, "Not to be so scared. And then since then, for whatever reason, people are like, 'We're gonna hire her to play the most unhinged people. She's great for that!'"
She'd earn another Golden Globe nomination for "Inventing Anna" (2022), playing Russian-born Anna Sorokin, who conned New York society into believing she was a German heiress.
But the 32-year-old began to be unnerved by the attention she was getting: "I just didn't like the feeling of being watched all the time and it kind of got to my head," she said.
During the actors' strike in 2023, Garner signed up for a clown school in France: "I failed miserably at it, a lot of times. And you know what? It was the best feeling."

It was there she realized she felt ashamed of her own success – that she wasn't worthy of it. In class, her clown instructor called her out one day: "He's like, 'You are hiding from something, you feel a lot of shame, you are not comfortable. Look, let me see your eyes.' So, I had to open up."
What did she learn by opening up? "Not being afraid to fail," Garner said.
I noted, "I find it very interesting that he calls you out on your eyes, and you are someone who does so much with your eyes."
"But I didn't want someone to see my eyes, you see?" Garner replied. "I got a lot out of it. I'm still sometimes looking for my inner clown."
Aren't we all? "Well, I have a clown certificate!" Garner laughed.

Perhaps Garner's most famous role is in a film yet to be shot. Madonna picked her to play the singer in a biopic that was in development, but has since been shelved. Garner doesn't know if the film will get made: "Every hour it changes in a way," she said, adding, "It's not up to me. I would love for the movie to get made, obviously, but I also feel whatever happens, I made a great friend. I love Madonna, I think she's incredible. She works, like, she taught me properly, like, how to work."
The audition process required Garner to sing, dance, and act as Madonna. "I wasn't a trained dancer," she said.

Did she surprise herself? "Yeah, but I always try to," Garner said. "It's the same thing with the Caroline Ellison role. I really didn't want to recognize myself, like, at all. That's my goal. The thing that I'm concerned about always when I'm working is, how am I going to move people? How am going to affect people? How am gonna make people feel less alone? Because I remember growing up when I felt alone, and I watched a movie. It gave me this endless sense of hope, because I didn't feel alone. And that's the beauty of, you know, good acting."

title: With "Thrasher," Brandon Flowers returns home
summary: Smalltown Nephi, Utah, was where the musical sensibilities of Killers frontman Brandon Flowers started to take form, before finding success as a rock star in Las Vegas. Now his solo album, "Thrasher," is filled with country songs like those beloved by his dad.
story: The year was 2002, in Henderson, Nevada, and no one at the bar that night realized they were watching what would become one of the biggest bands in the world: The Killers. No one, that is, except maybe Brandon Flowers, who was barely 23 years old when The Killers shot to stardom with their first single, "Mr. Brightside," a story about being cheated on ripped from Flowers' own life, which became the anthem for a generation.

"I noticed early on, people would talk about the storytelling in Killers music, that they didn't always associate with young rock bands," Flowers said. "And I think that was when it first started to maybe dawn on me, where was I getting this from?"

Where he was getting it from turns out is Nephi, Utah, an hour and a half south of Salt Lake. It has one stoplight, and feels about as far away from rock & roll stardom as you could get. The family moved there from Las Vegas when Flowers was eight. "It's funny to look at it now, to say it was a culture shock," he said. "It really was, even though I was just a kid. My unit was my family, but there was something in me that still really felt planted in Las Vegas, and felt like that was part of my identity, you know? And it was something that I always wanted to go back to."

Flowers struggled to fit in, missing school to help his dad work on an apartment building, a family business. (His sister's name is still on the mailbox.) And to buy music in Nephi back then, he headed to the closest thing Nephi had to a record store: The Flying J Truck Stop. "They used to have these bins inside our Flying J that would just be full of cassettes, and you'd kind of mine through them," he said. "One particular treasure that I found was a Depeche Mode record there."

Another formative location in town? The local golf course. "This is the bar of the town," said Flowers. "This is where people can congregate and play a sport they love, but they can also drink. And so, there's sort of a subculture of guys that played golf here a lot. And so, that was my experience – my first cigarettes and my first chewing tobacco and alcohol was all here also." It was as close to Las Vegas as he was going to get in Nephi.
Flowers did end up back in Las Vegas for his senior year of high school, and it's where The Killers established themselves and rocketed to fame.

Btu these days, it's places like Nephi that actually inspire Flowers, which might be why his new solo album is country western, the kinds of songs his dad played on the radio. "It just really lends itself to the stories and to the characters and to detail," he said. "I was secretly absorbing it."
Gold and silvеr, God and glitter Lights that flicker on hubcap chrome On the road to Heaven In Strauss and Stetson Swimming pools of horsepower Take me back home-- From "The American Dream"
Brandon Flowers performs "The American Dream"

Flowers' latest solo project is called "Thrasher," filled with stories of his childhood. "One of my strongest memories, more so than getting beat up by a couple of country kids that were stronger than me, was [my dad] trying to teach me to fight," he said. "So, it's just an interesting thing to look back on. Now I have three sons, and I teach them to not fight."

Nine years ago, Flowers moved back to Utah with his wife and children, something he's glad he did now that they're leaving the nest. "They don't prepare you for this," he said. "You know, watching kids be young and that innocence and raising them was maybe the best, you know, felt like the greatest time for me. And now we just took one and dropped them off in Pennsylvania yesterday. It's just a tough thing to wrap your head around, letting them go."

Flowers, who's been a lifelong practicing Mormon AND a rock star, says he's looked to rock & roll's past for guidance on how to handle that balance. "One of the things I love about Elvis is, I see him as sort of like a spiritual progenitor and someone that, no matter what mistakes he made, you know – and we all know everything about Elvis – but just he was still deeply religious, and I think about that with Johnny Cash also, a couple of the people that always come to mind," Flowers said. "And they struggled with it, and so I'm able to learn from them and make my decisions based on, you know, you can read the books, you watch the documentaries, you watch the movie, you know how it would happen."
And sometimes it's learning from Elvis what to avoid? "Absolutely, yeah," said Flowers. "I mean, he was the first. He did everything. He did everything wrong and he did everything right."

To hear Flowers tell it, his true success wasn't found on the Vegas Strip or even on stadium stages. For him, his bright side has been found at home. "I mean, it's been a wild ride," he said. "I've been lucky. I have three sons, and me and my wife have been married for 21 years and it's just, those are the things you start to realize, what is success? I try to instill that into my children and show them I have a great time on stage, I love writing songs, it's fulfilling for me. But I am so happy walking down the street with you right now. You know, I have dinner, our routine, the things that we have implemented, like those are the things that feel like true success."

title: Judi Dench on an actor's life
summary: A film producer once told Judi Dench she had "everything wrong with her face." One Oscar and a Damehood later, she's had the last laugh. The actress, now 91, talks about her new memoir, "Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It?"
story: Judi Dench has made a career out of delivering just the right words, such as ait ("It's an island in a river"). During a game of Bananagrams with a friend, we saw the 91-year-old is still very much in command. "Don't expect any vowels, because I've got them all," she laughed.
Although she can barely see the letters. "It's tricky if you're playing with an almost-blind person," she said.
Her eyesight is almost gone, robbed by macular degeneration, but there's no diminishing Dame Judi Dench.

She got her start on stage in 1957 as Ophelia in "Hamlet" at London's Old Vic Theatre. Her first starring role in film came 40 years later, in "Mrs. Brown." But her loyalties are clear. "Oh, theater, theater, theater, theater," Dench said.
Asked what she loves so much about the theater, she replied, "I love the fact of a group of people trying to get it better every night, whereas in film, they say 'Cut,' and you can't make it better."

A meeting with a movie producer early on was not encouraging: "'I'm sorry,' he said, 'you have every single thing wrong with your face.' So I said, 'Fine,' and I walked out and back to the glorious Old Vic."
She says that criticism didn't get to her: "No, because I didn't want to do films. But it must have stayed with me, and, I mean, I suppose my insides have dealt with it."

Her face would become one of the best-known in cinema. She has been nominated for eight Academy Awards, winning an Oscar for her portrayal of Queen Elizabeth I in "Shakespeare in Love"; and she's appeared in eight James Bond films as M, the steely MI6 boss, originally opposite Pierce Brosnan.

"Pierce came to lunch not long ago," Dench said. "When he got to the front door, what I'd forgotten was that I have a doormat which says, 'I've been expecting you, Mr. Bond…' He liked that. I think he thought I'd put it there for the occasion!"
What did they talk about? "Oh, everything, everything, of how frightened we were doing the first one together."
Why frightened of shooting a Bond film? "Well, the responsibility of the part," she said.

It's those sorts of stories that ended up in her new memoir, "Is It Too Late to Make a Run for It?" Written with her friend of 30 years and fellow actor Brendan O'Hea, it's a series of conversations – the books reads like the two of them having a chat. "That is exactly how it evolved," Dench said. "He knows too much about me, and what he doesn't know, he makes up."

"Not true!" O'Hea interjected. "Working on this book has made me realize I knew Jude to be fun and generous and kind, and a fantastic, life-affirming human being, and a mischief-maker. But you realize all that was in embryo in her childhood. It was all there, and I think when you read about the childhood and your faith, your Quakerism, I think that is what's kind of probably shaped you."
"And being part of a happy family," she said. "How lucky."

At her home in England, she's planted trees in memory of friends and family, including her late husband, actor Michael Williams. She says it was friendship at first sight: "Yes, and a sense of humor, and daftness."
She planted a crabapple for Maggie Smith: "Well, because she was a terrific friend, and because she was unbelievably witty and funny. And I thought it actually suited her very well!"
Over the years, Dench has found herself in rather good company. She recalls a knock on her door and Sidney Poitier walking in. She felt 'completely dumbstruck" she said.
Does she really get starstruck still? "You are joking!" Dench replied.
But you're Dame Judi Dench! "Seth, that doesn't matter – Sidney Poitier!"
Yet, Dench doesn't believe that others might feel the same sense of awe when meeting her. "No, they don't," she said.

O'Hea said to Dench, "I think you mean that. I think that you are genuinely surprised when people come up to you and say nice things. You have no vanity. I think it goes back to that moment when that film producer said you have everything wrong with your face. I think something was lodged there."
"Did me a good service," Dench said. "I don't think I do have much vanity."
In her book, Dench is also very frank about aging. "There's nothing to be said for it, at all," she said. "I can't now read, I can't go to the theater."
And so, she says, she cannot take on roles anymore. "It's because I can't see, so there's nothing I can do."
But she does remember lines. "Oh yes, I can remember all sorts of lines," she said. "I could do an hour of Shakespeare for you now."
And so, we asked if she could give us an example. She recited from "Antony and Cleopatra," and did so flawlessly: Dame Judi Dench still has these lines deep in her.

I dreamt there was an Emperor AntonyO, such another sleep, that I might seeBut such another man …His legs bestrid the ocean, his reared armCrested the world. His voice was propertiedAs all the tuned spheres, and that to friends …For his bounty, there was no winter in 't …In his livery walked crowns and crownets;Think you there was, or might be such a man,as this I dreamed of?

title: Enrolling in Medicare? Here's what to consider before Dec. 7.
summary: Medicare open enrollment, which runs from Oct.15 to Dec. 7, gives people a chance to change their health coverage. Here's what to know.
story: The Medicare open enrollment window has arrived, giving millions of seniors across the U.S. the chance to revisit their coverage choices. Even if you're happy with your plan, experts say it's still worth exploring your options.

Health plans change every year, meaning people could see updates to premium costs, prescription drug coverage and available providers in their network. New plans also come online, expanding the already broad list of coverage options.
"There's really no one who can't benefit from at least taking some time to take a look," Alex Cottrill, senior policy analyst with KFF's program on Medicare policy, told CBS News.

People enrolled in Medicare Advantage or a Part D prescription drug plan typically receive an "Annual Notice of Change" in September outlining any updates to their coverage, according to Medicare.gov, the government website for the program.

"Pay attention to those notices, and frankly, even if you don't receive an annual notice of change, you still want to review your current plan and make sure that it is the right one for you," said Jessica Rivkin, vice president of Reliance Medicare Advisors, an insurance agency that helps people enroll in Medicare Advantage plans.
Americans now have less than a month to make their Medicare choices, with open enrollment set to close Dec. 7. Here are some considerations as you navigate the process.
Choosing between Medicare and Medicare Advantage

One of the biggest decisions people face when enrolling in Medicare is whether to choose traditional Medicare or Medicare Advantage, a comprehensive plan in which private insurers are paid to manage your care.

By contrast, people who enroll in regular Medicare plans must separately select a Medicare Part D prescription drug plan and Medigap, private insurance people can layer on top of their plan to help defray out-of-pocket costs.
"You only have to pick one plan rather than having these modular options that you have in traditional Medicare," Cottrill said of Medicare Advantage.

A drawback of Medicare Advantage is its more stringent requirements. Some plans only allow you to visit in-network providers. If the plan does allow you to go out-of-network, you may face steeper cost-sharing rates, Cottrill said.

"That's a consideration for people who have either a preferred provider that they really want to stay with ...or people who have really complex health needs where they have to see maybe a lot of different specialists, or they need a very specialized type of care," he told CBS News.

For those leaning towards Medicare Advantage, Cottrill said it's worth double-checking that the providers you need are covered by the plan. People should also consider what it might mean for the Medigap coverage, he said.

If people enroll in Medicare Advantage and later switch back to traditional Medicare, they may face higher premiums due to their age or pre-existing conditions, compared to someone who enrolled in Medigap through a traditional Medicare plan from the outset, according to Cottrill.
Comparing plans

Cottrill said a good place to start is Plan Finder, a tool offered by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) that allows people to compare Medicare Advantage plans and Part D plans and to see whether providers are in-network.
The website, however, is just a jumping-off point. People should still conduct independent research to ensure their coverage needs are met, Cottrill said.
"If something is really crucial for somebody's care, they should reach out to the plan directly, talk to their provider directly and don't just rely on the website," he told CBS News.

For general information, people can contact 1-800-Medicare, the CMS-run helpline for Medicare information, or consult their State Health Insurance Assistance Program, which provides more tailored counseling.

Seniors may also consider working with a broker who can help sort through the different options. But they should keep in mind that these people may have a financial stake in their decision, Cottrill said.
"They're often paid on commission," he said. "That's not to say that they can't be helpful, but it's worth getting a second opinion from someone who doesn't have that financial stake."
Enrollment timeline
The plan you choose during open enrollment takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027, for the full calendar year.

While the deadline to make changes is Dec. 7, some people have some extra wiggle room. Medicare Advantage enrollees can switch to another Medicare Advantage plan from Jan. 1 through March 31 during a separate enrollment period.

"You can also choose to leave your Medicare Advantage plan and return to original Medicare during that same time frame, with the option of also enrolling in a Part D plan," said Will Kinkead, associate vice president of Reliance Medicare Advisors.
Some people also qualify for special enrollment periods if they move or lose access to their current health care coverage and need to make a change.

As people research Medicare plan options, they may find they need to chase down details from their providers or consult with an expert. So it's important not to wait until the last minute to start the enrollment process, Rivkin said.

"This can be a really complicated decision for some people, so take the time to get comfortable with the questions you have, what you need in 2027, and make sure that you're getting all of your needs covered," she told CBS News.

title: Seeking relief from chronic pain
summary: With about one in four American adults living with chronic pain, Dr. Jon LaPook examines some of the current treatments, from medications and surgery, to nerve stimulation, biofeedback and self-hypnosis.
story: Veterinarian Dr. Troy Hudnall enjoyed an active practice in Missouri. But in 2022, during an intense delivery of a calf, he felt a sharp pain, and heard a strange sound: "A snap or a pop, snap's probably the best way to describe it," he said.

Herniated discs and a pinched nerve in his neck caused numbness and severe muscle loss in Hudnall's right hand: "The first thing that I really remember is, I couldn't click my mouse on my computer. I started having trouble with instruments. Anything that required much agility in the fingers was almost gone."

Hudnall had multiple surgeries to help free up the nerves, but as sensation returned, he began experiencing severe pain … pain so bad, he says, he thought about amputating his own arm. Asked to describe how it felt, Hudnall replied, "For me, it's always been electricity. If you've ever touched an electric fence on a farm, or accidentally touched both prongs while you're plugging something in, it's that, but it's repetitive, it pulses."

That chronic pain has haunted Hudnall for three years now, forcing him to stop working. He treats it with a daily handful of pills, including opioids, and has tried red light therapy, physical therapy, electrical spine stimulation, and lidocaine injections. But despite all that, he says he experiences pain every second of every day. Rating his pain level from zero to ten, Hudnall says his "best days" rank at six to eight.
About one in four American adults lives with chronic pain, defined as pain lasting more than three months. Most are still suffering a year later.
"When you have chronic pain day in, day out, you're just inundated with this signal all the time; it's crushing you completely," said pain specialist Dr. Lara Crock.
A global problem

We followed Hudnall's care at one of the nation's top pain centers, the Washington University School of Medicine Pain Center in St. Louis, where, Crock explained, patients often end up trying many different approaches. "We throw medicines at it, we try different injections, we try different procedures," she said. "But really, we don't have a full understanding of why one person with the same injury continues to hurt while the other person heals and no longer hurts."

Treating chronic pain requires understanding the different ways a body can react to a painful stimulus. For example, when a person burns their hand, an electrical signal travels up nerves in the arm to the spine, then on to brain cells that interpret that signal as pain. In most people, once the painful stimulus stops, the sensation of pain stops. But not always.

Crock said, "The tissue that was injured before may be healed, or the injury that you had is recovered, but that signal continues to go and go." Why? "We don't know!" she said. "Your arm is totally normal, every scan, everything about your arm is completely normal, but there's an area of your brain that is affecting your hand that's damaged and causes your arm to hurt all the time."

Chronic pain is a global problem. Over the last 35 years, more than 900 journals in 86 countries have published thousands of articles about chronic pain. Approaches to treatment include using devices that stimulate the vagus nerve in the neck to lower pain in patients with rheumatoid arthritis or migraine headaches. And researchers are testing new non-opioid medications that block tiny gateways in nerve cells (called sodium channels) to keep pain signals from traveling to the brain.
Biofeedback

At Washington University, researchers are trying to lower pain by "retraining" the brain. Doctors Eric Leuthardt and Simon Haroutounian have come up with a headset, wearable at home, that uses biofeedback to train patients to increase certain brain waves that ease pain. "We have conducted a pilot in a small group of about six patients with chronic pain that was non-responsive to other treatments, like surgery, medications," said Haroutounian. "And everyone improved to some extent."

The positive assets of the device, Leuthardt said, include, "It's not a drug, it's got no pathologic side effects, it's not addictive, and in many ways, [it] empowers the patient to rehabilitate their own neural circuits for improvement."
Self-hypnosis

Still in early research stages, that headset isn't ready for patients like Troy Hudnall. But since last May, Hudnall has been trying hypnosis, in sessions conducted by pain psychologist Sarah Buday. "Clinical hypnosis is not your Las Vegas stage show; I'm not trying to make anyone cluck like a chicken or be under my control," Buday said. "The way I think of it is, I'm teaching somebody the skill of self-hypnosis. We are having them go into a very deep state of relaxation, at which point, I start to make suggestions about maybe the quality of the pain or the meaning of it, their emotions."
Several weeks ago, with the help of self-hypnosis, Hudnall endured another surgery. As for his future, he says he tries to remain positive.
And Buday is positive about Hudnall's outlook as well: "I think it's good. It's already getting better. And he is somebody that has a lot of optimism and hope."

And Lara Crock says, even if – despite all you throw at it – pain is only partially relieved, "It can be the difference from being able to get up and take your kid to school or eat breakfast or dinner with your family, versus laying in bed all day. So, that can be huge."

title: Microsoft says it "restored service" after major worldwide outage
summary: A Microsoft outage involving services like Outlook and Teams impacted many users, companies and government services.
story: Microsoft said early Saturday it had restored its services after a worldwide outage which involved services like Outlook and Teams impacted users, companies and government operations around the world.
In a post on X, the company said: "We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions."

The disruption, which lasted over 24 hours, affected a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down.
Microsoft said the outage was linked to a technical issue, not malicious or cyber activity, and apologised for the incident.

"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," the company said Friday on X. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."

The outage affected Microsoft's suite of business products, as well as those tailored for personal use by individuals, students and families. Users in more than 70 countries and territories experienced disruptions, according to Downdetector, a website that tracks technology outages.

"Microsoft in a Friday the 13th moment as global outage [causes] a very bad day in Redmond," Yorkville Ives and Co. tech analyst Dan Ives said in an X post Friday. "There will be major questions for MSFT in this global outage."

Charles Lamanna, executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform at Microsoft, said in a social media post Friday that "technical challenges and failure modes" made the recovery process "more difficult than normal."

"I'm working closely with the engineering team to complete the full post-mortem," Lamanna said in the post. "We will publish the post-mortem shortly covering the step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future."
Widespread impact
Microsoft first flagged technical issues just before 1 p.m. ET Thursday. The company updated users about its recovery progress through a series of posts on its Microsoft 365 Status X account.
More than 130,000 users reported issues with Microsoft on Thursday, Downdetector's website shows. However, those reports started to wane by Friday morning as Microsoft worked to restore its services.
The outage disrupted email for hours, hampering work activity for some employees.
"It's just challenging sending reports or things that needed to be approved," one woman told CBS News Los Angeles.
However, some took delight in the slowdown, with social media users posting videos celebrating the freedom of not having access to email.
It's unclear how many people were impacted. More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, according to Microsoft's website.
Companies worldwide report issues

OpenAI and Anthropic each reported problems connecting to Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects of outages as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies' software.
U.S.-based industrial technology company Workhorse Group Inc. delayed a conference call on its quarterly earnings because of the outage.
In Australia, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Friday that Microsoft had likened the widespread outage to the CrowdStrike outage in 2024.
Burke said he had spoken to Microsoft's top executive in Australia and the government's national cybersecurity coordinator about the global disruption.

"They (Microsoft) don't believe they are dealing with a cyberattack. They believe that they are dealing in some ways (with something) similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Burke told reporters in Sydney.

Texas-based cybersecurity company CrowdStrike blamed a bug in an update that allowed its systems to push bad data out to millions of customer computers, setting off a global tech outage in July 2024 that grounded flights, took TV broadcasts off the air and disrupted banks, hospitals and retailers.

Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum firm, said his company's Outlook accounts couldn't receive updates from its U.S. customers due to the outage. If the situation dragged on further, it could "impact the production timeline," he said.

Air India said its flight operations were unaffected by the Microsoft outage. However, it temporarily rerouted its email services to ensure customer queries continued to reach the airline without interruption, the company said in a statement.

IndiGo, another Indian airline company, said it also reported disruptions to its email support services, which affected its ability to receive customer queries. The airline in a statement on X said its other support channels remained operational and its flight operations were unaffected.
Singapore's Government Technology Agency said government email services were down and that it is working with Microsoft to resolve the issue.
The Philippines' Supreme Court said in a statement on social media that the ongoing Microsoft 365 service outage had affected some of its operations, including email responses.
In Japan, Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said the outage impacted the government's IT infrastructure and that officials were "keeping a close eye on the developments."

title: Lutnick agrees to testify as Bessent blames him for chip sales
summary: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10, according to a U.S. official.
story: Washington — Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10, according to a U.S. official, amid intensifying scrutiny of the Commerce Department's oversight of the export of powerful AI chips following the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

A growing number of Republicans are calling on Lutnick to answer questions about the Commerce Department's apparent delay in adding Singapore-based company Megaspeed International to the U.S. government's Entity List, which would have restricted the company's ability to get access to advanced AI chips.

Megaspeed was previously led by Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy who had an affair with Jensen Huang. The U.S. government suspects Megaspeed of directing advanced Nvidia chips to China, circumventing a U.S. export ban.

GOP Sen. Jim Banks of Indiana, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, told Fox News on Thursday that "we know that the Department of Commerce, Secretary Lutnick, it appears, used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur even though President Trump has directed his administration and the Department of Commerce not to allow that to happen."

On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent repeatedly emphasized that the Treasury Department and other parts of the executive branch had pushed for restrictions on Megaspeed, laying the blame for the delay at the feet of the Commerce Department.

"Treasury, War, [the U.S. Trade Representative] and State, they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the Entity List for months, but Commerce has the pen," Bessent told CNBC. "And you will have to ask them about their internal processes."
Bessent declined to comment on reported tensions between himself and Lutnick. The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.

title: Never bought Nvidia stock? Its slide could still hit your 401(k).
summary: Millions of Americans are exposed to Nvidia shares through their retirement plans. That's not as bad as it sounds (really!).
story: Even if you never bought a single share of Nvidia, the embattled chipmaker's steep slide this week could still ding your retirement savings.

Nvidia is a component of the S&P 500 and many other indexes, including the Nasdaq 100 and Dow Jones Industrial Average, all popular with retirement savers through funds offered by millions of employer retirement plans. About 97% of retirement plans now offer index funds, up from 79% in 2006, according to March research from the Investment Company Institute and ISS Market Intelligence.

That means even if you haven't directly bought Nvidia stock, your 401(k) is likely exposed to the chipmaker through an index fund, such as the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust or Vanguard's S&P 500 ETF (which trade under the tickers SPY and VOO, respectively).
Overall, Nvidia represents about 6% of the S&P 500 index, making it the second-largest component after Apple, according to Yahoo Finance.

Nvidia's shares started falling on Monday amid revelations that cofounder Jensen Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Huang resigned from his role as CEO on Thursday, causing a further drop in the stock.

Since Nov. 6, the company's value has declined by more than $550 billion — a decline of about 13% in one week. While that will certainly hurt investors who directly own Nvidia shares, it may also impact people with indirect investments through funds that hold the chipmaker.

Nvidia's woes underline the risks inherent in many big tech companies widely held by U.S. investors, Shiva Rajgopal, a Columbia Business School professor who studies corporate governance, told CBS News.

The "Magnificent Seven" tech stocks account for about one-third of the S&P 500. As with Nvidia, several of those companies are closely associated with CEOs whom investors see as central to their success, such as Elon Musk at Tesla, Rajgopal noted. And as Nvidia's selloff showed this week, trouble for a charismatic CEO can quickly spill over into the company's stock.

"They are amazing wealth creators for shareholders," Rajgopal said. "But hopefully, shareholders know what they are doing when they buy the stock of these companies, because the exact same structure also has a lot of fragility built into it."
A drag on the S&P 500

The AI industry's influence on Wall Street was evident this week, as turmoil at Nvidia triggered a broader slump in technology stocks. Yet more companies within the S&P 500 rose rather than fell this week, boosting the index by 2.9% for the week through Thursday's close. Excluding Nvidia, the index would have gained an estimated 3.8%.

"If you check your account today, tomorrow, you're going to see some sort of fluctuation, especially if you own shares of Nvidia," Sabrina Escobar, a reporter at Barron's, told CBS News. "The decline we saw over the past couple of days will certainly have some implications in your daily or weekly stock movements."

For investors, Huang's sudden downfall and Nvidia's wobbly stock highlight the importance of properly diversifying their portfolios, Mercer Advisors chief investment officer Donald Calcagni said in a blog post.

"Events like this — where the outcome hinges on one company's leadership — are a risk we try to minimize through diversification," he wrote. "This is the core principle behind portfolio diversification strategies: spread your risk broadly enough that no single company's troubles can derail your long-term plan."

Of course, that's the idea behind holding a broad-based index fund like the S&P 500 — rather than concentrating your money in a handful of individual stocks, you're spreading your bets across hundreds of types of companies. And the fact that the S&P 500 is on track to post a weekly gain despite Nvidia's turmoil points to how that strategy can pay off.
Timing is not on your side

Investors may be tempted to sell when the market, a stock or a fund tumbles, but research has repeatedly shown that trying to determine the right time to buy or sell an investment usually results in losses.

Meanwhile, tech experts noted that Nvidia's chips remain essential to the artificial intelligence sector, a key competitive edge unlikely to change in the near term even with Huang's abrupt departure. In other words, holding Nvidia shares may be a way to bet on the broader AI industry, rather than on its executive roster.

"When a single company's stock drops on unexpected news, the best response is usually the simplest one: pause, keep the news in perspective and let your diversified portfolio do what it was designed to do," Calcagni said.

title: Family Dollar to pay $63M after FTC says it overcharged customers
summary: The discount retailer failed to honor prices displayed on store shelves, on price tags and in ads, the FTC and multiple states alleged.
story: Family Dollar has agreed to pay $63 million to settle allegations that it routinely overcharged customers by millions of dollars.
The Federal Trade Commission and 17 U.S. states accused the budget retailer of failing to honor prices displayed on store shelves, on price tags and in advertisements.

A proposed order bans Family Dollar from misleading customers on prices and requires the company to adopt what the FTC described as a "pricing accuracy program" that is independently assessed and certified annually.

"Today's order will ensure Family Dollar stops deceiving consumers about its prices and returns money to consumers harmed by these practices," Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement on Thursday.
Family Dollar operates more than 7,000 stores across 48 U.S. states and Washington, D.C. The Chesapeake, Virginia-based company did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the settlement.

The FTC and the states' complaint alleged that pricing inaccuracies are widespread at Family Dollar stores and that the retailer failed to correct errors. Customers regularly reported being charged higher prices at the register than those displayed on goods' price tags, in stores, on the retailer's website and in its mobile app, according to the complaint.
The states include Alabama, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Iowa, Illinois, Kansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Nebraska, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin.
In October, the FTC and 20 states sued another discount retailer, Dollar General, over allegations of similar deceptive pricing practices. The litigation is ongoing.
Customer refunds and discounts
The proposed order requires Family Dollar to establish a $40 million fund to compensate eligible customers.

The retailer will notify customers of their eligibility for reimbursement through in-store notices and online. Eligible customers include anyone who made a purchase at a Family Dollar store from Jan. 1, 2023, to Oct. 1, 2026.

The order also establishes a separate $20 million discount program for customers. Under the program, Family Dollar must offer customers 15% off a range of goods for two days. State plaintiffs will receive $3 million to be divided among them.
The retailer must create a pricing accuracy program to ensure that it regularly monitors and verifies prices and trains employees to identify and correct pricing discrepancies.

title: Inflation isn't going away. Here's what that means for interest rates.
summary: As inflation seeps deeper into the U.S. economy, the Federal Reserve may have to step up the pace of rate hikes, according to Wall Street analysts.
story: The Federal Reserve is likely to accelerate the pace of interest rate hikes to rein in stubbornly high inflation, according to a growing number of Wall Street analysts.

Aditya Bhave, a U.S. economist with BofA Global Research, expects monetary policymakers to raise the Fed's benchmark rate by 0.25 percentage points at each of the central bank's next three meetings in December, January and March. Analysts at TD Securities also predict three straight quarter-point hikes, up from their previous forecast of two, because hotter inflation signals that price pressures across the U.S. are broadening.
The latest Consumer Price Index showed that inflation rose more than expected in October, climbing 0.4%.

"Inflation is not trending in the right direction," TD Securities said Friday in a note to investors. "The October report not only surprised our own forecast, it was also not driven by a particular factor or two as had been the case in recent reports. Price pressures appear to be broadening."

Hotter inflation in October was the third straight month that prices have risen faster than expected amid supply constraints and ample economic demand, according to EY-Parthenon chief economist Gregory Daco, who is penciling in rate hikes for December and January.

"For any borrower, this will mean a high cost of borrowing for any type of consumer loan people take out," Daco told CBS News. "A higher federal funds rate trajectory will generally mean higher long-term interest rates and increase the cost of borrowing for consumers across the country."

Interest rate traders put the odds of a quarter-point hike at the Fed's next meeting on Dec. 8-9 at nearly 90%, and also see a better-than-even chance of another such hike at the Jan. 26-27 gathering, according to CME FedWatch.

Some Fed officials themselves have said tightening may need to be more aggressive to bring inflation in line with their 2% annual target. At a conference in London on Tuesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said policymakers should consider a 0.50 percentage-point increase in December, adding that a smaller hike "would put our credibility at risk."
High energy prices continue to drive inflation, along with robust corporate spending on data centers and other equipment for powering AI.
"Together, these forces could keep inflation elevated into 2027 and weigh further on household purchasing power," Daco said in a report.

title: As Americans drown in medical debt, how one family found a lifeline
summary: Coy and Caty Smith are gainfully employed and have health insurance. But when illness struck, the bills piled up fast — here's how they found their way back to financial health.
story: Coy Smith and his wife were getting up to 16 phone calls a day, all to discuss the same topic — how they planned to pay off the thousands of dollars in medical bills their family had racked up after facing a series of serious healthcare issues.
By 2023, the family was more than $30,000 in the hole, including credit card debt they had taken on to help pay their medical bills.

"It's very stressful knowing that every time the phone rings, you have to pick it up and talk to someone who says you owe them thousands of dollars for something you couldn't help," Coy, 32, a Cypress, Texas, resident, told CBS News.
40% of Americans

The phone is also ringing off the hook for millions of other people facing overdue healthcare bills. Roughly 40% of Americans are saddled with debt for medical care not covered by insurance, treatment for complex medical conditions, and hospitalization costs for serious injuries or illnesses, according to health policy and research firm KFF.

Those debts are often financially debilitating, with high healthcare costs topping the list of financial worries for U.S. voters, a recent KFF poll shows. To stay on top of their medical bills, people may cut spending on essentials like food, exhaust emergency savings and tap their retirement funds.

"There's no other way to state it than as a parent and American, you dread having to go to the doctor and having to go to the hospital," Smith said. "You know it's going to cost thousands of dollars just to walk in the door."

Smith also said he was routinely advised to take out a personal loan to consolidate the family's crushing debt. But that approach carried its own financial risks. At the time, they calculated, it would've taken them 30 years and cost $150,000 in interest to pay down all of their debt.
Instead, the goal was "to change our relationship with credit and how we paid for things," he told CBS News.
How illness spawns debt
Smith and his wife, Caty, are both public school teachers, earning a combined income of roughly $100,000 per year plus benefits, including health insurance.

Their financial problems began in 2023, when their youngest son was hospitalized with lung problems shortly after birth. Their son's one-week stay in the hospital left the couple owing $10,000 even after insurance had covered its share.

The stress also triggered a flare-up of the autoimmune and inflammatory diseases Caty has suffered from since 2018, he told CBS News. After she missed some days at work because of her health issues, Caty's employer docked her pay, further straining the family's finances.
With lower income, the couple turned to credit to cover urgent medical costs and pay their grocery, electricity and daycare bills, resulting in a ballooning balance.

"We paid our electric bills with credit. We did anything we could to keep the lights on and make sure we could provide for the family," Smith said. "At one point, we even had to put daycare on our credit cards. We were unable to keep up with payments and interest rates, and found ourselves in this revolving cycle of debt."

Making ends meet was difficult, and even small unexpected expenses could make budgeting all but impossible, Smith told CBS News. To make matters worse, the family was paying interest rates of up to 30% on some of their debt.
"Any time we would get a little bit of air, we would blow a tire on the car, or an appliance would go out, or something along those lines would happen," he said.
Getting back on track

Knowing they needed help, the Smiths turned to Money Management International, a nationally accredited credit counseling firm. Working with a debt counselor, they took stock of all their obligations and set about negotiating lower interest rates with creditors. That allowed them to form a repayment plan.

"They would negotiate a lower interest rate and plan a time period where we would make X number of payments at X value, and within a set time period that debt would be paid off," Smith said of working with a counselor.

The family wanted to be aggressive, but realistic, in paying off debt. That meant thinking long-term — their goal was to have it all paid off by the time the Smiths' two children had left daycare and entered the local public school system.

"We wanted to have it paid off so we could enter the next phase of life without credit card debt hanging over our heads," Smith told CBS News. "We put together a plan we could afford, which was $400 less than if we'd continued to pay minimum monthly payments on our own."
Inevitably, escaping debt also required belt-tightening and greater prudence in how they spent money.

"We are very careful about where we spend money, avoiding any consumer debt, avoiding things like buy now, pay later loans," he said. "We are smarter about looking at interest rates before entering into agreements."

Four years later, the Smiths are on track to be fully out of debt by the end of 2027. The experience, while harrowing, has at least made Smith think long and hard about how to change the family's financial behaviors to avoid future problems.

Smith added, "If we have our debt paid off by the time our oldest son is 7, and our youngest is 4, they have the rest of their childhoods to enjoy trips together. We can enjoy them, too, knowing we are not burying ourselves in insurmountable debt while doing it."

title: U.S. gave Singapore scant help with Alice Huang probe, source says
summary: Singapore held Alice Huang's passport for 8 months and asked the U.S. to help investigate her firm's suspected Nvidia chip sales, but received little help, sources say.
story: Singaporean authorities seized the passport of then-Megaspeed chief executive Alice Huang in June 2025 and held it for eight months, preventing her departure while trying to engage the U.S. government to support their investigation into advanced Nvidia chips possibly being shipped to China.

One source with knowledge of the matter told CBS News on Friday the Singaporean government received no meaningful help from Washington during the time she was in the Asian city-state. This source said officials in Washington were "not forthcoming" in response to Singapore's requests for help, and no substantive assistance has been provided to date.
Singapore's government confirmed in a statement this week that it reached out to both the U.S. Department of Justice and the FBI for assistance with its investigation.
Alice Huang is the suspected Chinese spy at the center of the extramarital affair scandal that toppled Nvidia founder Jensen Huang from the helm of the global tech giant he built over three decades.

Since February 2025, Singaporean authorities have been investigating whether Alice Huang and Megaspeed worked with California-based Supermicro to ship the Silicon Valley firm's computer servers — equipped with advanced Nvidia chips — to China, the source told CBS News.
Alice Huang flew into Singapore in June 2025 for a voluntary interview with Singapore-based investigators from the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security, according to the source.

The agency sits within the U.S. Department of Commerce and regulates the export of sensitive products on national security and economic grounds. The American authorities requested the interview, according to a Thursday statement by Singapore's Home Affairs Ministry, as part of a post-shipment verification check, a process used to determine whether imported products have reached their declared recipient.
Singaporean police also interviewed Huang on the same day as the U.S. officials, and made the decision to impound her passport.
The source said it was not known where Huang, a Chinese national, arrived in Singapore from in June 2025.

By February 2026, however, the Singapore Police Force had not charged Huang with any crime and had no option but to return her passport, the source told CBS News. She was barred from ever returning to Singapore, as authorities assessed that she had given "inaccurate information" to downplay her role at Megaspeed, as noted in the statement from the home ministry.
That statement was released four days after Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman who sources confirmed to CBS News was Alice Huang.

Singapore's investigation has focused on whether the then-Megaspeed CEO may have broken domestic law by lying about the details of purchases of computer servers from Supermicro, a San Jose-based technology company. The company's servers use Nvidia's advanced chips to run artificial intelligence software, data centers and cloud computing.

"The suspected domestic offenses pertained to potential false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers and other related offenses," Singapore's Home Affairs Ministry said in its statement this week.
Singaporean investigators have tried to determine the true ultimate destination of the Supermicro servers ordered by Megaspeed.

A second source familiar with the investigation told CBS News it is believed they may have been sent to Malaysia, but Singaporean investigators suspect "some or all" of them may then have been shipped onward to China. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.
Singapore's home ministry attempted to contact Supermicro, but the U.S. company only "provided limited cooperation," according to the home ministry statement.

The New York Times reported Wednesday that Malaysia kept Nvidia's chips and installed them in its own data centers, but then rented use of those centers to China, rather than physically shipping any chips to China.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Friday that there was "no indication" any chips linked to the Nvidia-Megaspeed issue had been re-exported out of the country.

Beijing has dismissed the claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China." Asked Thursday about a Bloomberg report that she had returned to China, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters: "I do not have information on what you mentioned."
Since 2022, the U.S. has restricted the export of Nvidia's most powerful chips to China over national security concerns as the world's two biggest economies race for dominance in the AI sector.

The Singapore police first raised the issue with U.S. authorities in July 2025 to try to secure Supermicro's cooperation in revealing where its servers were ultimately ending up, repeating requests "on several occasions to the U.S. Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation," according to the Home Affairs Ministry's Thursday statement.

The second source confirmed to CBS News that Washington did not meaningfully engage with the requests for help on the investigation and said it "would be useful to know" what Supermicro declared about its exports to fulfill orders by Megaspeed, whether those products were registered as being bound for Malaysia, and whether some or all of those products were actually "bound for somewhere else," such as China.

The Singapore home ministry said in its statement that six other individuals linked to Megaspeed, in addition to Alice Huang, are wanted for questioning, but none have been in the country since the government launched its investigation in February 2025.
"One is a Singaporean citizen and the rest are foreigners," said the first person familiar with the case.

Singapore has charged five other people in a wider fraud conspiracy case related to the suspected transfer of Nvidia chips, including one Chinese man charged on Friday. The case was launched at the same time as the probe into Alice Huang and Megaspeed, the first source told CBS News, but it is separate.

"Singapore is committed to upholding our reputation as a trusted and reliable business hub. We will not allow companies or individuals to misuse Singapore's business environment to engage in fraud or dishonest practices," the home ministry said in its statement, adding that it would "conduct its own investigations independently, in accordance with our laws and based on the evidence available. We will cooperate with foreign authorities where appropriate, and take firm enforcement action wherever the evidence warrants it."

title: China warns against new U.S. export controls on computer chips
summary: China is warning the U.S. against putting new export controls on semiconductors in the wake of the scandal surrounding​ AI chip giant Nvidia and its now-former CEO Jensen Huang.
story: China warned the United States on Friday against imposing additional controls on exports of semiconductors in the wake of the scandal surrounding AI chip giant Nvidia and its now-former CEO Jensen Huang.

China "has consistently opposed the abuse of export control measures, which disrupts the stability of global industrial and supply chains and serves no party's interests," foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told a regular press briefing when asked about calls from U.S. lawmakers to impose more limits on exports of chip equipment to China.

"China and the United States should work together to implement the important consensus reached by their respective heads of state and maintain the stable development of China-U.S. economic and trade relations," Mao said.
Jensen Huang — who resigned Thursday — has admitted to an affair, reportedly with Alice Huang, a former senior executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. They're not related.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under fire from critics asking whether his ties to Chinese companies and friendship with Jensen Huang contributed to a lack of oversight by the federal agency over billions in Nvidia AI chip sales, CBS News has learned. The Commerce Department did not respond to a request for comment.

During an interview on CNBC on Friday morning, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent placed the blame on Lutnick's Commerce Department for not including Megaspeed on what's known as the Entity List, which would restrict their ability to access U.S. technology products.
Bessent said that his department as well as the Defense Department, State Department and U.S. trade representative all supported adding Megaspeed to the list.

"They were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the Entity List for months," Bessent said, before referring to the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security. "Commerce BIS has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes."
According to a U.S. official, Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10.

Last month, the New York Times reported that about a year ago, President Trump was briefed on intelligence that suggested that Alice Huang was a Chinese asset and that she had grown close to Jensen Huang and the president decided not to do anything with the information.
House Speaker Mike Johnson said there's a growing consensus in Congress on further tightening controls on chip exports to China.
According to the Times, U.S. officials circulated a memo last spring citing intelligence alleging that Alice Huang was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, its main intelligence service.
Beijing has rejected the allegations and said on Thursday that they are a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" to stop China advancing in artificial intelligence technology.

title: Major AI developers can't control their own tech, lawsuit alleges
summary: Companies including Anthropic, Meta and OpenAI are knowingly building technology that poses catastrophic risks to humanity, nonprofit groups claim in a lawsuit.
story: A coalition of nonprofit groups sued five major artificial intelligence developers on Thursday in a bid to block their development of AI models, alleging the companies knowingly created technology that poses catastrophic risks to humanity.

The lawsuit — filed in San Francisco Superior Court by the Alliance for Secure AI, alongside advocacy groups Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen and the Heat Initiative — named Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceXSI (SpaceX Super Intelligence).
"For years, the executives building these systems have warned us that their own frontier models pose catastrophic risks," Brendan Steinhauser, CEO of The Alliance for Secure AI, said in a statement.
"Yet they keep racing to develop and market increasingly powerful AI that they admit they cannot reliably control, and are now handing over AI research and development to AI itself," he added.
A Meta spokesperson for Meta declined to comment. The other tech companies targeted in the suit did not respond to a request for comment.
The litigation comes amid broader concerns about AI safety, sparked by several publicly reported incidents in which AI agents went rogue and carried out unauthorized actions.

The nonprofit groups contend that AI companies are developing technology they have admitted they can't control. The risk could grow as the companies rely more on their own AI models to develop future platforms without human intervention, a concept known as "recursive self-improvement," according to the suit.

"Defendants know these systems do not consistently act in accordance with their intentions," the lawsuit states. "And Defendants know there is no reliable method to control their AI systems and prevent them from causing harm."

The nonprofits also point to past comments by AI company executives acknowledging the potential harm from their technology. In 2015, for example, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said AI will "probably most likely lead to the end of the world." In 2025, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei suggested there was a 25% chance that the development of AI could lead to disastrous outcomes.

As scrutiny of their tech's safety grows, tech leaders have underlined their safety commitments. AI company leaders, including Altman, Amodei and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, in October voiced support for an industrywide slowdown in AI development after an Anthropic employee said there's a 10% chance AI "could kill all humans."
