title: New congressman faces sexual harassment allegation
summary: House Democrats are investigating an allegation of sexual harassment against Brian Poindexter, who defeated embattled GOP Rep. Max Miller.
story: Washington — House Democrats are investigating an allegation of sexual harassment against Brian Poindexter, who defeated embattled GOP Rep. Max Miller of Ohio in last week's elections.

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, House Democrats' campaign arm, said Friday that it had hired an independent firm to investigate "any instance of inappropriate behavior, conduct interviews and gather the facts."
"The DCCC has been made aware of the allegations and takes them seriously," the group's executive director, Julie Merz, said in a statement.
A spokesperson for Poindexter's campaign characterized his actions as "an innocuous compliment to a volunteer."

"He heard later that it made her feel uncomfortable and he felt awful," the spokesperson said in a statement. "When Brian learned about this, we immediately began to work to get to the bottom of it with an outside HR firm. Neither Brian nor the campaign ever wants anyone to feel uncomfortable."
The investigation comes as Congress grapples with how to overhaul how it handles allegations of sexual misconduct as numerous lawmakers have faced complaints.

The DCCC was made aware of the allegations from two political action committees — the Blue Dog PAC and the Congressional Progressive Caucus PAC — which said they were informed of a report of alleged sexual harassment in the final days before the election.

"We informed the DCCC and connected the individual with legal advocacy and support services so she could determine how she wanted to proceed," the PACs said in a joint statement Friday. "The individual requested that we did not disclose any details about this publicly because she did not want her identity becoming public and she wanted an opportunity to determine how she wanted to proceed while protecting herself."
The PACs said they pulled their endorsements from Poindexter "pending the investigation being completed."

title: Democrat Eileen Laubacher defeats Lauren Boebert in House race
summary: Colorado Democrat Eileen Laubacher has defeated incumbent Republican Congresswoman Lauren Boebert to represent the 4th Congressional District, CBS News projects.
story: More than a week after Election Day, the final votes have been tallied for Colorado's 4th Congressional District. Colorado Democrat Eileen Laubacher has defeated incumbent Republican Congresswoman Lauren Boebert to represent the 4th Congressional District, CBS News projected.
The race was very close, with just 1% of the vote separating the two candidates by the time the race was projected, 10 days after Election Day.
Earlier this week, Laubacher claimed victory over Boebert, even as thousands of votes separated the two candidates.
Boebert talked to reporters on the steps of the U.S. Capitol on Monday night, saying that all the ballots had yet to be counted.

"We've been curing ballots for over a week, and you know we... we need to make sure that every vote counts and every voice is heard. We still have military and overseas ballots that are coming in, and we'll see what that number is," said Boebert.

Laubacher is a retired two-star rear admiral in the Navy who worked on the National Security Council under President Biden. The Highlands Ranch resident used to be a Republican and then changed her party affiliation. She has described herself as a common-sense candidate who wants to get things done. She said her top priorities were keeping costs down, fighting corruption, and improving rural healthcare access.

Laubacher was at the U.S. Capitol on Monday in Washington, D.C., along with other newly-elected members of the 120th Congress for the first day of New Member Orientation after Democrats flipped both chambers in the midterm elections.
The district spans the eastern third of the state of Colorado and also includes part of Douglas County, located south of Denver, and Loveland, in Northern Colorado.
Boebert previously served two terms in the state's 3rd Congressional District before switching districts and winning in the 4th with 53.6% of the vote in 2024.

The outspoken Republican recently faced some challenges, including when a Weld County judge granted the congresswoman a temporary protection order against a man who she said is spreading lies about her and her staff. David Wheeler, who lives in North Carolina, has made claims that Boebert had sexual relationships with three of her staff members and arranged a $200,000 payment to one former aide to keep the alleged involvement quiet.
Boebert did not face a challenger in the primary election earlier this year.

title: Democrats have flipped 45 House seats. Here's the breakdown.
summary: Democrats won control of the House by flipping more than 40 Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red.
story: Washington — Democrats won control of the House of Representatives on Nov. 3 by flipping more than 40 Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red. The party's wins ranged from suburban areas in the northeastern United States to areas of South Texas that were once viewed as increasingly GOP-friendly.

The 2026 midterm elections were also shaken up by last year's nationwide mid-decade redistricting gambit, with Texas Republicans shifting several districts rightward at President Trump's behest, California Democrats moving districts to the left and several other states tweaking their House maps for partisan purposes. Democrats notched several wins under the new maps, while the GOP's pickups have been more limited so far.
Winners in a dozen House races have yet to be projected by CBS News.
So far, 45 districts have shifted to Democrats and three have shifted to Republicans. Here's a look at the seats that swung:
Upsets
In several districts, Democrats ousted GOP lawmakers who won by double digits two years ago.

New Jersey's 2nd District: Republican Rep. Jeff Van Drew lost to Democrat Zack Mullock in a South Jersey district that was widely seen as solid red. Van Drew, who won by 16.9 points in 2024, is known for switching from the Democratic Party during the first Trump impeachment saga in 2019. Ohio's 10th District: GOP Rep. Mike Turner was ousted by Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker, ending Turner's nearly quarter-century tenure in Congress just two years after he won reelection by more than 18 points.Missouri's 2nd District: Democrat Fred Wellman unseated GOP Rep. Ann Wagner, who won by 12 points in 2024. Republicans tried to make the St. Louis-area seat slightly redder last year, but the new maps were tossed out in the courts. As recently as September, the Cook Political Report viewed it as solid-red.Indiana's 5th District: Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz lost to Democrat J.D. Ford in one of several election night surprises. Spartz won reelection by just over 18 points in 2024.Kentucky's 6th District: The race between Democrat Zach Dembo and Republican Ralph Alvarado for the open seat was not expected to be competitive, but the election forecasters moved the GOP-held seat toward Democrats in recent weeks. Outgoing Rep. Andy Barr won it by 26 points two years ago.Wisconsin's 1st District: Republican Rep. Bryan Steil, who was first elected in 2018, lost his race to Democrat Mitchell Berman. A Democrat has not represented the district in more than 30 years. Steil won his last reelection by just over 10 points, outperforming Mr. Trump, and the Cook Political Report rated it "Likely Republican" until late September.Nevada's 2nd District: Teresa Benitez-Thompson will be the first Democrat to represent Northern Nevada in decades, after she defeated Republican David Flippo. The seat was left open by the retirement of longtime GOP Rep. Mark Amodei, who won by a nearly 19-point margin in 2024.Ohio's 15th District: Democrat Don Leonard defeated GOP Rep. Mike Carey, who won reelection by 13 points in 2024.

Both parties invested in districts in the Northeast, including seats with a history of swinging from one party to another, and a competitive Pennsylvania seat that was held by an overperforming Republican for a decade.

title: These House and Senate midterm races don't have winners yet
summary: Democrats won sizable House and Senate majorities in the 2026 midterm elections, but the exact margins are unclear because some races haven't been projected yet. Here's where the results stand.
story: Washington — The makeup of Congress shifted dramatically in the 2026 midterm elections, as Democrats decisively won control of the Senate and picked up dozens of House seats — in what's on track to be one of the largest midterm routs in recent decades.

The exact margins of Congress are not yet clear, as winners have not yet been projected in one Senate race and more than a dozen House races. They include GOP-held districts with razor-thin margins, a few Democratic seats that could flip to Republicans and several races in California and other Western states that still need to count ballots.
Here's a look at the congressional races that CBS News has not yet projected, including where the results stand:
Senate Battlegrounds
Democrats are set to enter next year with at least 55 Senate seats, compared to Republicans' 44. A winner still hasn't been projected in one race.

Alaska Senate: Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is running for reelection against Democrat Mary Peltola, a razor-thin race rocked by a last-minute scandal over how another Dan Sullivan got on the ballot. The count could drag on due to both outstanding ballots and Alaska's ranked choice voting system, which allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate is the top choice of a majority of voters, the last-place candidate is eliminated and the counting process moves to a second round. Final results aren't expected until 15 days after Election Day. Both the Sullivan and Peltola campaigns have argued they have the upper hand.
Democrats on Defense

The dozens of red districts that Democrats flipped were the primary story of Tuesday night, but a few Republican House candidates tried to swim against the tide, either due to redistricting or a favorable local political makeup.

Louisiana's 6th District: This formerly blue-leaning, majority-Black district was redrawn after the Supreme Court voided the state's maps, finding that mapmakers relied too heavily on race and narrowing the Voting Rights Act. It's now significantly redder, but since no candidate won a majority under the state's "jungle" primary system, it will go to a runoff between Democrat Chauna Banks and Republican Blake Miguez.
GOP-Held Battlegrounds
Several races held by Republicans still don't have projections — including in districts that Democrats are hoping to flip.

Minnesota's 1st District: Republican Rep. Brad Finstad is locked in a tight battle against Democrat Jake Johnson, after Finstad won by 17.2 points in 2024. Under state law, candidates who are behind by less than 0.25 points can request a recount.
Tennessee's 4th District: GOP Rep. Scott DesJarlais is defending his seat against Democrat Victoria Broderick. It's a red district, though it was made somewhat less red in redistricting.
North Carolina's 3rd District: GOP Rep. Greg Murphy is running against Democrat Raymond Smith. The district was made slightly bluer during redistricting last year, but it still favors Republicans.

North Carolina's 5th District: GOP Rep. Virginia Foxx is facing Democrat Chuck Hubbard. First elected over 20 years ago, Foxx is the longest-serving member of the Tar Heel State's congressional delegation, which was shaken up in the midterms, with Democrats flipping several House seats and a Senate seat.
North Carolina's 7th District: Republican Rep. David Rouzer is running against Democrat Kimberly Hardy.
North Carolina's 10th District: Republican Rep. Pat Harrigan faces Democrat Ashley Bell.
Please hold...

Results could take a while in some House districts, either because ballots still need to be counted or because of runoffs. In some California districts, both candidates belong to the same party, so they don't have any implications for the makeup of Congress.

Alaska's At-Large District: Republican Rep. Nick Begich is running against Bill Hill, an independent endorsed by Democrats, and a few other candidates. Remember: Alaska has ranked-choice elections, so further tabulation may be needed.
California's 4th District: In the Napa Valley area, longtime Rep. Mike Thompson is running against businessman and fellow Democrat Eric Jones.
California's 23rd District: Republican Rep. Jay Obernolte is running against Democrat Tessa Hodge.

Louisiana's 5th District: Democrat Patricia Moore and Republican Gabe Firment are headed to a December runoff in this deeply conservative district. It's currently held by GOP Rep. Julia Letlow, who was elected to the Senate this week.

title: Supreme Court takes up case over asylum access at border
summary: The case involving President Trump's directives suspending access to the asylum system is the latest involving the president's second-term immigration agenda.
story: Washington — The Supreme Court on Friday said it will take up a legal fight over President Trump's directive suspending access to the asylum system and other legal protections for migrants illegally crossing the southern border.

The case is the latest involving Mr. Trump's second-term immigration agenda that the Supreme Court will decide in the coming months. The justices are also considering the legality of removing migrants to third countries and indefinitely detaining immigrants in the U.S. illegally without access to a bond hearing.
A decision in the cases is expected by the end of June or early July.

Mr. Trump has made cracking down on immigration a cornerstone of his second term, which has seen enhanced enforcement operations in major U.S. cities and mass deportations of people in the U.S. illegally. Unlawful crossings at the U.S.-Mexico border have reached historic lows and immigration detentions have set new highs under the president's second administration.

As part of his efforts to curb illegal immigration into the U.S., Mr. Trump issued a proclamation on his first day back in the White House claiming that there is an "invasion" at the southern border. The president suspended the entry of migrants crossing the southern border between ports of entry and barred them from seeking asylum and other legal protections that would allow them to remain in the U.S.

The Department of Homeland Security then issued guidance implementing the president's directive. Immigration authorities have since relied on the policy to summarily remove migrants entering the country illegally without allowing them to apply for asylum.

In February 2025, three nonprofit groups and 13 people filed a class-action lawsuit challenging Mr. Trump's proclamation and the administration's guidance. Several months later, a federal judge in Washington set aside the Trump administration's asylum restrictions and found them unlawful.

The judge, Randolph Moss, found that neither the Constitution nor federal immigration law gave the Trump administration the authority to replace the rules and procedures enacted by Congress. The judge also said that immigration law does not give the president the unilateral authority to limit the rights of noncitizens in the U.S. to apply for asylum or other protections.
As part of his decision, Moss certified a class of all people covered by the president's proclamation and blocked the Trump administration from enforcing the directive against them.

The Trump administration appealed, and in April, a divided three-judge panel upheld the district court's decision and ruled that the proclamation and guidance exceeded the president's authority. The two judges in the majority also found that the president does not have the power to suspend migrants' right to apply for asylum or deport migrants under his administration's new summary removal proceedings.

The Trump administration has continued to enforce its policy suspending access to asylum while legal proceedings have continued, and the D.C. Circuit halted its ruling against DHS pending Supreme Court review.

title: Top doctor for Congress resigns amid misconduct allegations
summary: Dr. Brian Monahan, the attending physician of the U.S. Capitol, has resigned from his post as lawmakers' top doctor.
story: Washington — Dr. Brian Monahan, the attending physician of the U.S. Capitol, has resigned from his post as lawmakers' top doctor, Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Thursday, amid allegations of misconduct.
"My understanding is he's resigned," Thune said.

One source familiar with the matter told CBS News that Monahan, a two-star Navy admiral, resigned after allegations of misconduct related to what he chose to do and asked the sailors under him to do in terms of providing care.
The resignation comes in conjunction with a report by the Defense Department's inspector general that found lax oversight of the Office of the Attending Physician.

The public version of watchdog report, while light on specifics and including numerous redactions, said investigators found a "gap in clinical quality management." The report found that some prescription drugs, including sleep aids and pain medication, were not properly inventoried or tracked.
These shortfalls, the inspector general said, could "result in OAP beneficiaries unknowingly assuming health and safety risks because clinical and prescribing practices were not monitored."
CBS News has learned the Navy is also conducting an inquiry into the Office of the Attending Physician.

Monahan has served as the attending physician since 2009. He is also a professor at Uniformed Services University in Bethesda, Maryland, and previously served as its chairman of medicine. He is certified by the American Board of Internal Medicine in internal medicine, hematology and medical oncology.
His removal was first reported by Punchbowl News. The Office of the Attending Physician did not reply to multiple requests for comment.

Since 1928, the Navy — through the Office of the Attending Physician — has been tasked with medical care of Congress, staff, the Supreme Court and visitors to the Capitol complex. In addition to administering minor first aid services and providing other general medical support, the office participates in planning for and responding to disasters that may involve the Capitol.

CBS News asked House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries on Thursday if he had any knowledge about the circumstances surrounding Monahan's dismissal. Jeffries said he did not but wants to ensure member health is protected.

The Navy Times reported military personnel in the office were pressured to endure 70-80 hour work weeks and do tasks "no one else wants to do ... like cutting a congressman's toenails or bringing their medication to their private residence at 3 a.m."

The inspector general's report included five recommendations for improving OAP, including designating an outside group to oversee quality control and establishing policies and procedures for OAP employees.

title: Brother of cartel leader "El Mencho" gets 22.5 years in prison
summary: The brother of the slain prominent cartel leader known as "El Mencho" was sentenced on Friday to 22 and a half years in prison.
story: Washington — The brother of the slain prominent cartel leader known as "El Mencho" was sentenced on Friday to 22.5 years in prison, after he pleaded guilty to drug trafficking and firearms offenses, the Justice Department said.
Antonio Oseguera Cervantes, 67, worked for cartels with his brother Nemesio Rubén Oseguera Cervantes, or El Mencho, who was killed by the Mexican army in February.

Antonio Cervantes, also known as "Tony Montana," pleaded guilty in July to conspiring to distribute five kilograms or more of cocaine and 500 grams or more of methamphetamine for importation into the U.S. He also pleaded guilty to using, carrying and possessing a firearm in furtherance of the drug trafficking conspiracy.
El Mencho co-founded and led the Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generación, also known as CJNG. Last year, the Trump administration designated the CJNG and other cartels as foreign terrorist organizations.

"For more than two decades, Antonio Oseguera Cervantes helped fuel one of the world's most dangerous drug trafficking organizations, flooding America's communities with deadly drugs while enriching himself and his associates," said Tysen Duva, the assistant attorney general for the Justice Department's Criminal Division, in a statement.

title: China warns against new U.S. export controls on computer chips
summary: China is warning the U.S. against putting new export controls on semiconductors in the wake of the scandal surrounding​ AI chip giant Nvidia and its now-former CEO Jensen Huang.
story: China warned the United States on Friday against imposing additional controls on exports of semiconductors in the wake of the scandal surrounding AI chip giant Nvidia and its now-former CEO Jensen Huang.

China "has consistently opposed the abuse of export control measures, which disrupts the stability of global industrial and supply chains and serves no party's interests," foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told a regular press briefing when asked about calls from U.S. lawmakers to impose more limits on exports of chip equipment to China.

"China and the United States should work together to implement the important consensus reached by their respective heads of state and maintain the stable development of China-U.S. economic and trade relations," Mao said.
Jensen Huang — who resigned Thursday — has admitted to an affair, reportedly with Alice Huang, a former senior executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. They're not related.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under fire from critics asking whether his ties to Chinese companies and friendship with Jensen Huang contributed to a lack of oversight by the federal agency over billions in Nvidia AI chip sales, CBS News has learned. The Commerce Department did not respond to a request for comment.

During an interview on CNBC on Friday morning, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent placed the blame on Lutnick's Commerce Department for not including Megaspeed on what's known as the Entity List, which would restrict their ability to access U.S. technology products.
Bessent said that his department as well as the Defense Department, State Department and U.S. trade representative all supported adding Megaspeed to the list.

"They were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the Entity List for months," Bessent said, before referring to the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security. "Commerce BIS has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes."
According to a U.S. official, Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10.

Last month, the New York Times reported that about a year ago, President Trump was briefed on intelligence that suggested that Alice Huang was a Chinese asset and that she had grown close to Jensen Huang and the president decided not to do anything with the information.
House Speaker Mike Johnson said there's a growing consensus in Congress on further tightening controls on chip exports to China.
According to the Times, U.S. officials circulated a memo last spring citing intelligence alleging that Alice Huang was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, its main intelligence service.
Beijing has rejected the allegations and said on Thursday that they are a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" to stop China advancing in artificial intelligence technology.

title: Critics say Lutnick failed to cut off diversion of Nvidia chips to China
summary: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under fire from critics asking whether his ties to Chinese companies and friendship with ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang contributed to a lack of oversight over Nvidia AI chip sales.
story: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under fire from critics asking whether his ties to Chinese companies and friendship with Nvidia's ousted CEO Jensen Huang contributed to the federal agency's lack of oversight over billions in Nvidia AI chip sales, CBS News has learned.

Before President Trump nominated Lutnick to lead the Commerce Department, Lutnick was the chairman and CEO of Cantor Fitzgerald, a New York investment bank which held about $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time.

Lutnick developed a warm relationship with Huang, who resigned Thursday as reports of a growing number of affairs caused new uncertainty about the world's dominant AI chipmaker. One of Huang's alleged relationships was with Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen Huang), who is believed by the U.S. to be a Chinese spy. She ran Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based company that became one of Nvidia's biggest customers for AI chips and is suspected of illegally shipping Nvidia's most advanced AI chips to Chinese entities, circumventing a U.S. ban.
As commerce secretary, Lutnick took the helm of an agency responsible for policing exports of sensitive technology to adversaries and global rivals.

One way the Commerce Department keeps this information and technology out of the hands of China and other adversaries is by putting foreign companies and individuals on its Entity List. This restricts their ability to access U.S. technology products, and inclusion on the list means that the department believes there's a risk that the entity is involved in activities that are contrary to U.S. national security or foreign policy interests.

In 2024, under the Biden administration, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security launched an investigation into Nvidia's chip sales to Megaspeed to determine whether they were being redirected to China. But according to The New York Times, the probe was abruptly transferred to the Department of Justice. The Justice Department would not comment about the investigation.
The Commerce Department has not added a company to the Entity List since October 2025.
Last week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Lutnick over the Commerce Department's failure to place Megaspeed on the Entity List, Axios reported.
Chris McGuire, an expert on China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, said, "The real scandal here is the lack of enforcement of export controls."

He added that the Commerce Department had known for as long as a year that Megaspeed was being run by a woman who is believed by the U.S. to be a Chinese spy, "and they did nothing." The New York Times reported that about a year ago, Mr. Trump was briefed on intelligence that suggested that Alice Huang was a Chinese asset and that she had grown close to Jensen Huang.
"Either Lutnick doesn't know how to do his job or he is protecting Huang," McGuire said.
The Commerce Department did not respond to a request for comment.

On Thursday, after Jensen Huang's resignation became public, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, called on Lutnick and his deputy, Jeffrey Kessler, to "explain why they have not closed export control loopholes." Kessler is the undersecretary who led the Commerce Department's probe into Megaspeed.

Warren urged the two to "act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military." In March, Warren wrote to Lutnick to demand the "immediate pausing" of all export licenses of Nvidia chips destined for China.
Questions about Lutnick's own relationship with Chinese state companies have further complicated the ongoing Nvidia crisis.

A financial services firm Lutnick ran, BGC Group, had a 33% stake in a joint venture with China Credit Trust, a Chinese state-owned company whose largest shareholder is the China People's Insurance Company, another state enterprise.

Another firm he ran, Cantor Fitzgerald, is still overseen by his two eldest sons. That firm helped several Chinese companies go public in the U.S. Cantor Fitzgerald was also a key investor in Satellogic, a satellite company that is under contract with a Chinese data science company, Zhong Ke Guang Qi Space, until 2033.

His close China ties emerged as a topic at his Senate confirmation hearing last year. Senators questioned whether he could be unduly influenced by Chinese officials, and how he would safeguard U.S. technology.

Sen. Maria Cantwell, a Democrat from Washington state, grilled Lutnick on potential conflicts of interest with respect to his investments in Chinese companies, and Cantor Fitzgerald's financial interest in Tether, a cryptocurrency company with a large footprint in China.
Other senators asked about how he would safeguard U.S. technology from the Chinese Communist Party.
"How will you address different threats that we see coming from the CCP within these information and technology markets?" asked GOP Sen. Deb Fischer, of Nebraska.
Lutnick promised to be vigilant against threats from China.
"I take a very jaundiced view of China," he said in response to Fischer. "I think they only care about themselves and seek harm to us, and so we need to protect ourselves."
Before he was sworn in as commerce secretary in February 2025, Lutnick resigned from all of his corporate leadership posts, transferring his business empire to his children.

Since his tenure as commerce secretary began, Lutnick and his family's net worth doubled to $7.3 billion, thanks to his indirect stake in Tether, according to Forbes, which valued his holding in Tether at $5.4 billion. The stake, worth $1.7 billion in early 2025, has more than tripled in value.

"Can we be confident that he is looking out for the public interest?" asked Kathleen Clark, a law professor and expert on government ethics at Washington University in St. Louis. "What's going on with him raises a lot of red flags."
Lutnick's friendship with Jensen Huang may also be problematic, Clark told CBS News.
Huang met Lutnick soon after Lutnick began his term as commerce secretary, Huang told podcaster Joe Rogan last year.

"He started our conversation with, 'Jensen, this is Secretary Lutnick,'" said Huang. "'I just want to let you know that you're a national treasure. Nvidia is a national treasure. And whenever you need access to the president, the administration, you call us.'"
Huang added that every time he called the commerce secretary's office, "if I want to get something off my chest, express some concern, they're always available."

Huang also visited with Mr. Trump. He attended a $1 million-per-person dinner at Mar-a-Lago in April 2025. At that time, Huang tried to convince Mr. Trump to lift restrictions on the company's less advanced H20 chip sales to China, according to The New York Times. Less than three months later, in July 2025, Mr. Trump lifted the restrictions. Nvidia's most advanced chip, the Blackwell, still cannot be sold directly to China.

In July 2025, Lutnick posted a photo to Instagram showing Huang in his trademark black leather jacket standing in the Oval Office next to Mr. Trump, who was seated at his desk. Lutnick is also in the photo along with other visitors.
"Great to meet in the Oval Office with Jensen Huang on the very day Nvidia crossed $4 trillion in market cap," the post said.

title: Van Hollen will challenge Schumer for Senate majority leader
summary: Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland announced Thursday that he will challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader.
story: Washington — Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland announced Thursday that he will challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader.

"In this election, Americans called on us to unrig an economy rigged against working people & fueled by political corruption. To deliver, we need new leadership. This isn't about any one person – it's about answering that call," Van Hollen said in a post on X. "That's why I'm running for Senate Majority Leader."

The decision by Van Hollen, who said earlier this week he was in "listening mode" about running for majority leader, marks the most significant step by a high-profile Democrat to challenge the party's existing leadership since it decisively won last week's midterms.

Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont quickly threw his support behind Van Hollen on Thursday. Some other Democrats have not yet committed to voting for Schumer in leadership elections, which are expected early next month, but haven't explicitly endorsed another candidate.

Van Hollen, 67, has been in the Senate since 2017 after representing the state in the House for more than a decade. The Maryland Democrat has gained attention from progressives in recent years. In 2024, he vocally supported restricting weapons shipments to Israel and criticized the Biden administration's posture toward the war in Gaza. Van Hollen also gained attention when he traveled to El Salvador last year to meet with Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran national who lived in Maryland and had been sent to the country's notorious CECOT prison.

Supporters see Van Hollen as someone who's willing to speak to the issues progressives hold most dear. Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed told NPR in an interview this week that Van Hollen is "willing to take risks when it matters," citing his trip to El Salvador.
Schumer, 75, responded to Van Hollen's announcement in a post on X, saying he welcomes "any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead."

"I'm proud of what we've accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader," he wrote. "I look forward to leading our new Democratic majority and delivering for the American people."
Schumer has led Senate Democrats since 2017, when he succeeded retiring Sen. Harry Reid of Nevada.
Democratic Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand of New York, who chairs the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, defended Schumer at a news conference earlier this week, crediting his "strategic leadership."

"You will see, despite all the grumblings, enormous gratitude for the hard work he has done to get us to this position," Gillibrand said. "We are about to win nine Senate seats — that has never happened in my political history."

Democratic Sen. Jacky Rosen of Nevada endorsed Schumer late Thursday, praising his work ahead of the midterms and writing, "I know he has the experience and the fight to continue leading our diverse caucus at this crucial moment."

The challenge comes as Schumer is still widely expected to hold on to the top leadership post, especially after the strong showing for Democrats in the midterm elections. Despite a Senate map that appeared unfavorable for the party heading into the cycle, Democrats flipped at least eight Senate seats — with one race remaining up in the air in Alaska — securing a sizable majority in the new Congress.

With the election results, Schumer has appeared to improve his position with the caucus, following a tumultuous tenure in recent years. The pushback took hold after the New York Democrat maneuvered to avoid a government shutdown in early 2025, prompting frustration from his party's left flank.
Later that year, he changed course and kept Democrats largely united through a record-breaking government shutdown as they sought to prevent the expiration of health insurance tax credits.

In an interview with MS NOW announcing his run for majority leader, Van Hollen acknowledged he is an "underdog," but said he has spoken with caucus members and believes the race is "very much in flux."

Asked what he would do differently from Schumer, Van Hollen suggested the current leader hasn't taken a firm enough stance on using the power of the purse to force the Trump administration to end the Iran war. He told host Jen Psaki that Democrats should use the Dec. 11 deadline to fund the government as leverage, saying it "should not be a finger-in-the-wind issue."
Van Hollen also criticized Schumer for, in his view, moving behind the scenes to back certain candidates in Democratic primaries — a longstanding point of contention for progressives.

"On the political side of the equation, we shouldn't have a Democratic leader who is getting involved in picking sides in open Democratic primaries. … We have two senators right now in the United States Senate who wouldn't be there if the current majority leader had his way," Van Hollen said, referring to El-Sayed and Minnesota Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan.
Some members of the Democratic caucus — including both progressives like Sanders and moderates like Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton of Kansas — have called for new leadership.

Sanders endorsed Van Hollen in a social media post late Thursday, writing: "The American people voted for change. They want a Democratic Party that will stand up to powerful special interests, take on the billionaire class and fight for working families."

Two days earlier, Sanders announced in a news conference he would not support Schumer. Sanders was flanked by the more moderate Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, who said she was "not actively seeking this job" but is "seeking change."
"Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that's definitively different," Slotkin said. "I'm a no until and unless I see that from anyone."

title: GOP lawmakers press Huang and Lutnick to testify over Nvidia
summary: Republicans on Capitol Hill are negotiating for now-resigned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang​ to appear before Congress.
story: Republicans on Capitol Hill are pressing now-resigned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to appear before Congress early next month about the scandal that has rocked one of the most important companies in the world — as a Senate panel asks Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify.

"We need to know the full extent to which our national security has been put at risk," the chairs of the House Select Committee on China, Foreign Affairs Committee and Intelligence Committee said in a statement requesting Huang's presence.

The three committee chairs wrote a letter Thursday asking Huang to appear for a closed-door interview on Dec. 1. They said if he does not accept their request by Friday evening, the House Foreign Affairs Committee will issue a subpoena.

The upper chamber has also pushed Huang to appear. Republican Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina, who chairs the Senate Banking Committee, asked Huang to testify voluntarily before the panel in the first week of December, but warned the committee is prepared to use its subpoena power if needed.
"The American people deserve answers," Scott wrote on X.

Nvidia, whose chips have fueled the AI boom, announced on Thursday that Huang had stepped down following a scandal over his affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at the company Megaspeed who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Huang's resignation from the company he co-founded has not dampened calls from members of Congress for answers about Nvidia's relationship with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that gained access to highly prized chips that are banned from being exported to China. Megaspeed is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China — allegations Megaspeed has denied.

Moments before Nvidia announced Huang's resignation, Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer of North Dakota said on CNBC on Thursday morning that he would happily support subpoenaing Huang. A Cramer spokesperson said he would still support subpoenaing the tech founder.

The controversy has also raised questions about whether the federal government has done enough to prevent Nvidia's chips from being diverted to China — and about the Trump administration's close relationship with Huang.

Scott asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to appear for a public hearing next month. The House Foreign Affairs Committee also requested testimony from Under Secretary of Commerce Jeffrey Kessler, who leads the Bureau of Industry and Security, an agency that oversees export controls.

Some critics have argued Lutnick's Commerce Department should have taken action to prevent Megaspeed from buying chips. The New York Times reported that a Bureau of Industry and Security probe into the firm was halted last year.
Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana told CNN on Thursday he wanted to hear from both Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, saying: "This is serious as an aneurysm."

Earlier Thursday, the chairman of the House Select Committee on China, GOP Rep. John Moolenaar of Michigan, said lawmakers were "in discussions" with Huang "on a date to come and meet with us." But he added, "If for some reason that were not to happen, all three committees, all three chairs have said we will use our subpoena power."

Moolenaar and two other chairs — Rep. Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and Rep. Rick Crawford of the Intelligence Committee — first asked Huang to appear in a letter last week. They said the purpose of the closed-door briefing would be to discuss Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset." The lawmakers gave Huang a deadline of Wednesday to respond.

Mast and Moolenaar told reporters on Thursday that they received a response. Mast said Huang indicated he's willing to appear. Moolenaar said that Huang's resignation "does change the dynamic" surrounding his potential testimony.
"I think right now our goal is to get him in as soon as possible, so that we have a full understanding of the facts and get to the bottom of the truth of this situation," Moolenaar said.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune also told CBS News that he expects "there'll be an interest in doing oversight" in the Senate. Asked whether he wants Huang to testify, Thune said, "I think that it would make sense because of the, again, the nature of the association and the governments and the national security interests, what we're talking about here."
Democrats will take control of both the House and Senate in January. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said Democrats have questions for the Trump administration, too.

"Despite Jensen Huang's resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk," Schumer said on X. "The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset."

President Trump, a friend of Huang's, has downplayed the scandal and said he doesn't believe Huang knew the Megaspeed executive was a spy. The president said Thursday that Huang had done a "fantastic job."
"NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place — TIM COOK of Apple," the president posted to Truth Social.

title: Hegseth awards medal to soldier who reprimanded group near tomb
summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth awarded a medal to the service member who reprimanded his group for making noise at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier​.
story: Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth awarded a medal on Thursday to the service member who reprimanded his group for making noise at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Veterans Day.

Hegseth posted a series of photos on X with the soldier, Spc. Thomas Iglesias, and other members of the unit who guard the tomb at Arlington National Cemetery around the clock. One of the photos showed Hegseth pinning a medal to Iglesias' chest.
"We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist," Hegseth wrote. "Carry on Patriots."
We love soldiers.We love standards.Well done, Specialist.Carry on Patriots. pic.twitter.com/Uk6ek6oOso

A Pentagon official said Hegseth "welcomed the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, the Old Guard, to the Pentagon where he proudly awarded Specialist Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026."

Iglesias was guarding the tomb following a Veterans Day event that included Hegseth, President Trump and other administration officials. Footage showed Hegseth, his wife, his chief of staff and other aides posing for photos near the tomb. Someone laughed, and Iglesias shouted: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."

In the aftermath, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told CBS News: "The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored-and will always honor-the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe. While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."

Soldiers reminding visitors to maintain decorum at the tomb is not uncommon. One member of the regiment that guards the tomb said in an Army interview in 2022 that sentinels react to the crowd two or three times per day.

title: White House warns of "blatant criminality" in Democratic probes
summary: White House counsel Will Scharf warned that congressional subpoenas could lead to investigations from the executive branch.
story: Washington — The top lawyer in the White House warned the leading Democrat on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee that investigations into the Trump administration that lawmakers plan to pursue in the next Congress "may cross the line into blatant criminality" and said congressional subpoenas could prompt probes from the executive branch.

The message from White House counsel Will Scharf to Rep. Robert Garcia, a California Democrat who is set to chair the Oversight Committee as of January, foreshadows a brewing fight between the Trump administration and congressional Democrats, who are poised to launch investigations in a slew of issues arising over the first two years of President Trump's second term.
Scharf sent a letter to Garcia, dated Monday, reminding him that investigative acts by Congress must be backed by a "legitimate legislative purpose."

"Beyond being inconsistent with the clear, well-recognized constitutional limitations on your investigative functions, threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality," Scharf wrote. "And issuing unlawful subpoenas with the intention of depriving citizens of their constitutional rights and privileges may warrant further investigation."

Scharf cited recent statements from Democratic members of Congress who previewed investigations into the Trump administration they plan to pursue once they take control of the House and Senate. He claimed that Democrats are intent on crossing the Constitution's limits on congressional investigations and subpoenas.

"Abusive threats and public statements about the indiscriminate issuance of subpoenas, along with threats directed at prospective targets within the Administration make it abundantly clear that any forthcoming investigative processes will be deployed to harass and aggrandize rather than to advance any legitimate end," he wrote.
Scharf accused Democrats of making "abusive and capricious threats" and said they are seeking to "abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with lawful functioning of government."
Garcia said in response to Scharf that the White House is threatening to infringe on his committee's right to conduct oversight.

"It appears Donald Trump has something to hide," the California Democrat said in a statement. "Let's be clear: Congress' authority comes from Article I of the Constitution, not from the permission of the White House. Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate."
Garcia accused the Trump administration of weaponizing the executive branch against Congress.
"We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President's lawyers," he said.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to become speaker in January, told reporters that in the first two years of Mr. Trump's second term, the White House has been used to a GOP-led Congress that he said has been a "reckless rubber stamp" for the president's agenda.

"A Democratic Congress is going to be a check and balance on an out-of-control executive branch in the face of unprecedented corruption that they've unleashed on the American people, and if they don't like it, consult the Constitution," he said.
Molly Nixon, a senior fellow in executive power at the Cato Institute, said Scharf's warnings may be more political than legal in nature.

"This letter, I think, is sort of an opening salvo in what will ultimately be a political debate or a public argument about whether Congress is using its power legitimately, and I don't think that's likely to wind up in court, especially on a criminal charge, but is something Americans will be able to judge with their own eyes," she told CBS News.

While the executive branch could attempt to bring a criminal indictment, any prosecution would run into roadblocks because of the Constitution's Speech or Debate Clause, which immunizes lawmakers from criminal or civil actions stemming from legislative duties.
"I think it's incredibly unlikely that any court would find merit in any criminal charge against a member of Congress for their vote on issuing a subpoena," Nixon said.

Separate from Scharf's warning to House Democrats, Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, accused Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal of threatening people who associated with Mr. Trump, after Blumenthal announced his plans to launch a congressional investigation into the companies and individuals who donated to the White House ballroom project.

In his Nov. 11 letter posted on X, Reitz appeared to accuse the senator of possibly committing a crime, citing two civil rights statutes that make it a crime to conspire to deprive people of their rights or to deprive someone of their rights "under the color of law."
He also ordered Blumenthal to preserve all records and correspondence.
It was not immediately clear how the top federal prosecutor in Houston would have jurisdiction to potentially pursue criminal charges against a U.S. senator from Connecticut.
Blumenthal accused Reitz of trying to intimidate him and suppress his First Amendment-protected speech, in a letter he sent the U.S. attorney in response.

"Since you appear to have evidence of the Trump Administration's efforts to protect corporate donors and Administration officials from legitimate oversight, I accordingly direct you to preserve all records and correspondence," Blumenthal wrote.

Although Reitz made it sound as though he is launching a criminal investigation, Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters Thursday that the department does not have any open criminal investigations into members of Congress.
"There's no ongoing ... criminal investigations into words that incoming senators or congressmen have said," Blanche told reporters.

"But I do think that the rhetoric that we saw starting Tuesday night — the night of the election — continuing up until as recently as today, is something that we have to be careful of as Americans," he said.

Mr. Trump's first administration turned to the courts to fight congressional subpoenas after Democrats took control of the House in 2019, and the president could do so again to fight Democrats' demands in the final two years of his second term. In those earlier legal battles, the Justice Department argued Democrats' subpoenas for documents lacked a legitimate legislative purpose, an argument government lawyers could reprise.
While a court may agree that a subpoena does not serve a valid legislative purpose, that doesn't mean it's criminal, Nixon said.
"That might just mean the subpoena doesn't get enforced or that it's quashed," she said. "The criminality question is not coterminous with the legislative purpose question."
Following last week's midterm elections, Democrats are poised to hold at least 254 seats in the House and 55 seats in the Senate, giving them control of congressional committees and subpoena power.
Garcia had a brief message to the Trump administration on the heels of Democrats' rout of Republicans in the fight for control of Congress: "Lawyer up."

Once he takes the gavel of the Oversight Committee, the panel is expected to look into the Trump family's business dealings, corporate corruption, actions by federal immigration authorities and the scandal involving convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
Garcia said his investigative agenda could also include:

Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding festivities in the Bahamas that were partially paid for by a Russian oligarch.A $2 billion investment that the private equity fund of Mr. Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, received from Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund.The Trump family's crypto ventures.Companies linked to the president's sons that have received Pentagon contracts.Allegations of a pay-to-play scheme and other kickbacks related to Department of Homeland Security contracts.Corporate donations to fund the new White House ballroom.
Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding festivities in the Bahamas that were partially paid for by a Russian oligarch.
A $2 billion investment that the private equity fund of Mr. Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, received from Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund.
The Trump family's crypto ventures.
Companies linked to the president's sons that have received Pentagon contracts.
Allegations of a pay-to-play scheme and other kickbacks related to Department of Homeland Security contracts.
Corporate donations to fund the new White House ballroom.

Faced with investigations once Democrats regain congressional majorities, Mr. Trump on Sunday accused Democrats of threatening senior members of his administration and claimed they were engaging in "extortion." The president said on Truth Social the Democrats "should be held accountable for this," and he directed the Justice Department to look into their oversight push.
"These SLEAZEBAGS should go to jail for what they are doing," he wrote in a second Truth Social post.

Democrats in Congress have in the past faced resistance from the White House in their efforts to investigate Mr. Trump and his administration. During the president's first term, Democratic-led House committees sought a trove of Mr. Trump's financial records from his accounting firm and two banks as part of an investigation into potential misconduct before and after he took office, whether he had undisclosed conflicts of interest and if he was complying with the Constitution.

Mr. Trump attempted to block the firms from complying with the subpoenas and took the dispute to the Supreme Court. In a 2020 decision, the high court declined to immediately give Congress access to the financial records, but reiterated that subpoenas must serve a "legitimate legislative purpose" and acknowledged that lawmakers have "significant legislative interests."

title: New federal housing rule could displace thousands, experts warn
summary: Since 1995, mixed-status families have been permitted to live together in federally funded housing, but a revised rule changes that.
story: Residents of federally funded public housing will be required to show proof of U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status under a new rule published Thursday by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.

The measure could displace nearly 80,000 people, including tens of thousands of citizens in mixed-status families, from their homes, according to the Center for Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan research and policy institute.

Since 1995, mixed-status families have been permitted to live together in HUD-funded housing as long as federal subsidies covered only eligible household members. The new rule may force these families to decide whether to remain together in nonpublic housing or split up their households.
"This is tearing apart families and sowing division," said Marie Claire Tran-Leung, director of the Evictions Initiative Project and managing attorney at the National Housing Law Project.

The rule's prior status, which allowed mixed-status families to live together, worked well for all parties, Tran-Leung said. Mixed-status households often paid a higher share of rent because their subsidies were prorated, experts say. If those families are forced to leave public housing, HUD will likely face financial shortfalls, Tran-Leung said.
About 20,000 mixed-status families, or 80,000 people, could be affected by the rule, CBPP's data shows. About 37,000 of those are children, mostly U.S. citizens, CBPP said.
The rule is scheduled to take effect on Dec. 14.

"President Trump warned that the days of illegal aliens and ineligible noncitizens exploiting government-funded welfare programs would be over," HUD Secretary Scott Turner said in a statement. "It's unacceptable that America's homeless veterans, disabled, elderly, and victims of domestic violence languish on waitlists while illegals and ineligibles scam our system. American taxpayers will no longer foot the bill. Promises made, promises kept."

Turner's statement said a recent audit identified nearly 200,000 tenants with incomplete or unverified eligibility status. Currently, HUD-funded housing serves only a quarter of eligible households in need.

Families in all 50 states will be affected, with the largest concentration in New York, California and Texas. The rule would impact more than 7,000 mixed-status households in California and 2,500 mixed-status households in New York, according to a coalition of 22 state attorneys general who opposed the rule.
They wrote in an April letter that it "would inflict significant economic costs on the States and exacerbate the affordable housing crisis."
CBS News reached out to housing authorities in California, New York and Texas to learn how the rule would be implemented and enforced locally.

During the first Trump administration in 2019, HUD attempted to revise the longstanding provision, but the proposed change was withdrawn in 2021. In February 2026, the agency reintroduced the proposed rule, drawing more than 11,000 public comments from individuals, advocacy groups and members of Congress during the three-month comment period.
Reactions also came from individual members of the public.

Claire Stanley, a senior living in public housing in Auburn, Washington, wrote: "There is no justification for this rule — it won't save money because the increase in homelessness will cost more than just allowing families to stay together."
Another commenter, Mark Smith of Oconto Falls, Wisconsin, urged in March: "Please withdraw the proposal and think about what Jesus would do."

title: With Jim Jordan as leader, House GOP signals it's ready to fight
summary: Republicans described the incoming minority leader as a "fighter" who can go head to head with Hakeem Jeffries.
story: Washington — Former House Speaker John Boehner once described Rep. Jim Jordan, the next House Republican leader, as a political "terrorist."
"I just never saw a guy who spent more time tearing things apart, never building anything, never putting anything together," the former GOP leader told CBS News in 2021.

On Tuesday, House Republicans selected Jordan to lead the party in the next Congress, a significant shakeup in the party's leadership that signaled they're ready for a fight after losing more than 40 seats in the midterm elections.

Jordan — who was a founding member of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, which routinely makes legislating difficult for GOP leaders — built his reputation confronting Democrats in combative hearings as the top Republican on the powerful House Judiciary Committee. There, the Ohio Republican defended President Trump against the first impeachment inquiry, which centered on the president's conduct toward Ukraine.

"Jim's a fighter," said GOP Rep. Nicole Malliotakis of New York, who sees Jordan, a former college wrestling coach, as someone who can unite the various factions in the party. "I think a lot of the reasons why we couldn't get more done this Congress was because we could not unite the team. I think Jim Jordan is somebody who everybody respects and can bring everyone together."
GOP Rep. Ralph Norman of South Carolina, who is retiring after losing a Senate primary, said Jordan represents "the side of the party that's willing to fight."
Norman suggested that the conference chose Jordan over current Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana for the role because he "represented more of what they wanted to see as a minority leader."
"There's nobody that can debate any better. There's nobody that can fight any more," Norman said.

Republican Rep. Andy Harris of Maryland, the chair of the House Freedom Caucus, called Jordan a "superb communicator" who can go up against Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is expected to become House speaker in January.
"I want to see the first time they go head to head," Harris said. "Jim Jordan will hold his own in that."

GOP House Speaker Mike Johnson, who represents Louisiana, said Jordan was a mentor to him when he was first elected to Congress a decade ago. The two also served on the Judiciary Committee together, before Johnson unexpectedly became speaker in 2023 after Kevin McCarthy's historic ouster.

After McCarthy was removed, Republicans struggled to coalesce behind a replacement for nearly a month, bringing the House to a standstill. Jordan was one of the candidates who failed to secure enough support, though he ran three times in the elections to replace McCarthy before giving up.

It wasn't the first time Jordan sought the House's top leadership position. He also failed in his 2018 bid to be speaker after Paul Ryan's retirement. And he then ran unsuccessfully for minority leader after Democrats took back the majority.
"He's always been regarded as a leader by the conference, and he's going to do an extraordinary job," Johnson said Tuesday after the leadership elections.
Jordan may be viewed by his Republican colleagues as a leader, but his record as a legislator is thin: He has never been a primary sponsor of legislation that passed in the House.

Then again, for this Republican minority, passing bills may not be the point. No measure that has only GOP support will get through the House, particularly not when Democrats are approaching a nearly 90-seat margin. Johnson thinks Jordan will have an easier time leading Republicans in the minority than he did as speaker. With his less enviable five-seat majority, Johnson has constantly had to navigate GOP infighting and Mr. Trump's shifting demands to get anything through the House.
"It is easier to keep a group together when you're in the minority," Johnson said.

Beyond resisting Democrats' investigations and legislation, it remains to be seen what Jordan will be fighting for. Significant bipartisan legislation is not likely to be on his agenda. But Jordan is sure to have a strong ally in the White House with the rise of likeminded hardliner Stephen Miller as Mr. Trump's new White House chief of staff.
Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, who has served with Jordan on the Judiciary Committee, called Jordan "a guy of real talent and real gifts."
"I wish that he would use them in defense of the public interest and not in defense of Donald Trump," he said Wednesday.
Jeffries, when asked Tuesday whether he could work with Jordan in the next Congress, told reporters, "That remains to be seen." He added, "He's going to have to chart out where he moves forward."

title: ICE deportations and arrests hit record high
summary: New Department of Homeland Security figures show more than 483,000 deportations and 491,000 immigration arrests in fiscal year 2026.
story: Immigration and Customs Enforcement deported a record 483,200 people in fiscal year 2026, according to new Department of Homeland Security figures obtained by CBS News, marking a historic escalation in President Trump's signature immigration crackdown, even as voters grapple with the increase in interior enforcement.

The total number of individuals deported represents the highest annual figure in ICE's reported history, surpassing the law enforcement agency's previous record of 442,640 in fiscal year 2025. ICE also reported more than 491,000 immigration arrests during the fiscal year ending Sept. 30, including nearly 475,000 administrative arrests — another record, according to DHS. Administrative arrests are those in which alleged undocumented immigrants are arrested for civil violations rather than criminal charges.

The records underscore a defining feature of Mr. Trump's second presidency — a sweeping enforcement campaign reshaped by dramatic immigration policy and the operational expansion of the federal law enforcement footprint in communities far from the border. But they also arrive at a politically complicated moment for Mr. Trump.

Following sweeping Republican losses in the midterm elections, the president has publicly acknowledged that parts of his deportation campaign may have gone too far. Yet that admission was coupled with a decision to elevate Stephen Miller, the architect of many of his most restrictive immigration policies, to White House chief of staff.

These new figures underscore a tension further reflected within American public opinion. CBS News polls have shown widespread support for border security alongside increasing discomfort with how immigration laws are enforced in communities nationwide.
Behind the record-breaking numbers

According to DHS, the new deportation total is approximately 18% higher than the 409,849 removals ICE recorded in fiscal year 2012, during the Obama administration, a longstanding agency benchmark. The new record is also nearly 78% higher than the 271,484 deportations recorded in fiscal year 2024, the last full fiscal year under President Biden.

ICE reported a total of 50,925 arrests in the month of August alone, eclipsing the previous monthly high set in July. By September, the agency was still carrying out more than 48,000 arrests a month, according to DHS, reflecting a sustained rapid pace of enforcement.

Still, a record number of reported deportations does not necessarily mean a record number of formal removal orders carried out. ICE's deportation figures do not include governmentwide statistics, which include actions by U.S. Customs and Border Protection and distinguish between formal removals, voluntary returns and voluntary departures. Using broader measures, nationwide deportations reached higher thresholds during portions of the early 2000s.

A new analysis published Wednesday by Syracuse University's Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, or TRAC, raised additional questions about how DHS counts deportations. Based on case-by-case federal immigration records, researchers found that formal removals accounted for just 63% of deportations in July and August 2026, with the remainder consisting of voluntary departures and returns.

"I couldn't be prouder of the brave men and women of ICE, who just broke more historic records," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement Thursday that accompanied the new numbers. "Fiscal Year 2026 saw the highest number of ICE deportations and arrests for any year in ICE's history. September 2026 was the best September in ICE's history in terms of arrests. The total number of ICE arrests in Fiscal Year 2026 was more than all three full fiscal years under Biden combined, as the patriots of ICE work around the clock to make America safe again. Thanks to President Trump's leadership, ICE has been unleashed to target and remove illegal aliens so that we can save American lives."
The "worst of the worst" — and a broader reality

The Trump administration has consistently defended its campaign as a public safety mission, boasting arrests and deportations of people accused or convicted of serious crimes, those DHS has repeatedly described as the "worst of the worst." It is also something Mr. Trump made a central focus of his campaign in his successful 2024 presidential run.

In its accounting of the 2026 fiscal year's deportations, DHS has highlighted several such cases: Raul Genesis Ortiz Moran, a Mexican national charged with second-degree murder and aggravated sexual assault in connection with the death of a 2-year-old girl in Virginia. The Louisa County Sheriff's Office independently confirmed the charges.
The department also cited Soili Xiomara Aparicio-Santos, a Honduran national deported in April who, according to DHS, was convicted of attempting to murder her newborn son in New York.
The cases illustrate the serious public safety threats immigration officers can encounter, but are not representative of hundreds of thousands in arrests.

DHS has repeatedly argued that immigrants without U.S. criminal records can still have criminal histories overseas or pose security risks to the public. The department also often notes that immigration law alone justifies civil arrest and deportation. Still, federal authorities have not publicly provided comprehensive evidence showing how many arrested immigrants without U.S. criminal records have committed crimes abroad.

An August CBS News analysis found that in July 2026, for the first time during Mr. Trump's second term, more than half of ICE arrests involved immigrants who had neither criminal convictions nor pending criminal charges. That analysis also found that approximately 6% of people booked into ICE detention during Mr. Trump's second administration had convictions for violent crimes.

Separately, the nonpartisan Migration Policy Institute found that only about 20% of approximately 980,000 deportations carried out collectively by ICE and CBP between January 2025 and July 2026 involved someone with a criminal conviction. Among deported immigrants who had lived in the U.S. for at least two years, 71% had no criminal conviction.
Many Americans believe immigration enforcement has gone too far

According to CBS News national exit polling from the 2026 midterm elections, 58% of voters said the Trump administration's immigration enforcement had gone too far. Another 22% said it had been about right, while 20% believed it had not gone far enough.
While support for border security remains high, it does not necessarily translate into support for tactics and operations used to enforce immigration law in American cities and towns nationwide.
In a "60 Minutes interview," the president acknowledged that his immigration crackdown had taken a political toll.
"I think it was too tough," Mr. Trump told "60 Minutes" correspondent Ross Douthat.

Trump added that his administration received high marks for securing the border and removing dangerous criminals, but faced criticism for deporting longtime immigrants who held jobs, worked in industries such as landscaping and hospitality, and in some cases paid taxes.

Mr. Trump also expressed interest in working with congressional Democrats in the new Congress to create and pass immigration legislation, a shocking acknowledgment from a president who built much of his political identity around the promise of mass deportations.
A new White House chief of staff

As Stephen Miller — a longtime aide of President Trump who has historically pushed for higher arrest targets — takes the helm as chief of staff, multiple administration officials tell CBS News that they do not expect the crackdown to slow down following the election.

In recent weeks, ICE officials have been instructed to aim for approximately 19,000 arrests per week, according to sources familiar with the agency's planning — a target established before the midterms and substantially above its historical pace.

The targets come as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress in January, with some voicing support for more scrutiny of the administration's immigration operations, spending and enforcement tactics. But their ability to force changes could be constrained by the billions already appropriated to ICE, in addition to presidential veto power.

A sweeping tax and spending law signed by Mr. Trump in July 2025 allocated roughly $170 billion for immigration enforcement and border security, including $75 billion in additional funding for ICE. Of that, $45 billion was designated to expand immigrant detention capacity, while nearly $30 billion was allocated for arrests, transportation, deportation operations and additional personnel.
For years, Mr. Trump's immigration message rested on a premise that resonated with millions of voters: the U.S. needed to regain control of its border and enforce its immigration laws.
But the sharp decline in illegal border crossings and the surge in ICE enforcement come as the political landscape has shifted, too.

The question facing Mr. Trump in the final two years of his presidency is whether an enforcement campaign that has achieved unprecedented scale by ICE's own accounting can harness the confidence of an American public increasingly divided over how the presidential mandate to crack down on immigration is being carried out.

Camilo  Montoya-Galvez

title: Hegseth's group reprimanded for noise at Tomb of Unknown Soldier
summary: A guard at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier reprimanded a group of people that included Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for making noise at the site.
story: Washington — A guard at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday loudly reprimanded a group of people that included Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for making noise at the site.

Hegseth, his wife and several aides — including chief of staff Ricky Buria — visited the tomb for a Veterans Day wreath-laying, followed by a ceremony at the nearby Memorial Auditorium. President Trump and first lady Melania Trump also attended the event.

After the ceremony, the defense secretary and his team posed for a photo. As they began walking away, a member of the group audibly laughed, leading a U.S. Army sentinel to belt out: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."
It is not clear who laughed, or whether Hegseth made any noise.

Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell told CBS News: "The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored—and will always honor—the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe. While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."

A group with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was reprimanded by a U.S. Army sentinel at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery on Veterans Day after someone in the group appeared to laugh following a photo.“All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of… pic.twitter.com/40qRCTy2Df
CNN was first to report on the incident.

The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier memorializes deceased American service members from World War I and later conflicts whose remains were never identified. The sentinels who march in front of the tomb for 24 hours a day — a prestigious posting within the Army — are a well-known presence at the cemetery, famous for their guard-changing ceremony.

It is not unusual for sentinels to reprimand visitors who interrupt the solemnity expected at the memorial. Army Staff Sgt. Chadwick Winget, who belonged to the regiment that guards the tomb, said in a 2022 Army interview that sentinels react to the crowd two or three times per day.
