title: Microsoft says it "restored service" after major worldwide outage
summary: A Microsoft outage involving services like Outlook and Teams impacted many users, companies and government services.
story: Microsoft said early Saturday it had restored its services after a worldwide outage which involved services like Outlook and Teams impacted users, companies and government operations around the world.
In a post on X, the company said: "We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions."

The disruption, which lasted over 24 hours, affected a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down.
Microsoft said the outage was linked to a technical issue, not malicious or cyber activity, and apologised for the incident.

"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," the company said Friday on X. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."

The outage affected Microsoft's suite of business products, as well as those tailored for personal use by individuals, students and families. Users in more than 70 countries and territories experienced disruptions, according to Downdetector, a website that tracks technology outages.

"Microsoft in a Friday the 13th moment as global outage [causes] a very bad day in Redmond," Yorkville Ives and Co. tech analyst Dan Ives said in an X post Friday. "There will be major questions for MSFT in this global outage."

Charles Lamanna, executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform at Microsoft, said in a social media post Friday that "technical challenges and failure modes" made the recovery process "more difficult than normal."

"I'm working closely with the engineering team to complete the full post-mortem," Lamanna said in the post. "We will publish the post-mortem shortly covering the step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future."
Widespread impact
Microsoft first flagged technical issues just before 1 p.m. ET Thursday. The company updated users about its recovery progress through a series of posts on its Microsoft 365 Status X account.
More than 130,000 users reported issues with Microsoft on Thursday, Downdetector's website shows. However, those reports started to wane by Friday morning as Microsoft worked to restore its services.
The outage disrupted email for hours, hampering work activity for some employees.
"It's just challenging sending reports or things that needed to be approved," one woman told CBS News Los Angeles.
However, some took delight in the slowdown, with social media users posting videos celebrating the freedom of not having access to email.
It's unclear how many people were impacted. More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, according to Microsoft's website.
Companies worldwide report issues

OpenAI and Anthropic each reported problems connecting to Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects of outages as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies' software.
U.S.-based industrial technology company Workhorse Group Inc. delayed a conference call on its quarterly earnings because of the outage.
In Australia, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Friday that Microsoft had likened the widespread outage to the CrowdStrike outage in 2024.
Burke said he had spoken to Microsoft's top executive in Australia and the government's national cybersecurity coordinator about the global disruption.

"They (Microsoft) don't believe they are dealing with a cyberattack. They believe that they are dealing in some ways (with something) similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Burke told reporters in Sydney.

Texas-based cybersecurity company CrowdStrike blamed a bug in an update that allowed its systems to push bad data out to millions of customer computers, setting off a global tech outage in July 2024 that grounded flights, took TV broadcasts off the air and disrupted banks, hospitals and retailers.

Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum firm, said his company's Outlook accounts couldn't receive updates from its U.S. customers due to the outage. If the situation dragged on further, it could "impact the production timeline," he said.

Air India said its flight operations were unaffected by the Microsoft outage. However, it temporarily rerouted its email services to ensure customer queries continued to reach the airline without interruption, the company said in a statement.

IndiGo, another Indian airline company, said it also reported disruptions to its email support services, which affected its ability to receive customer queries. The airline in a statement on X said its other support channels remained operational and its flight operations were unaffected.
Singapore's Government Technology Agency said government email services were down and that it is working with Microsoft to resolve the issue.
The Philippines' Supreme Court said in a statement on social media that the ongoing Microsoft 365 service outage had affected some of its operations, including email responses.
In Japan, Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said the outage impacted the government's IT infrastructure and that officials were "keeping a close eye on the developments."

title: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop that disrupted thousands of flights
summary: The rare nationwide ground stop lasted about five hours Friday. Sources told CBS News an update to the network connecting the air traffic control system caused a reboot, crash and outage.
story: A rare nationwide ground stop on all departing U.S. flights that lasted several hours Friday has been lifted, and flights are resuming, the Federal Aviation Administration said. Officials said the issue stemmed from a "telecommunication outage."

"At 8:15 tonight, Eastern time, we've opened up the airspace," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said during a news briefing Friday night. "Now does that mean every flight is going to fly right now? It's going to be slow. So if you're watching, you're at an airport, check with your airline."
In a social media post following the briefing, the FAA said that "before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable."
The FAA had issued the ground stop on all departing flights due to "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." The ground stop lasted about five hours.
Duffy attributed the ground stop to outdated air traffic control technology and routers overloaded by data.

"What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system," Duffy said during the news conference. " ... Our routers actually got overloaded with data and … they started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down."

"The FAA lifted the ground stop and some flight departures are resuming," the FAA confirmed in a social media post following the briefing. "Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable."

An update to the private communications network that connects America's air traffic control system caused the system to reboot, leading to a crash and a communications outage, multiple sources told CBS News earlier Friday. The system is operated by L3Harris, which did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in Friday's briefing that new security patches introduced into the older system appeared to "overwhelm" its routers.
Duffy said the FAA would try to move as many flights as possible Friday night depending on crew capacity.
"If not, we're going to start tomorrow [Saturday] morning with our airline partners moving those aircraft. But it's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened this afternoon," Duffy said.
There were more than 10,000 delays and over 4,000 cancellations listed Friday, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware.
Duffy said he thinks flights will be "back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel" during the Thanksgiving holiday later this month.

Mullin told reporters in an earlier briefing outside the White House Friday that "there was no indication, as of yet, that this was a nefarious act against us. It was just a telecommunication outage, as of right now."

"There is no indication, we had no reason to believe, that as of right now, that this was a threat to the United States," Mullin said. "This was a telecommunication outage throughout FAA. Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all the flights. And all the flights are accounted for."
Mullin reiterated Friday night that there was no cyberattack and the ground stop was not related to the massive global Microsoft outage.

"I want to make sure everybody understands that there is no connection between this and Microsoft," Mullin said during the news briefing with Duffy. "I know a lot of people are making that jump. This is so far what we've seen. There is actually no cyberattack. We're still working through that process."
He also said flights will be able to land safely.

"We are assured that everybody is safe. Everybody that's going to be in the air, that's currently on the plane, the loved ones, as I said, we're going to get you on the ground and we're doing it in a safe manner," Mullin said.
Federal agencies are all working together on the situation, Mullin added.
"I don't want to say that this is a crisis, but it is because we're ... we had to do a nationwide ground stoppage," he said.
According to the flight tracking site Flightradar24, there were about 3,100 airborne aircraft bound for U.S. airports when the ground stop began.
Delays began piling up at major airports across the country in Boston, Atlanta, Miami, Pittsburgh, New York City, Los Angeles and Baltimore.

"This is absolutely unprecedented," said Robert Sumwalt, a former chair of the National Transportation Safety Board and a CBS News transportation safety expert. "I was an airline pilot for 24 years. I was in the air on 9/11. That was the last major ground stop. There was one back in 2023 for just a few hours. This is absolutely unbelievable that this could happen in this day and age."
On Friday night, Duffy renewed his call for Congress to approve emergency funding to modernize the nation's air traffic control system.
"But you will have more of these," Duffy said during the news conference. "You will have more of them unless the American people and the Congress tell us to build."

Mullin argued that the incident demonstrated why he believed piecemeal modernization was insufficient and said the Trump administration wants a complete replacement of the air traffic control system, at an estimated cost of $50 billion.

The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure, known as FTI, is the communications backbone that connects air traffic control centers and other FAA facilities. It supports the transmission of essential voice communications and operational data used to manage air traffic.
The FAA awarded Harris Corp., the predecessor to L3Harris, a contract to modernize, operate and manage the network in July 2002, more than 24 years ago.
A November 2023 FAA-commissioned safety review described the FTI network as obsolete and said it depended on an older communications technology known as TDM.

The review also warned that the technology was no longer supported by the telecommunications infrastructure on which it relied and that an unexpected failure could leave individual FAA facilities, or even an entire regional air traffic control center, disconnected from the broader network.

In January 2023, a nationwide ground stop was ordered for a few hours, and domestic flights were delayed nationwide due to an FAA system outage. The FAA said at the time that its flight personnel alert system went down overnight.

title: Passengers rescued after tanker hit river cruise in New Orleans
summary: A tanker struck a river cruise ship on the Mississippi River near the Port of New Orleans Friday, partially submerging the passenger boat.
story: A major rescue operation took place Friday after a tanker struck a river cruise ship on the Mississippi River near the Port of New Orleans, leaving the American Heritage passenger boat on its side and largely submerged in the water.
Everyone aboard both vessels has been accounted for, officials said, and there were no fatalities reported.

The much larger tanker, identified as the Atlantic Asphalt, crashed into the paddlewheel cruise boat while it was docked at about 12:30 p.m. local time, the Port of New Orleans said. The American Heritage had docked about two hours earlier for passengers to disembark.

In a news briefing late Friday afternoon, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said 32 passengers from the cruise ship were taken to area hospitals for treatment, but none with critical injuries. No one aboard the tanker was hurt, Moreno said.
New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said two of her officers were also hospitalized during the rescue operation, but were in good condition.
There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, aboard the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to Port NOLA.

Moreno said the tanker "lost control" and crashed into the cruise ship. As passengers were disembarking from the cruise ship, it "began to sink, and then eventually toppled over and flipped," sending people into the water, the mayor said.

Some people were seen in the water in life jackets or standing near the railing as the other side of the ship listed farther into the water. Nearby boats reported rescuing more than a dozen people from the water.

Emergency responders, including Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department and the U.S. Coast Guard, conducted rescue and response operations, Port NOLA said. Moreno said that along with local and federal agencies, private vessels that happened to be on the river at the time responded "as volunteers to try and get people out of the water."
Moreno described the successful rescue operation as a "miracle on the Mississippi."

One witness, Jamie Holford, told CBS News he saw the American Heritage hit the dock after the collision. He described seeing people hurrying off the boat. Then, as it rolled over, some were climbing over the railings of the boat, he said.
"It looked like something off the Titanic," he said.
Asked what the collision sounded like, Holford said, "It sounded like a war movie. Just imagine tons of steel crunching. That's what it sounded like."
U.S. Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said Coast Guard investigators were on scene working to determine what caused the tanker to lose control.
"The investigation is still ongoing, there seems to be some kind of a loss of steering," Burnham told reporters. "The exact reason why, we don't know that."

The National Transportation Safety Board said in a statement that it was sending a "Go Team" to the scene Saturday to begin its own investigation into the cause. However, in a follow up social media post, the NTSB clarified that because of the nationwide ground stop earlier Friday that canceled and delayed thousands of flights, it would no longer be sending one of its board members to the scene, and its team of investigators would be driving instead of flying to New Orleans.
Burnham also noted that she was working to reopen the river, which the Coast Guard had closed when the collision occurred.
"We're going to start evaluating how to reopen it as soon as possible," Burnham said.

In a Truth Social post, President Trump praised the response of the Coast Guard and other law enforcement agencies for "doing such an incredible job of rescue, and other work, having to do with the crash of the two ships in Louisiana."
The American Heritage was built in 2015 and is operated by American Cruise Lines. It is five stories and can hold up to 150 passengers.

The Associated Press reports that the tanker is owned by a subsidiary of the China State Shipbuilding Corporation, a sprawling Chinese state-owned conglomerate, according to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic. The tanker specializes in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semisolid substance that is often used for road construction and roofing, according to MarineTraffic.
CBS News has reached out to the tanker's owner for comment.

title: How "Banana Man" took a small Indiana town by storm
summary: Banana Man began popping up around Linton, Indiana, a few months ago. Videos that also began circulating on social media appeared to show a boy biking all over town in a banana suit.
story: In Linton, Indiana, there have been reports and sightings of a superhero of sorts, "Banana Man."
"Just boom, like a yellow streak goes by," one Linton resident said. "... And everybody is like, 'It's the Banana Man.'"
"Little bitty legs and tights on," stated another.
Banana Man began popping up around town a few months ago. Videos that also began circulating on social media appeared to show a boy, about middle school age, biking all over town in a banana suit.
So CBS News came to Linton to investigate and find out who and why, but it wasn't easy.
Because Banana Man's other trademark is that he doesn't ever talk. In fact, by all accounts, he has never spoken a word publicly. That is, until now.
In an interview, CBS News disguised his voice to protect his identity.

"So my mom bought a banana costume from Goodwill, and I put it on and rode my bike as a joke," Banana Man explains as to how his alter ego took shape. "And I saw that it made a lot of people smile, and I like making people smile."
Banana Man said that when he was younger, he dreamed of being a superhero.
"But I didn't expect to be a banana," he said.
But as a banana, he has so much more appeal. Linton residents have now thoroughly embraced the legend, and many even dressed up as him for Halloween.
A local girls cross country team did a run in his honor. Some people are even wearing Banana Man T-shirts.
"People honk and yell and wave," one Linton resident said of Banana Man sightings.
In gratitude to his legions, Banana Man hands out autographed cards, which have become quite the collector's item in Linton.
What started out as a joke has now made a serious difference. Banana Man has brought the town together.
"Yeah, feels good. I feel proud," Banana Man said. "And I'm just going to keep doing the same thing that I've been doing."

title: Lutnick agrees to testify as Bessent blames him for chip sales
summary: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10, according to a U.S. official.
story: Washington — Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10, according to a U.S. official, amid intensifying scrutiny of the Commerce Department's oversight of the export of powerful AI chips following the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

A growing number of Republicans are calling on Lutnick to answer questions about the Commerce Department's apparent delay in adding Singapore-based company Megaspeed International to the U.S. government's Entity List, which would have restricted the company's ability to get access to advanced AI chips.

Megaspeed was previously led by Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy who had an affair with Jensen Huang. The U.S. government suspects Megaspeed of directing advanced Nvidia chips to China, circumventing a U.S. export ban.

GOP Sen. Jim Banks of Indiana, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, told Fox News on Thursday that "we know that the Department of Commerce, Secretary Lutnick, it appears, used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur even though President Trump has directed his administration and the Department of Commerce not to allow that to happen."

On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent repeatedly emphasized that the Treasury Department and other parts of the executive branch had pushed for restrictions on Megaspeed, laying the blame for the delay at the feet of the Commerce Department.

"Treasury, War, [the U.S. Trade Representative] and State, they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the Entity List for months, but Commerce has the pen," Bessent told CNBC. "And you will have to ask them about their internal processes."
Bessent declined to comment on reported tensions between himself and Lutnick. The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.

title: Man whose wife, son were injured in building collapse wants answers
summary: The world crumbled around Anderson Velez's family on Wednesday when the multi-use Brooklyn building where they resided collapsed.
story: The world crumbled around Anderson Velez's family on Wednesday when the multi-use Brooklyn building where they resided collapsed.

Video from a baby monitor showed his terrified sons and wife, Joanna, inside their third-floor apartment as the walls broke open and crashed. CBS News also obtained surveillance video capturing the apartment building and storefront crashing down.
Eight people, ranging in age from 9 to 31, died in the collapse, including two children. Another 18 were injured.

Joanna Velez remains hospitalized, as does their 9-year-old son, Pablo Alvarez, who is recovering from surgery for a severe head injury. Miraculously, their 2-year-old son Joseph Alvarez survived with barely a scratch.
Anderson Velez, who was not home at the time, told CBS News his fear when he heard of the collapse was that his children had "lost their lives."
The building where the Velez family resided collapsed into an adjacent construction site and also tore off the side of another building in the process.
Now, the search for answers and accountability is underway, as the Brooklyn District Attorney's Office has launched a criminal investigation into the incident.
The collapsed building had 98 open violations, according to records from the New York City Department of Buildings.

The same agency had also earlier this year ordered a contractor to stop demolition work that was underway at the adjacent construction site. When the contractor continued the demolition work despite the stop-work order, the buildings department issued a violation in April.
In May, though, the violation was addressed and the stop-work order was lifted, the buildings department said.
That contractor, Townhouse Builders, has been sued at least 67 times since 2012, according to court records reviewed by CBS News.

"Buildings do not simply collapse without systemic failures," Farah Louis, a member of the New York City Council, said in a news conference Friday. "Especially when records show a building with nearly 100 open violations sitting next to an excavation site cited for violating a stop-work order."
Anderson Velez believes that construction taking place in the site next door led to the collapse.
"The building had no reason to fall on its own," he said.
Asked about his thoughts when he sees the video of the collapse, Anderson Velez responded, "Honestly, I still watch it and tears come to my eyes."
CBS News has reached out to the owner of the collapsed building for comment but has not heard back.

title: Democrats strategize on how to deliver on midterm mandate
summary: Democrats gathered in Denver this week for a conference on what comes next as they prepare to take control of Congress.
story: Democrats received the message loud and clear from the midterm elections that Americans want results, not "shallow litmus tests," as Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro put it at a conference in Denver this week. But it was evident that Democrats, who gathered at a summit on the way forward as they take control of the House and Senate next year, are still working out just how to achieve those results while President Trump is still in the White House.

Shapiro helped Democrats flip four House seats in his state, and he spoke after an election that delivered decisive majorities to Democrats in the Senate and the House. He said voters had rejected "chaos" and "corruption" and are demanding results-focused governance. Shapiro urged congressional Democrats to focus on lowering costs, building affordable housing, protecting consumers and expanding economic opportunity — and not on ideological fights.

The Pennsylvania governor, who has been mentioned as a possible 2028 presidential candidate, focused on national issues, arguing the "beginning of the mandate" from voters called for aggressive action on competition, AI, innovation and economic fairness. He advised Democrats to use their majorities to deliver a stronger "American bargain" for working families.

While some newly elected Democrats, like Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas, have some optimism about the new Congress' ability to work with the Trump administration, others, including New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, encouraged new members of Congress to be pragmatic in approaching dealmaking with Mr. Trump.
In his remarks Thursday, Talarico, who won his seat in a heavily Republican state, said that Democrats "must" work with President Trump because "the American people cannot wait two years for change."
"We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history," Talarico said.
But Sherrill suggested that may be harder than it sounds.

"The art of the deal to Trump is, he figures out what you want. He leverages the you-know-what out of you and keeps taking, taking, taking and never delivers. He does not follow through on his commitments," Sherrill said of her experience in working with him as New Jersey's governor.
She told Democrats to take advantage of the power they amassed this election cycle and use it to their advantage.
"My advice to Senator Talarico is, if Trump wants to work with us, we will lay out the agenda and he can sign it," Sherrill said.
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, who won the governorship in 2025, the same year as Sherrill, agreed that trying to make deals with Mr. Trump may be futile.

"It is foolish to think if you ever make a deal, if you ever give anything, you give an inch to the president, there is no reason to believe—he has no track record of ever following through—that if you make a deal with President Trump, he will ever actually abide by it," Spanberger said.

Spanberger, who represented Virginia in the House before she was elected governor, offered this advice to next year's Democratic Congress: "Congress should pass bill after bill after bill that is broadly, very clearly popular, and is responsive to what folks across the country campaigned on, and send it to the president's desk. No pre-negotiations, no discussions. Eventually he'll want to do a signing ceremony. And eventually, he might sign a couple of them. And if not, then in 2028, folks say, look at these bills that passed through the House, passed through the Senate. The president didn't take action."

Despite the celebratory mood in Denver, Democratic officials repeatedly sent the message that they understand that last week's victories do not represent a long-term realignment, and there's no guarantee that the voters who supported them will continue to do so.
"This isn't a blank check," Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona said. "If anything, it is a short-term loan that we need to keep paying — or we will lose it."

title: New congressman faces sexual harassment allegation
summary: House Democrats are investigating an allegation of sexual harassment against Brian Poindexter, who defeated embattled GOP Rep. Max Miller.
story: Washington — House Democrats are investigating an allegation of sexual harassment against Brian Poindexter, who defeated embattled GOP Rep. Max Miller of Ohio in last week's elections.

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, House Democrats' campaign arm, said Friday that it had hired an independent firm to investigate "any instance of inappropriate behavior, conduct interviews and gather the facts."
"The DCCC has been made aware of the allegations and takes them seriously," the group's executive director, Julie Merz, said in a statement.
A spokesperson for Poindexter's campaign characterized his actions as "an innocuous compliment to a volunteer."

"He heard later that it made her feel uncomfortable and he felt awful," the spokesperson said in a statement. "When Brian learned about this, we immediately began to work to get to the bottom of it with an outside HR firm. Neither Brian nor the campaign ever wants anyone to feel uncomfortable."
The investigation comes as Congress grapples with how to overhaul how it handles allegations of sexual misconduct as numerous lawmakers have faced complaints.

The DCCC was made aware of the allegations from two political action committees — the Blue Dog PAC and the Congressional Progressive Caucus PAC — which said they were informed of a report of alleged sexual harassment in the final days before the election.

"We informed the DCCC and connected the individual with legal advocacy and support services so she could determine how she wanted to proceed," the PACs said in a joint statement Friday. "The individual requested that we did not disclose any details about this publicly because she did not want her identity becoming public and she wanted an opportunity to determine how she wanted to proceed while protecting herself."
The PACs said they pulled their endorsements from Poindexter "pending the investigation being completed."

title: Never bought Nvidia stock? Its slide could still hit your 401(k).
summary: Millions of Americans are exposed to Nvidia shares through their retirement plans. That's not as bad as it sounds (really!).
story: Even if you never bought a single share of Nvidia, the embattled chipmaker's steep slide this week could still ding your retirement savings.

Nvidia is a component of the S&P 500 and many other indexes, including the Nasdaq 100 and Dow Jones Industrial Average, all popular with retirement savers through funds offered by millions of employer retirement plans. About 97% of retirement plans now offer index funds, up from 79% in 2006, according to March research from the Investment Company Institute and ISS Market Intelligence.

That means even if you haven't directly bought Nvidia stock, your 401(k) is likely exposed to the chipmaker through an index fund, such as the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust or Vanguard's S&P 500 ETF (which trade under the tickers SPY and VOO, respectively).
Overall, Nvidia represents about 6% of the S&P 500 index, making it the second-largest component after Apple, according to Yahoo Finance.

Nvidia's shares started falling on Monday amid revelations that cofounder Jensen Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. Huang resigned from his role as CEO on Thursday, causing a further drop in the stock.

Since Nov. 6, the company's value has declined by more than $550 billion — a decline of about 13% in one week. While that will certainly hurt investors who directly own Nvidia shares, it may also impact people with indirect investments through funds that hold the chipmaker.

Nvidia's woes underline the risks inherent in many big tech companies widely held by U.S. investors, Shiva Rajgopal, a Columbia Business School professor who studies corporate governance, told CBS News.

The "Magnificent Seven" tech stocks account for about one-third of the S&P 500. As with Nvidia, several of those companies are closely associated with CEOs whom investors see as central to their success, such as Elon Musk at Tesla, Rajgopal noted. And as Nvidia's selloff showed this week, trouble for a charismatic CEO can quickly spill over into the company's stock.

"They are amazing wealth creators for shareholders," Rajgopal said. "But hopefully, shareholders know what they are doing when they buy the stock of these companies, because the exact same structure also has a lot of fragility built into it."
A drag on the S&P 500

The AI industry's influence on Wall Street was evident this week, as turmoil at Nvidia triggered a broader slump in technology stocks. Yet more companies within the S&P 500 rose rather than fell this week, boosting the index by 2.9% for the week through Thursday's close. Excluding Nvidia, the index would have gained an estimated 3.8%.

"If you check your account today, tomorrow, you're going to see some sort of fluctuation, especially if you own shares of Nvidia," Sabrina Escobar, a reporter at Barron's, told CBS News. "The decline we saw over the past couple of days will certainly have some implications in your daily or weekly stock movements."

For investors, Huang's sudden downfall and Nvidia's wobbly stock highlight the importance of properly diversifying their portfolios, Mercer Advisors chief investment officer Donald Calcagni said in a blog post.

"Events like this — where the outcome hinges on one company's leadership — are a risk we try to minimize through diversification," he wrote. "This is the core principle behind portfolio diversification strategies: spread your risk broadly enough that no single company's troubles can derail your long-term plan."

Of course, that's the idea behind holding a broad-based index fund like the S&P 500 — rather than concentrating your money in a handful of individual stocks, you're spreading your bets across hundreds of types of companies. And the fact that the S&P 500 is on track to post a weekly gain despite Nvidia's turmoil points to how that strategy can pay off.
Timing is not on your side

Investors may be tempted to sell when the market, a stock or a fund tumbles, but research has repeatedly shown that trying to determine the right time to buy or sell an investment usually results in losses.

Meanwhile, tech experts noted that Nvidia's chips remain essential to the artificial intelligence sector, a key competitive edge unlikely to change in the near term even with Huang's abrupt departure. In other words, holding Nvidia shares may be a way to bet on the broader AI industry, rather than on its executive roster.

"When a single company's stock drops on unexpected news, the best response is usually the simplest one: pause, keep the news in perspective and let your diversified portfolio do what it was designed to do," Calcagni said.

title: Family Dollar to pay $63M after FTC says it overcharged customers
summary: The discount retailer failed to honor prices displayed on store shelves, on price tags and in ads, the FTC and multiple states alleged.
story: Family Dollar has agreed to pay $63 million to settle allegations that it routinely overcharged customers by millions of dollars.
The Federal Trade Commission and 17 U.S. states accused the budget retailer of failing to honor prices displayed on store shelves, on price tags and in advertisements.

A proposed order bans Family Dollar from misleading customers on prices and requires the company to adopt what the FTC described as a "pricing accuracy program" that is independently assessed and certified annually.

"Today's order will ensure Family Dollar stops deceiving consumers about its prices and returns money to consumers harmed by these practices," Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement on Thursday.
Family Dollar operates more than 7,000 stores across 48 U.S. states and Washington, D.C. The Chesapeake, Virginia-based company did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the settlement.

The FTC and the states' complaint alleged that pricing inaccuracies are widespread at Family Dollar stores and that the retailer failed to correct errors. Customers regularly reported being charged higher prices at the register than those displayed on goods' price tags, in stores, on the retailer's website and in its mobile app, according to the complaint.
The states include Alabama, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Iowa, Illinois, Kansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Nebraska, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin.
In October, the FTC and 20 states sued another discount retailer, Dollar General, over allegations of similar deceptive pricing practices. The litigation is ongoing.
Customer refunds and discounts
The proposed order requires Family Dollar to establish a $40 million fund to compensate eligible customers.

The retailer will notify customers of their eligibility for reimbursement through in-store notices and online. Eligible customers include anyone who made a purchase at a Family Dollar store from Jan. 1, 2023, to Oct. 1, 2026.

The order also establishes a separate $20 million discount program for customers. Under the program, Family Dollar must offer customers 15% off a range of goods for two days. State plaintiffs will receive $3 million to be divided among them.
The retailer must create a pricing accuracy program to ensure that it regularly monitors and verifies prices and trains employees to identify and correct pricing discrepancies.

title: Democrats have flipped 45 House seats. Here's the breakdown.
summary: Democrats won control of the House by flipping more than 40 Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red.
story: Washington — Democrats won control of the House of Representatives on Nov. 3 by flipping more than 40 Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red. The party's wins ranged from suburban areas in the northeastern United States to areas of South Texas that were once viewed as increasingly GOP-friendly.

The 2026 midterm elections were also shaken up by last year's nationwide mid-decade redistricting gambit, with Texas Republicans shifting several districts rightward at President Trump's behest, California Democrats moving districts to the left and several other states tweaking their House maps for partisan purposes. Democrats notched several wins under the new maps, while the GOP's pickups have been more limited so far.
Winners in a dozen House races have yet to be projected by CBS News.
So far, 45 districts have shifted to Democrats and three have shifted to Republicans. Here's a look at the seats that swung:
Upsets
In several districts, Democrats ousted GOP lawmakers who won by double digits two years ago.

New Jersey's 2nd District: Republican Rep. Jeff Van Drew lost to Democrat Zack Mullock in a South Jersey district that was widely seen as solid red. Van Drew, who won by 16.9 points in 2024, is known for switching from the Democratic Party during the first Trump impeachment saga in 2019. Ohio's 10th District: GOP Rep. Mike Turner was ousted by Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker, ending Turner's nearly quarter-century tenure in Congress just two years after he won reelection by more than 18 points.Missouri's 2nd District: Democrat Fred Wellman unseated GOP Rep. Ann Wagner, who won by 12 points in 2024. Republicans tried to make the St. Louis-area seat slightly redder last year, but the new maps were tossed out in the courts. As recently as September, the Cook Political Report viewed it as solid-red.Indiana's 5th District: Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz lost to Democrat J.D. Ford in one of several election night surprises. Spartz won reelection by just over 18 points in 2024.Kentucky's 6th District: The race between Democrat Zach Dembo and Republican Ralph Alvarado for the open seat was not expected to be competitive, but the election forecasters moved the GOP-held seat toward Democrats in recent weeks. Outgoing Rep. Andy Barr won it by 26 points two years ago.Wisconsin's 1st District: Republican Rep. Bryan Steil, who was first elected in 2018, lost his race to Democrat Mitchell Berman. A Democrat has not represented the district in more than 30 years. Steil won his last reelection by just over 10 points, outperforming Mr. Trump, and the Cook Political Report rated it "Likely Republican" until late September.Nevada's 2nd District: Teresa Benitez-Thompson will be the first Democrat to represent Northern Nevada in decades, after she defeated Republican David Flippo. The seat was left open by the retirement of longtime GOP Rep. Mark Amodei, who won by a nearly 19-point margin in 2024.Ohio's 15th District: Democrat Don Leonard defeated GOP Rep. Mike Carey, who won reelection by 13 points in 2024.

Rematches

title: Inflation isn't going away. Here's what that means for interest rates.
summary: As inflation seeps deeper into the U.S. economy, the Federal Reserve may have to step up the pace of rate hikes, according to Wall Street analysts.
story: The Federal Reserve is likely to accelerate the pace of interest rate hikes to rein in stubbornly high inflation, according to a growing number of Wall Street analysts.

Aditya Bhave, a U.S. economist with BofA Global Research, expects monetary policymakers to raise the Fed's benchmark rate by 0.25 percentage points at each of the central bank's next three meetings in December, January and March. Analysts at TD Securities also predict three straight quarter-point hikes, up from their previous forecast of two, because hotter inflation signals that price pressures across the U.S. are broadening.
The latest Consumer Price Index showed that inflation rose more than expected in October, climbing 0.4%.

"Inflation is not trending in the right direction," TD Securities said Friday in a note to investors. "The October report not only surprised our own forecast, it was also not driven by a particular factor or two as had been the case in recent reports. Price pressures appear to be broadening."

Hotter inflation in October was the third straight month that prices have risen faster than expected amid supply constraints and ample economic demand, according to EY-Parthenon chief economist Gregory Daco, who is penciling in rate hikes for December and January.

"For any borrower, this will mean a high cost of borrowing for any type of consumer loan people take out," Daco told CBS News. "A higher federal funds rate trajectory will generally mean higher long-term interest rates and increase the cost of borrowing for consumers across the country."

Interest rate traders put the odds of a quarter-point hike at the Fed's next meeting on Dec. 8-9 at nearly 90%, and also see a better-than-even chance of another such hike at the Jan. 26-27 gathering, according to CME FedWatch.

Some Fed officials themselves have said tightening may need to be more aggressive to bring inflation in line with their 2% annual target. At a conference in London on Tuesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said policymakers should consider a 0.50 percentage-point increase in December, adding that a smaller hike "would put our credibility at risk."
High energy prices continue to drive inflation, along with robust corporate spending on data centers and other equipment for powering AI.
"Together, these forces could keep inflation elevated into 2027 and weigh further on household purchasing power," Daco said in a report.

title: Alex Murdaugh wants murder indictments tossed, saying agent lied
summary: Alex Murdaugh is facing a retrial on murder charges after the South Carolina Supreme Court threw out his convictions and life sentence.
story: Attorneys for Alex Murdaugh asked a judge Friday to throw out the original murder indictments for killing his wife and son, saying the chief investigator in the case lied to the grand jury.

Murdaugh is facing a retrial on the murder charges after the South Carolina Supreme Court threw out his convictions and life sentence, ruling that a court clerk improperly influenced jurors against him during his 2023 trial.

Even if the request to dismiss the indictments is granted, it may not stop or even postpone an April retrial for the disgraced lawyer. Prosecutors can seek another set of grand jury indictments, and defense attorneys said they won't stop them.
Judge ends hearing with interesting question
Judge Debra McCaslin did not immediately decide on the defense request, promising a written ruling next week. But one of her last comments at the hearing may have indicated where she is going.
"If you had to go back to the grand jury, could you have it all done and ready to go by April 5th?" she asked prosecutor Creighton Waters.
"Your honor, I'm always working ahead," Waters responded.
Throwing out indictments could be another rebuke of agent on case
A ruling throwing out the indictments would be another rebuke of the chief investigator in Murdaugh's case, State Law Enforcement Division agent David Owen.

A judge last year threw out a different murder case Owen was involved in because the dead woman's mother told the agent about a suicide threat her daughter made days before she died that Owen never relayed to prosecutors or defense attorneys. She was found dead by the same method she told her mother she was going to use to kill herself.
Owen abruptly retired in 2024, not long after he was honored as State Law Enforcement Officer of the Year.

Prosecutors pointed out while Owen is accused of hiding or not revealing evidence in that case, all the issues in the Murdaugh case involved evidence and reports the defense had at the original trial.
The grand jury heard several questionable assertions

Prosecutors said Murdaugh, 58, killed his wife, Maggie, and younger son, Paul, on their sprawling property in the South Carolina Lowcountry in 2021. Murdaugh is spending decades in prison for stealing millions of dollars from clients, and has admitted in court that he is a thief, insurance cheat, bad lawyer and longtime opioid addict. But he denies being a killer.

Defense lawyers said that as prosecutors sought the indictments, Owen told the Colleton County grand jury that blood spatter was found on a T-shirt Murdaugh was wearing the night of the killings. An earlier report from state agents said there were no blood stains, and no such evidence was introduced at trial.

Owen also told grand jurors that the same ammunition load of buckshot in one chamber and large birdshot in the other used to kill Paul Murdaugh was found loaded in weapons all over the Murdaugh property, which wasn't the case.

The grand jury may have heard about plenty of evidence, including the video Paul Murdaugh recorded in which Alex Murdaugh's voice could be heard at the scene, contradicting his claims that he wasn't at the kennels near where his wife and son were killed any time close to their deaths.
But defense attorney Jim Griffin said the false evidence of the blood of Murdaugh's son was the only thing anyone heard that could link him to the place and time of the killings.
"A phone call doesn't put him there. The video doesn't put him there," Griffin said. "The blood from his murdered son sprang through the air — it's raining back on him — puts him there."
Prosecutors call it a mistake, cite other evidence against Murdaugh
Prosecutors said they had plenty of other evidence supporting the murder charges, and wrote in court papers that "a single mistake is not bad faith."

Along with the kennel video, Owen told the grand jury about the family's mounting debts, guns missing from the house that matched what could have been used in the killings and how Murdaugh's schemes to steal from clients and his law firm were close to being discovered.

"This is what the agent understood at the time. And it's ultimately not something that would cause a substantial effect on the grand jury or cast grave doubt when we look at all the other evidence that was presented," Waters said.
Prosecutors said Murdaugh killed his wife and son because he thought the sympathy generated by the killings would buy him time to cover up his thefts.

Murdaugh's lawyers have repeatedly pointed out how little evidence prosecutors have. No DNA or blood was found splattered on Murdaugh or any of his clothes, even though the killings were at close range with powerful weapons that were never found.
"What we're asking, your honor, is to reboot — go back to square one," Griffin said.
Even with the original convictions overturned, Murdaugh remains in prison on separate financial crime sentences. The outcome of the murder case will not determine when he could be released.

title: Supreme Court takes up case over asylum access at border
summary: The case involving President Trump's directives suspending access to the asylum system is the latest involving the president's second-term immigration agenda.
story: Washington — The Supreme Court on Friday said it will take up a legal fight over President Trump's directive suspending access to the asylum system and other legal protections for migrants illegally crossing the southern border.

The case is the latest involving Mr. Trump's second-term immigration agenda that the Supreme Court will decide in the coming months. The justices are also considering the legality of removing migrants to third countries and indefinitely detaining immigrants in the U.S. illegally without access to a bond hearing.
A decision in the cases is expected by the end of June or early July.

Mr. Trump has made cracking down on immigration a cornerstone of his second term, which has seen enhanced enforcement operations in major U.S. cities and mass deportations of people in the U.S. illegally. Unlawful crossings at the U.S.-Mexico border have reached historic lows and immigration detentions have set new highs under the president's second administration.

As part of his efforts to curb illegal immigration into the U.S., Mr. Trump issued a proclamation on his first day back in the White House claiming that there is an "invasion" at the southern border. The president suspended the entry of migrants crossing the southern border between ports of entry and barred them from seeking asylum and other legal protections that would allow them to remain in the U.S.

The Department of Homeland Security then issued guidance implementing the president's directive. Immigration authorities have since relied on the policy to summarily remove migrants entering the country illegally without allowing them to apply for asylum.

In February 2025, three nonprofit groups and 13 people filed a class-action lawsuit challenging Mr. Trump's proclamation and the administration's guidance. Several months later, a federal judge in Washington set aside the Trump administration's asylum restrictions and found them unlawful.

The judge, Randolph Moss, found that neither the Constitution nor federal immigration law gave the Trump administration the authority to replace the rules and procedures enacted by Congress. The judge also said that immigration law does not give the president the unilateral authority to limit the rights of noncitizens in the U.S. to apply for asylum or other protections.
As part of his decision, Moss certified a class of all people covered by the president's proclamation and blocked the Trump administration from enforcing the directive against them.

The Trump administration appealed, and in April, a divided three-judge panel upheld the district court's decision and ruled that the proclamation and guidance exceeded the president's authority. The two judges in the majority also found that the president does not have the power to suspend migrants' right to apply for asylum or deport migrants under his administration's new summary removal proceedings.

The Trump administration has continued to enforce its policy suspending access to asylum while legal proceedings have continued, and the D.C. Circuit halted its ruling against DHS pending Supreme Court review.

title: TSA agent finds live snakes in luggage at California airport
summary: X-ray images of the luggage showed what appeared to be a rope but turned out to be two live snakes concealed in a pillowcase.
story: Video by the Transportation Security Administration shows the moment officers discovered two live snakes inside a checked bag at California's Ontario International Airport in October.
TSA said the snakes were discovered during a routine inspection of a bag.
X-ray images showed what appeared to be a rope but turned out to be two live snakes concealed in a pillowcase.
"When I realized the item in my hand was alive, I told myself, 'I need to escalate this immediately,'" said TSA Officer Benjamin Andrade-Carillo, who discovered the pillowcase.
Andrade-Carillo notified a supervisor who further inspected the pillowcase. Supervisory TSA Officer Suggey Flores said he felt the pillowcase tense up and start moving.
"I have held snakes before, so I wasn't too spooked," Flores said. "I was more impressed, because it's not something you see every day."
After the discovery of the snakes, TSA said screening operations in the immediate area were paused due to safety concerns.
"Safety was a concern because we didn't know what kind of snakes they were," Flores said. "They could have been venomous."
Airport police took possession of the bag and brought it to the airline ticketing area. The passenger removed the snakes and gave them to a non-traveling family member, TSA said.
After the snakes were removed, TSA rescreened the bag and the passenger was cleared for travel.
According to the Los Angeles TSA Coordination Center, the passenger said the snakes were pets and he had previously traveled with them on another airline.
"In my two years of service, I had not found anything like this," Andrade-Carillo said. "In San Diego, I experienced a gentleman trying to bring live lobsters as a carry-on."
TSA encourages travelers to contact their airline before traveling with pets to understand the carrier's rules and requirements.

title: Top doctor for Congress resigns amid misconduct allegations
summary: Dr. Brian Monahan, the attending physician of the U.S. Capitol, has resigned from his post as lawmakers' top doctor.
story: Washington — Dr. Brian Monahan, the attending physician of the U.S. Capitol, has resigned from his post as lawmakers' top doctor, Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Thursday, amid allegations of misconduct.
"My understanding is he's resigned," Thune said.

One source familiar with the matter told CBS News that Monahan, a two-star Navy admiral, resigned after allegations of misconduct related to what he chose to do and asked the sailors under him to do in terms of providing care.
The resignation comes in conjunction with a report by the Defense Department's inspector general that found lax oversight of the Office of the Attending Physician.

The public version of watchdog report, while light on specifics and including numerous redactions, said investigators found a "gap in clinical quality management." The report found that some prescription drugs, including sleep aids and pain medication, were not properly inventoried or tracked.
These shortfalls, the inspector general said, could "result in OAP beneficiaries unknowingly assuming health and safety risks because clinical and prescribing practices were not monitored."
CBS News has learned the Navy is also conducting an inquiry into the Office of the Attending Physician.

Monahan has served as the attending physician since 2009. He is also a professor at Uniformed Services University in Bethesda, Maryland, and previously served as its chairman of medicine. He is certified by the American Board of Internal Medicine in internal medicine, hematology and medical oncology.
His removal was first reported by Punchbowl News. The Office of the Attending Physician did not reply to multiple requests for comment.

Since 1928, the Navy — through the Office of the Attending Physician — has been tasked with medical care of Congress, staff, the Supreme Court and visitors to the Capitol complex. In addition to administering minor first aid services and providing other general medical support, the office participates in planning for and responding to disasters that may involve the Capitol.

CBS News asked House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries on Thursday if he had any knowledge about the circumstances surrounding Monahan's dismissal. Jeffries said he did not but wants to ensure member health is protected.

The Navy Times reported military personnel in the office were pressured to endure 70-80 hour work weeks and do tasks "no one else wants to do ... like cutting a congressman's toenails or bringing their medication to their private residence at 3 a.m."

The inspector general's report included five recommendations for improving OAP, including designating an outside group to oversee quality control and establishing policies and procedures for OAP employees.

title: Brother of cartel leader "El Mencho" gets 22.5 years in prison
summary: The brother of the slain prominent cartel leader known as "El Mencho" was sentenced on Friday to 22 and a half years in prison.
story: Washington — The brother of the slain prominent cartel leader known as "El Mencho" was sentenced on Friday to 22.5 years in prison, after he pleaded guilty to drug trafficking and firearms offenses, the Justice Department said.
Antonio Oseguera Cervantes, 67, worked for cartels with his brother Nemesio Rubén Oseguera Cervantes, or El Mencho, who was killed by the Mexican army in February.

Antonio Cervantes, also known as "Tony Montana," pleaded guilty in July to conspiring to distribute five kilograms or more of cocaine and 500 grams or more of methamphetamine for importation into the U.S. He also pleaded guilty to using, carrying and possessing a firearm in furtherance of the drug trafficking conspiracy.
El Mencho co-founded and led the Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generación, also known as CJNG. Last year, the Trump administration designated the CJNG and other cartels as foreign terrorist organizations.

"For more than two decades, Antonio Oseguera Cervantes helped fuel one of the world's most dangerous drug trafficking organizations, flooding America's communities with deadly drugs while enriching himself and his associates," said Tysen Duva, the assistant attorney general for the Justice Department's Criminal Division, in a statement.

title: As Americans drown in medical debt, how one family found a lifeline
summary: Coy and Caty Smith are gainfully employed and have health insurance. But when illness struck, the bills piled up fast — here's how they found their way back to financial health.
story: Coy Smith and his wife were getting up to 16 phone calls a day, all to discuss the same topic — how they planned to pay off the thousands of dollars in medical bills their family had racked up after facing a series of serious healthcare issues.
By 2023, the family was more than $30,000 in the hole, including credit card debt they had taken on to help pay their medical bills.

"It's very stressful knowing that every time the phone rings, you have to pick it up and talk to someone who says you owe them thousands of dollars for something you couldn't help," Coy, 32, a Cypress, Texas, resident, told CBS News.
40% of Americans

The phone is also ringing off the hook for millions of other people facing overdue healthcare bills. Roughly 40% of Americans are saddled with debt for medical care not covered by insurance, treatment for complex medical conditions, and hospitalization costs for serious injuries or illnesses, according to health policy and research firm KFF.

Those debts are often financially debilitating, with high healthcare costs topping the list of financial worries for U.S. voters, a recent KFF poll shows. To stay on top of their medical bills, people may cut spending on essentials like food, exhaust emergency savings and tap their retirement funds.

"There's no other way to state it than as a parent and American, you dread having to go to the doctor and having to go to the hospital," Smith said. "You know it's going to cost thousands of dollars just to walk in the door."

Smith also said he was routinely advised to take out a personal loan to consolidate the family's crushing debt. But that approach carried its own financial risks. At the time, they calculated, it would've taken them 30 years and cost $150,000 in interest to pay down all of their debt.
Instead, the goal was "to change our relationship with credit and how we paid for things," he told CBS News.
How illness spawns debt
Smith and his wife, Caty, are both public school teachers, earning a combined income of roughly $100,000 per year plus benefits, including health insurance.

Their financial problems began in 2023, when their youngest son was hospitalized with lung problems shortly after birth. Their son's one-week stay in the hospital left the couple owing $10,000 even after insurance had covered its share.

The stress also triggered a flare-up of the autoimmune and inflammatory diseases Caty has suffered from since 2018, he told CBS News. After she missed some days at work because of her health issues, Caty's employer docked her pay, further straining the family's finances.
With lower income, the couple turned to credit to cover urgent medical costs and pay their grocery, electricity and daycare bills, resulting in a ballooning balance.

"We paid our electric bills with credit. We did anything we could to keep the lights on and make sure we could provide for the family," Smith said. "At one point, we even had to put daycare on our credit cards. We were unable to keep up with payments and interest rates, and found ourselves in this revolving cycle of debt."

Making ends meet was difficult, and even small unexpected expenses could make budgeting all but impossible, Smith told CBS News. To make matters worse, the family was paying interest rates of up to 30% on some of their debt.
"Any time we would get a little bit of air, we would blow a tire on the car, or an appliance would go out, or something along those lines would happen," he said.
Getting back on track

Knowing they needed help, the Smiths turned to Money Management International, a nationally accredited credit counseling firm. Working with a debt counselor, they took stock of all their obligations and set about negotiating lower interest rates with creditors. That allowed them to form a repayment plan.

"They would negotiate a lower interest rate and plan a time period where we would make X number of payments at X value, and within a set time period that debt would be paid off," Smith said of working with a counselor.

The family wanted to be aggressive, but realistic, in paying off debt. That meant thinking long-term — their goal was to have it all paid off by the time the Smiths' two children had left daycare and entered the local public school system.

"We wanted to have it paid off so we could enter the next phase of life without credit card debt hanging over our heads," Smith told CBS News. "We put together a plan we could afford, which was $400 less than if we'd continued to pay minimum monthly payments on our own."
Inevitably, escaping debt also required belt-tightening and greater prudence in how they spent money.

"We are very careful about where we spend money, avoiding any consumer debt, avoiding things like buy now, pay later loans," he said. "We are smarter about looking at interest rates before entering into agreements."

Four years later, the Smiths are on track to be fully out of debt by the end of 2027. The experience, while harrowing, has at least made Smith think long and hard about how to change the family's financial behaviors to avoid future problems.

Smith added, "If we have our debt paid off by the time our oldest son is 7, and our youngest is 4, they have the rest of their childhoods to enjoy trips together. We can enjoy them, too, knowing we are not burying ourselves in insurmountable debt while doing it."

title: Criminal probe into cruise ship over potential "magic pipe"
summary: The U.S. Coast Guard launched an investigation into a so-called "magic pipe" case, in which a ship transfers its oil discharge into its gray water system.
story: The MSC Poesia cruise ship, which was cleared to depart the Port of Miami on Thursday after being detained earlier this month, is under investigation for allegedly discharging oil illegally at sea, according to a U.S. official familiar with the probe.
The U.S. Coast Guard launched the criminal investigation into a so-called "magic pipe" case, in which a ship transfers its oil discharge into its gray water system. This is illegal under federal law.
Gray water — which includes anything from a sink or shower — can be discharged at sea as long as the ship is a safe distance from the shore.
The investigation could target crew members, the owner of the vessel, and whoever may have been directly involved and therefore potentially criminally liable, according to the U.S. official.
CBS News has reached out to MSC Cruises, which operates the ship, for comment.

The MSC Poesia was detained at the Port of Miami earlier this month after the U.S. Coast Guard, which has jurisdiction to inspect foreign-flagged vessels entering U.S. ports, "identified deficiencies with systems on board the vessel." At the time, MSC Cruises described the issue as a "regulatory matter" and no further details were provided.
More than 2,000 people were on board the MSC Poesia at the time of its detention, a source familiar with the matter told CBS News.
Using a so-called "magic pipe" could lead to hefty fines.

In 2016, Carnival's Princess Cruises was ordered to pay a $40 million fine for dumping oily waste into the ocean. It was the largest penalty of its kind at the time. The company also pleaded guilty to seven felony charges.

title: Major AI developers can't control their own tech, lawsuit alleges
summary: Companies including Anthropic, Meta and OpenAI are knowingly building technology that poses catastrophic risks to humanity, nonprofit groups claim in a lawsuit.
story: A coalition of nonprofit groups sued five major artificial intelligence developers on Thursday in a bid to block their development of AI models, alleging the companies knowingly created technology that poses catastrophic risks to humanity.

The lawsuit — filed in San Francisco Superior Court by the Alliance for Secure AI, alongside advocacy groups Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen and the Heat Initiative — named Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceXSI (SpaceX Super Intelligence).
"For years, the executives building these systems have warned us that their own frontier models pose catastrophic risks," Brendan Steinhauser, CEO of The Alliance for Secure AI, said in a statement.
"Yet they keep racing to develop and market increasingly powerful AI that they admit they cannot reliably control, and are now handing over AI research and development to AI itself," he added.
A Meta spokesperson for Meta declined to comment. The other tech companies targeted in the suit did not respond to a request for comment.
The litigation comes amid broader concerns about AI safety, sparked by several publicly reported incidents in which AI agents went rogue and carried out unauthorized actions.

The nonprofit groups contend that AI companies are developing technology they have admitted they can't control. The risk could grow as the companies rely more on their own AI models to develop future platforms without human intervention, a concept known as "recursive self-improvement," according to the suit.

"Defendants know these systems do not consistently act in accordance with their intentions," the lawsuit states. "And Defendants know there is no reliable method to control their AI systems and prevent them from causing harm."

The nonprofits also point to past comments by AI company executives acknowledging the potential harm from their technology. In 2015, for example, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said AI will "probably most likely lead to the end of the world." In 2025, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei suggested there was a 25% chance that the development of AI could lead to disastrous outcomes.

As scrutiny of their tech's safety grows, tech leaders have underlined their safety commitments. AI company leaders, including Altman, Amodei and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, in October voiced support for an industrywide slowdown in AI development after an Anthropic employee said there's a 10% chance AI "could kill all humans."

title: Billy Evans calls his portrayal in Elizabeth Holmes documentary "crazy"
summary: Billy Evans, the partner of Elizabeth Holmes, opened up about his portrayal in a hit documentary on "CBS Sunday Morning."
story: Billy Evans, the long-time partner of disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, opened up about his reaction to the hit documentary "You Can See Everything" during his first TV interview.

"You Can See Everything," directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, follows Holmes and Evans in the weeks before she began her prison sentence for defrauding investors. Holmes claimed that she had invented technology that could run a battery of medical tests from a single drop of blood. Those claims were found to be fraudulent. Holmes is currently serving a 10-year sentence in federal prison on charges of wire fraud and conspiracy. She maintains her innocence.

Evans' full interview will air on "CBS Sunday Morning" this weekend. In a preview clip, Evans told CBS News chief correspondent Matt Gutman that he loved the three-hour documentary, while also acknowledging it makes him appear "crazy," like a manipulative partner or even a villain.
"I would have preferred for that not to be the case, but it's entertainment. I didn't get to control that edit," Evans said.

Fans of the movie fixated on scenes where Evans appeared controlling or manipulative towards Holmes and Fielder. In one scene, Evans takes a bowl of eggs away from Holmes and claims she's not whisking them correctly. In another, he claims to know what Fielder is thinking. Later in the documentary, he reveals he has power of attorney over Holmes while she serves her sentence and controls her social media accounts. Holmes and Evans share two children.
Evans said that while he disagrees with his portrayal, he thinks the documentary captures Holmes accurately.
"I think my goal was to have people see Elizabeth. And when I watch that movie, I see the person that I love in exactly who she is," Evans said.
Evans said that it was Holmes' advice that inspired him to share his side of the story with CBS News.

"You gotta learn really painful lessons sometimes in life. And with Elizabeth going through everything she did in the press, the lesson that was ingrained in us is 'You can't lose your voice,'" Evans told Gutman. "So I look forward to speaking with you."

"You Can See Everything" has become a sensation in the weeks since it was released. It has grossed over $80 million worldwide, and there is speculation that it could become the first documentary to be nominated for best picture at the Academy Awards.

title: GOP lawmakers press Huang and Lutnick to testify over Nvidia
summary: Republicans on Capitol Hill are negotiating for now-resigned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang​ to appear before Congress.
story: Republicans on Capitol Hill are pressing now-resigned Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to appear before Congress early next month about the scandal that has rocked one of the most important companies in the world — as a Senate panel asks Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify.

"We need to know the full extent to which our national security has been put at risk," the chairs of the House Select Committee on China, Foreign Affairs Committee and Intelligence Committee said in a statement requesting Huang's presence.

The three committee chairs wrote a letter Thursday asking Huang to appear for a closed-door interview on Dec. 1. They said if he does not accept their request by Friday evening, the House Foreign Affairs Committee will issue a subpoena.

The upper chamber has also pushed Huang to appear. Republican Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina, who chairs the Senate Banking Committee, asked Huang to testify voluntarily before the panel in the first week of December, but warned the committee is prepared to use its subpoena power if needed.
"The American people deserve answers," Scott wrote on X.

Nvidia, whose chips have fueled the AI boom, announced on Thursday that Huang had stepped down following a scandal over his affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at the company Megaspeed who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Huang's resignation from the company he co-founded has not dampened calls from members of Congress for answers about Nvidia's relationship with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that gained access to highly prized chips that are banned from being exported to China. Megaspeed is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China — allegations Megaspeed has denied.

Moments before Nvidia announced Huang's resignation, Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer of North Dakota said on CNBC on Thursday morning that he would happily support subpoenaing Huang. A Cramer spokesperson said he would still support subpoenaing the tech founder.

The controversy has also raised questions about whether the federal government has done enough to prevent Nvidia's chips from being diverted to China — and about the Trump administration's close relationship with Huang.

Scott asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to appear for a public hearing next month. The House Foreign Affairs Committee also requested testimony from Under Secretary of Commerce Jeffrey Kessler, who leads the Bureau of Industry and Security, an agency that oversees export controls.

Some critics have argued Lutnick's Commerce Department should have taken action to prevent Megaspeed from buying chips. The New York Times reported that a Bureau of Industry and Security probe into the firm was halted last year.
Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana told CNN on Thursday he wanted to hear from both Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, saying: "This is serious as an aneurysm."

Earlier Thursday, the chairman of the House Select Committee on China, GOP Rep. John Moolenaar of Michigan, said lawmakers were "in discussions" with Huang "on a date to come and meet with us." But he added, "If for some reason that were not to happen, all three committees, all three chairs have said we will use our subpoena power."

Moolenaar and two other chairs — Rep. Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and Rep. Rick Crawford of the Intelligence Committee — first asked Huang to appear in a letter last week. They said the purpose of the closed-door briefing would be to discuss Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset." The lawmakers gave Huang a deadline of Wednesday to respond.

Mast and Moolenaar told reporters on Thursday that they received a response. Mast said Huang indicated he's willing to appear. Moolenaar said that Huang's resignation "does change the dynamic" surrounding his potential testimony.
"I think right now our goal is to get him in as soon as possible, so that we have a full understanding of the facts and get to the bottom of the truth of this situation," Moolenaar said.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune also told CBS News that he expects "there'll be an interest in doing oversight" in the Senate. Asked whether he wants Huang to testify, Thune said, "I think that it would make sense because of the, again, the nature of the association and the governments and the national security interests, what we're talking about here."
Democrats will take control of both the House and Senate in January. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said Democrats have questions for the Trump administration, too.

"Despite Jensen Huang's resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk," Schumer said on X. "The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset."

President Trump, a friend of Huang's, has downplayed the scandal and said he doesn't believe Huang knew the Megaspeed executive was a spy. The president said Thursday that Huang had done a "fantastic job."
"NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place — TIM COOK of Apple," the president posted to Truth Social.

title: Hegseth awards medal to soldier who reprimanded group near tomb
summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth awarded a medal to the service member who reprimanded his group for making noise at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier​.
story: Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth awarded a medal on Thursday to the service member who reprimanded his group for making noise at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Veterans Day.

Hegseth posted a series of photos on X with the soldier, Spc. Thomas Iglesias, and other members of the unit who guard the tomb at Arlington National Cemetery around the clock. One of the photos showed Hegseth pinning a medal to Iglesias' chest.
"We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist," Hegseth wrote. "Carry on Patriots."
We love soldiers.We love standards.Well done, Specialist.Carry on Patriots. pic.twitter.com/Uk6ek6oOso

A Pentagon official said Hegseth "welcomed the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, the Old Guard, to the Pentagon where he proudly awarded Specialist Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026."

Iglesias was guarding the tomb following a Veterans Day event that included Hegseth, President Trump and other administration officials. Footage showed Hegseth, his wife, his chief of staff and other aides posing for photos near the tomb. Someone laughed, and Iglesias shouted: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."

In the aftermath, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told CBS News: "The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored-and will always honor-the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe. While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."

Soldiers reminding visitors to maintain decorum at the tomb is not uncommon. One member of the regiment that guards the tomb said in an Army interview in 2022 that sentinels react to the crowd two or three times per day.
