title: Severe allergic reaction after sipping energy drink traced to unexpected source
summary: A teen's severe allergic reaction to an energy drink was traced to cod collagen, revealing how fish-derived ingredients can hide in unexpected products.
story: Fox News medical contributor Dr. Jessica Gray joins 'Fox & Friends' to discuss a new study linking energy drinks and supplements to reports of heart problems, warning about potential risks for young adults.
Anaphylaxis – a severe, potentially life-threatening allergic reaction – is usually tied to peanuts or shellfish, but a recent case has brought up a new concern.
According to a report by the American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology (ACAAI), a teen experienced a severe allergic reaction from an energy drink.

The case, which was presented at the ACAAI’s 2026 Annual Scientific Meeting held Nov. 12–16 in Phoenix, Arizona, involved a 15-year-old boy who developed "widespread hives," wheezing and difficulty breathing after trying a new beverage.
POPULAR DRINKS LINKED TO HEART ATTACKS, CARDIAC ARREST IN YOUNG ADULTS, STUDY FINDS

The teen was reportedly taken to the hospital, where he received two doses of epinephrine, albuterol — a medication commonly used in rescue inhalers to help open the airways — an antihistamine and IV fluids. His symptoms resolved after treatment.
A 15-year-old boy (not pictured) developed "widespread hives," wheezing and difficulty breathing after trying a new energy drink. (iStock)
A review of the drink’s label revealed that it contained 5 grams of collagen derived from cod.

According to the report, the teen reported mild throat itching and lip swelling when eating canned tuna, although he had eaten salmon without an issue. He also has eczema, asthma and allergic rhinitis (commonly called hay fever).
WHY STACKING SUPPLEMENTS WITHOUT A BLOOD TEST FIRST CAN DO MORE HARM THAN GOOD
Despite the teen's symptoms, a skin prick testing for tuna, cod and flounder allergy all returned negative.
These findings represent initial research presented at the ACAAI conference, and have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.
The teen received two doses of epinephrine, often administered as an EpiPen, as well as other treatments before his symptoms resolved. (iStock)
Allergist Annabelle Rowland, M.D., study author and ACAAI member based in Georgia, commented in a news release that this case shows "how tricky fish allergy can be."

"Collagen from fish is showing up in a growing number of products, from drinks to supplements," she said. "Standard fish allergy tests mostly look for a different fish protein and contain very little collagen, so a person can test negative and still react."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In a statement sent to Fox News Digital, a spokesperson for the Council for Responsible Nutrition in Washington, D.C., said that collagen ingredients can come from several animal sources, like fish, cattle and pigs.

"While collagen has been studied for potential benefits related to skin and joint health, consumers should consider their individual health needs and sensitivities when choosing products," they advised.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Fish-derived collagen can pose an allergy risk for people sensitive to fish, and processing or hydrolysis does not necessarily eliminate that risk."

The spokesperson recommended those with fish allergies should carefully review product labels, which are required to identify major food allergens, such as fish. Consumers should also consult with their healthcare provider before considering these products.
Experts recommend that consumers with fish allergies carefully review product labels. (iStock)
"The case presented at ACAAI highlights the importance of allergen awareness, but a single suspected reaction does not establish how frequently such reactions occur," they added.
"Product manufacturers are required by law to provide accurate ingredient information and major allergen disclosures so consumers can make informed choices."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Sung Poblete, Ph.D., CEO of Virginia-based Food Allergy Research & Education, told Fox News Digital that fish collagen is increasingly being used in products like supplements, beverages and wellness items.

"While many people with fish allergy avoid all finned fish, reactions can vary between individuals and between different fish-derived proteins," she said. "So someone can be allergic to one type of fin fish and not another."
"Consumers with fish allergy should look for fish-derived ingredients and the specific fish species on food, beverage and supplement labeling," an expert advised. (iStock)
Poblete added that labels must identify the species of fish. Crustacean shellfish, such as shrimp, crab and lobster, must also be specifically identified, according to the FDA.

"For someone managing fish or shellfish allergy, 'marine collagen' on a label calls for a closer look at the ingredient list and 'contains' statement," she said. "If the source still isn’t clear, FARE encourages people to call the manufacturer before using the product."
"A single suspected reaction does not establish how frequently such reactions occur."
Consumers are encouraged to ask the manufacturer what the collagen is made from, and how the product is sourced, packaged and tested for allergens.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"This case offers a timely reminder to read every label, including on drinks and supplements, and talk with an allergist about any reaction, even if a test came back negative," Poblete added.
Fox News Digital reached out to energy drink manufacturers for comment.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Widely used diabetes drug may offer unexpected health benefit
summary: A Stanford study found Type 2 diabetes patients on metformin had a 39% lower risk of dying in the year after a COVID-19 infection than others.
story: Erin Palinski-Wade, a dietitian and diabetes educator, talks about important factors that affect blood sugar and gives an opinion on a recent study suggesting eating with a partner can decrease blood sugar levels.

For decades, doctors have relied on metformin to help people with type 2 diabetes manage their blood sugar. Now, new research suggests the widely prescribed drug may offer benefits beyond blood sugar control.

Researchers at Stanford University found that adults with type 2 diabetes who were taking metformin before catching COVID-19 had a 39% lower risk of dying in the year following their infection than patients taking a different type of diabetes medication.
The findings, published in the journal Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, point to potential protective effects that go beyond basic glucose control.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY PREVENT PREDIABETES FROM TURNING INTO DIABETES

High blood sugar can weaken immune defenses, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Metformin lowers blood sugar and helps the body use insulin more effectively, though it's unclear whether these effects explain the study’s findings.

A Stanford-led study of 53,332 U.S. adults with type 2 diabetes found that patients taking metformin before catching COVID-19 had a 39% lower risk of dying over the following year than those taking DPP-4 inhibitors. (iStock)

Researchers noted that the drug may help regulate a biological pathway involved in blood pressure and fluid balance that influences the severity of COVID-19. Earlier studies have also indicated that metformin can reduce inflammation and lower viral levels in the body during an active infection.
DIABETES DRUG COULD SLASH RISK OF FATAL HEART CONDITION IN ONE GROUP, SCIENTISTS REVEAL
To assess the impact on long-term survival, the team analyzed U.S. medical records for 53,332 adults with type 2 diabetes who tested positive for COVID-19 between October 2021 and November 2023.

All patients were between 30 and 85 years old and had been prescribed either metformin or another diabetes drug, known as dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor (DPP4i), at least a month before their diagnosis.

An independent epidemiologist noted that patients on metformin are generally healthier and younger than those prescribed DPP-4 inhibitors, which are typically reserved for older patients or those with kidney disease. (iStock)

"Metformin is the first drug most people with type 2 diabetes are given. DPP-4 inhibitors usually come later, or go to people who cannot take metformin, often because they are older or have kidney disease or other health problems," Ziyad Al-Aly, M.D., a senior clinical epidemiologist at Washington University in St. Louis, told Fox News Digital.
"Put simply, people on metformin are generally healthier than people on DPP-4 inhibitors," added Al-Aly, who was not involved in the study.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Most of the group, 50,965 patients, were taking metformin, while 2,367 were taking a DPP4i. Patients on metformin were slightly younger on average, 60 years old compared with 64 for those on the alternative medication.
After adjusting for age, gender and other variables, the researchers found that patients taking metformin were more likely to survive over the following year.
The data initially suggested a 13% drop in long COVID symptoms among metformin users, though further statistical testing found no statistically significant link. (iStock)
The data initially suggested a 13% drop in long COVID symptoms among metformin users, though further statistical testing found no statistically significant link.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The new analysis aligns with other recent research, including a study from the University of Minnesota Medical School that showed patients who were prescribed metformin within six days of a COVID-19 diagnosis were less likely to die or develop long COVID.

"There is some evidence from the same group that metformin, started early in a COVID infection, may lower the risk of long COVID, [but] that still needs to be confirmed in large, well-designed randomized trials," Al-Aly noted.
Both the study authors and an outside expert emphasized that more clinical trials are needed, and advised diabetes patients not to alter their current medications based on these findings. (iStock)
Because the Stanford review relied on existing medical records rather than a clinical trial, the authors cautioned that the study cannot prove metformin directly caused the higher survival rate.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Patients taking DPP4i medications tended to be older and had more underlying health conditions, which could have contributed to their higher mortality risk, the researchers noted.
The team also lacked complete records on patients' COVID-19 vaccination status.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"This is not enough evidence to change treatment," Al-Aly cautioned. "People take a DPP-4 inhibitor because they need it to control their diabetes, usually because metformin was not enough or was not an option for them."
"No doctor is choosing between these two drugs for the same patient. The comparison in this study is not a real choice in any clinic. If you take either drug, do not change it because of this study."

title: Healthy runner suffers sudden stroke at 27 as doctors discover possible cause
summary: Patrick Mascoli was running 40 miles a week when a stroke struck at 27. Doctors found a patent foramen ovale that likely sent a clot to his brain.
story: Patrick Mascoli, an engineer and fitness enthusiast, shares the story of the sudden stroke that sidelined him, and the possible cause that doctors uncovered.
As stroke rates continue to rise among young adults, one Boston man is sharing his experience of a life-threatening event at just 27 years old.

Patrick Mascoli, an engineer and fitness enthusiast, was regularly running 40 miles a week at the time of his medical emergency. Beyond a history of migraines, there were no obvious symptoms or warning signs, he shared with Fox News Digital.
On a Sunday in July 2024, Mascoli went for a 10-mile run and headed to the gym for a lifting session. As he was changing alone in the locker room, something felt suddenly wrong.
STROKES NEARLY DOUBLE AMONG ADULTS UNDER A CERTAIN AGE IN DISTURBING TREND
"It just felt like a bomb went off my head," he shared with Fox News Digital. "The right side of my brain just felt like a severe burning sensation, a lot of pain. And that came out of nowhere."
At first, Mascoli assumed it was related to blood pressure-related fainting episodes he’d had when he was younger, but then his vision grew blurrier and the pain intensified.
Patrick Mascoli, pictured at left with his father after his life-threatening stroke at just 27 years old in 2024, ran in the Chicago Marathon (right) in October 2026. (Patrick Mascoli)
"This wasn’t something I had ever experienced before," he said.
When Mascoli tried to stand up and step forward, his leg moved to the right instead, sending him into the wall.

"No matter what I was telling my body to do, it just wasn’t working," he said. "My legs just went in completely opposite directions of the way that I wanted them to. And my vision was a complete swirling mess."
WHAT TO DO IF SOMEONE IS HAVING A STROKE, AFTER JILL BIDEN REVEALED DEBATE-NIGHT FEARS
Mascoli managed to text his sister before collapsing again. As his sister drove to the gym, he lay on the floor, repeatedly vomiting, unable to control his legs and struggling to see.
Stroke briefly crossed his mind, he said, but his age and fitness level made him dismiss it.
"I thought a stroke was something that happens to someone who is elderly or has other pre-existing conditions," Mascoli said. "And in my mind, I’m like, ‘I don’t fit that.’"

In October 2026, Mascoli completed the Chicago Marathon as part of Team Abbott, the company that made his heart implant. He is pictured at right with his girlfriend, Christine Bonarrigo. (Patrick Mascoli)
When his sister arrived, she found Mascoli on the bathroom floor of the gym, drenched in sweat, and called 911.

First responders initially suspected dehydration because Mascoli was young, appeared healthy and had just run in the heat. He received IV fluids, but there was no improvement, he shared. Clinicians also treated him for suspected vertigo, but that didn’t relieve the symptoms.
EVEN OCCASIONAL MARIJUANA USE LINKED TO HIGHER STROKE RISK, STUDY FINDS
Clinicians at Boston Medical Center later identified the stroke on a CT scan and confirmed it with an MRI, according to Mascoli.
The next morning, Mascoli’s head pain had subsided, but he still had significant movement problems, particularly on his right side, which he described as "completely useless."
"No matter what I was telling my body to do, it just wasn’t working."
He spent a few days in the hospital, during which he slowly began walking again with the use of a walker.
The diagnosis left Mascoli fearful about his future. "It was very jarring and terrifying," he said.
Searching for answers
Once the stroke was identified, Mascoli’s care team investigated possible causes. He underwent extensive blood testing for clotting disorders and other conditions, without clear answers.
A heart ultrasound using tiny bubbles injected into a vein revealed a patent foramen ovale (PFO) — an opening between the heart’s upper chambers that normally closes shortly after birth.

"In most people, it closes shortly after birth – but in others, it does not shut completely," Dr. Dheeraj Khurana, chief of cardiology at Episcopal Health Services in New York, told Fox News Digital. Khurana did not treat Mascoli.
"In rare cases, a blood clot passes through this opening, travels to the brain and causes a stroke," Khurana said.
Mascoli’s doctors considered the opening the likely route by which a clot reached his brain.
Mascoli is pictured with the entire Abbott running team prior to the Chicago Marathon. (Patrick Mascoli)
Most people with the opening experience no related health problems, according to the American Stroke Association.

In younger stroke patients who lack common risk factors and whose initial tests reveal no clear cause, doctors may look for a PFO using an ultrasound of the heart called an echocardiogram, Khurana said.
SILENT HEART THREAT FOUND IN ADULTS UNDER 30 WITH NO KNOWN CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE
Mascoli does have a lingering uncertainty about why a clot formed in the first place.
"I had none of the genetic predispositions to it. I had no clear physical issues that were causing it. So that is a little bit of a mystery," he said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
About a month after the stroke, Mascoli underwent a catheter procedure to close the opening in his heart, using an Abbott device that resembled a mesh, double-sided umbrella.
He said his cardiologist’s reassurance that the suspected pathway had been addressed helped ease his fears.

Although his mobility has improved with therapy, Mascoli said he still has lingering difficulty with fine motor skills. "I was very hard on myself, and I still get mad if my hands are shaking and my writing looks bad."
Source of motivation
Returning to running brought its own anxiety. Before the stroke, Mascoli said he would head out for miles without tracking his distance, but afterward, he worried about getting stranded.
"I need to know how far I’m going because I don’t want to be too far away and have something happen," he recalled thinking.
During his recovery, Mascoli’s girlfriend gave him a fitness watch and encouraged him to start racing.
"It was something that kept me motivated, because I knew it was helping me both physically and mentally," he said.

Anyone experiencing sudden loss of balance, vision changes, face drooping, arm weakness or difficulty speaking should call 911 immediately, regardless of age or fitness level, according to the American Stroke Association. (iStock)
In October 2026, Mascoli completed the Chicago Marathon as part of Team Abbott, representing the company that made his heart implant.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
After finishing, he listened to an emotional voice message from his sister, who had helped rescue him at the gym.
"She was the one who saved me, so it meant a lot to me," he said.

Factors that may raise stroke risk in younger adults include high blood pressure, smoking, unhealthy cholesterol levels, clotting disorders, certain heart conditions and tears in the arteries supplying the brain. (iStock)

To others who have experienced health emergencies, Mascoli urged them to be patient with themselves and to not let the traumatic event define them, emphasizing that recovery looks different for everyone.
"Just take as many steps as you can," he said. "It might not be running a marathon. It doesn’t need to be this big thing."
Risks, symptoms and prevention

Factors that may raise stroke risk in younger adults include high blood pressure, smoking, unhealthy cholesterol levels, clotting disorders, certain heart conditions and tears in the arteries supplying the brain, Khurana said.

"Younger adults with stroke may experience dizziness, altered mental status, vomiting and headaches, which they can easily mistake for exhaustion, especially after exercise or migraine," he told Fox News Digital.
"I had none of the genetic predispositions to it. I had no clear physical issues that were causing it."
"Other common symptoms include visual disturbances, speech problems, weakness, lethargy or seizures."
Dr. Sean Levchuck, chair of pediatric cardiology at St. Francis Hospital & Heart Center in New York, shared some general best practices for young adults to prevent a first stroke.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Young, active adults should stay active and exercise. Following strenuous activity, fluid replacement is necessary," he advised.
The cardiologist also recommends avoiding smoking and tobacco products.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Anyone experiencing sudden loss of balance, vision changes, face drooping, arm weakness or difficulty speaking should call 911 immediately, regardless of age or fitness level, according to the American Stroke Association.
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Highly contagious bird flu detected in Wisconsin as officials euthanize infected flock
summary: Wisconsin officials euthanized a backyard poultry flock in Rusk County after confirming a case of highly pathogenic avian influenza in the birds.
story: Wisconsin officials confirmed a highly contagious bird flu outbreak in a backyard poultry flock in Rusk County, prompting the depopulation of affected birds and renewed warnings to livestock owners.

A highly contagious strain of bird flu has struck a backyard poultry flock in Wisconsin, prompting officials to euthanize the birds amid ongoing concerns about the spread of the potentially deadly disease.
The Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection (DATCP) confirmed Thursday a case of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) in a backyard poultry flock in Rusk County.
Officials did not specify how the flock became infected.
DATCP said all birds on the property were euthanized and will not enter the food system.
H5N1 BIRD FLU CONFIRMED IN AUSTRALIA FOR THE FIRST TIME, MEANING VIRUS HAS NOW REACHED EVERY CONTINENT

Wisconsin agriculture officials confirmed an outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza in a backyard poultry flock in Rusk County, prompting the depopulation of birds on the affected property. (Emily Elconin/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
HPAI, a highly contagious virus that is often fatal to domestic poultry, has circulated among wild and domestic birds in North America since December 2021, according to DATCP.
The disease is caused by influenza type A viruses and can vary in severity depending on the strain and affected species.
The virus can spread through contact with infected birds, wild birds or their droppings, as well as contaminated equipment or clothing worn by people working with the animals, according to DATCP.
JD VANCE INSTALLS CUSTOM CHICKEN COOP AT NAVAL OBSERVATORY AND WILL PERSONALLY CARE FOR BIRDS

A highly contagious strain of bird flu was detected in a backyard poultry flock in Wisconsin, according to the state's Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection. (Bernadett Szabo/Reuters)
When HPAI is confirmed in a backyard poultry flock, officials may establish a 10-kilometer surveillance zone, though surrounding poultry premises would not face movement restrictions.

DATCP urged livestock owners to take precautions to protect their flocks and herds, including washing hands, disinfecting equipment, restricting access to animals and separating new additions for at least 30 days.

Wisconsin officials confirmed a case of highly pathogenic avian influenza in Rusk County, where birds on the affected property were depopulated to prevent the spread of the disease. (Tiksa Negeri/Reuters)
The agency also recommended that poultry owners keep their birds indoors when possible.

title: Hospital sewers may be breeding grounds for dangerous superbugs, study finds
summary: A Nature Communications study found hospital wastewater promotes antibiotic-resistant E. coli, with bacteria on sewer pipes three times as resistant.
story: Hospital wastewater has been shown to promote the growth of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, potentially making sewer systems hotspots for antimicrobial resistance, according to a new Swedish study published in Nature Communications.

Hospital wastewater has been shown to promote the growth of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, potentially making sewer systems hotspots for antimicrobial resistance, according to a new Swedish study published in Nature Communications.
Antibiotics taken by patients can pass through their bodies and enter hospital sewer systems, creating conditions that favor the growth of resistant bacteria.

Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria develop the ability to survive drugs designed to kill them, making some infections harder to treat. More than 9.3 million drug-resistant infections occur in the U.S. each year, resulting in more than 39,000 deaths, according to the CDC's 2026 Antimicrobial Resistance Threats Report.
DANGEROUS DRUG-RESISTANT FUNGUS SPREADS ACROSS US, REACHING 27 STATES
How hospital wastewater promotes antibiotic resistance
The researchers conducted a study involving wastewater from 10 hospitals and eight municipal wastewater treatment plants.
They wanted to determine whether hospital wastewater actually promoted the growth of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, rather than simply carrying resistant bacteria from patients.
Hospital wastewater has been shown to promote the growth of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, potentially making sewer systems hotspots for antimicrobial resistance. (iStock)

First, the researchers filtered hospital wastewater to remove existing bacteria, then exposed other bacteria to the filtered water in laboratory experiments. All 10 hospital samples significantly favored the growth of E. coli strains resistant to ciprofloxacin and cefotaxime, two antibiotics used to treat bacterial infections.
None of the eight municipal wastewater samples showed the same effect.
DEATH REPORTED IN E COLI OUTBREAK LINKED TO CALIFORNIA PUMPKIN PATCH AS MORE CASES EMERGE
This suggested that something in the wastewater itself was helping antibiotic-resistant bacteria thrive, according to the researchers.

The team also placed plastic plates in sewer pipes to study bacteria growing on their surfaces. After 30 days, bacteria growing on surfaces inside the pipes were about three times as likely to be resistant to the two antibiotics as bacteria in the surrounding wastewater. This pattern was not observed in municipal sewers.
The researchers conducted a study involving wastewater from 10 hospitals and eight municipal wastewater treatment plants. (iStock)

The researchers also measured antibiotic levels in the wastewater and tested whether those same concentrations helped resistant bacteria grow in laboratory experiments. They found that ciprofloxacin was a major contributor, while cefotaxime also played a role.
BEACHGOERS WARNED AFTER DEADLY 'FLESH-EATING' BACTERIA KILLS 5 IN SOUTHERN STATE

"The discovery [suggests] that hospital sewers could be a spawning ground for bacteria that are difficult to treat with antibiotics," Joakim Larsson, professor of environmental pharmacology at the University of Gothenburg and Director of Centre for Antibiotic Resistance Research, told Fox News Digital.
"The patients’ need for antibiotics must not be compromised."

"Knowing where resistant bacteria are promoted — and where they are less likely to be — is crucial when deciding how resources and efforts should be allocated to limit risks for antibiotic resistance development."

The study had several limitations. All sampling sites were in Sweden, and researchers focused primarily on E. coli and a limited number of antibiotics, so the findings may not apply to all bacteria or locations.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The sewer experiment lasted approximately 30 days, leaving longer-term effects unclear. The study also did not determine whether the growth of resistant bacteria in hospital sewers leads to more infections in patients or surrounding communities.
Although the study did not directly link hospital wastewater to human infections, Larsson said resistant bacteria could potentially reach people through contaminated water.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"When it rains heavily, treatment plants are typically overloaded, and release untreated or partially untreated wastewater with lots of bacteria," Larsson told Fox News Digital.

"If people get in contact with such waters, they can acquire those bacteria and then continue spreading them from person to person," he went on. "One thing that remains uncertain is how much you need to be exposed for resistant bacteria to colonize your gut or infect you."
Preventing antibiotic resistance
The researchers identified two possible approaches to reducing antibiotic resistance in hospital sewers.
One involves using alternative antibiotics that are less likely to pass through patients' bodies unchanged and promote the growth of resistant bacteria in wastewater.
All 10 hospital samples significantly favored the growth of E. coli strains resistant to ciprofloxacin and cefotaxime, two antibiotics used to treat bacterial infections. (iStock)

"But – and it is an important but – the patients’ need for antibiotics must not be compromised," Larsson said, emphasizing that equally effective alternatives may not always be available, and patients' medical needs must come first.

The second approach involves treating wastewater at hospitals to remove antibiotics that promote resistance, particularly fluoroquinolones and beta-lactams (two classes of antibiotics used to treat bacterial infections), while also removing harmful bacteria.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Larsson said treating wastewater at municipal plants would likely be less effective because antibiotic concentrations are high enough to favor resistant bacteria, primarily in hospital sewers.
Existing technologies can remove antibiotics from wastewater, but they can be costly and require additional treatment, he noted.

"When we know more about the drivers, we think it might be possible to develop technical solutions that are targeted and hopefully less expensive," Larsson added.

title: Ozempic and Zepbound users face 6 rebound risks after stopping, doctor warns
summary: Thinking of quitting a GLP-1? A physician outlines six risks, from weight regain and muscle loss to worsening biomarkers and mental health consequences.
story: Internal medicine physician Dr. Frank Dumont discusses why patients may experience renewed cravings, changes in body composition and worsening blood sugar levels when discontinuing popular injectable treatments for obesity and diabetes.
While GLP-1 medications like Ozempic, Wegovy and Zepbound have reshaped weight management and diabetes control, research shows that many patients stop taking them within a year.
Research has found that cycling off these medications can bring potential rebound risks, ranging from rapid weight regain to the loss of cardiovascular protection.

Dr. Frank Dumont, internal medicine physician and executive medical director at Virta Health in San Francisco, spoke with Fox News Digital about why patients stop taking GLP-1s, the potential risks and how to maintain progress afterward.
TYPE 2 DIABETES PATIENTS 21 TIMES MORE LIKELY TO ACHIEVE REMISSION WITH INTENSIVE LIFESTYLE CHANGES
Why patients stop
Some patients may stop taking GLP-1 medications because of medical concerns or side effects, while others prefer not to remain on long-term medication, Dumont said.
Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, constipation and diarrhea.

"Those types of things can become troublesome enough that people actually have a hard time eating enough food to get good nourishment," he told Fox News Digital. "Working with your physician to make a decision about whether it's right for you to stay on the medicine or not is important."
Other serious side effects, like acute pancreatitis, would prompt immediate discontinuation of the drug.
4 SIMPLE HABITS CAN HELP SLOW MUSCLE LOSS AS YOU AGE, FITNESS EXPERT SAYS
"We know that's fairly rare, but if the pancreas becomes involved, that is not a good thing," Dumont said. "It can be very serious. It can even be life-threatening."
Certain GLP-1 medications carry a warning about thyroid tumors based on animal studies, though the risk in humans remains unknown.
"When people take the GLP-1 medications, they lose weight, but they tend to lose both fat mass and lean muscle mass."
These medications should not be used by people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or a condition called multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).
Dumont outlined six potential risks patients may face after stopping a GLP-1.
No. 1: Return of hunger and cravings
The most immediate side effect patients notice after stopping a GLP-1 is the return of intense cravings and a sharp spike in appetite, often referred to as "food noise," according to Dumont.
Many patients assume they can treat GLP-1s like a short-term prescription, taking the drug to hit a target weight or blood sugar goal and then stopping, the doctor noted.
Hunger and cravings typically increase after stopping a GLP-1, the doctor said. (iStock)

However, major medical organizations, including the American Medical Association (AMA) and the Obesity Medicine Association, classify obesity as a chronic condition that typically requires ongoing management.

"Unless you have significantly changed what you're doing in terms of the types of foods you're eating, it's likely you'll go back to the same foods you were eating before, and hunger and cravings will go up," Dumont said.
No. 2: Weight regain
It is typical for GLP-1 users to experience weight regain after quitting, according to Dumont.
In the STEP 1 trial extension, participants regained about two-thirds of the weight they had lost within a year of stopping semaglutide and lifestyle interventions.
WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY FIGHT 7 SERIOUS HEALTH PROBLEMS BEFORE THE POUNDS EVEN COME OFF

In the SURMOUNT-4 trial for tirzepatide, patients who were switched to a placebo after 36 weeks of treatment regained more than half the weight they had lost over the following year, even while receiving diet and exercise counseling.
"That's just so devastating for people who felt like they'd finally found a solution that would work," Dumont said.
No. 3: Change in biomarkers

Biomarkers — which are measurable indicators of what’s happening inside the body, such as blood sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol levels — tend to improve while taking a GLP-1, which is beneficial for those with prediabetes or diabetes.
When a GLP-1 is stopped, these markers can reverse if not countered with a change in diet, according to Dumont.
Early trials have found that people regained more than two-thirds of the weight they lost while taking a GLP-1 within a year of stopping the medication. (iStock)
Improvements in fatty liver disease may also fade after treatment stops, the doctor said.

"We know that these medications can help to decrease some of that steatotic or fatty liver disease that occurs," he noted. "And when you go off the medicine, if you go back to eating the way you did before, those numbers have a tendency to worsen."
No. 4: Worsening body composition
Weight loss while taking GLP-1 medications can include a loss of muscle, raising concerns about body composition and long-term physical function, according to Dumont.
"When people take the GLP-1 medications, they lose weight, but they tend to lose both fat mass and lean muscle mass," he told Fox News Digital.
In a body-composition study of tirzepatide, about 25% of the weight lost was lean mass, which includes muscle and other nonfat tissue. The remaining 75% was fat.
Dumont expressed concern that patients who regain weight after stopping treatment may not fully replace the muscle they lost.
Studies have linked GLP-1s to a reduced risk of chronic health conditions like cardiovascular disease and stroke. (iStock)

"So, there's a bit of a ratcheting-down effect if someone is on and off these medications, where they lose fat and muscle, stop the medicine, regain fat, go back on the medicine, and lose fat and muscle," he added.
The doctor emphasized that preserving muscle is important for metabolism, injury prevention and everyday activities.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
No. 5: Mental health effects
In addition to the physical consequences, Dumont noted that stopping a weight-loss drug can take a heavy toll on mental health.
Many patients have spent years cycling through diets and programs without lasting success, often viewing GLP-1s as a final solution, according to the doctor.
In addition to the physical consequences, the doctor noted that stopping a weight-loss drug can take a heavy toll on mental health. (iStock)

When the medication isn't right for them — adding to a history of past weight-loss setbacks — experiencing a "regression on all fronts" can be "really devastating from a mental health standpoint," Dumont said.
"It can make you feel disheartened and like you don’t have the control you thought you did," he added.
No. 6: Loss of health protection

An observational study published in BMJ Medicine found that adults with type 2 diabetes who stopped GLP-1 treatment had a higher risk of major cardiovascular events than those who continued. Longer periods without treatment were associated with greater risk.
Dumont noted that the stakes of stopping a GLP-1 go far beyond weight, pointing to the broader risk of losing metabolic benefits.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
While taking a GLP-1, lower inflammation and improved cholesterol and blood sugar levels help reduce the risk of major events like heart attacks and strokes, the doctor said.

"But again, if you stop the medicine and you haven't changed the way that you eat, then all of those numbers can worsen … and that can then increase the risk of those bad things happening — things that can be devastating from a life quality standpoint, but also can shorten your life," he warned.

"The GLP-1 is not the only solution," the doctor said. "It needs to be coupled with ... a way of eating that's going to work for you for the long term that allows you to stop the medicine successfully if you need to." (iStock)
Making your progress last
Reaching metabolic goals and making lasting lifestyle changes may help patients maintain their progress after stopping a GLP-1, according to Dumont.
"We actually have peer-reviewed published data demonstrating that you can indeed stop one of these medications when you reach your metabolic goals," he said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The Virta-affiliated observational study examined selected patients with type 2 diabetes in a structured nutrition program, so the findings may not apply to all GLP-1 users.
The doctor recommended adopting sustainable eating habits before stopping a GLP-1.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"The GLP-1 is not the only solution," he said. "It needs to be coupled with ... a way of eating that's going to work for you for the long term that allows you to stop the medicine successfully if you need to."
Dumont recommended working with the prescribing clinician on a plan for stopping treatment and monitoring weight and blood sugar afterward.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Death reported in E coli outbreak linked to California pumpkin patch as more cases emerge
summary: An E. coli outbreak linked to California’s Brookshire Farms has left one person dead, five confirmed infections and 10 suspected cases.
story: Dr. Tyler Evans, an infectious disease physician and founder of Wellness Equity Alliance in California, speaks with Fox News Digital about E. coli infections linked to a California pumpkin patch that closed just days before Halloween.
One person has died in an E. coli outbreak linked to a California pumpkin farm, San Luis Obispo County health officials confirmed Tuesday. Officials have not released the person’s age or identity.

The death follows confirmation of five cases of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli infection, potentially originating from Brookshire Farms in San Luis Obispo, according to an advisory issued by the County of San Luis Obispo Public Health Department.

"We can confirm that one individual associated with the E. coli outbreak has died. We are sharing this information with the permission of the individual’s family," Tom Cuddy, public information officer for the department, said in a statement to The Tribune of San Luis Obispo on Nov. 10.
E. COLI OUTBREAK LANDS 3 IN HOSPITAL; HEALTH OFFICIALS INVESTIGATE LINK TO PUMPKIN PATCH

"This is truly a heartbreaking development, and our thoughts are with the family and everyone affected by this outbreak. The entire team at Public Health extends our deepest condolences to the family and loved ones during this difficult time."
In a Nov. 6 statement, the health department said an additional 10 individuals who visited the farm between Oct. 16 and Oct. 26 and developed symptoms have been deemed "suspect cases."
One person has died in an E. coli outbreak linked to a California pumpkin farm, San Luis Obispo County health officials confirmed Tuesday.  (Getty Images)
Tests of water, food and other samples from the farm found some bacteria, including other E. coli strains, but did not detect the strain responsible for the outbreak, officials said.
People who became ill shared possible exposures to corn cups, pumpkins, hay and water not intended for drinking, but officials could not pinpoint the source.
FDA WIDENS CYCLOSPORA OUTBREAK INVESTIGATION TO SIX MORE STATES AS CONFIRMED CASES TOP 6,000
No farm animals or petting zoos, which are known to be common sources of this type of infection, were accessible to visitors or operating at the farm.

Investigators faced several limitations, including numerous possible sources, items no longer available for testing and delays between exposure and sampling. No further environmental testing is planned, according to the report.
Tests of water, food and other samples from the farm found some bacteria, including other E. coli strains, but did not detect the strain responsible for the outbreak, officials said. (iStock)

"Based on the findings of our investigation, we believe the risk of additional exposure associated with this incident has passed, and there is no longer an ongoing public health threat," said County Health Officer Dr. Christy Mulkerin.

"Our hearts go out to the families affected by this outbreak. We thank all those who have helped protect our community in response to this outbreak, and we encourage community members to continue practicing good handwashing and food safety to protect themselves and their families."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Typical symptoms of E. coli include cramping, severe abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea and signs of dehydration, which usually begin within three to 10 days of exposure.

Young children under 10 are typically at the highest risk for complications, which can include hemolytic uremic syndrome, a serious condition that damages blood cells and can lead to kidney failure, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Young children under 10 are typically at the highest risk for complications, which can include hemolytic uremic syndrome, a serious condition that damages blood cells and can lead to kidney failure. (iStock)
Dr. Tyler Evans, an infectious disease physician and founder of Wellness Equity Alliance in California, warned that diarrhea can lead to dehydration and fatigue.
"The diarrhea is really the key component here, and the stomach cramps," he told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Evans said younger children and older adults can be particularly vulnerable, emphasizing the need to closely watch children younger than 5.
Speaking generally about potential exposure routes in pumpkin patches, Evans said E. coli can spread when bacteria from feces reach someone’s mouth.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
He pointed to potentially contaminated food or water, animal contact and person-to-person transmission as possible transmission routes.
Evans also noted that not all E. coli bacteria cause illness. The confirmed cases in this investigation involve Shiga toxin-producing E. coli.
Typical symptoms of E. coli include cramping, severe abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea and signs of dehydration, which usually begin within three to 10 days of exposure. (iStock)
The health department shared the following safe practices to protect against these types of infections.

Washing hands thoroughly with soap and water after being in outdoor environments or touching animals.Washing fruits and vegetables before eating them.Keeping raw foods separate from other foods during preparation and storage.Avoiding consumption of untreated water.Drinking milk and juices that have not been pasteurized.When selling or otherwise providing food to the public, always follow state and County health regulations.
Washing hands thoroughly with soap and water after being in outdoor environments or touching animals.
Washing fruits and vegetables before eating them.
Keeping raw foods separate from other foods during preparation and storage.
Avoiding consumption of untreated water.
Drinking milk and juices that have not been pasteurized.
When selling or otherwise providing food to the public, always follow state and County health regulations.

title: New weight-loss drug wipes out chronic knee pain in some patients, researchers say
summary: Northwestern University-led trials found retatrutide helped two-thirds of obese knee osteoarthritis patients cut pain by half in late-stage studies.
story: A non-surgical knee procedure provided yearlong pain relief for 80% of patients in a new study. The treatment reduces inflammation without permanent implants, but researchers note important limitations.

An experimental weight-loss drug significantly reduced chronic knee pain and improved mobility in people with obesity and knee osteoarthritis, according to two clinical trials led by researchers at Northwestern University.
The trials, which were funded by Eli Lilly and published in The New England Journal of Medicine, evaluated retatrutide, a once-weekly injectable medication developed by Eli Lilly and Co.
Retatrutide, which is not yet FDA-approved, mimics three hormones involved in appetite and metabolism — GLP-1, GIP and glucagon — and has produced substantial weight loss in clinical trials.
WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY FIGHT 7 SERIOUS HEALTH PROBLEMS BEFORE THE POUNDS EVEN COME OFF
The late-stage trials enrolled more than 1,000 adults who were overweight or obese, did not have diabetes, and experienced painful knee osteoarthritis.

After 68 weeks in one trial and 80 weeks in the other, participants receiving the highest dose of retatrutide lost about a quarter of their body weight on average. A pooled analysis found that roughly two-thirds of those treated with the drug achieved at least a 50% drop in knee pain, compared with 38% of those receiving a placebo.
Painful knee osteoarthritis affects an estimated 15 million Americans.
Beyond pain relief and functional gains, participants experienced reductions in blood pressure, lower blood lipid levels and decreased systemic inflammation, according to the researchers.
Gastrointestinal problems were the most common side effects, and serious adverse events were more common among participants receiving retatrutide than among those receiving placebo.
KNEE TREATMENT WITHOUT SURGERY OFFERS LASTING PAIN RELIEF FOR 80% OF ARTHRITIS PATIENTS, STUDY FINDS

Dr. Thomas J. Schnitzer, a professor at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine and lead author of the study, said the findings offer therapeutic potential for specific groups of patients.

"For people who are obese, not diabetic, have radiographically confirmed knee osteoarthritis that has not progressed to bone on bone, and have consistent moderate knee pain, retatrutide treatment has the potential to result in a significant and meaningful reduction in their knee pain and improvement in their physical function while providing cardiometabolic benefit," Schnitzer told Fox News Digital.
An experimental weight-loss drug significantly reduced chronic knee pain and improved mobility in people with obesity and knee osteoarthritis. (iStock)
While researchers anticipated benefits from the weight reduction, the "complete relief of knee pain" in one of every eight patients taking the drug was a surprise, Schnitzer said.
Painful knee osteoarthritis affects an estimated 15 million Americans, often turning routine activities such as standing, walking and climbing stairs into painful challenges.
YOUR FAVORITE SNACKS COULD BE QUIETLY WRECKING YOUR KNEES, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS
Conventional treatments include physical therapy, anti-inflammatory medications and steroid injections, which often offer only limited or temporary relief, according to the researchers.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

While earlier research has found that losing 5% to 10% of body weight through diet and exercise can ease knee osteoarthritis symptoms, losing more than 10% through those measures alone can be difficult, particularly when knee pain limits exercise, Schnitzer said.
In addition to physical pain relief, some participants experienced broader health improvements, including reduced blood pressure, lower lipid levels and decreased systemic inflammation. (iStock)
Despite the study's promising outcomes, Schnitzer stressed that there were some limitations.
"People with knee OA who were not overweight or obese were not studied, and individuals who were obese and had more advanced OA were also excluded, so we have no information on them," he said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
The trials excluded patients who needed knee replacement surgery. Whether retatrutide slows osteoarthritis progression or reduces the need for future joint replacements remains unknown.
While researchers anticipated benefits from the weight reduction, the "complete relief of knee pain" in one of every eight patients taking the drug was a surprise, the researcher said. (iStock)
For individuals experiencing joint pain who may meet the study criteria, Schnitzer recommended discussing options with a healthcare provider.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"If someone fits the profile noted above, and they have been unsuccessful at losing weight, they should speak to their physician about the possibility of being treated with a medication that would help them lose weight, as that could also reduce their knee pain as well as provide cardiometabolic benefits," Schnitzer said.
At the same time, he emphasized that medication should not replace healthy daily habits.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Before starting pharmacologic treatment for knee pain, people who are overweight should try diet and exercise and consider interventions such as physical therapy," Schnitzer advised.
"Also, even for people on weight-loss medications, exercise is an important part of any treatment plan to maintain as much muscle as possible."
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Woman claims hospital injected wrong drug into her spine during knee surgery, leaving her unable to walk
summary: Linda Gilbert's lawsuit alleges Ascension Saint Thomas Midtown injected potassium phosphate instead of mepivacaine, causing incomplete paraplegia.
story: A non-surgical knee procedure provided yearlong pain relief for 80% of patients in a new study. The treatment reduces inflammation without permanent implants, but researchers note important limitations.
A Nashville woman is seeking $150 million from Ascension Saint Thomas Midtown, alleging that a medication error during knee replacement surgery left her with a permanent spinal cord injury.
Linda Gilbert, who was 78 at the time of the incident, alleges that hospital staff injected the wrong drug into her spinal canal during the procedure.

A total of four surgery patients received potassium phosphate instead of the intended anesthetic, mepivacaine, on Aug. 14, according to an Aug. 21 statement published on the hospital system’s website.
ORGAN HARVESTING BEGAN WHILE PATIENTS STILL SHOWED ‘SIGNS OF LIFE,’ FEDERAL INVESTIGATION FINDS

The Nov. 6 complaint, which was provided to Fox News Digital by Gilbert’s attorney, alleges the injection severely injured her spinal cord and nerves, leaving her with incomplete paraplegia, severe weakness in both legs and the inability to walk, drive or live independently.

A Nashville woman (not pictured) is seeking $150 million from a hospital where she underwent surgery, alleging that a medication error during knee replacement surgery left her with a permanent spinal cord injury. (iStock)

Gilbert also developed shock and respiratory failure requiring a ventilator, according to the filing. The lawsuit alleges that the patient’s injuries are permanent and says she remained in inpatient rehabilitation at a spinal cord injury center in Atlanta at the time it was filed.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Gilbert’s lawsuit claims that staff continued using syringes from the same batch after two earlier patients reported burning pain. It also alleges medication preparation and verification failures, along with delays in treatment.
The patient is seeking $50 million in compensatory damages and $100 million in punitive damages.

A total of four surgery patients received potassium phosphate instead of the intended anesthetic, mepivacaine, on Aug. 14, according to an Aug. 21 statement published on the hospital system’s website. (iStock)

Potassium phosphate is used to treat low phosphorus levels and to supply phosphorus in intravenous nutrition. Its prescribing information specifies that it must be diluted and administered through a vein.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

The label warns that excessive doses or overly rapid intravenous administration can cause dangerous heart rhythms, cardiac arrest, seizures and death, according to prescribing information available on NIH’s DailyMed. Those warnings concern intravenous use, rather than injection into the spinal canal as alleged in Gilbert’s lawsuit.
"Our hearts remain with the four patients and families impacted by the recent medication error that occurred at Ascension Saint Thomas Midtown."

In a statement published by local NBC affiliate WSMV on Nov. 9, Ascension Saint Thomas said it was aware of the complaint and was cooperating with the legal process, but could not share additional details because the case was ongoing.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Our hearts remain with the four patients and families impacted by the recent medication error that occurred at Ascension Saint Thomas Midtown," the hospital wrote in a Sept. 11 statement on its website.

In a Sept. 16 update, the hospital said it was working with an independent quality consultant to "guide and verify the full scope of our corrective actions and process enhancements," adding that it remained "committed to learning from this and upholding the standards of patient safety, quality, and compassionate care."
About 790,000 total knee replacements are performed each year in the U.S., according to the American College of Rheumatology. (iStock)
About 790,000 total knee replacements are performed each year in the U.S., according to the American College of Rheumatology.
Most patients experience substantial pain relief and improved mobility, with only 2% reporting serious complications, the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons states.

Medication safety recommendations emphasize the importance of clear labeling of drugs, including their names and concentrations, and reading the label to correctly identify each medication before administration.

title: Common heart pill under scrutiny for older patients as study weighs risks of stopping
summary: A new clinical trial found 13% of older adults who stopped statins had a heart attack, stroke or died, compared with 9% who continued treatment.
story: Dr. Christopher Kelly, a UNC Health cardiologist, emphasized individualized decisions based on overall health and expected lifespan when deciding whether to continue statin use.
Some older adults may be able to stop taking statins with little added risk over two years, but a new study raises concerns about longer-term safety.

That’s according to a randomized clinical trial that was presented on Nov. 7, 2026, at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions in Chicago, and published in The New England Journal of Medicine.

Statins are prescription medications that lower LDL, or "bad," cholesterol by reducing how much cholesterol the liver makes. They are known to help reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke, according to the National Heart, Lung and Blood Institute.
COMMON CHOLESTEROL DRUG LINKED TO LOWER DEMENTIA RISK WHEN STARTED EARLY

The study — conducted by researchers from the University of Bern in Switzerland, the University of California, San Francisco, and other institutions — included 1,880 adults aged 70 years and older, all of whom were taking statins to prevent a first heart attack or stroke.
Some older adults may be able to stop taking statins with little added risk over two years, but a new study raises concerns about longer-term safety. (iStock)

All participants had at least two chronic medical conditions, but did not have established cardiovascular disease or previous cardiovascular events. Half of the participants stopped taking statins, and the other half continued.
After two years, the added risk from stopping statins was small enough to fall within the limits researchers had set for the study. However, that did not mean stopping carried no added risk.
5 HABITS THAT COULD HELP KEEP YOU OUT OF A NURSING HOME, FROM AN ORTHOPEDIC SURGEON

Over the full follow-up, which lasted about two years for the typical participant and up to four years for some, about 13% of those assigned to stop statins had a heart attack, an ischemic stroke or died from any cause, compared with 9% assigned to continue treatment.

The study’s safety monitoring board also recommended that participants who were assigned to stop statins discuss restarting treatment with their healthcare team, according to the American College of Cardiology.
Statins are prescription medications that lower LDL, or "bad," cholesterol by reducing how much cholesterol the liver makes. (iStock)
For other outcomes, the researchers found no meaningful differences between the two groups in reported quality of life, muscle pain, falls or loss of muscle mass and strength.
Dr. Christopher Kelly, a UNC Health cardiologist, emphasized that continuing statins did not worsen reported muscle pain or quality of life in the trial.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Although guidelines support lowering high cholesterol earlier in life, the benefits of continuing statins in older age are less certain, said study author Dr. Rita F. Redberg, a cardiology professor at the University of California, San Francisco, in a press release.
"This small, increased risk of cardiovascular events means that one cannot make a general recommendation about stopping statins in this patient population."
Earlier studies found no difference in mortality after adults 70 and older stopped statins for primary prevention, she noted.

"One study suggested quality of life improvements after stopping statins," Redberg said, adding that her team explored whether stopping was safe for older adults taking the drugs to prevent a first cardiovascular event.
Study limitations

The study had several limitations. About 14% of participants did not stick with their assigned treatment plan. Some who were told to stop taking statins resumed them, while others assigned to continue treatment stopped taking the drugs, according to the researchers.
The findings also may not apply to all older adults, as the study was limited to people aged 70 and older who had multiple chronic health conditions but no history of heart disease or stroke.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Although some participants were followed for up to four years, the study primarily assessed outcomes over about two years. Longer follow-up is needed to determine how stopping statins affects patients over many years.
Weighing the risks
"This small, increased risk of cardiovascular events means that one cannot make a general recommendation about stopping statins in this patient population," Redberg said.

"There should be shared decision-making between the patient and the healthcare professional to know if it is appropriate for an individual to discontinue the medication," the researcher said. (iStock)

"There should be shared decision-making between the patient and the healthcare professional to know if it is appropriate for an individual to discontinue the medication. In general, however, discontinuation is safe for most people who are in this age group and without a previous CVD event."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Kelly, who was not involved in the study, noted that a healthy 70-year-old could live another 20 years, leaving questions about the effects of stopping treatment over that longer period.
The doctor also emphasized individualized decisions based on overall health and expected lifespan, noting that he "errs on the side of caution" with his own patients.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I typically recommend that they continue taking it unless they have specific concerns about that medication, such as side effects, or if they are taking a lot of medicines, and they're just really eager to stop taking one of them."

title: Viral ‘heightmaxxing’ trend has teen boys taking cancer drugs to grow taller, doctors warn of risks
summary: Erdafitinib, a cancer medication, is being misused by teens chasing height growth. Medical experts detail the severe risks of the heightmaxxing trend.
story: Dangerous 'heightmaxxing' trends see teenagers taking a bladder cancer drug to grow taller. Family physician Dr. Jessica Gray warns of severe skeletal health risks. Manufacturer Johnson and Johnson released a statement confirming the medication is not approved for children, while separate reports analyze tens of thousands of FDA energy drink cases.
Medical experts are warning of a dangerous new social media trend known as "heightmaxxing," amid reports that teenagers are taking black-market cancer medications in an effort to grow taller.
Adolescents, primarily teenage boys, are reportedly turning to erdafitinib — often referred to online as "ERDA" or "Erta" — a targeted prescription drug approved to treat advanced bladder cancer.
Teenagers are reportedly experimenting with the prescription medication after encountering online discussions suggesting it could increase height.
DOCTORS WARN OF ‘LOOKSMAXXING’ DANGERS AFTER INFLUENCER’S LIVESTREAM EMERGENCY

"It’s extremely concerning that teenagers are experimenting with powerful cancer medications in an attempt to grow taller," Dr. Stephanie Widmer, a New York City-based emergency medicine physician and Fox News medical contributor, told Fox News Digital.

"These drugs were developed to treat serious medical conditions, not to enhance physical appearance, and taking them without a legitimate medical indication or physician supervision can have devastating consequences."

Medical experts are warning of a dangerous new social media trend known as "heightmaxxing," amid reports that teenagers are taking black-market cancer medications in an effort to grow taller. (iStock)

The drug maker, Johnson & Johnson, pushed back against the practice in a statement to Rolling Stone, emphasizing that the medication has never been approved to stimulate height growth and that its safety and effectiveness have not been established for any pediatric or adolescent use.

Medical research has documented unexpected growth spurts in children receiving erdafitinib for brain tumors. A 2024 study published in Hormone Research in Paediatrics described accelerated growth in two pediatric patients, while a separate case report documented a teenager who grew more than 5 inches during treatment but developed serious skeletal complications.
CALLOUT:

Physicians caution that these spurts do not equal healthy skeletal growth. Dr. Jessica Gray, a family physician in Lubbock, Texas, warned that forced, rapid growth can trigger dangerous structural problems, including premature growth plate damage and bone fractures.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS FACE NUMEROUS LAWSUITS OVER RARE ‘EYE STROKE’ LINKED TO VISION LOSS
The drug works by blocking specific cellular signaling pathways involved in cancer cell growth, Widmer shared during an appearance on Fox News' "America's Newsroom."
Those same pathways also play a role in bone development, which may help explain why some pediatric patients experienced unexpected growth during treatment.

Widmer noted that height is overwhelmingly governed by genetics, and biological shortcuts do not exist. Once growth plates close near the end of puberty, medications cannot reopen them, meaning older adolescents taking the compound are incurring catastrophic health hazards without any chance of gaining height, she said.
The drug works by blocking specific cellular signaling pathways involved in cancer cell growth. (iStock)

"One of the biggest concerns is that these medications can cause serious side effects, including potentially permanent vision damage, elevated phosphate levels and other metabolic abnormalities," Widmer said.
"We’re talking about adolescents whose bodies are still developing, and exposing them to these risks for a cosmetic goal is particularly troubling."

Other warning signs and side effects linked to the medication include skeletal pain — especially in the hips or knees — as well as mouth sores, loose nails and skin disorders.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The trend has also raised concerns about the influence of social media on teenagers' decisions about their health. Widmer noted that online discussions about physical appearance and self-improvement can expose young men to potentially unsafe practices that lack medical evidence.
"Parents need to understand that this goes beyond teenagers being insecure about their height," the doctor said.
Medical experts warn that taking the drug can cause irreversible harm, including permanent vision damage, metabolic abnormalities and severe skeletal fractures. (iStock)

"We’re talking about young people potentially obtaining prescription cancer medications and experimenting with them outside of medical supervision. If a child has concerns about their growth, that conversation belongs in a pediatrician’s office, not on an internet forum."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Doctors advise parents to watch for symptoms such as unusual joint pain or unexplained physical changes, and to speak with their children if they suspect they are using medications obtained online.
Teenagers concerned about their height or growth should consult a pediatrician before considering any medication.

"We should be encouraging teenagers to prioritize their health, not teaching them to gamble with it," Widmer said. "No amount of additional height is worth risking permanent damage to your vision or other serious and potentially unknown medical complications."

title: Aggressive cancer type linked to common chemical exposure in new study
summary: A new NIH study links PFOA and PFOS forever chemicals to a 67% and 93% higher rate of ER-negative breast cancer, raising urgent questions. Experts weigh in.
story: Dr. Tiffany Troso-Sandoval breaks down research examining potential cancer risks associated with PFAS and offers advice on reducing exposure.
Two "forever chemicals" have been associated with a higher risk of aggressive breast cancer, according to research from the National Institutes of Health (NIH).
Forever chemicals, known as PFAS, are a group of synthetic chemicals that break down extremely slowly and can build up in the environment and the human body.
PFAS have been used in nonstick cookware, upholstery and clothing, as well as some food packaging and personal care items.
CANCER RISK MAY BE HIGHER FOR PEOPLE WITH ONE PARTICULAR TYPE OF JOB

The study, published in the Journal of Clinical Oncology, found that women with higher blood levels of two types of PFAS — perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) — were more likely to develop estrogen receptor-negative (ER-negative) breast cancer.

ER-negative breast cancers tend to be "more aggressive" and have worse outcomes compared to breast cancers that respond to estrogen, according to a U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) press release.

Data was drawn from a large U.S. research project called the Sister Study, which investigated environmental and genetic factors related to breast cancer. All participants had a sister diagnosed with breast cancer at enrollment but did not have breast cancer themselves.

Researchers measured 17 PFAS in blood samples collected before diagnosis from 1,609 women who later developed breast cancer and a comparison sample of 2,269 women, then examined links between PFAS levels and breast cancer risk by tumor type.
EATING LESS OF COMMON INGREDIENT EARLY IN LIFE MAY SLASH CANCER RISK DECADES LATER

The highest PFOA exposure group had a 67% higher rate of ER-negative breast cancer. The rate was 93% higher in the highest PFOS group compared to those in the lowest group. These figures represent relative differences between groups, not an individual woman’s chance of developing breast cancer.
"We know little about how they may influence health outcomes."
The researchers found no clear association between PFOA or PFOS and breast cancer overall.

"This study, along with the accompanying meta-analysis of previous studies, provides evidence that two PFAS are related to a higher ER-negative breast cancer risk," study leader Alexandra White, Ph.D., a researcher at the National Institutes of Health, told Fox News Digital.
Two "forever chemicals" have been associated with a higher risk of an aggresive type of cancer, according to research from the National Institutes of Health. (iStock)

As this study focused mainly on older PFAS chemicals that have been largely phased out, the researcher said experts know "very little" about the PFAS that are replacing them, which could serve as a limitation.
MICROPLASTICS DETECTED IN MOST HEART ATTACK PATIENTS' BLOOD IN STARTLING NEW STUDY

"They tend to be shorter-chain compounds and may be less persistent in our bodies and the environment, but we know little about how they may influence health outcomes, such as breast cancer," she said.
The findings show an association, not proof of causation, between forever chemical exposure and breast cancer risk, as the authors noted that more research is needed.
ER-negative breast cancers tend to be more aggressive and have worse outcomes compared to breast cancers that respond to estrogen hormones, according to the HHS. (iStock)
HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said that "women deserve clear answers about how chemicals in their environment may affect their health," calling for further investigation.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Under President Trump’s leadership, we will pursue the evidence, confront environmental health risks and give women the information they need to protect their health," he said.

Medical oncologist Dr. Tiffany Troso-Sandoval, a New York City-based breast and gynecological cancer specialist who worked at Memorial Sloan Kettering for more than 25 years, also acknowledged that forever chemicals can increase cancer risk.
Forever chemicals, known as PFAS, are a group of human-made synthetic chemicals that break down extremely slowly and can build up in the environment and the human body. (iStock)

"Oftentimes, once you've been exposed to them, they will accumulate in your body and cause havoc, and can actually increase the risk of carcinogenic transformation of cells," she told Fox News Digital. "What was interesting about this study is that the link was found only in ER-negative breast cancers, which is a known aggressive subtype of cancer."

Few risk factors beyond genetic predispositions are known for ER-negative breast cancer, Troso-Sandoval noted, adding that "the study did not show that it increased the risk of all breast cancers in general."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
She suggested PFAS might damage DNA or interfere with the body's ability to repair that damage or destroy cancerous cells.
While patients with ER-negative breast cancer had higher levels of these compounds in their bodies, that does not prove the chemicals caused their cancers, according to Troso-Sandoval.
Reducing PFAS exposure

First author Che-Jung Chang, Ph.D., a former research fellow at NIH and a current researcher at DLH, noted that although PFAS are "persistent" in the environment and in the human body, exposure is "potentially modifiable."
"People can take steps to reduce their exposure, and these findings could open new avenues for prevention," she said.
One doctor recommended considering cooking with stainless steel pots and pans. (iStock)
Troso-Sandoval recommends reviewing everyday sources of exposure to PFAS and other potentially harmful chemicals, including the following:
Drinking waterCookware and utensilsCosmetics and personal care products
Drinking water
Cookware and utensils
Cosmetics and personal care products
Her concerns about black plastic utensils involve other chemical contaminants, including flame retardants.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Try to look at the products that you are using very frequently, and those are the first ones to swap out," she advised.

"Maybe consider cooking with stainless steel pots and pans ... I recommend not heating up any food in plastic containers, because as you heat these plastics, they tend to leach more of the compounds into our foods."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
She recommends reviewing cosmetics and personal care products that may contain some of these compounds.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: New California law will restrict sales of some muscle-building supplements to minors
summary: Gavin Newsom signed AB 2030 restricting diet pills and muscle building supplements for minors, but questions remain about creatine and protein products.
story: Fox News medical contributor Dr. Jessica Gray discusses research connecting energy drinks and workout supplements to increased heart problems.
Gavin Newsom has signed legislation banning the sale of some "muscle-building supplements" to Californians under 18 years of age.
The legislation (AB 2030), which was signed on Sept. 28, covers over-the-counter diet pills and dietary supplements for weight loss or muscle building. It will go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

"Nonprescribed, medically unapproved products may cause dangerous side effects," the governor’s office said in its announcement. "Products can be mislabeled or contaminated with substances such as steroids."
WHY STACKING SUPPLEMENTS WITHOUT A BLOOD TEST FIRST CAN DO MORE HARM THAN GOOD

California’s law restricts minors’ access to supplements marketed for muscle building – specifically, those that are "labeled, marketed or otherwise represented for the purpose of achieving weight loss or building muscle."
New California legislation will ban the sale of some "muscle-building supplements" to Californians under 18 years of age. (iStock)
Courts may consider whether a product contains "creatine, green tea extract, raspberry ketone, garcinia cambogia or green coffee bean extract," the legislation states.
The law does not impose an outright ban on all creatine products. Restrictions depend on how the supplements are labeled, advertised and marketed to consumers.
TAKING DAILY SUPPLEMENT MAY HELP PRESERVE MUSCLE AS YOU AGE — EVEN WITHOUT EXERCISE
The law does not apply to people under 18 who have a prescription for an over-the-counter diet pill or dietary supplement for weight loss or muscle-building.
The release cites research indicating that nearly one in 10 adolescents have used such products.
The legislation (AB 2030), which was signed on Sept. 28, covers over-the-counter diet pills and dietary supplements for weight loss or muscle building. (iStock)
It also references studies linking over-the-counter diet pill use to a sixfold greater likelihood of an eating disorder diagnosis within three years.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The announcement does not specify whether whey protein or creatine products are included in the ban.
Sellers who do not adhere to the new law will face civil fines of up to $500 per violation.
"Nonprescribed, medically unapproved products may cause dangerous side effects."
The American Herbal Products Association, based in Maryland, released a statement opposing the law.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Lacking any scientific justification, AB 2030 casts a shadow over safe, beneficial products," said Robert Marriott, the association's vice president of regulatory and government affairs, in the statement.
The organization argues that the law's scope is unclear and notes that it does not explicitly exempt protein products.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The Center for Science in the Public Interest, based in Washington, D.C., shared public support of the new legislation.
POPULAR DRINKS LINKED TO HEART ATTACKS, CARDIAC ARREST IN YOUNG ADULTS, STUDY FINDS

"Manufacturers of these products often prey on kids and teens with deceptive claims that lack any scientific evidence," said Jensen Jose, a regulatory counsel at CSPI, which co-sponsored the legislation.
"Studies show that many supplements contain harmful substances that go undetected," one physician warned. (iStock)

Dr. Sigrid Wolf, a pediatric sports medicine physician at Lurie Children's Hospital of Chicago, recently addressed the use of creatine products among teenagers, stating that evidence of benefits is limited.
POISON CENTERS LINK GROWING BENADRYL ABUSE AMONG TEENS TO DANGEROUS SOCIAL MEDIA TRENDS

"In some cases, they might even be dangerous," wrote Wolf, who is a member of the American Academy of Pediatrics' sports medicine committee, in an article published on HealthyChildren.org, the American Academy of Pediatrics' parenting website.
"Creatine can come with negative side effects such as weight gain, dizziness, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Studies show that many supplements contain harmful substances that go undetected," she added, instead recommending prioritizing nutrition, training, sleep and hydration.
Fox News Digital reached out to Newsom's office for comment.
