title: Men and women who smoke marijuana may experience different effects, study suggests
summary: UCLA researchers found occasional male cannabis users reported stronger effects like anxiety and elevated heart rate than women with similar THC levels.
story: Family physician Dr. Jessica Gray discusses the rising trend of daily marijuana use in America. She warns against the common misconception that cannabis is naturally safe and highlights the lack of evidence supporting its mental health benefits.
Men who use cannabis occasionally may feel stronger effects from the drug than women with similar use habits, new research suggests.

The UCLA Health study, published in the journal Neuropsychopharmacology, included 44 healthy adults between the ages of 21 and 55, evenly split between men and women. Researchers divided participants based on whether they used cannabis frequently or occasionally.
Each participant took part in three separate sessions: smoking cannabis with no THC, a lower amount of THC or a higher amount. They did not know which one they were receiving at the time.
MARIJUANA USERS MAY FACE HIDDEN DRIVING DANGER THAT STANDARD TESTS CAN MISS
Among those who used cannabis occasionally, men reported feeling more high, sedated and impaired than women with similar use habits, according to the study.
The men also reported more unpleasant effects, including anxiety, and their heart rate rose significantly after using active cannabis.
Men who use cannabis occasionally may feel stronger effects from the drug than women with similar use habits, new research suggests. (iStock)
Blood THC levels alone did not appear to explain the difference.
Men and women who used cannabis occasionally had similar peak THC levels, even though the men reported stronger effects, researchers found.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
The pattern was different among people who used cannabis more often. Men and women in the frequent-use group generally responded similarly to active cannabis.
Frequent users were also more likely than occasional users to say they liked the effects, wanted to use cannabis again and chose to take more during the study, regardless of gender.
Men who smoke cannabis occasionally may experience greater intoxication, sedation and impairment than women who use the drug at similar frequencies. (iStock)
The findings challenge some previous research suggesting women may be more sensitive to the effects of cannabis.

"Much of what we thought we knew about sex differences in cannabis effects came from animal research and from human studies that pooled data from different trials," Dr. Ziva Cooper, the study's principal investigator and director of the UCLA Center for Cannabis and Cannabinoids, said in a press release.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES
"When we designed a study to look at sex and frequency of use at the same time, and controlled for hormones, the picture changed," she added.
The researchers controlled for menstrual cycle timing among the women in the study, who were not using hormonal birth control.
The findings suggest that a person's history of cannabis use may be an important factor in determining how strongly the drug affects them. (iStock)
The findings suggest that a person's cannabis habits may be important when considering how men and women respond to the drug.

"Sex and cannabis use history can both shape how someone experiences the effects of cannabis," lead author Dr. Stephanie Lake, a researcher at the UCLA Center for Cannabis and Cannabinoids, said in the release.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Studying both together is key to understanding who is most at risk of higher-risk, unpleasant or beneficial experiences from cannabis."
There were several limitations to the findings, the researchers acknowledged.
Researchers noted that cannabis products sold today commonly contain THC concentrations of 20% or higher, exceeding the strengths tested in the study. (iStock)
The study was small, with just 44 participants, and several of the findings involving occasional male users came from exploratory analyses, meaning they need to be confirmed in larger studies.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The cannabis used in the experiment contained 4% or 10% THC, which researchers noted is weaker than many cannabis products sold today, where THC levels are commonly 20% or higher.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Researchers said larger studies are needed to better understand whether men and women develop tolerance to cannabis differently and how those differences could affect the risk of cannabis use disorder.
Fox News Digital reached out to the researchers for comment.

title: 6-minute daily habit could help Ozempic users preserve muscle, expert says
summary: Gary Brecka says just six minutes of daily resistance training can help protect lean body mass during Ozempic and Wegovy weight loss journeys.
story: Gary Brecka, a biologist and longevity expert in Miami, Florida, shared with Fox News Digital his simple strategy for helping people preserve muscle — starting with just six minutes of exercise a day.
As more Americans turn to popular GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Zepbound to lose weight or manage diabetes, there is a growing focus on protecting muscle as pounds are shed.
The concern comes as 11% of U.S. adults report taking these drugs for weight loss, up from 3% in 2024, according to Gallup.
Lean mass, which includes muscle and other tissues, accounts for roughly a quarter to a third of the weight lost with these obesity treatments, research suggests.
4 SIMPLE HABITS CAN HELP SLOW MUSCLE LOSS AS YOU AGE, FITNESS EXPERT SAYS

Gary Brecka, a biologist and longevity expert in Miami, Florida, shared with Fox News Digital his simple strategy for helping people preserve muscle — starting with just six minutes of exercise a day.

"GLP-1s can be life-saving for people, especially for people who are morbidly obese or have type 2 diabetes, but they can also be fascinating shifts in someone's trajectory of their wellness journey," he said.
Lean mass, which includes muscle and other tissues, accounts for roughly a quarter to a third of the weight lost with GLP-1 medications. (iStock)
"What's critically important for people who embark on a GLP-1 journey is to make sure that they are mitigating the lean body-mass loss."
Brecka emphasized that weight loss is not exclusively fat loss.
OZEMPIC USERS MAY BE MAKING A MAJOR WEIGHT-LOSS MISTAKE, NEW STUDY SUGGESTS

"When most people say, ‘I want to lose weight,’ what they're really saying is, ‘I want to lose fat,’" he said. "But with GLP-1s, you have a double-edged sword. About 20% to 40% of the weight that you lose is what we call lean body mass."

Lean body mass includes not only muscle, but also water, organs, blood and connective tissues, such as tendons and ligaments. Brecka emphasized that preserving lean tissue should be a priority during treatment.
"You don't have to lift like a bodybuilder to mitigate lean body mass loss."
Maintaining strength also helps people remain independent as they age, supporting everyday activities such as bathing, dressing and walking.
"The more that we can maintain control and dominion over those, the more independent we can be," Brecka said.
WEEKLY WEIGHTLIFTING SWEET SPOT MAY BE LINKED TO LONGER LIFE, STUDY FINDS
Strength in minutes
Challenging the body through exercise encourages it to adapt and grow stronger, Brecka said.
"But when it comes to a GLP-1 journey, you've got to give up a little bit of that comfort to reach your goals," he said.
Challenging the body through exercise encourages it to adapt and grow stronger, the expert said. (iStock)
Brecka recommends starting with six minutes of resistance exercise each day.

"People think of weight-training or resistance training as something they've got to dedicate 60 to 90 minutes to every day, and therefore they think they don't have enough time in their day," he said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
It’s also important to pair the strength training with adequate protein to help preserve muscle during weight loss.
Protein provides amino acids that help the body build and maintain muscle and other tissues, including tendons, ligaments and cartilage, Brecka said.
‘Snacking’ on exercise
Busy people who don’t have time for lengthy gym sessions can fit resistance training into their day by "snacking" on exercise, the longevity expert said.
Brecka suggested simple exercises such as holding a plank with the knees on the floor, progressing to a full plank as strength allows, or doing body-weight squats and abdominal crunches.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

He also recommended resistance exercises using dumbbells or barbells, preferably moving through a full range of motion. One example is a goblet squat, which involves holding a dumbbell near the chest while squatting and standing.

"You don't have to lift like a bodybuilder to mitigate lean body mass loss," he said. "All you have to do is provide resistance for these tissues so that your body doesn't begin to reabsorb them while you're on this GLP-1 journey."
Busy people who don’t have time for lengthy gym sessions can fit resistance training into their day by "snacking" on exercise, the longevity expert said. (iStock)

In terms of frequency, Brecka said exercise should be "non-negotiable" as a daily practice. He recommends a minimum of three days of resistance training and a minimum of three days of cardiovascular training.

"Cardiovascular training can be as simple as walking outside, taking your dog for a 20-minute walk," he said, adding that a weighted vest can make the same walk more challenging by increasing the load the body carries.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"If you're going to an airport, skip the moving walkway, skip the escalator, just take the steps," Brecka suggested. "There are simple things that you can do every single day … that have a dramatic impact on your body's ability to rebuild these tissues."
"These small choices throughout our lifetime are what build resilience for the decades ahead."
Prioritizing protein
Protein does more than just support muscle, according to Brecka.

Whether protein comes from chicken, beef or plant-based foods, the body breaks it down into amino acids that help build and repair muscle and other tissues, including tendons, ligaments and cartilage.
The body breaks down protein from foods such as chicken, beef and plants into amino acids, which help build and repair muscle and other tissues, including tendons, ligaments and cartilage. (iStock)
"Protein is important for so many more things than just muscle and the physical things that we see on the outside," Brecka said. "It's also responsible for building these lean body mass structures."
Current federal dietary guidelines recommend 1.2 to 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight daily.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
A joint advisory on GLP-1 treatment discusses the same range during active weight loss, while emphasizing that targets should be tailored to the individual.

Brecka also urged patients to pay attention to declining energy or exercise performance, such as finding a previously easy flight of stairs suddenly difficult, and discuss those changes with a doctor.

title: Forget prunes: Popular green fruit shows promise for constipation relief
summary: A review of 33 studies links eating two green kiwis daily for four weeks to more regular bowel movements in people with constipation or IBS-C.
story: Christopher Gardner, PhD, a nutrition scientist at Stanford University, says increasing fiber is crucial in a healthy diet and recommends eating more fruits, vegetables and minimally processed foods rather than eliminating an entire food group.
Eating two green kiwis a day could help people struggling with constipation, a new review suggests.
The research, published in the journal Food, Nutrition and Health, looked at 33 previous studies and reports on kiwifruit and digestive health.

Eating two fresh green kiwis a day for about four weeks was linked to more regular bowel movements, less straining and better digestive comfort in people with constipation or irritable bowel syndrome with constipation (IBS-C).
COMMON KITCHEN STAPLE MAY HELP RELIEVE MILD CONSTIPATION, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS

In one international trial included in the review, people with constipation had about 1.5 more complete bowel movements per week, while those with IBS-C had about 1.7 more per week. Both groups also reported improved digestive comfort.
The new review suggests there may be several reasons kiwi helps with constipation.
Eating two green kiwis a day could help people struggling with constipation, a new review suggests. (iStock)

Its fiber can add bulk and hold water in stool, while the fruit's natural water and sorbitol may help make stool easier to pass. Researchers said the benefit likely comes from several parts of the whole fruit working together rather than one component alone.
Kiwi was not necessarily more effective than other constipation treatments.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

One U.S. trial included in the review found that green kiwi, psyllium fiber and prunes all helped improve chronic constipation. Kiwi was associated with fewer side effects and was well-tolerated by many participants.
The evidence is strongest for fresh green kiwi, the researchers noted. There is less research on gold kiwi, powders and extracts, so those forms should not be assumed to have the same effect.
Researchers found that consuming two green kiwis daily for about four weeks was linked to more regular bowel movements and less straining. (iStock)

Jason Heiselman, a New York-based certified nutritionist and professional chef at Hungryroot in New York City, previously told Fox News Digital that kiwi is an easy fruit to work into a person's diet.
"It feels like a no-brainer to include a few slices with any meal," said Heiselman, who was not involved in the new review.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Kiwi contains fiber along with a natural enzyme called actinidin, which can help with digestion, the nutritionist noted.
"Pairing kiwi with some good fat sources, like seeds, nuts or full-fat dairy, allows your body to absorb more nutrients," he said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
For people who do not want to eat kiwi on its own, the fruit can also work in savory meals, according to Heiselman. "Raw kiwi slices often make their way to my dinner table," he said.
Heiselman said he pairs the fruit with salty cheeses, toasted pistachios and shaved red onion, and has also used kiwi as the base for chutneys and relishes.
Although green kiwi showed promise for constipation relief, researchers said it was not necessarily more effective than other dietary options. (iStock)
There were some limitations to the findings.

The paper reviewed previous research rather than conducting a new clinical trial, and the studies differed in the people involved, the types and amounts of kiwi consumed, and the results researchers measured.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Most of the research also looked at relatively short periods of time, so more studies are needed to determine whether the benefits continue long-term.
Fox News Digital reached out to the researchers for comment.
Andrea Margolis of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.

title: Pro-life pregnancy center expands mission to help patients embrace their God-given gender
summary: By listening to the Holy Spirit, Heidi Matzke, executive director of the Alternatives Pregnancy Center, said her clinic helps women embrace the gender they were given by God.
story: A mother shares her experience with pro-life crisis pregnancy centers, Life First in Manassas, Virginia, opened its doors to Fox News Digital to discuss how it helps pregnant women in crisis.
Helping a transgender man detransition to being a woman again is not something the pro-life, gospel-led Alternatives Pregnancy Center even notes on its website.

But because it is a full-service women's health clinic with doctors who specialize in hormone therapy, it's simply something they do in order to give women the care they need to fully embrace their God-given gender.
It is all based on listening to the Holy Spirit, said executive director Heidi Matzke.
STUDY REVEALS UNEXPECTED HEALTH BENEFITS AFTER 5 MINUTES OF PRAYER

Based in Sacramento, California, Alternatives is one of hundreds of like-minded pregnancy help centers across the country. These venues may have different names, but they all work to help women with unplanned pregnancies.
Still, years ago when Matzke took over, she knew she needed help — heavenly help.
A health center located in Sacramento, California, not only helps women with unplanned pregnancies — it is also a full-service women's health clinic propelled by faith (not pictured). (iStock)

Matzke told Fox News, "When God called me into this ministry... I felt the Holy Spirit impress upon my heart back then, 'Heidi, you're right. You have no idea what you're doing, and that's why you'd better be face-down before me every single day. You better be fasting and praying.'"
She did fast. And she prayed and listened, she said.
The result today is a pregnancy help center that is also a full-service health clinic for women.
New challenges
It wasn't long before another challenge came Matzke's way, involving listening to God.
She asked the Holy Spirit to direct her very short talk at a church soon after launching the full-service clinic. The pastor gave her just two minutes.
By listening to the Holy Spirit, Heidi Matzke became the angel in Jessica Rose's life.
Matzke heard the Holy Spirit say to talk only about the women's health services the center offered and nothing else — not even the unplanned pregnancy help.

She did as directed. While the congregation received her respectfully and politely, Matzke said she felt a sense of defeat.
Then, between services, a man dressed as a woman came to her in the pews.
It wasn't long before another challenge arrived that involved listening closely to God. (boonchai wedmakawand via Getty Images)
It was just the two of them.
He said the words that changed both their lives.

He said to her, "What you don't know about me is that I'm biologically female, and I encountered Christ. The Holy Spirit has done work in my heart, and I am now trying to detransition. But my current doctors have basically abandoned me and I have nowhere to go."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH NEWS
That "man dressed as a woman" was Jessica Rose. Her story is all over the internet.

On that faith-filled day, Rose told Matzke she had been sobbing uncontrollably during Matzke's short presentation, as she had been praying that morning that God would provide her with free women's medical care.
The woman had been "sobbing uncontrollably" — and praying God would help her with her serious medical issues. (iStock)
By listening to the Holy Spirit, Matzke became the angel in Jessica Rose's life.
Her doctors had been eager to start her on hormones and surgery to remove her breasts after just a 30-minute consultation.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Now, in the pew, Matzke was the answer to spirit-leading prayer.
The women's heath clinic at that moment became more full-service than Heidi Matzke could ever imagine.
Heidi Matzke, executive director of the Alternatives Pregnancy Center in California, is pictured during an appearance in 2022 before the Senate Judiciary Committee. (Senate Judiciary Committee)
It became a place where all women, meaning adult females, can be strengthened and shown to love themselves as they are in the light of the Gospel of Christ.
On an episode of the "Lighthouse Faith" podcast, Matzke talks about her encounter with Jessica Rose.

She also shares how a series of events strengthened her resolve to develop a full-service health clinic led by the Gospel — and how listening to the Holy Spirit brings healing to many more people than we could ever imagine.

title: Struggling with depression? Psychiatrist says 6 habits may be making it worse
summary: Dr. Daniel Amen reveals the everyday habits that worsen depression, from alcohol use and isolation to processed foods and unchecked negative thoughts.
story: Dr. Daniel Amen, founder of Amen Clinics, identifies six behaviors people should avoid when experiencing depression, including drinking alcohol, withdrawing from others and consuming highly processed foods.

Depression rates among Americans ages 12 and older rose nearly 60% over a decade, increasing from 8.2% in 2013–2014 to 13.1% in 2021–2023, according to a recent report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Finding the right treatment for depression can take time, and antidepressants usually take four to eight weeks to work, per the National Institute of Mental Health.

For those struggling with the condition, clinical psychiatrist Dr. Daniel Amen – founder of Amen Clinics in California – says avoiding the following habits may help to manage symptoms and support mental health.
IS DRINKING EVERY DAY ALCOHOLISM? EXPERTS EXPLAIN WHERE CULTURE AND ADDICTION COLLIDE
No. 1: Drinking alcohol
Alcohol may offer temporary relief from depression symptoms, but as its effects wear off, mood can worsen.
Dr. Daniel Amen (right) is the founder of brain scan company Amen Clinics in California. (Katie Levine; iStock)
As the brain adjusts to alcohol’s relaxing effects, it can leave people feeling more anxious and restless after the buzz fades, making them feel "worse than before," Amen warned.
Drinking can also disrupt sleep, adding to next-day fatigue, according to the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism.
No. 2: Staying in bed
It might be tempting to linger in bed when you wake up, but Amen encouraged people with depression to get up and start their day.

"When people are depressed, they tend to have pretty low activity, especially in the front part of their brain, but burying yourself under the covers just makes things worse," he said. "Get up, get out."
SCIENTISTS REVEAL SURPRISINGLY EASY EXERCISE THAT MAY BOOST YOUR MOOD IN JUST 10 MINUTES
Amen's advice aligns with a broader approach called behavioral activation, a type of therapy that helps people gradually return to meaningful activities rather than withdraw from them.
Behavioral activation has been shown to be beneficial for treating depression, according to a 2020 Cochrane review of 53 studies involving 5,495 adults.
"Burying yourself under the covers just makes things worse," Amen said in reference to depression. (iStock)
No. 3: Believing your negative thoughts
A negative mindset can make it easier to believe things that aren’t true — or, as Amen puts it, every "stupid" thought. He refers to these as "ANTs," or automatic negative thoughts.
"The thoughts that come into your mind automatically and ruin your day – they drive depression," he said.
"Burying yourself under the covers just makes things worse … get up, get out."
When feeling strong emotions – such as sadness, anger, anxiety or just lack of control – Amen recommends writing down what you’re thinking and then asking yourself if it’s true.
"My favorite part – and there's a whole method to this – is flipping the thought and actually meditating on the opposite of the thought you have," he said. "So, taking each thought captive."
No. 4: Isolating yourself
Depression can lead people to withdraw from others, but social isolation may worsen symptoms, Amen said.
"The more isolated you get, the louder the ANT chorus gets, and it makes [depression] worse," he cautioned.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

A 2025 study published in General Hospital Psychiatry tracked more than 339,000 U.K. adults for roughly 12 years. Loneliness was associated with a 77% higher risk of developing depression, while social isolation was linked to a 14% higher risk.
No. 5: Eating highly processed foods
Eating more ultraprocessed foods, including many fast-food items, has been linked to a higher risk of depression, Amen said, although research has not established cause and effect.
"There's actually a lot of consensus now among psychiatrists that inflammation drives certain types of depression," the doctor told Fox News Digital.
A negative mindset can make it easier to believe things that aren’t true — which Amen refers to these as "ANTs," or automatic negative thoughts. (iStock)
A 2025 review in the American Journal of Psychiatry supports inflammation’s role in some cases, but notes that elevated inflammatory markers occurred in only a subset of people with depression.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Amen recommends adhering to an anti-inflammatory diet emphasizing "vegetables, healthy protein and healthy fats."

A 2024 review of five randomized trials involving 1,507 adults found that Mediterranean-style diets reduced depressive symptoms compared with control groups, although results varied considerably among studies.
No. 6: Taking medication without a proper assessment
Depression treatment is individualized, so not every medication is right for everyone — and not every patient requires medication.
Amen emphasized the importance of receiving a thorough assessment prior to receiving antidepressants, which he said can be "lifesaving."
Some supplements, like omega-3 and saffron, have been found to be more effective than antidepressants in recent research. (iStock)

For milder depression, psychotherapy is often the first approach. People with moderate or severe depression are usually prescribed medication as part of their initial treatment plan, according to the National Institute of Mental Health.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

For those who have done "all the right things" but still struggle, Amen encouraged seeking further medical evaluation. Depending on symptoms and medical history, a clinician may order blood tests to check for conditions such as anemia or thyroid disease that could contribute to symptoms.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The doctor also recommended considering approaches beyond medication, such as exercise — or, as Amen suggested, "walking like you're late" — which has been proven in studies to perform better than some depression medications.
Some supplements, like omega-3 and saffron, have been found to be more effective than antidepressants in recent research.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Inside the House GOP strategy to capitalize on Democrats' warring factions in the new Congress
summary: Tom Emmer says House Republicans will use committee hearings and floor votes to hold Democrats accountable as the GOP shifts to minority status.
story: Incoming House Minority Whip Rep. Tom Emmer, R-Minn., joins ‘The Ingraham Angle’ to discuss the GOP’s legislative priorities, efforts to support American manufacturing and whether Democrats will work with Republicans to advance their agenda.
EXCLUSIVE: House Republicans are heading into the next Congress ready to brawl.

Rep. Tom Emmer, R-Minn., who is set to go from the No. 3 most powerful House Republican to No. 2 next year, told Fox News Digital that the GOP will hold the new Democrat majority "accountable" for their far-left faction's ideas over the next two years, even if they cannot control what bills get a vote.

Emmer, who has served as House majority whip for the past four years, was elected Tuesday to serve as minority whip alongside incoming House Minority Leader Jim Jordan, R-Ohio. The Speaker of the House position turns over to Democrats, and will likely be won by current minority leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y.
And despite Jeffries poised to take control of what legislation gets to the House floor, Emmer signaled House Republicans would find ways to push their agenda as well.
JIM JORDAN BECOMES NEW HOUSE GOP LEADER AFTER CLOSED-DOOR VOTE, DEFEATING STEVE SCALISE
U.S. House Majority Whip Tom Emmer speaks during a press conference after the House GOP elected new leadership on Capitol Hill on Nov. 10, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images)

"What's their answer to dealing with costs and wages? We're going to investigate Trump," Emmer said in reference to Democrats. "That's not going to solve the problems that they created. So that's going to be the job of the whip, is to make sure that we have a coordinated process — committee hearings, floor votes — to expose and define exactly who these people really are."
PROGRESSIVE GROUP'S 182-PAGE BLUEPRINT MAPS OUT POTENTIAL DEM INVESTIGATIONS INTO TRUMP, CORPORATE ALLIES
Emmer, in his first print interview since winning the House minority whip job, would not go into detail about how Republicans would utilize floor votes, however.
"There's a toolbox with a bunch of different tools, and you're going to have to build that strategy as you go from week to week," he said.
The Minnesota Republican also signaled there would be little appetite for bipartisanship over the next two years, a sentiment he suggested would come from the other side of the aisle.
"Well look, they're not going to work with us, that's pretty clear, and I don't even know if they're going to be able to work with each other," Emmer said.
HAKEEM JEFFRIES FACES PROGRESSIVE HOLDOUTS BUT NO RIVAL AS HOUSE SPEAKER RACE TAKES SHAPE

Congressman Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., address a press conference during the congressional delegation's visit to Denmark, in Copenhagen on Friday, April 25, 2025 (EMIL NICOLAI HELMS/Ritzau Scanpix/AFP via Getty Images)

He repeated a short time later, "I see nowhere where they're going to work with Republicans. And Republicans who think they are should think again, because they will tell you nice things, and then they will just go do what they do."
Meanwhile other House Republicans are already coming up with ideas on how to put Democrats on the spot on the House floor in the new Congress.
"We'll file amendments," said Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla. "And I think that'll be where having good debaters and communicators would be important."

Holding amendment votes is commonplace before large pieces of legislation like the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), which Congress has enacted annually for decades to update and reauthorize critical national security policies.

Rep. Nick LaLota, R-N.Y., suggested an emphasis on a parliamentary procedure called the "motion to recommit," which allows the minority party to get a vote on altering or even killing a bill in its tracks.

"I expect we'll use that smartly," LaLota said. "But as well, a Speaker Hakeem Jeffries will be wise to work these problems backwards, to know that anything he puts on the floor that he wants to become law or budget needs President Trump's signature and probably 60 votes in the Senate."
Rep. Mark Harris, R-N.C., said "there's been a lot of conversation about going on offense."
"We want to make sure that they know when they come to the floor, they're gonna dread it, I hope," Harris said.
DEMOCRATS RALLY BEHIND GOP LAWMAKER'S HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT PUSH, SIGNAL MORE TO COME IN JANUARY
But there's another mechanism for forcing a House vote that's been used more and more often in recent years — often by their fellow Republicans.

Privileged resolutions allow lawmakers on either side to get a vote on a given bill within two days of its introduction. It generally begins with a procedural vote on whether to "table" the bill or refer it to committee in order to stop it, before a vote on the measure itself.

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., most recently invoked it to force the House to consider impeaching Secretary of War Pete Hegseth. But that was defeated when the rest of the House GOP banded together to refer the bill to committee.
The GOP lawmakers who spoke with Fox News Digital, however, signaled little appetite for using it.

U.S. Rep. Jim Jordan speaks during a press conference after House Republicans elected new leadership for the upcoming session of Congress at the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 10, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images)

"I think either party would be wise to build consensus around things that help actually deliver for the American people," LaLota said. "The privileged resolutions have been abused in my time here, and there's a better way to do business."
And Emmer said his main goal for the next two years would be winning back the House majority in 2028 — which he insisted was a realistic goal.
He said at least 38 seats flipped by Democrats would be "ready to return to Republican hands," and could see some old faces return.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Asked whether he wanted to see some of those losing GOP incumbents run for their seats again, Emmer said, "I absolutely hope so, I've talked to several already."
Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.
Follow on Twitter at @liz_elkind and send tips to elizabeth.elkind@fox.com

title: Trump keeps signaling an end to Iran war, but expert warns a crucial piece of his strategy is missing
summary: President Donald Trump declared on Truth Social the U.S. no longer needs a deal with Iran, one day after proclaiming victory at Arlington.
story: During a speech at Arlington National Cemetery on Wednesday, President Donald Trump thanked U.S. service members for their ongoing sacrifices and argued that the U.S. has been pitted against Iran since 1979, when the Islamic Revolution happened.

President Donald Trump declared Thursday that the United States no longer needs a deal with Iran, abruptly shifting his diplomatic message just three days after expressing optimism about negotiations and directing Vice President JD Vance to focus on domestic issues instead.
"We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!"

Trump's latest declaration came just one day after he proclaimed victory over Iran during a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery, while acknowledging that the conflict had not yet formally ended.
"We won," Trump said Wednesday. "It’s just a question of when we end it. I want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93 percent victory."
TRUMP DEFENDS IRAN WAR DURING VETERANS DAY ADDRESS, SAYS HE IS MAKING THE WORLD 'SAFER'

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a ceremony at Memorial Amphitheater at Arlington National Cemetery to mark Veterans Day on November 11, 2025 in Arlington, Virginia. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
The president also thanked veterans "working to ensure the world’s number one sponsor of state terrorism, the Islamic Republic of Iran, will never have a nuclear weapon."

An administration official defended Trump's strategy, arguing that the United States has substantial leverage over Iran through its naval blockade and continued military pressure, even as questions remain about how the conflict will end.

"The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz and the Iranian economy collapsing. The President has been clear that the greatest naval blockade in history, Operation Economic Outcast, and the new Operation Iron Gate will continue with full effect," a U.S. official told Fox News Digital.
"President Trump holds all the cards, will do what is best for the United States, and will make sure that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon," the official added.
Trump's latest words follow months of predictions that an agreement could be reached soon, including comments earlier this week that Tehran "would love to make a deal."

Trump's declaration raises questions about the future of U.S.-Iran negotiations, including whether diplomatic efforts will continue through other administration officials as Washington maintains its military and economic pressure on Tehran.
AFTER 47 YEARS OF CONFRONTING IRAN, DOES AMERICA HAVE A STRATEGY FOR ENDING THIS WAR?

An Iranian flag is displayed at Iran's Bushehr nuclear power plant during an official ceremony on Nov. 10, 2019, to kick-start work on a second reactor at the facility. Bushehr is Iran's only nuclear power station and currently operates on imported fuel from Russia that is closely monitored by the UN's International Atomic Energy Agency. (AFP via Getty Images)
Trump has suggested on at least a dozen occasions since February that Iran wanted to negotiate or that an agreement could be reached soon, according to a preliminary review of his public remarks.

Ludovic Hood, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, said the administration's combination of economic coercion, military force and regional partnerships is sensible, but warned that a crucial diplomatic component remains underdeveloped.

"What’s lacking is disciplined diplomacy to complement the economic squeeze and possible airstrikes," Hood told Fox News Digital. "Our Gulf partners are singing from different hymn sheets and we need to draw European partners in more meaningfully."

Trump's optimistic assessments began before U.S. military operations against Iran commenced. On Feb. 13, he suggested Tehran could avoid an attack by accepting Washington's terms. After military operations began, he increasingly emphasized Iran's weakened capabilities and the prospect of ending the conflict.
IRANIAN NEGOTIATORS KICKED OUT OF US AS TALKS STALL, TRUMP LAYS OUT 'POSSIBLE' TIMELINE FOR MORE STRIKES
President Donald Trump arrives to deliver remarks at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 2, 2026. (Umit Bektas/Reuters)
On March 20, Trump said the United States was "getting very close" to achieving its military objectives.

The administration agreed to a ceasefire in April and continued pursuing a diplomatic settlement, but subsequent military actions and disagreements over Iran's nuclear program and regional shipping have left the broader conflict unresolved.
Trump continued expressing confidence that Iran wanted an agreement, including in May, when he suggested Tehran was eager to negotiate because of the damage inflicted on its military.

During an unscheduled appearance in the White House briefing room Monday, Trump said, "Iran, militarily, is effectively over," while warning that U.S. forces remained "locked and loaded" should circumstances change.
Hood said Trump's seemingly contradictory messages could be part of a deliberate negotiating strategy.
"The administration is pursuing a sensible hybrid strategy of economic coercion, selective use of force, and reliance on capable regional allies," Hood said.
TRUMP SAYS IRAN IS 'NEGOTIATING ON FUMES,' BELIEVES REGIME THOUGHT THEY COULD OUTWAIT HIM

Senior military leaders listen as U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth speaks at Marine Corps Base Quantico on September 30, 2025 in Quantico, Virginia. In an unprecedented gathering, almost 800 generals, admirals and their senior enlisted leaders have been ordered into one location from around the world on short notice. (robynmac)
"Trump’s messaging seems designed to both signal his preference for a diplomatic solution while preserving the option of force," he added.
Hood defended the president's willingness to maintain military pressure.
"Bluster, bluffing and brinkmanship are inherent in the public dimension of negotiations like this; Trump does it, Rubio does it, and senior figures in Tehran do it," he said.
"Strategic patience is essential in this standoff, which has essentially been 40 years in the making."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
But Hood also suggested that securing meaningful nuclear concessions or a more cooperative government in Tehran would require coordination with regional partners.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Socialist LA mayor's bold homelessness promise ahead of 2028 Olympics hit with reality check: 'Not optimistic'
summary: Los Angeles mayor-elect Nithya Raman pledges to halve homeless encampments before the 2028 Olympics, but a local activist warns it won't work.
story: John Alle, co-founder of the Santa Monica Coalition, spoke to Fox News Digital about potential gaps in incoming Mayor Nithya Raman's plan to cut the number of people sleeping in tents and encampments by at least 50% before the 2028 Olympics.

Incoming Los Angeles Mayor Nithya Raman has promised to cut the number of people sleeping in tents and homeless encampments by at least 50% before the 2028 Summer Olympics, but one local activist believes her vision may not be realistic.

The blue city’s growing homeless population became a major focus of Raman’s mayoral campaign. A member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), she plans to expand shelter and housing options while stretching "every dollar as far as possible."

John Alle, a business owner and co-founder of the Santa Monica Coalition, told Fox News Digital Raman won’t be able to "hide" the city’s homelessness problem from tourists arriving for the Games and raised concerns about potential gaps in in her plan to deliver lasting results.
"I don't think we're going to be able to hide that before the crowds," Alle said, adding that the city has become a "third-world country."
4 OF NATION'S LARGEST CITIES NOW LED BY SOCIALIST MAYORS AFTER TUESDAY'S ELECTION, AFFECTING TENS OF MILLIONS

John Alle, co-founder of the Santa Monica Coalition, told Fox News Digital he has concerns that incoming Mayor Nithya Raman's homelessness plan could be a temporary fix ahead of the 2028 Olympics. (Mario Tama/Getty Images; Allen J. Schaben / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

"We're not hiding it now. We're seeing tourists being attacked in Santa Monica, we're seeing tourists being attacked in LA. Our tourism, everything that funds our general fund, our retail sales taxes are all down. The morale of the police, which we need, is down."
Alle warned that Raman’s plan will be a temporary solution that will have homeless people moved off the streets ahead of the Olympics and returning once the Games are over.
"When the Olympics come, they'll be picked up, they'll be bused, they’ll be sent elsewhere, and they'll wander right back after the three-week Olympic and Paralympic events."

Former Mayor Karen Bass accepted the Olympic flag during the closing ceremony in Paris two years ago, marking the handoff of hosting duties. This will be the first time LA has hosted the Games since 1984.
According to the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority’s 2026 annual count, homelessness rose 3.4% in LA and 1.2% across the broader LA area, undoing two consecutive years of declines under Bass.
But how does Raman plan to follow through on that promise?

By the end of her first term, Raman has pledged to expand housing, shelter capacity and rental assistance to eliminate long-term encampments. Raman has previously called the city's "desensitization to homelessness" a "moral failing." Her plan calls for sending medical teams directly into encampments to provide mental health and addiction treatment and help with transitions into long-term housing or care within 90 days.

Raman has also criticized Bass' Inside Safe program, which often places homeless people in costly hotels and motels. Instead, Raman wants to shift funding toward less expensive alternatives, like rental vouchers.
SEATTLE MAYOR KATIE WILSON'S SOCIALIST AGENDA STALLS AMID HOMELESSNESS AND PUBLIC SAFETY CONCERNS
A woman pushes a stroller past a homeless encampment on Cesar E. Chavez Avenue in downtown Los Angeles on Friday, Aug. 21, 2026. (Christina House / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

Other parts of Raman’s proposal include sending unarmed crisis response teams rather than police officers to certain emergencies, auditing stalled housing projects and increasing oversight of homelessness spending.
Despite Raman’s ambitious vision, Alle said he isn't convinced her plan will bring meaningful change and argued that city leadership has gone "from bad to worse."
"It's not that much different than Mayor Karen Bass's plan," Alle said.

Alle, who manages roughly 1 million square feet of commercial property across Los Angeles, said he sees the homelessness crisis firsthand and raised concerns about its impact on local businesses and workers.
He warned that treating homeless people on the streets will only prolong the crisis, saying that many Angelenos avoid parts of the city that have been left untouched.
"Pick up the individuals and take them to their facilities away from the parks, away from kids, away from seniors," he said.
Alle said there must be more transparency over how the city has handled more than $1 billion in homelessness funding before allocating more taxpayer dollars.
"She’s got a billion-dollar problem on her hands right now, and she knows," he said.
FURIOUS RESIDENTS CONFRONT HOMELESS HOUSING LEADERS AS POPULAR BEACH COMMUNITY HITS BREAKING POINT
Los Angeles City Council member Nithya Raman, left, talks with Mayor Karen Bass, right, at Hazeltine Park in Sherman Oaks on Feb. 10, 2024. (Mel Melcon/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

Raman chaired the City Council's Housing and Homelessness Committee from 2023 until her removal this year amid her mayoral campaign. Alle said Raman will have to explain where the money went but acknowledged her push to investigate the spending.

"To her credit, she wants to audit every single non-profit and every single agency that spent money, including the non-profits that are supported by the city with taxpayer funds for programs," he said.
One of the biggest red flags in Raman’s plan is the proximity of supportive housing to families and children, according to Alle. He added that some facilities don't require residents to remain sober.
"There is no commitment for anyone not to use drugs while they're there," he said.
Pointing to her past opposition to restrictions on camping in public spaces and near schools, Alle argued Raman's approach isn’t "aggressive enough."
"I don't see the solutions that have been put forth that could work being used and so I'm not optimistic," he said.
Alle described LA as having a drug and mental health problem, not a homelessness problem. He said the city needs to stop making life on the streets more comfortable for those who refuse help.
"Until those two issues are addressed, we're not gonna solve homelessness," he said.
He urged Raman to find a more practical solution by moving outreach services off the streets and ending LA's sanctuary city status for good.
"Of course I want her to succeed," he said. "If Nithya succeeds, we all succeed."
Raman ousted Bass in the midterm elections and will take office in December as mayor of Los Angeles, a city of roughly 4 million residents.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to Raman's team and LA28 for comment.
Kiera McDonald is a Production Assistant for Fox News Digital.

title: Democrats seize on midterm wins to push massive minimum wage hikes, but economists see trouble ahead
summary: Josh Shapiro says he wants to more than double Pennsylvania's minimum wage and codify abortion rights with the new Democratic trifecta.
story: Research Director at the Employment Policies Institute, Rebekah Paxton, warns local officials about raising the minimum wage as Alameda County advances highest mandate in U.S. history.

Democrats are pushing major minimum-wage increases after their midterm victories, but economists warn the proposals could come with unintended consequences for small businesses and inexperienced workers.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro is pledging to more than double his state's $7.25 minimum wage, while Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker is calling for a federal increase as Democrats make affordability a central part of their governing agenda.

The renewed push comes as Seattle, which has one of the nation's highest minimum wages, faces concerns about rising business costs and employment opportunities — raising questions about the tradeoffs of higher wage mandates.

"We’re going to more than double Pennsylvania‘s minimum wage," Shapiro wrote in an X post this month. "Codify abortion rights into our state Constitution. Fund mass transit. Build more housing. These are the commonsense things that Pennsylvanians want done."
AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro speaks during a re-election campaign kickoff event in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, on Thursday, Jan. 8, 2026. (Rachel Wisniewski/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"And with a Democratic trifecta, we will deliver on all of them," he continued.

Shapiro's proposal would raise Pennsylvania's minimum wage from $7.25 to $15 an hour, an increase of roughly 107%, prompting questions about how small businesses would absorb the additional labor costs.

Tom Savidge, an economist with the American Institute for Economic Research, warned in an interview with Fox News Digital that steep wage increases could force small businesses to raise prices, reduce workers' hours or cut back on hiring.

"A federal minimum wage hike will worsen the affordability crisis," Savidge told Fox News Digital. "A one-size-fits-all mandate ignores regional differences in wages and business costs. It risks higher prices, fewer hours, and fewer jobs, especially for inexperienced workers. Politicians can mandate higher wages, but they cannot mandate that businesses can afford to pay them."

"Small businesses employing minimum-wage workers cannot absorb such a sharp increase without adjusting elsewhere," he added. "Some may raise prices, cut hours, or stop hiring. A higher minimum wage means little to workers who cannot find a job."
The debate comes as Democrats seek to deliver on campaign promises to make life more affordable, even as businesses in cities with higher minimum wages report growing financial pressures.

Seattle, where the minimum wage is currently $21.30 an hour and will rise to $22.14 in January, offers one example of the economic questions surrounding such policies. While proponents have asserted that minimum wage increases will be a boon to employees, some Seattle business owners have previously raised concerns about facing additional cost burdens, KOMO News reported in December 2025.

Rising labor costs have been among the financial pressures cited by Seattle restaurant owners who have closed locations, alongside higher food prices, declining customer demand and other operating expenses, Fox News Digital previously reported.

A January survey by The Intentionalist found that 67% of 136 independent small businesses surveyed in Seattle and surrounding Washington communities reported greater financial strain than during the pandemic, with respondents pointing to rising labor costs, rent, insurance and weaker customer demand.

A 2022 study published in the American Economic Journal: Economic Policy found that Seattle's 2015 and 2016 minimum-wage increases boosted pay for longer-tenured workers but reduced hours worked, particularly among less-experienced employees, and limited opportunities for people entering low-wage jobs.

However, a separate 2017 study by University of California, Berkeley researchers found that Seattle's earlier minimum-wage increases raised wages in the food-service industry without a statistically significant decline in restaurant employment.
Savidge went on to say that steep minimum wage increases often benefit major corporations over Main Street businesses.

"Higher minimum wages can favor big corporations over small businesses," he explained. "Large corporations can spread higher labor costs across more sales, invest in automation, or relocate operations. Small businesses have fewer options."
FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: HOW DEMOCRATS TOOK CONTROL OF THE SENATE

Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, at the Democratic National Convention, speaks with activists from New Hampshire at a delegation breakfast, on Aug. 21, 2024 in Chicago, Illinois. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

Despite concerns about the potential economic consequences, Shapiro has made raising Pennsylvania's minimum wage one of his first priorities after Democrats won control of both chambers of the state legislature.

"Half a million workers in Pennsylvania still make less than $15 an hour — you can’t live off of that in 2026," Shapiro said. "Now, we’re finally able to change that. The very first bill that I will sign into law with our new Democratic majority this January will be to raise our minimum wage — and make sure every Pennsylvania worker has a livable wage. It’s long overdue."
His comments come after Democrats secured a trifecta in Harrisburg in the 2026 midterms after flipping the Pennsylvania state Senate.
$25 AN HOUR? MAJOR CITIES EYE MASSIVE WAGE HIKES AS LABOR ACTIVISTS SEEK FEDERAL MANDATE
When reached for comment, Shapiro's office referred Fox News Digital to the governor’s comments on raising the minimum wage during an interview with former CNN host Don Lemon released on Sunday.

"Some of your some of your viewers and listeners are going to think it's crazy, but job number one is going to be raise the minimum wage to 15 bucks an hour, and now your listeners like, 'What do you mean 15 bucks an hour?'" Shapiro said during the interview. "Everybody's at 15 bucks an hour. Well, we're not in Pennsylvania. We've been stuck at $7.25 an hour for decades, right? Because the Republicans in the state senate, every time we've sent a bill over there, have blocked it."
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker speaks during a press conference at the UI Health Mile Square Health Center on Feb. 28, 2025. (Eileen T. Meslar/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
The minimum-wage push is also gaining traction beyond Pennsylvania.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who signed legislation in 2019 gradually raising his state's minimum wage to $15 an hour, is now calling on Congress to increase the federal minimum wage as part of his post-election economic agenda.

"Americans made their voices heard and this is an opportunity for Congress to immediately address the challenges of working people – higher wages, lower costs, rooting out corruption," Pritzker said in a statement. "The people of Illinois cannot afford to wait."
AOC-BACKED $25 MINIMUM WAGE PLAN SOUNDS GREAT — BUT AT WHAT COST?
Savidge told Fox News Digital that Pritzker and Shapiro's minimum wage proposals "risk giving large corporations a competitive advantage while squeezing out smaller competitors."
Critics question whether higher wage mandates translate into better overall economic outcomes, particularly for workers with little job experience.
Adam Gorcyca, a policy researcher at the Illinois Policy Institute, warned that employers may respond to higher labor costs by reducing hours, limiting hiring or raising prices.

"Mandating higher wages doesn't immediately guarantee workers will take home more money," Gorcyca added. "Employers often respond to these policies by cutting back hours, slowing hiring or raising prices. It can help select workers, while also making it harder for entry-level or younger workers."
Gorcyca also questioned whether Illinois' minimum-wage increases had delivered broader employment gains, pointing to the state's slow pandemic recovery as evidence of its economic struggles.

"In Illinois, Gov. J.B. Pritzker passed a minimum wage hike in 2019, slowly increasing the state’s minimum wage to $15 an hour by 2025," he said. "While he has campaigned that it was the ‘right thing to do,’ the state doesn’t have a stronger labor market for workers. In fact, Illinois was one of the slowest to recover from the pandemic."
Pritzker's office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on Tuesday.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The push is also emerging as a priority for congressional Democrats.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said Monday that the federal minimum wage needs to be raised and that he plans to discuss the issue with members of both chambers of Congress.

"It's a conversation that I look forward to having with not simply the members of the House Democratic caucus, but with the Senate as well, to see what is possible," Jeffries said. "It certainly needs to be increased. It's a disgrace that the minimum wage hasn't been raised in 20 years and is currently $7.25 per hour."

title: Massie's push to impeach Hegseth splits constituents in his own backyard: 'Pure spite'
summary: Northern Kentucky residents offer sharply divided takes on Thomas Massie's push to impeach Pete Hegseth over the Iran war and his true motives.
story: Northern Kentucky voters talk to Fox News Digital and give differing opinions of their firebrand libertarian representative, who was defeated in the Republican primary and will leave office.

KENTON COUNTY, Ky. — Rep. Thomas Massie's push to impeach War Secretary Pete Hegseth over the Iran war drew sharply different reactions from northern Kentucky residents interviewed by Fox News Digital, who offered competing assessments of the outgoing Republican congressman — and whether his latest confrontation with the Trump administration reflects principle or political payback.

Fox News Digital visited Covington, the population center of Massie’s district, along with Newport, Erlanger and other communities across the river from Cincinnati, to ask residents about their outgoing congressman and his efforts to impeach the Pentagon chief.
Richard Hassebrock, a Covington resident who said he has not always agreed with Massie, welcomed the impeachment effort.
"I'm not always a huge fan of Thomas Massie, but on this point I am," Hassebrock told Fox News Digital.
TRUMP DEFENDS PENTAGON CHIEF AS MASSIE TARGETS HIM: 'HEGSETH SHOULD BE PRAISED, NOT IMPEACHED'

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth takes questions from reporters during a news conference at the Pentagon on Nov. 10 in Arlington, Va. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday, alleging he violated the Constitution by waging war in Iran without congressional authorization, among other charges. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Craig Cuskey, who works in the Covington area but lives just outside the bounds of Massie’s district in Louisville, described the impeachment push as "pure spite" and "petty," saying his opinion of the congressman had deteriorated.

The contrasting reactions came after House Republicans voted to refer Massie's impeachment effort against Hegseth to committee, adding another confrontation to the Kentucky Republican's long-running disagreements with President Donald Trump and his party's leadership.
Democrats poised to take the gavel in January, however, signaled they will likely take up Massie’s mantle and seek the Pentagon chief’s impeachment.
Hassebrock said he was disappointed by Massie's electoral defeat and praised the congressman's independence.
"He stands up for himself, he stands up to what he believes in, he's got principles unlike 99% of the other congress people out there," he said.
Rilla, a Fort Wright resident who provided only her first name, offered a more complicated assessment.
"I think he's just trying to get back at Trump," she said, while adding that she had been proud of Massie for standing up to the president and was disappointed by his defeat.
7 REPUBLICANS REBEL AGAINST TRUMP, VOTE WITH DEMS TO REIN IN IRAN WAR POWERS
Rilla said she opposed the Iran war, particularly the prospect of military action without congressional involvement.
"I don't think anyone should just go in and declare war without Congress being a part of it," she said.
Phil Wiseman, an Independence resident, said he doubted the impeachment effort would accomplish much, even as he questioned the administration's military strategy.
"I don't see a definable outcome," Wiseman said. "And if you're going to fight a war, there needs to be a definable outcome."

Wiseman said he identifies as a "RINO" — a term often used derisively by conservatives for "Republican in Name Only" — and voted for an independent instead of supporting Rep.-elect Ed Gallrein, the Trump-endorsed Republican who defeated Massie in Kentucky's primary earlier this year.
He said his family has discussed Hegseth, noting that his father was a 27-year military veteran and his son served in the Marine Corps.
"We all had the same discussion," he said. "Who is advising him? Because this [war] is very ill-thought-out and not well-planned."
Wiseman compared that aspect of the Iran conflict to how the U.S. previously became mired in Afghanistan.
"So I seriously question the military advisors that are giving them this advice, or maybe they gave them contrary advice and it was ignored," he said.
Anthony Tuemler of Covington supported impeachment and accused Hegseth of violating the Constitution through his conduct of the war.
Tuemler's assessment of Massie was similarly mixed. Although he said he was glad the congressman was leaving office, he credited Massie with speaking up when he believed it was necessary.
"I'm glad he's gone," Tuemler said of Massie. "But the only thing I'm distressed about or sorry about is like when it came time to say the right things, Massie was the one who did it."
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Randall Thompson of Newport, dressed in a military uniform for Veterans Day as he walked with his children near Covington's Mainstrasse Village corridor, said he supports the defense secretary and pointed to their shared military experience in the Middle East.
"I support the troops and Pete Hegseth," Thompson said, adding off-camera that he was in the same area of Iraq as the former Fox News host when they were both deployed.
Cuskey also defended Hegseth, saying he had initially been skeptical of his nomination but had grown more impressed with his performance.
"I think for his background, he's done a remarkable job," Cuskey said, arguing that Hegseth was carrying out directives from the commander in chief.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has voiced support for impeaching the Pentagon chief, while other Democrats have signaled plans to revisit his conduct when they take control of Congress in January.

Some lawmakers are also eyeing investigations and potential impeachment proceedings involving other senior Trump administration officials, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and border czar Tom Homan — setting the stage for a broader confrontation between congressional Democrats and the White House.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: Blue wave meets ballot box surprises as voters split on abortion, voter ID and billionaire taxes
summary: Voters in three states approved voter ID measures, while California rejected a billionaire wealth tax and Idaho turned down a proposal to expand abortion rights.
story: Americans from across the country shared their midterm voting decisions with Fox News Digital, driven by everything from President Donald Trump to abortion, immigration enforcement and gun rights. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

While Democrats’ midterm sweep dominated Election Night, voters in several states delivered consequential — and sometimes crosscutting — verdicts on voter ID, abortion access, taxes and English-language laws.
But the down-ballot decisions largely unfolded beneath the shadow of the GOP’s crushing losses, offering a separate look at the policy priorities voters chose to elevate in their states.
Read on to learn more about some of the most significant ballot measure results that will be shaping the lives of thousands of Americans.
New voter ID voting requirements
More than a dozen states are holding ballot measures on Election Day that are related to voting. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)
DEMOCRATS ‘DIVORCED FROM VOTERS’ AS 5 STATES BACK CITIZEN-ONLY VOTING, BOLSTERING GOP PUSH

Voters in Nevada, North Carolina and Ohio all voted to pass voter ID requirements, even as talks among federal lawmakers have stalled on the issue, showcasing that the issue remains a point of public interest.

In North Carolina, the state has required photo ID for in-person voting since 2018. But with the adoption of a constitutional amendment in a 59.6% to 40.3% vote, the Tar Heel State expanded the requirement to all forms of voting.

Similarly, in Ohio, voters passed Issue 3 in a 65.3% to 34.6% vote. Although Ohio already had pre-existing in-person voter-ID laws, Issue 3 codified the requirement in the state’s constitution, making it harder to overturn later.

Finally, in Nevada, Question 7 passed in a 62.1% to 37.8% vote, establishing a constitutional amendment to enact the state’s first voter-ID requirement. It compels voters to show ID when voting in person and, for mail and absentee ballots, asks voters to provide the last four digits of their driver's license or Social Security number.
English is the official language of Idaho
The Idaho state capitol building in Boise, Idaho. (Getty Images)
EVERYTHING TO KNOW ABOUT HOUSE AND SENATE CONTROL, BALLOT MEASURES AND 2026 ELECTION DAY POLL CLOSING

In Idaho, voters approved HJR6 in a 63.1% to 36.8% outcome, a measure that makes English the official language of the state, codifying it for use in public proceedings with a constitutional amendment.
English had already been made Idaho’s official language through statute since 2007.

State Rep. Dale Hawkins, one of the champions behind HJR6, called it reflective of efforts from the Trump administration to make English the official language of the United States through executive order.
"Our current administration signed an executive order doing this for the entire United States so we are just in line with what’s going on," Hawkins said in public remarks.
In an interview with local media, Hawkins also cited a concern that many newcomers to the U.S. had, in his view, overlooked the country’s linguistic identity.

"One of the things that unites us all as a culture, as a country, as a state, is language. And what used to be the desired effect, which was assimilation — learn the language, learn the culture, learn the history — those things have slipped away. And we don’t see assimilation anymore. And I believe that if we have a common language, then our culture will survive," Hawkins told the Idaho Capital Sun.
Voters reject a ‘viability’ right to abortion

Marjorie Dannenfelser, president of the Susan B. Anthony List, speaks as she introduces former U.S. Vice President Mike Pence at the National Press Club on November 30, 2021 in Washington, D.C. (Drew Angerer/Getty Images)
DEM GOV MAURA HEALEY SIGNS SWEEPING MASSACHUSETTS BILL ALLOWING ABORTIONS UP TO BIRTH

Alongside their English language constitutional amendment, voters in Idaho rejected Proposition 1, which would have created a right to abortion up to the point of fetal viability, except in cases of medical emergency.

In the words of the proposition itself, it "would support creating a right to abortion before fetal viability—defined as a fetus’ ability to survive without extraordinary medical measures—and after fetal viability in cases of medical emergency; providing protections against professional discipline and civil and criminal liability for healthcare providers; and codifying a statutory reproductive right to freedom and privacy."
Proposition 1 failed in a 44.0% to 55.9% outcome.
Had it been successful, the measure would have greatly reduced the state’s current limits on abortion except to save the life of a pregnant woman or in cases of rape or incest.

To onlookers like Marjorie Dannenfelser, president of Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, the outcome demonstrates that protecting life in the womb remains a priority and an ongoing contest at the state level.

"We are incredibly grateful for Stop Prop 1 and all who stood up to defend the unborn. This is a hard-fought win and an example to pro-life voters, candidates and elected officials across the country… Voters were not fooled because pro-life leaders spoke up boldly to expose this initiative," Dannenfelser said in a statement.
Socialist-backed 5% tax for billionaires goes up in smoke
California Gov. Gavin Newsom, left, pictured alongside a group of DSA supporters holding a banner, right. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images; Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE

In California, voters rejected the implementation of a 5% billionaire tax that carried the backing of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). The measure, Proposition 40, failed in a 47.5% to 52.4% loss.
The proposition would have applied a 5% tax on assets like businesses, securities, art, collectibles and intellectual property while excluding select pensions, real estate and retirement accounts.
To prevent billionaires from simply leaving the state, Proposition 40 was designed to retroactively apply to billionaires who were residents of California on Jan. 1, 2026.
The DSA framed the measure as a way to distribute wealth and as a kind of scaled-up version of a progressive tax, a tax that scales relative to income.

"We have the money in California to pay for the quality schools and healthcare that we need. It just needs to be transferred from the wrong pockets to the right ones. We can do that by taxing the rich," the slideshow reads.
Notably, Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom opposed Proposition 40, arguing that it would lessen California’s competitiveness relative to other states.
California rejects voter ID
California Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks while campaigning for then-Senate candidate Chris Pappas at Exeter Town Hall on Oct. 17, 2026, in Exeter, N.H. (John Tully/Getty Images)

Alongside Proposition 40, voters in California also rejected Proposition 39 — a proposed constitutional amendment that would have required ID for in-person voting and checks for the state’s voter registration lists.
Like Nevada's Question 7, it also would have asked absentee voters to provide the last four digits of a unique government-issued ID number before securing a mail-in ballot.
The measure failed in a 39.4% to 60.5% vote.
Ahead of Election Day, Gov. Newsom characterized Proposition 39 as an extension of efforts to restrict access to voting rights.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Trump and his MAGA allies tried to rig our elections once, and California voters shut them down with Prop 50. Prop 39 is just their latest attempt to silence us, because they know they can’t win in California in a fair fight. It’s voter suppression, full stop, and Californians will vote it down in November," Newsom said in a statement.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Democrat flips Alaska governor's mansion after Trump-backed GOP infighting
summary: President Trump endorsed Republican Bernadette Wilson for Alaska governor, but bitter GOP infighting and ranked-choice voting complicated the race to succeed Mike Dunleavy.
story: After a midterm rally in Alaska, President Donald Trump told Fox News' Matt Finn "we are looking into" Dan Sullivan, an independent challenger who goes by the same name as the Republican incumbent, Sen. Dan Sullivan.
Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has won Alaska's gubernatorial election, defeating Trump-endorsed Republican Bernadette Wilson and flipping the governor's mansion.
The Associated Press called the race for Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state lawmaker, Friday evening local time. He is the first Democratic governor in Alaska since 1998.
Alaska's gubernatorial election became an unusual contest as Republicans battled among themselves over who should succeed Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who was barred from seeking a third consecutive term.
A BLUE WAVE IN GOVERNORS' MANSIONS COULD HURT FAMILIES MORE THAN A BLUE CONGRESS
Former State Representative Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democrat from Alaska, during the What's Next conference in Denver, Colorado, on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. (Chet Strange/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Wilson, a conservative activist and former political operative, received President Donald Trump's endorsement during a campaign in which multiple Republicans competed for the governor's office.
Trump publicly criticized fellow Republicans Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor, accusing them of dividing conservative voters and potentially jeopardizing the party's hold on the governorship.
Bronson, a former Anchorage mayor, and Taylor, a former Alaska attorney general, remained part of the Republican field, creating a complicated general-election contest.
ALASKAN POLITICAL SCION HOPES TO HOLD ONTO STATE'S SINGLE HOUSE SEAT
Alaska gubernatorial candidate Bernadette Wilson was the only Trump-endorsed candidate in the race, despite being one of three Republican options. (Courtesy: Bernadette Wilson for Governor)
Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state representative from Sitka, emerged as the Democratic contender, seeking to return his party to the governor's mansion after Dunleavy's two terms.
The election unfolded under Alaska's ranked-choice voting system, which allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

If no candidate receives a majority of first-choice votes, the lowest-performing candidate is eliminated and those ballots are redistributed according to voters' next preferences. The process continues until a candidate secures a majority among continuing ballots.
The system has added an unusual dynamic to Alaska politics, allowing multiple candidates from the same party to compete in the general election without a traditional partisan runoff.

Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy speaks at a rally in Wasilla, Alaska, in October 2026. President Trump endorsed GOP gubernatorial candidate Bernadette Wilson at this rally, but Dunleavy did not offer an endorsement for any candidate. (Nathaniel Wilder/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The contest also came as Alaska remained a reliably Republican state in presidential elections, despite occasionally electing Democrats and independents to statewide office.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: Rep Lauren Boebert projected to lose House seat in another Democratic flip
summary: Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., lost her congressional seat to Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher. Boebert, an ally of President Trump, was seeking a fourth term.
story: Incoming House Minority Leader Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, discusses the GOP’s agenda during the post-midterm election lame-duck session, Democrats’ lawfare threats and his priorities as House GOP leader on ‘Hannity.’
GOP firebrand Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., is projected to lose her seat in the House to Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher.
The Associated Press made the call in the razor-thin race Friday afternoon in favor of Laubacher, who maintained her slim 48.7% lead over Boebert’s 47.9% once 99% of the ballots had been counted.
Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., arrives to a Republican caucus meeting at the U.S. Capitol September 13, 2023, in Washington, DC.  (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
GOP SENATOR SAYS REPUBLICANS CAN 'FORGET 2028' AS PARTY LOOKS TO RECLAIM UPPER CHAMBER
Libertarian candidate Douglas Mangeris came in third with a little more than 3% of the vote.
Laubacher is projected to win Colorado’s 4th Congressional District, according to the AP.
Boebert was running for her fourth term in the state. She served her first two terms in Colorado’s third district and was running for her second term in the state’s fourth district.
2026 MIDTERMS: PRIMARIES, KEY RACES AND ELECTION RESULTS
The 39-year-old congresswoman’s loss comes amid a blue wave that saw Democrats flip seats in Republican strongholds like Texas, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.
Democrats now have 256 seats in the House of Representatives to Republicans’ 169. A party needs 218 for a majority.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
Several races nationwide remain uncalled nearly two weeks after Election Day.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.
Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Former CIA Director John Brennan's son arrested after FBI uncovers dozens of alleged child porn images
summary: Kyle Brennan, 40, son of former CIA Director John Brennan, was arrested on a federal child pornography charge after an FBI investigation, prosecutors say.
story: An image shows former CIA Director John Brennan in front of a Central Intelligence Agency crest. (William B. Plowman/NBC/NBC Newswire/NBCUniversal via Getty Images; Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)
The son of former CIA Director John Brennan was arrested for allegedly possessing child pornography, Fox News has learned.
Kyle Brennan, 40, was charged with transportation of child pornography, according to a federal complaint.
The case originated when Adobe CyberTipline reports flagged accounts linked to Brennan for uploading illicit files involving minors.

In April and June 2024, Adobe submitted two reports to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) regarding an account allegedly used to upload suspected child sexual abuse material.
FEDERAL JUDGE BLOCKS BLUE STATE'S LAW PROHIBITING ICE AGENTS FROM WEARING MASKS ON THE JOB

Former CIA Director John Brennan speaks during a forum on election security, "2020 Vision: Intelligence and the U.S. Presidential Election" at the National Press Club in Washington, D.C., Oct. 30, 2019. (Joshua Roberts/Reuters)
The FBI's Washington field office is involved in the investigation.

Around April 7, 2024, three files were uploaded to the Adobe account. A review of the files indicated a file that appeared to be a morphed image combining the face of a minor girl, later identified as a 12-year-old, with the naked body of another minor, federal prosecutors said.
Comcast records showed that the IP address used to upload the files was registered to Kyle Brennan at an address in Warrenton, Virginia, where he lives.
Records from Apple later confirmed that the private relay account was registered to Brennan, authorities said.
DOJ LAUNCHES GRAND JURY PROBE INTO MARXIST MOGUL NEVILLE ROY SINGHAM'S FUNDING OF LEFTIST GROUPS
President Barack Obama in the East Room of the White House in Washington, announcing he was nominating John Brennan, right, as CIA director. (Brooks Kraft LLC/Corbis via Getty Images)
In July 2024, authorities searched Brennan's home and seized his iPhone.
The case was referred to the FBI in October, and a judge signed off on a warrant so investigators could examine the records and seize Brennan's phone.

On Friday, an FBI analysis of the iPhone, which was named "Kyle’s iphone (2)" contained a photograph of Brennan’s Virginia driver’s license and revealed approximately 88 images depicting girls under the age of 18 engaged in sexually explicit conduct, prosecutors said.
One image appeared to be a "fully nude, pubescent minor girl on a locker bench," the complaint states.
