title: Pence leaves door open to 2028 White House run, issues stark warning to GOP after midterm disaster
summary: Mike Pence says he's heard from people across the country about a 2028 presidential bid and warns the GOP must return to conservative principles.
story: Former Vice President Mike Pence, in an exclusive Fox News Digital interview, leaves door open to 2028 White House run and warns GOP must abandon Trump-era policy shifts

EXCLUSIVE - Former Vice President Mike Pence isn't ruling out another run for the White House in 2028, telling Fox News Digital that he has heard from people across the country about a potential presidential bid.

The former vice president also delivered a warning to his party following the GOP's severe setbacks in the 2026 midterm elections, arguing that Republicans risk another defeat unless they abandon departures from the traditional conservative principles that have defined the party for decades.

Pence, who unsuccessfully campaigned for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination, said at an event in September at the Economic Club of Washington that he had "no plans" to run for president or any other elected office in 2028.

But in his first interview since the midterms, Pence appeared to leave the door open to another White House bid, telling Fox News Digital he's received outreach urging him to consider another White House bid.
ONLY ON FOX NEWS: PENCE DELIVERS SCATHING REBUKE TO VANCE, TRUMP
Former Vice President Mike Pence, in a Fox News Digital interview, leaves the door open to another White House run in 2028. (Jose Sarmento Matos/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"We've been hearing from a lot of people around the country. I've been very humbled by that," he said.
Pence didn't reveal any timeline for making a 2028 decision.

Instead, he repeatedly emphasized that "the most important thing is that we win the presidency in 2028. And to do that, I think it will be essential that we focus first on what we're for before we focus on who we're for."
WILL TRUMP AVOID MAKING AN ENDORSEMENT IN THE 2028 GOP NOMINATION RACE?

Pence, who has seen Advancing American Freedom, his policy and advocacy organization, dramatically expand over the past year, highlighted that he's going to "continue to lean into advocating that broad mainstream conservative agenda that's defined the Republican Party for the last 50 years."

"The truth is, if we don't return the Republican Party to the principles of a strong defense, limited government, fiscal responsibility and the right to life, it won't matter who we nominate in 2028."

Pence partially blames the GOP's midterm shellacking, which saw the Democrats win a large House majority and also regain control of the Senate, on what he argues is President Donald Trump's second term retreat from conservative principles and towards a populist agenda.

Pence, who served as Trump's first-term vice president, claimed that "this version of Republicanism was just rejected by the American people" in what he called "the wreckage of the 2026 midterm elections."

Asked for comment, White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Fox News Digital, "Mike Pence’s total and complete lack of courage caused untold damage to our great country. If Republican voters cared what Mike Pence had to say, he wouldn’t have had to drop out of the presidential race months before the Iowa caucuses."
VANCE, CRUZ, DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS 2028 BATTLE BEGINS

Looking ahead, Pence said, "I don't know what the future holds, but all of my energies, all of my focus and my calling now is to be a champion and an advocate for the conservative principles that have defined our party, led us to our greatest successes, and always made America strong and prosperous and free."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Asked if he doesn't run, he could support Vice President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio if either seeks the GOP nomination, Pence answered, "What I'm gonna be looking for is men and women who embrace that historic traditional conservative agenda of the Republican Party."

He argued that "there's a lot of folks on the populist right that suggest that people that that hew to that old Reagan tradition don't know what time it is, and I think the midterm elections have given a verdict on their approach to Republicanism."
Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: Android TV box malware found in 1.3M devices
summary: Google says Videostrong deliberately installed backdoor malware in over 1.3 million Android TV boxes, turning them into a botnet for criminals.
story: Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson warned of worrying privacy clauses in smart devices in a recent episode of the "Beyond Connected" podcast.

You buy a streaming box, plug it into your television and connect it to Wi-Fi. A few minutes later, you're watching your favorite show. Everything seems perfectly normal. But what if that little box has been secretly working for criminals since the day you brought it home?

That's the alarming discovery behind a massive Android TV box malware operation involving more than 1.3 million devices worldwide. According to a Nov. 2 report from Google's Threat Intelligence Group, investigators concluded with high confidence that a device manufacturer deliberately installed hidden software inside streaming hardware. That backdoor gave outsiders remote access without the owners knowing.

And here's what makes this particularly concerning. The malware was built directly into the devices, and some affected products made it through Google's own security certification process. In other words, buyers could do everything right and still end up with compromised hardware.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
CHEAP ANDROID PHONES FOUND WITH MALWARE ALREADY INSTALLED
Researchers discovered preinstalled malware in a MECOOL KM9PRO Max streaming box, allowing criminals to access the device without the owner's knowledge. (MECOOL)
Google uncovers malware hiding inside Android TV boxes

Google says the operation involved Videostrong Technology, a China-based company that manufactures Android-powered devices for different brands. According to investigators, Videostrong developed and installed malicious software called XCPE. Google assesses with high confidence that the company deliberately operated the backdoor for financial gain. The software allowed remote operators to maintain access to devices long after customers purchased them.

According to Google, Videostrong sold access to compromised devices to criminal affiliates, who installed additional malware and turned those products into part of a botnet. That's a network of infected devices controlled remotely without their owners' permission. Researchers identified more than 1.3 million affected devices across the globe. Most were Android TV streaming boxes, although the operation also reached other types of connected hardware. And many people using these products had no idea anything was wrong.
What criminals were doing with infected streaming boxes

While people were watching television, hidden software could be working behind the scenes for someone else. One of the biggest operations involved residential proxy networks. These services allow someone to route their internet activity through another person's home connection. That means a criminal could use your internet address to make suspicious online activity appear to originate from your household.

Think about that for a moment. Someone you've never encountered could be using your internet connection without your permission, while your streaming box continues playing Netflix or YouTube. Google also found malware capable of generating fake advertising activity. Some modules secretly loaded ads or simulated interactions to generate revenue for the operators.

Other capabilities were more invasive. Researchers observed operators capturing screenshots, injecting keystrokes and collecting sensitive account information from compromised devices. They could also install additional software remotely. And because much of this activity happened in the background, users might never see an obvious warning.
5 WORRISOME PRIVACY CLAUSES HIDDEN IN SMART HOME DEVICES
Google's diagram shows how the XCPE backdoor connected infected Android TV boxes to remote servers that could install additional malware and control devices. (Google Threat Intelligence Group)
How the Android TV malware bypassed Google's security

Normally, manufacturers must pass Google's compatibility and security checks before shipping certified Android devices with Google's services. However, Google says Videostrong found a way around those protections. The company allegedly concealed malicious software during testing. The backdoor then loaded additional malicious code after the device's first startup, exploiting a gap in Google's review process.

Even more concerning, the malware could disable Google Play Protect app verification. That's one of Android's built-in defenses against harmful applications. The backdoor also had staying power. Researchers discovered that XCPE was embedded in the device's firmware, the software responsible for basic hardware operations. If someone removed the visible malware package, the system could reinstall it after a reboot. So even a factory reset might leave the underlying infection intact.
Which Android TV boxes are affected?

This is probably the first question people will ask after hearing about this investigation. Unfortunately, Google has not released a complete consumer-friendly list of every infected retail product. However, cybersecurity company Synthient published its own investigation identifying specific hardware and model names connected to the operation.

Researchers purchased and examined a MECOOL KM9PRO Max Android TV streaming box in late 2025. They found the XCPE backdoor preinstalled under the package name com.oemservice. The tested device used firmware version C1.0.8_20250325, according to Synthient's technical documentation. This identifies the specific research sample, although it does not establish that every unit running that version is infected.

Synthient also published model identifiers observed in the wider botnet. These include KM9PRO_MAX, KM9PRO, KM2PLUSDELUXE, KM2PLUS, KM7PLUS, KT1, IPx1, IPx3, Q96MAX and TX3MINI. These identifiers appeared in data associated with the malicious operation. However, researchers explicitly warn that a matching model name alone cannot confirm that an individual device is compromised. You can review Synthient's published device model list at github.com/synthient/public-research/blob/main/2026/11/Videostrong/README.md to compare it with your own hardware.

The investigation also identified infections in Android-powered karaoke machines, digital signage equipment and some telehealth devices. Google says the malware appeared across many models and brands over several years. And that's why checking the exact product you own is so important. The retail brand on the box may differ from the company responsible for manufacturing its hardware or firmware.
Google shuts down the XCPE botnet and bans manufacturer

Google worked with Japan's National Police Agency and several cybersecurity companies to dismantle the XCPE operation. Google took legal action to shut down the domains and servers Videostrong used to control infected devices and install malware. The company also pursued legal action against command-and-control domains associated with more than a dozen additional malware families. According to Google, those additional actions were expected to sever criminal access to at least 10 million other compromised devices. That estimate involves malware networks beyond the 1.3 million devices identified in the XCPE operation.

Google also cut ties with Videostrong and banned the company, along with future subsidiaries and affiliates, from building or selling certified Android devices or supplying software to other certified vendors. The company says it has also strengthened its security review process to better detect similar threats, including improvements to how it verifies the integrity of firmware on certified Android TV devices. That's encouraging news, but there's an important catch. Disrupting the servers used to control malware doesn't automatically remove malicious firmware from devices already sitting in people's homes. For owners of affected hardware, that leaves an important question about whether their devices can ever be trusted again.
Google's investigation uncovered more than 1.3 million compromised devices worldwide, revealing how widely the XCPE malware operation had spread. (Google Threat Intelligence Group)
How to protect yourself from Android TV box malware

Now, before you start unplugging every streaming device in your house, understand that Google has not suggested every Android TV or Google TV product is compromised. However, this investigation offers a good reason to take a closer look at the equipment connected to your home network.

Start by identifying the exact make and model of your streaming device. Look on the underside of the box, its original packaging or the device information screen in Settings. Compare that information with Synthient's list of observed models. If your device matches a listed model, investigate further. Remember, a model match alone does not confirm an infection. If you own the MECOOL KM9PRO Max examined by researchers, take the warning seriously and consider replacing it.

If you have strong reason to suspect your streaming box contains malicious firmware, disconnect it from Wi-Fi or unplug it entirely. Contact the manufacturer or retailer about a verified clean firmware update, replacement or refund. Synthient recommends permanently removing affected devices from use because they may contain additional malware. Don't assume a factory reset will solve the problem. The XCPE backdoor was designed to reinstall itself.

On devices with the Google Play Store, open the Play Store, tap your profile icon and select Settings > About to check the Play Protect certification status. You can also open Play Protect from your profile menu to review security scanning. However, certification alone cannot guarantee a device is free of malware. Some devices associated with this investigation passed Google's certification checks. A certified label offers an additional layer of reassurance, but it cannot guarantee that a device is free of malware.

Be cautious about streaming products promising unlimited premium channels or paid entertainment for a suspiciously low one-time price. The FBI has previously warned about questionable streaming hardware that arrives with malware or installs it during setup. Stick with reputable manufacturers that provide regular security updates. Also, avoid installing streaming applications from unofficial websites or unknown app marketplaces.

Your router connects your streaming equipment to the rest of your home network. Make sure its firmware is current and review the list of connected devices for unfamiliar equipment. If your router supports a separate guest or smart-home network, consider placing streaming boxes and other connected gadgets there. That can help limit their access to your personal computers and other sensitive devices. If you discover an infected device, disconnect it before changing your Wi-Fi password. A password change alone will not remove malware already embedded in the box.

Check your router's activity logs or connected-device information if those features are available. Unexplained bandwidth consumption or unfamiliar network connections can be warning signs, although they do not prove a device has malware. Keep in mind that an infected streaming box may show no obvious symptoms. Normal performance doesn't guarantee that the hardware is secure.

If you've signed into streaming services or a Google account on a device you believe was compromised, change those passwords using a trusted computer or phone. Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) where available. Also, review your account activity for unfamiliar sign-ins. Google observed operators collecting sensitive information from compromised devices, so protecting those accounts is a sensible precaution.

Strong antivirus software can help protect your computers and smartphones from malicious downloads and other threats. Keep those protections enabled, especially when dealing with unfamiliar applications. However, traditional antivirus software on your computer won't remove a backdoor embedded in a streaming box's firmware. If the box itself is compromised, disconnecting and replacing it may be the safest solution. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

Some services offer compensation in exchange for allowing others to use your unused internet connection. Google specifically warns that these arrangements can expose devices and home networks to additional security risks. Before installing any bandwidth-sharing or proxy application, understand exactly who can access your connection and what activity they may conduct through it.
Kurt's key takeaways

What really gets my attention about this investigation is how little someone would have needed to do to become a victim. You could buy a streaming box from an online retailer, connect it to your television and end up with malware that was already installed before you opened the package. And there's another part of this story I find particularly frustrating. Some affected devices made it through Google's certification process. People rely on those certifications because they assume someone has checked the hardware for security problems. In this case, that trust was exploited. Google deserves credit for working with investigators to disrupt the operation. But I think the bigger responsibility starts with manufacturers and the companies selling these products. If a company puts compromised hardware into someone's home, it should be held accountable for fixing the problem. For me, the takeaway is pretty simple. Know what you're connecting to your home network. Stick with brands that have a solid record of security updates. And if researchers confirm that a streaming box contains malicious firmware, I wouldn't keep using it simply because the picture on the television still looks fine.

If a streaming box can pass Google's security checks and still arrive with hidden malware, should manufacturers be required to recall compromised devices and compensate customers? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: Eric Trump-partnered robotics CEO addresses 'Terminator' fears as he sends combat humanoids into war zones
summary: Foundation Future Robotics co-founder Mike LeBlanc says the MK 2 humanoid is ready to engage enemies with machine guns in Ukraine's combat zone.
story: Mike LeBlanc, a former U.S. Marine Corps officer and co-founder of Foundation Future Robotics, told Fox News Digital he believes the majority of warfare will be fought by robots. Foundation deployed its first humanoid robots to Ukraine in February.
Foundation Future Robotics, an Eric Trump-backed robotics company, became the first company to deploy humanoid robots to a combat zone when it sent its Phantom MK 1 robots to Ukraine in February.
Now in talks to ship more MK 1 units to Israel, expanding its war theater footprint, Foundation co-founder Mike LeBlanc sees a near future in which the majority of warfighting is done by robots.

"In the next five to 10 years, I would expect that humanoids, ground vehicles, drones, will be doing most of the major fighting, with humans really only doing special forces, special operations, small surgical operations on the side," LeBlanc, a former Marine Corps officer with three tours of duty in the Middle East, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview.
ZELENSKYY ANNOUNCES 'THE FUTURE IS HERE' AFTER WAR'S FIRST ALL-ROBOT CAPTURE

LeBlanc stressed that, while robotics companies have been creating both warfare drones and household humanoid robots, Foundation is the first company to create humanoid robots specifically for warfare.
Foundation says its Phantom humanoid robot can autonomously navigate uneven terrain, detect people and map its surroundings. (Foundation)

The MK 1 units deployed to Ukraine have a roughly 88-pound carrying capacity, making their best fit in combat situations one of a supplementary role, assisting human soldiers with ordnance, munitions loading, manual labor and other ancillary tasks.
However, LeBlanc explained that the units were simply a "proof of concept" for the broader application of humanoid robots in war, claiming that Foundation is already close to shipping out the MK 2.
"It is 6 feet tall, 185 pounds, as I say, created in my own image," LeBlanc joked.
THIS ROBOT DOG WAS MADE TO SAVE SOLDIERS' LIVES AS US RACES INTO NEW ERA OF AUTONOMOUS WARFARE
"But this thing is ready to engage by making small and medium machine guns, by engaging with enemies.

"The Mark II is going to be the biggest, fastest, strongest humanoid on the market. This robot is already able to pick me up. So, it's a much larger payload than anybody else. That allows us to do heavy industrial work, but it also lets us set up heavy machine guns, bullfrogs, etc.," LeBlanc told Fox News Digital.
ARMY CUTS HELICOPTERS, PUSHES ‘AMAZON FOR WAR’ AS DRONE COMBAT RESHAPES MILITARY
Product specs for the Phantom MK I humanoid robot, which serves as a precursor to Foundation's MK II units (Foundation Future Robotics)
LeBlanc said Ukraine will likely be the first place the MK 2 is deployed, a fitting testing ground, he explained, as the war between Ukraine and Russia is largely being fought by machines already.
"In Ukraine, robots are very much a question of today and today's battlefield," LeBlanc explained.
PENTAGON JUMPS FROM $225M TO $55B ON DRONES AS CHEAP ATTACKS OVERWHELM US DEFENSES
He then marveled at how quickly the combat environment has shifted, contrasting today’s battlefield with those he engaged in during his tours of duty.

"It's amazing how quickly things change. I was in Afghanistan in 2012, and then again in 2013. And, at that time, they would have very small drones that it was almost like you were looking through a toilet paper roll," LeBlanc told Fox News Digital.
PENTAGON CONSOLIDATES DRONE OVERSIGHT AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PUSHES RAPID UNMANNED WARFARE EXPANSION
"It was a very small supplementary tool. Today, when you go to Ukraine, it's actually drones first that are doing the fighting and the humans that are the small supplement," he said.
Russia launched its largest aerial assault on Ukraine since the war started as fires burned in Kyiv May 25, 2025. (Reuters/Gleb Garanich)
Still, LeBlanc did not see a future in which humans would become obsolete in warfare.
"I don't think you'll ever see a battlefield where you have no humans," he said.

"I was just in New York at a fancy restaurant, and, you know, even there, the waiter had to come by because our table was unbalanced, and he put some napkins in the bottom to make sure that it didn't wobble," he said.

"We are a species of workarounds, and that's what has made humans so incredible is that we can adapt to just about any situation. And, so, I think that it's unlikely that we'll see a battlefield without any humans, but we should drastically see that number drop."
DAVID MARCUS: BIG TECH INVENTED AI DOOMSDAY TO DUCK REAL LIFE PROBLEMS
The Foundation founder did address concerns that his robots could incur public fears about a "Terminator" situation.
"I think that anyone who's been far away from the battlefield could get rightfully very concerned that we have Terminator going out and deciding who to kill and who not to kill," he said.
A Foundation humanoid robot loads a mortar in the desert. (Foundation Future Robotics)
But, ultimately, he argued that anybody who has served on the front lines is going to be in favor of taking human beings out of harm's way.

"We had a saying in the Marine Corps: Never send a Marine where you could send a bullet first. And at Foundation, we always say, 'Don't send a Marine where you can send a humanoid first,'" LeBlanc quipped.
An additional fear he’s had to grapple with is the public’s increased trepidation about artificial intelligence, a technology that served as the catalyst for his company’s breakthrough.
"The AI is what really brings humanoids alive," he told Fox News Digital.

"I think there are rightfully a lot of concerns about AI and what AI companies are doing. Because, in some way, it's kind of the digital nuclear program. So you are seeing all of these companies that are kind of able to engage in their own atom bomb, in a way," LeBlanc said.
"And, so, especially companies like ours that are willfully putting these in combat and pressing to get these into combat, certainly should be questioned. But we've been having a lot of oversight."

LeBlanc foresees even further scrutiny when Democrats take control of Congress in January after one prominent Democrat already highlighted Foundation’s relationship with investor and chief strategy officer Eric Trump.

President Donald Trump and his son, Trump Organization Executive Vice President Eric Trump, attend the third day of the 2026 Amgen Irish Open at Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg, County Clare, Ireland. (Brendan Moran/Sportsfile via Getty Images)

"Senator [Elizabeth] Warren has called out our company by name because we have Eric Trump as a strategic advisor. He was an investor first, and now he helps us mostly with planning our real estate, our building of manufacturing facilities, and he just loves to talk about mechanical things," LeBlanc said.
After Foundation secured a $24 million Pentagon contract for research into humanoid robots, Warren criticized the deal in a post on X.

"Eric Trump went on FOX to brag about winning ANOTHER multimillion-dollar contract from the Trump administration. I've been sounding the alarm and pushing for answers. Is the Pentagon just a cash machine for Trump's kids now? This looks like corruption in plain sight," she wrote.
LeBlanc pushed back on the criticism.

"She has called us out on, you know, ‘Do the Trumps think that the Pentagon is their own personal ATM?’ For me, this just kind of goes against all of the facts and experience that I have in it," LeBlanc said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Sen. Warren did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

title: Could AI reduce shipping costs and grocery bills?
summary: EAIGLE says its AI camera technology cuts truck check-ins from 10 minutes to under 30 seconds, potentially reducing fuel waste across supply chains.
story: AI is transforming the multi-trillion dollar consumer packaged goods industry, and giving you more choices at the grocery store.

You walk into the grocery store and notice that some of your favorite products cost more than they used to. Then you order something online and discover the delivery fee has gone up, too. It's frustrating, especially when it feels like you're paying more for the same things. Now, here's something you probably haven't considered. Part of what you pay for everyday products can be tied to delivery trucks sitting in long lines outside warehouses. Those trucks can burn expensive diesel while drivers wait to check in. Meanwhile, transportation companies face higher operating expenses that can eventually find their way into retail prices.

According to the most recent update from the U.S. Energy Information Administration, the national average diesel price was $6.13 per gallon for the week of Nov. 9. That's still a significant expense for businesses moving products across the country. But what if artificial intelligence could help eliminate some of that waste?

A company called EAIGLE says its AI-powered camera technology can reduce truck check-ins at distribution centers from roughly 10 minutes to under 30 seconds. That could save trucking companies money. And if those savings spread across supply chains, they could potentially help reduce some of the cost pressures behind your grocery bill.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
TRUMP'S DIESEL IDEA COULD HAVE UNLEASHED A PROBLEM AMERICANS NEVER SAW COMING
A semi-truck passes through a freight facility where AI-powered gate automation could help reduce delays, fuel waste and shipping costs. (EAIGLE)
Why expensive diesel can make your groceries cost more

You may never fill your car with diesel. However, chances are that much of the food in your kitchen traveled on a diesel-powered truck. Fresh produce often travels hundreds of miles before reaching your neighborhood supermarket. Many grocery products also move through distribution centers, where trucks unload incoming merchandise before stores receive their deliveries. Each trip costs money. When diesel prices rise, transportation companies often add fuel surcharges or increase shipping rates to cover the additional expense.

Those costs can eventually reach the companies selling products to you. In fact, a USDA-supported study examined how diesel prices and truck-driver availability affect food transportation. The researchers found that higher transportation costs generally increased food prices in the scenarios they studied. Potatoes were especially sensitive to changes in transportation expenses, partly because they're often shipped long distances from growing regions to major markets. So, while fuel prices are only one factor behind grocery inflation, they can have a real impact on what shoppers pay. And here's where AI could help.
How AI could reduce shipping costs before trucks leave the warehouse

Think about driving through an E-ZPass lane. Instead of stopping at a toll booth, technology handles the payment while traffic keeps moving. EAIGLE wants to bring a similar experience to warehouse gates. At many distribution centers, truck drivers still go through manual check-ins. Security personnel may need to review shipping documents and verify that the right truck has arrived for the right load.

During busy periods, those checks can create long lines. And when drivers leave their engines running, they're consuming fuel before they've even reached the loading dock. EAIGLE uses artificial intelligence and existing security cameras to automate much of that process. Its Automated Vehicle Access Control system, known as AVAC, identifies arriving vehicles and compares information against facility records. The company says its computer vision technology can capture more than 25 truck and trailer data points in under 30 seconds. That includes license plate numbers and other identifying details that help determine whether a vehicle should enter the property.

When the information matches, an automated gate can allow the driver to proceed. If something looks suspicious, the system can flag the vehicle for additional review. EAIGLE says this reduces a process that typically takes around 10 minutes to less than 30 seconds. Now, saving a few minutes might not sound like much. But consider a major distribution center processing hundreds of trucks every day. Reducing repeated delays could help companies use less fuel and avoid unnecessary operating expenses.
AI-powered gate technology can help process arriving trucks in under 30 seconds, reducing the time drivers spend waiting to enter distribution centers. (EAIGLE)
Could faster shipping mean lower grocery prices?

Here's the question I think is worth asking. If artificial intelligence helps companies spend less money moving products, could some of those savings reach shoppers? Potentially, yes. But there's an important catch. Transportation costs are built into the economics of getting products onto store shelves. If a grocery chain can reduce those expenses, it may have more room to hold prices steady when other costs increase. The same idea applies to online shopping. Shipping companies often include fuel surcharges in their rates, which can affect what retailers charge for delivery.

Reducing wasted fuel could help offset some of that expense. However, there's currently no evidence that EAIGLE's technology has directly lowered grocery prices or delivery fees for shoppers. Retailers could use the savings to offset other expenses or improve their profits. And because freight-yard check-ins account for only a small part of overall transportation costs, any savings would need to add up across many facilities to have a noticeable impact on what families pay. Still, with shipping expenses affecting so many products, it's an area worth watching.
Could AI also help prevent late deliveries and empty shelves?

Price is one concern. But what about finding the products you actually want? We've all gone shopping for something specific, only to discover that the store is out of stock. And there's nothing particularly satisfying about tracking an online order that seems stuck somewhere between a warehouse and your front door. Distribution delays can contribute to those frustrations.

If trucks spend less time waiting at warehouse gates, facilities may be able to process incoming shipments more efficiently. That could help retailers keep merchandise moving through their networks. For example, a grocery distribution center that receives deliveries more smoothly may have an easier time keeping scheduled shipments moving toward individual stores.

However, faster check-ins alone won't guarantee fuller shelves or earlier deliveries. Trucks can still encounter traffic delays, and warehouses may face shortages or loading dock congestion. The potential benefit comes when companies reduce delays throughout the entire shipping process.
DELIVERY DRONES COULD BE WAITING BEFORE YOU EVEN ORDER
Faster truck check-ins could help major shipping companies move merchandise more efficiently, potentially easing some of the transportation costs behind retail prices. (EAIGLE)
EAIGLE says its AI technology could save $726,000 annually

EAIGLE estimates that a facility using its technology could save approximately $726,000 annually through improvements in gate operations and other efficiencies. The company also estimates that a facility processing around 200 trucks daily could eliminate approximately 110,000 pounds of carbon dioxide emissions each year by reducing unnecessary idling. That's roughly 55 U.S. tons of carbon dioxide. These are company-provided estimates, and actual results would depend on the facility and its operations.
AI may also help protect products from cargo theft

There's another expense that can affect the supply chain. Cargo theft. Criminals sometimes pose as legitimate transportation companies to collect shipments they have no authority to take. According to a June 2026 FBI warning, estimated cargo theft losses across the United States and Canada reached nearly $725 million in 2025. That's an enormous amount of stolen merchandise.

EAIGLE says its system can help identify suspicious pickups by comparing truck information with shipping records. If a vehicle arrives with incorrect identification or paperwork, the software can flag the problem. The company claims its technology can reduce theft and fraud exposure by more than 50%. Preventing stolen shipments could help retailers avoid some expensive losses. It may also reduce disruptions when merchandise disappears before reaching its destination.
Walmart and Loblaw are bringing AI into distribution centers

According to EAIGLE, its technology is already being used in major North American distribution facilities, including operations associated with Walmart. Meanwhile, Loblaw Companies Limited, one of Canada's largest grocery and pharmacy retailers, is expanding its relationship with EAIGLE. In a September 2026 announcement, Loblaw confirmed plans to expand the company's AI-powered gate technology across multiple distribution centers. The retailer says early results showed improvements in processing times and data accuracy. The technology also helped improve the experience for truck drivers arriving at its facilities.

Wael Yehia, Loblaw's vice president of national transportation, explained that the company is looking for practical ways to move products more efficiently through its distribution network. That's worth paying attention to because grocery retailers handle enormous volumes of merchandise. Improvements at busy distribution centers could help make those operations more reliable.
Cameras positioned beside a truck trailer can capture identifying details, helping automated systems verify vehicles and flag potential security concerns. (EAIGLE)
What this means to you

Here's why I think this technology is worth following, even if you never visit a freight yard. Every product that reaches your home has a transportation story behind it. Fuel costs affect that journey, and inefficiencies can add expenses long before a retailer puts a price tag on an item. AI systems like EAIGLE's could help transportation companies reduce some of those costs. Faster gate operations may also help retailers keep deliveries on schedule, which could improve product availability. For shoppers, the biggest potential benefit is relief from rising prices. If companies can operate more efficiently, they may be better positioned to absorb transportation costs instead of passing every increase along.
Kurt's key takeaways

I think one of the most interesting things about AI right now is where it's starting to show up. We hear so much about robots taking over jobs in warehouses and trucks that drive themselves. But here's an example of AI tackling something as simple as a long line of trucks waiting to enter a warehouse. And when you start connecting those delays to fuel expenses and the cost of shipping everyday products, you can see why this technology has potential. What I like about EAIGLE's approach is that companies can use cameras they may already have installed. They don't necessarily need a fleet of new trucks or expensive changes to their facilities to start improving operations. For now, I see this as a promising example of AI addressing a real supply chain problem. The next step is proving that the improvements go beyond the warehouse gate. And if those savings eventually help keep grocery prices or delivery fees from climbing even higher, that's something we can all appreciate.
If AI helps Walmart and other major retailers save hundreds of thousands of dollars moving merchandise, should they pass those savings on to shoppers? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: Fox News AI Newsletter: 'Godfather of AI' resigns, testing American juggernaut
summary: The Fox News AI Newsletter covers the latest artificial intelligence technology advancements, including the challenges and opportunities AI presents.
story: After allegations of multiple affairs, one being with a suspected Chinese spy, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned as top of a company pivotal to the AI rollout.
IN TODAY’S NEWSLETTER:
- Nvidia loses its 'Godfather of AI' and now faces first big test without him
- Trump's FAA touts new AI-powered tool helping thousands of passengers avoid flight delays
- Red counties with data center projects swung away from GOP in midterms, analysis finds
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned following a reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy. (Kiyoshi Ota/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
UNCHARTED WATERS: The resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday roiled the company's stock, as investors and analysts assessed the path forward for the AI giant.

SMARTER SKIES: The Trump administration's new AI-supported air traffic management tool has already helped reroute nearly 180 flights carrying approximately 24,000 passengers to avoid congestion, cutting flight times by more than 10 minutes on average, according to new Department of Transportation (DOT) data shared exclusively with Fox News Digital.

ELECTION RIPPLE: A new analysis from a conservative AI safety group found that deep-red counties with large data centers or proposed projects shifted further toward Democrats in last week's midterm elections than comparable counties without such projects.

EYES INSIDE: New York announces the launch of the Center for AI Responsibility and Research at Binghamton University, where researchers will scrutinize registered AI models. Billionaire Bloomberg cofounder Tom Secunda, a major Democratic Party donor, led a group that gave $30 million to launch the center.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul speaks unveiled a plan that will allow researchers to scrutinize existing AI models. (Lev Radin/Pacific Press/LightRocket)

PRICE TAGGED: You probably know that hackers want your passwords, credit card information and other personal details. But what if they could also figure out how much you're worth to them? That's exactly what researchers say a newly discovered malware strain is designed to do. It steals information from your computer, studies your digital life and then uses artificial intelligence to build a detailed profile of you. The goal? Help criminals decide which victims deserve more attention and which stolen accounts could bring in the most money.

TOO MUCH INFORMATION: You post a few photos from a concert on Instagram. The next day, an email arrives that appears to be from the venue, offering you access to exclusive photos from the show. It mentions the artist you saw and even references the night you attended. Sounds legitimate, right? You might be tempted to click without giving it a second thought. But what if that email came from a scammer who used artificial intelligence to study your social media posts?

BIG TECH, BIG BETS: Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, is seeking a valuation of up to $1.02 trillion in a blockbuster initial public offering, falling short of earlier expectations as Wall Street grows increasingly cautious about the enormous costs fueling the AI boom.
Google and Adobe are strengthening their partnership. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
NEXT LEVEL: Adobe and Google are announcing an AI-focused strategic partnership on Tuesday that will deepen the integration of the two companies' products.

HIDDEN AGENDAS: Nvidia’s reported spy scandal is shaking markets and rattling the tech world, raising urgent questions about how close foreign agents can get to America’s most powerful corporate leaders.

NOWHERE TO HIDE: My own niece has told me for years that she and her friends could get around age restrictions on Facebook and Instagram when they were younger. They knew how easy it was to make themselves appear older online. And I suspect plenty of parents have heard similar stories. So when I heard that Meta was expanding its AI technology to identify teens who lie about their age, my first thought was, it's about time.

NEXT CHAPTER: The abrupt resignation of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia Thursday following reports he engaged in multiple extramarital affairs leaves the AI giant facing an uncertain future, and a longtime company executive is stepping in as interim CEO.

OPINION: With Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation on Thursday, an accused Chinese spy has taken out the No. 1 player on America’s AI roster. This is worse than a first-and-goal fumble. It’s a body blow that puts the U.S.-China AI race in flux.

title: Nonprofit offers veterans second career through commercial drone pilot training
summary: After the military, some veterans are left wondering what's next? Nonprofit organization Vets to Drones is helping them take on a new path by becoming certified drone pilots.
story: The nonprofit Vets to Drones helps veterans use their skills to become certified commercial pilots in the drone industry, allowing them to take up a second career after the military.
NEW ORLEANS – Each year more than 200,000 service members leave active duty and return to civilian life, but the transition is not the easiest.
Vets to Drones, a nonprofit that helps veterans gain training and experience in the drone industry, is trying to change that by helping veterans find a second career after leaving the military.
Kickstarted by Marine Corps veteran Chris Lewis after a recent trip to California aiding in wildfire mitigation, Lewis knew what it was like to leave the military and search for a new path forward.
"I ended up right back in the civilian world, searching for answers I guess," Lewis said.
AI FIREFIGHTING DRONES TAKE AIM AT WILDFIRES
Chris Lewis, founder of Vets to Drones, watches a drone he is flying. (Chelsea Torres)

Lewis handled drones for a short time while deployed, but realized there's a bigger future with unmanned aircraft systems. He started Vets to Drones with a fellow Marine who died in 2022, which ultimately pushed him even harder to help other veterans through the organization.
He believes the drone industry is a true fit for military members looking to enter the civilian workforce, adding that many of their field and infantry skills cross over seamlessly.
Vets to Drones has become a pipeline for the drone workforce, while bringing a new sense of purpose and community to veterans.
MARINE REFUSES TO BACK DOWN IN 16-YEAR FIGHT
When Marine veteran Dusty Lopez left the military, he got into disaster recovery and insurance, then started his own business in insurance claims and assessment.

Lopez came into contact with Vets to Drones at an event after clients asked him if he had drones to help with some of the jobs. That meeting led to a partnership with his company, Struction Solutions.
"I still live by the Marine Corps motto: honor, courage, and commitment," Lopez said, adding that the branch helped him shape his career outside the military.
Dusty Lopez shows his drone used for several jobs under his business.  (Chelsea Torres)

Now, Lopez has nearly a dozen drones for different jobs. One hefty drone, typically used by law enforcement or first responders for security over watch, is tethered and can stay in the air for days at a time.
PENTAGON CONSOLIDATES DRONE OVERSIGHT
Veterans across the country train under Vets to Drones, then become FAA Commercial Drone certified, which leads them to jobs in several sectors.

Through the organization, veterans have participated in search and rescue, helped farmers, guided first responders during natural disasters and provided assistance for security operations, according to Lewis.
In the aftermath of Hurricane Ida's landfall in Louisiana, Lewis said they created a 360 view similar to Google Earth, but "from the sky with the drone."
Dusty Lopez, a Marine veteran, wears his FAA commercial drone pilot vest. (Chelsea Torres)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Today, Vets to Drones has nearly 8,000 members with hundreds already licensed as commercial drone pilots.
"It's [an] incredible feeling when I get that phone call [that] says, 'hey, man, thank you. I had no idea this was a thing. And now I'm able to feed my family with this new skill,'" Lewis said.
Chelsea Torres joined Fox News in 2023 as a Multimedia Reporter based in Charlotte.

title: Cop fired over fake Facebook page targeting mom
summary: Natasha Lopez says a Flock camera system helped a Georgia deputy track her family, and after she spoke out, a fake Facebook page targeted her children.
story: A Georgia deputy lost his job over a fake Facebook page targeting a mother he arrested. The woman says the page featured AI images and records involving her children.

You come home with your kids after an afternoon at a trampoline park. A sheriff's deputy is waiting outside. He's investigating your adult son and later demands that everyone leave your house. You ask whether he has a search warrant. Minutes later, you're being arrested while your terrified children watch. That's how Georgia mom Natasha Lopez describes the police encounter that changed her family's life. But what happened afterward took an even more disturbing turn.

In my conversation with Natasha on The CyberGuy Report podcast, she described how a Flock license plate camera system allegedly helped a deputy track someone to her home. After Natasha publicly challenged her arrest, a fake Facebook page began attacking her family. The page allegedly shared sensitive records involving her children and AI-generated images designed to humiliate her.

The deputy who arrested her has since been fired. In a statement provided to CyberGuy, the Cherokee County Sheriff's Office confirmed that its investigation found him responsible for the Facebook page's content. However, the department strongly disputes Natasha's account of the original arrest and how authorities handled her complaints. Now, with a protective order in place and her criminal case still unresolved, Natasha says her family continues to live with the consequences.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
YOUR BUMPER STICKER COULD HELP FLOCK CAMERAS TRACK WHERE YOU GO — NEW BILL AIMS TO STOP IT
Home security footage captures the confrontation between Natasha Lopez and then-Cherokee County Sheriff's Corporal Charles Mills outside her home on August 30, 2025. (Natasha Lopez)
How Flock cameras allegedly led police to Natasha's home

The trouble began on August 30, 2025, when Cherokee County Sheriff's Corporal Charles Mills was investigating Natasha's adult son. Authorities suspected him of fleeing police on a motorcycle during an earlier encounter. According to Natasha, Mills used Flock automated license plate readers to follow the movements of her son's girlfriend as she traveled to Natasha's house. "He was investigating my adult son, who he alleged was speeding on a motorcycle the night before," Natasha told me.

Flock cameras capture passing vehicles and record license plates along with their location and time. Police can search those records to identify where a vehicle appeared. Multiple camera sightings can reveal someone's movements across an area. Natasha believes those camera searches led Mills to her home. When Natasha returned from the trampoline park with her younger children, deputies were already at her home. Natasha questions how Mills connected her son to the motorcycle involved in the alleged incident. She says Mills relied on a Flock camera image captured approximately six hours before the reported encounter and at a different location. She believes that evidence did not establish that her son was the rider.
She asked for a warrant and ended up arrested

Mills had an arrest warrant for Natasha's adult son. However, authorities had not yet obtained a search warrant for Natasha's home. After taking her son into custody, the deputy demanded that everyone leave the house. Natasha wanted to know why he needed to enter. "Do you have a warrant?" she recalled asking. She says she repeatedly requested documentation authorizing a search. Instead, Mills walked past her and entered the house. "And I remember saying, like, my kids and my dogs are in there, like, what are you doing?" Natasha told me.

She followed him inside because her children were there. At the same time, she called 911 because she believed the deputy had entered without proper authorization. Her home surveillance cameras captured the confrontation. Natasha says she never expected an argument over a warrant to end with her being placed in handcuffs. "I felt very helpless, very scared, very scared for my children because they were taking the only parent that they had," she said.

The Cherokee County Sheriff's Office disputes Natasha's characterization of the encounter. In a statement provided to CyberGuy, the department said Mills believed evidence connected to the felony traffic investigation was inside the home. According to the agency, he attempted to conduct a protective sweep to clear individuals from the residence and preserve potential evidence before obtaining a search warrant.

The department maintains that Mills believed his actions were permitted under established Fourth Amendment case law. It also says Natasha interfered with his efforts despite repeated lawful orders. The sheriff's office emphasized that Mills was wearing his full uniform, operating a marked patrol vehicle and had identified himself as a law enforcement officer. After securing the residence, Mills obtained a search warrant from a judge. Natasha was transported to the Cherokee County Adult Detention Center, processed and later released on bond. Authorities charged her with obstruction of a law enforcement officer under Georgia law.

The sheriff's office also told CyberGuy that prosecutors independently reviewed body-camera footage and determined there was probable cause to pursue the case. An additional obstruction charge was subsequently filed. Natasha maintains that she was exercising her rights and trying to protect her children. Her attorneys have challenged the legal basis for the deputy's actions. The court would later address those arguments, but the encounter had already set off another chain of events.
Why Natasha took her story to social media

After leaving jail, Natasha began asking questions about what happened. She told me she had asked supervising deputies to review her home security footage before taking her into custody. She believed the recording would show that the arresting deputy had misrepresented the encounter. "I told them the arresting officer wasn't telling the truth, and they would not," she said, referring to her requests that officials review the footage.

After her release, Natasha says she contacted the sheriff's office and prosecutors. She hoped someone would investigate her complaint. Instead, she felt that authorities had dismissed her concerns. She eventually began sharing her experience publicly through a social media page called Natasha Noble. She wanted people in her community to see what happened and decide for themselves.

The sheriff's office offered a different perspective on the social media activity that followed. In its response to CyberGuy, the department described Natasha's posts as an online campaign targeting Mills, other deputies, elected officials, prosecutors and their families. It also said employees and their families had received hateful messages and death threats from individuals across the country.

The department reported that its phone lines had been inundated with disturbing calls and said the attention surrounding the case had adversely affected employees and their families. Its statement did not establish that Natasha personally made those threats. Meanwhile, Natasha's public criticism of her arrest was followed by another problem.
A fake Facebook page starts attacking Natasha's family

Natasha noticed an anonymous Facebook page while checking reactions to one of her posts. The account was called Not So Noble, a play on the name of her own page. It used her branding and published material criticizing her. At first, she did not know who was behind it. Then the posts became increasingly personal. "It was a like, harassment page that somebody had made, that they were attacking me and my children on," she told me.

Natasha says the page accused her children of criminal behavior and published personal information about them. Some posts allegedly included unredacted school and incident reports involving minors. That frightened her because she could not understand how the person behind the page was obtaining those records.

She also noticed people connected to local law enforcement interacting with the content. However, she had no proof at that point of who controlled the page. As the posts continued, her concern shifted toward her children's safety. "I felt desperate, like, how, how how do I protect my children, you know?" she said. Natasha told me she filed a complaint with the sheriff's department because she feared for her family's safety. She says she wanted investigators to identify the person behind the page but felt authorities were unwilling to help.
TENNESSEE COPS RAIDED MAN'S HOME AFTER HE CRITICIZED OFFICER FOR SPEEDING: LAWSUIT
Indoor security camera footage shows deputies inside Natasha Lopez's home during the August 2025 encounter that led to her arrest. (Natasha Lopez)
What the sheriff's office says about Natasha's complaint

The Cherokee County Sheriff's Office disputes Natasha's description of how investigators handled her report. In its response to CyberGuy, the department said Natasha filed a complaint concerning Not So Noble in June 2026. According to the agency, she initially suggested that a woman known to her might have created the page and provided screenshots for investigators to review.

The department said detectives did not believe the screenshots established criminal conduct at that time. However, investigators identified reported telephone calls that could potentially violate Georgia's harassing telephone call statute. According to the sheriff's office, detectives asked Natasha to come in for a formal interview and possible additional evidence collection. The department says she did not communicate with investigators for approximately one week and later advised that she was unavailable to meet with the assigned detective.

The agency maintains that the investigation could not move forward without her participation. Natasha disputes how authorities handled her requests for assistance. During our podcast conversation, she described feeling abandoned while the online targeting escalated.
Then came the AI-generated intimate images

The online targeting eventually took an especially disturbing turn. According to Natasha, the Facebook page began posting personal photographs of her and digitally manipulated images designed to make her appear connected to an OnlyFans account. Some photographs were years old. Natasha says she still does not know how the original images were obtained. "I don't know, we still don't know," she told me when I asked where the photographs came from.

The images allegedly included AI-generated material created using her likeness. Natasha says the posts also directed people to folders on Google Drive, where copies of the images and other material could be viewed. She repeatedly reported the content to Facebook and Google. Although some images were removed, she says additional versions continued appearing online. What upset her most was the apparent effort to expose her children to the material. "They wanted, like, my children to see it," Natasha said. For Natasha, the situation became especially frightening because she still did not know who was responsible.

We reached out to Meta, Facebook's parent company, for comment on the page and Natasha's reports of harassment. A Meta representative told CyberGuy that the account appears to have already been removed.
The deputy who arrested her was behind the Facebook page

The biggest revelation came during a September 18, 2026 court hearing. Natasha says her attorney questioned Mills about records he had obtained involving her. Then the attorney asked whether he had created fake social media accounts. Mills acknowledged using fake Facebook profiles to monitor Natasha's posts after she blocked him.

That admission did not immediately establish that he operated Not So Noble. However, prosecutors subsequently disclosed that Mills was the page's creator and owner. When I asked Natasha how she reacted to learning that the arresting officer was connected to the page, she struggled to describe the shock. "Disgust. Anger. Sadness. Fear," she said. "I couldn't believe it." Natasha says she suspected someone connected to law enforcement might be involved because of the records appearing online. But she had never expected the person responsible to be the deputy who arrested her.
Mills and his wife fired as investigation continues

The Cherokee County Sheriff's Office told CyberGuy that prosecutors formally notified the department on September 21, 2026, that Mills was potentially involved in the Not So Noble Facebook page. The following day, September 22, Mills was placed on administrative leave while the department opened an internal investigation. On October 2, the department terminated his employment. The sheriff's office confirmed its investigation determined that Mills was responsible for the page's content and that his actions violated department policy.

In its statement to CyberGuy, the department emphasized, "The personal actions of Charles Aaron Mills do not reflect the values and ethical standards of the Cherokee Sheriff's Office." Meanwhile, Cherokee Judicial Circuit District Attorney Erle Newton confirmed to CyberGuy that his office was assigned to investigate Mills' actions alongside the Georgia Bureau of Investigation. Newton said that the investigation remains ongoing and that no criminal charges had been filed at the time of his response.

CyberGuy has also confirmed that Mills' wife was fired from her position at the Blue Ridge Judicial Circuit District Attorney's Office on September 30, 2026. The office said her termination was based on policy violations but declined to provide further details, citing its recusal from investigations involving social media content about Natasha Lopez. It remains unclear whether her firing was connected to the allegations involving her husband.

Despite those developments, important questions remain. The department's findings establish Corporal Mills' responsibility for the Facebook page's content, but they do not explain how sensitive records involving Natasha's children were obtained or who generated each allegedly manipulated image. Natasha also questioned whether other local government employees knew about the page. It's still unclear whether anyone else knew about it or helped Corporal Mills.
We reached out to Mills' attorney for comment on the allegations and the sheriff's office's findings, but did not hear back before our deadline.
Natasha wins a protective order, but her fight continues

The deputy's termination did not bring Natasha the closure she wanted. She sought legal protection from Mills after identifying him as the person behind the Facebook page. On October 20, 2026, a Cherokee County Superior Court granted her a 12-month stalking protective order against the former deputy.

Natasha told me the process had been extremely expensive. She estimated that one day of legal proceedings connected to obtaining protection cost her about $7,000. That financial burden added another source of frustration to an experience that had already taken an enormous emotional toll. During our conversation, she repeatedly questioned when the ordeal would finally end. "At what point do they stop, you know?" she asked.
Judge upholds the legal basis for the home search

Meanwhile, Natasha's original obstruction case remains unresolved. In an October 2026 ruling, a Cherokee County judge declined to dismiss the charges stemming from her August 2025 arrest. According to the sheriff's office, the court determined that the protective sweep and subsequent search of Natasha's residence were lawful and consistent with the Fourth Amendment.

The judge found that Mills had probable cause to enter the home and that it was reasonable for him to believe urgent circumstances justified securing the property before obtaining a search warrant. The ruling allows the obstruction prosecution to continue. Natasha maintains that her arrest was unjustified. Her attorneys have challenged the deputy's actions throughout the proceedings.
FLOCK SAFETY CAMERAS NEED CONSTITUTIONAL GUARDRAILS BEFORE FURTHER DEPLOYMENT, TENNESSEE MAYOR ARGUES

Former Cherokee County Sheriff's Corporal Charles Mills testifies in court during a hearing in Natasha Lopez's case, where questions about fake Facebook accounts led to new revelations. (Cherokee County State Court)
What happened to Natasha's children?

The original investigation also led to the arrest of Natasha's adult son, Joseph Christopher Helms. Natasha says Mills arrested him outside her home shortly before taking her into custody. She maintains that her son was wrongly identified as the motorcyclist suspected of fleeing police and says he continues to deny the allegation.

Cherokee County court records show he was indicted on November 10, 2025, under case number 25CR1207. District Attorney Erle Newton told CyberGuy that the Blue Ridge Judicial Circuit District Attorney's Office recused itself from Helms' case. Newton said the Prosecuting Attorneys' Council informed him that the case had been assigned to the Paulding Judicial Circuit District Attorney's Office.

Paulding Judicial Circuit District Attorney Robert S. Lane subsequently confirmed to CyberGuy that his office has been appointed to handle the case. Helms faces two counts of fleeing or attempting to elude a police officer. Lane said the case remains pending and no trial or hearing had been scheduled at the time of his response. Helms has not been convicted of those charges.

But what stayed with me most from our conversation was what Natasha shared about her youngest son. He was 9 when deputies entered their home and arrested his mother. She says he has needed therapy since the encounter and still fears police will take her away again. "You know, we go somewhere and he'll ask me like, mom, are they going to take you?" she told me.

Natasha says her son was hyperventilating after officers took her away. "Nobody even asked him if he was okay," she recalled. Meanwhile, she says some of the online posts targeted her teenage son and damaged his personal relationships. For this family, the consequences extend far beyond the courtroom.
Why Natasha wants Flock cameras removed

The Flock camera system remains central to Natasha's concerns about the case. She believes access to vehicle location records helped Mills follow her son's girlfriend, who Natasha says was not suspected of a crime. She also questions whether existing department policies provide enough oversight to prevent officers from abusing the system.

When I asked Natasha how the experience changed her opinion of Flock cameras, she told me, "We want them gone because policies aren't enough." She believes state lawmakers need to establish stronger restrictions on how police use license plate reader data.

Flock cameras can provide valuable leads in criminal investigations. However, officers may have access to large amounts of vehicle movement information. Flock Safety says its systems include search logs and auditing tools to help departments monitor access. Still, those safeguards cannot prevent every potential misuse.

The Cherokee County Sheriff's Office did not specifically address Mills' use of Flock cameras or whether investigators identified any violations involving the technology. We previously covered a Flock camera hit that helped send the wrong woman to jail. Prosecutors eventually dropped the charges in that case. Both cases raise questions about how police use license plate surveillance and who holds them accountable.
Natasha says she would speak up all over again

Toward the end of our conversation, I asked Natasha a question that had been on my mind. Knowing everything she has endured, would she have stayed quiet if she could go back and do it again? "No, it wouldn't be me," she said. Natasha told me she has never been someone who stays silent when she believes something wrong has happened. "I believe in accountability. Right is right and wrong is wrong," she said.

When I asked what justice would look like for her, she had a specific answer. "Accountability. I want Charles Mills to be charged. I want him to lose his post certification so he can not be law enforcement officer and harm somebody else like this again." Post certification refers to the professional credentials required for law enforcement officers in Georgia. Losing that certification could prevent Mills from serving as an officer in the state.

Natasha also wants investigators to examine whether anyone else played a role in the harassment or the release of personal records. Whether those demands lead to additional consequences remains to be seen. But Natasha says she has no intention of stopping her efforts.
What you can do if someone targets you online

Natasha's experience also highlights how difficult online harassment can become when someone uses fake accounts and manipulated images. If something similar happens to you, preserving the evidence early can make a difference.

Save evidence before reporting posts: Take screenshots showing the account name and content. Keep copies of the URLs and record when the material appeared.Report impersonation accounts: Facebook and other platforms provide ways to report fake profiles, impersonation and harassment.Request removal of intimate images: Google allows people to report nonconsensual explicit imagery, including AI-generated images using their likeness. In Google Images, open the image, select the three-dot menu, choose Remove result and select It shows a sexual image of me. You can also use Google's image removal instructions.Review your family's privacy settings: Limit public access to photographs, locations and personal details, particularly those involving children.Seek legal guidance when harassment escalates: If someone publishes private records or threatens your family, an attorney can help explain your legal options.
Save evidence before reporting posts: Take screenshots showing the account name and content. Keep copies of the URLs and record when the material appeared.
Report impersonation accounts: Facebook and other platforms provide ways to report fake profiles, impersonation and harassment.

Request removal of intimate images: Google allows people to report nonconsensual explicit imagery, including AI-generated images using their likeness. In Google Images, open the image, select the three-dot menu, choose Remove result and select It shows a sexual image of me. You can also use Google's image removal instructions.
Review your family's privacy settings: Limit public access to photographs, locations and personal details, particularly those involving children.
Seek legal guidance when harassment escalates: If someone publishes private records or threatens your family, an attorney can help explain your legal options.

Keep in mind that removing something from Google Search does not necessarily delete the original material from the website hosting it. For additional guidance, see our article on protecting your family from deepfakes and online abuse.
Kurt's key takeaways

I understand why police use Flock cameras. If someone steals my car, I'd want investigators to have technology that could help find it. But who's making sure officers use these systems responsibly? What stayed with me most from Natasha's story was hearing that her youngest son still worries police might take his mother away again. That's heartbreaking. I appreciate the Cherokee County Sheriff's Office responding to our questions. A judge upheld the legal basis for entering Natasha's home, while the department confirmed Mills violated its policies through his involvement with the fake Facebook page. Mills was fired, and Natasha secured a protective order, but her criminal case continues. I hope the remaining questions get answered, especially how this was allowed to happen. title: 5 myths about data broker opt-outs that expose retirees
summary: Data broker opt-outs may not keep your personal information private for long. Five common myths leave retirees especially vulnerable to scams.
story: Artificial intelligence is rapidly accelerating elder fraud schemes across the U.S., targeting older Americans who hold a significant share of household wealth. ScamSkeptic founder Matt Sanner joins 'America's Newsroom' to highlight how fraudsters utilize AI to mimic voices and create deepfakes. Sanner provides key strategies for families to identify these scams and protect their vulnerable loved ones.

Have you already tried removing your personal information from data broker sites? If so, you might have Googled your name, disliked what you saw and spent an afternoon filling out opt-out forms on sites like Spokeo, Whitepages and BeenVerified. That took real effort, and it wasn't wasted. Unfortunately, completing a few data broker opt-outs doesn't necessarily mean your information will stay private.

It comes down to how data brokers operate. Their practices can be confusing, and some common misconceptions leave people exposed without realizing it. For retirees, the stakes can be especially high. Decades of public records, property ownership history and family connections can give scammers plenty of information to work with.

I've spent years covering how scammers operate. And here's something I've noticed. Sometimes, people take reasonable steps to protect themselves, then assume the problem has been solved. That's where trouble can begin. Let's clear up five myths about data broker opt-outs that could put your privacy and financial security at risk.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

WHY CAREFUL PEOPLE STILL END UP ON DATA BROKER SITES
Even after removing your personal information from data broker websites, your name, address and family details could still be exposed online. (Getty)
Myth 1: "I already opted out, so my data is gone"

This may be the most dangerous misconception, especially for retirees who've already taken steps to protect their privacy. Here's the reality. Hundreds of data brokers operate in the United States. When you submit an opt-out request to Spokeo, you've addressed your information on that particular service. What about everyone else? Other data brokers may still have your name, home address, phone number and information about your relatives. Some also compile estimates about your finances and property. And even the site you opted out of could eventually list your information again.

According to the Federal Trade Commission, information can reappear on people-search websites when the underlying public records change. Those records may include property filings and other government documents that remain publicly accessible. That's why one round of data broker opt-outs may only provide temporary relief.
Myth 2: "My family's personal information doesn't affect me"

This one concerns me because it involves the people closest to us. Data broker profiles frequently include information about relatives and household members. That means your information could still appear in someone else's listing even after you've removed your own profile. Let's say your daughter completes several opt-outs. Her personal listing disappears from those sites.

However, your profile could still identify her as a relative and reveal details about where she lives. Now consider what happens when a scammer uses that information to research your family. Your phone rings. "Grandpa, it's me. I'm in the hospital. Please don't tell Mom. She'll worry. Can you wire me $1,200?" The caller knows your granddaughter's name and how you're related. Those details can make the emergency sound believable. And with AI voice cloning, criminals may even imitate a loved one's voice if they have access to a suitable audio sample. This type of fraud is commonly called the grandparent scam. The consequences can be devastating.

According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, people 60 and older filed more than 201,000 complaints involving over $7.7 billion in reported losses. The average reported loss was approximately $38,500 per complaint. Those figures cover internet crime reported by older adults, not grandparent scams alone. Still, they show the financial danger facing this age group. A family code word and a rule to call relatives back using a trusted number can help stop these scams before money changes hands.
Myth 3: "My information isn't interesting enough to target"
I understand why this feels true. You're probably not a celebrity. You may not post much on social media. Perhaps you've lived a relatively private life. Why would a scammer care about you?
Here's what someone searching data broker websites might discover:

Your home address and estimated property valuePrevious addresses going back decadesNames of relatives and possible household connectionsYour approximate age and past employmentInformation suggesting your income range or financial circumstances
Your home address and estimated property value
