WINDOWS MALWARE USES GROK AI TO HELP STAY HIDDEN, RESEARCHERS SAY
VOLTA-AUTODOXER steals sensitive information from Windows computers, then uses artificial intelligence to assess which victims could be most valuable to criminals. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How this new AI malware works

Most information-stealing malware follows a familiar pattern. It gets onto your computer, collects whatever sensitive information it can find and sends that data back to criminals. VOLTA-AUTODOXER takes that process further by using AI to evaluate the information after collecting it. According to Cisco Talos, the Windows malware can steal saved browser passwords, payment card information and login sessions. It also targets cryptocurrency wallets and certain work-related credentials. Once it collects that information, it builds a detailed report about the person using the computer.

That report can include your location, employer and clues about your age. The malware can also collect saved Wi-Fi passwords, screenshots and information from applications such as Microsoft Outlook and Slack. Researchers even found that it attempts to crack cryptocurrency wallet vaults. Then comes the AI component. The malware sends the information to an AI model through a platform called OpenRouter. The model receives instructions to act like an intelligence analyst and determine which stolen information could be the most valuable.

Think about that for a moment. Instead of a criminal manually reviewing hundreds of stolen accounts, AI can help sort through the information and identify potentially profitable targets. And the AI analysis is optional. Even if that part fails or cannot run, the malware can still collect information and send it to the attacker.
Your food delivery history could reveal more than you think

Here's where this gets especially personal. VOLTA-AUTODOXER can search for clues about your home address, employer and financial information. Researchers found that it can also use stolen account access to examine Gmail receipts and food delivery orders. For example, the malware looks for purchase information from services such as Uber Eats and DoorDash. It can also examine receipts from Amazon and other retailers. Those records may help confirm where you live.

And it goes further. Using stolen login sessions, the malware can retrieve order histories directly from Uber Eats and DoorDash. It can also search Gmail for receipts from Grubhub, Walmart and PayPal. That gives criminals another way to connect your online activity to your actual identity.

The information goes well beyond your address. The malware can collect clues about your age, workplace and online accounts. It can even look at Roblox accounts to estimate the value of virtual items. Individually, some of these details might seem harmless. But when AI combines them, criminals could develop a much clearer understanding of your personal and financial life.
AI decides which stolen information could be worth money

The most concerning part of VOLTA-AUTODOXER comes after the information has been collected. The malware asks AI to create a report that ranks the victim's assets according to their potential value. Researchers found that the instructions include a section called "WHAT THEY'RE WORTH." The AI is asked to identify valuable information and assign low, medium or high rankings.

Another section called "THEIR OPSEC" examines the victim's security habits, including password practices. In other words, the malware is designed to help criminals understand what they might gain and how well someone has protected their accounts. Cisco Talos found that the malware uses Anthropic's Claude as its default AI model. If the model refuses the request, the malware can try Moonshot AI's Kimi K2 and Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash.

That fallback system is especially revealing. Whoever developed the malware anticipated that an AI model might refuse to help and built a way to try another model. The malware can also send the resulting assessment to criminals through Telegram. That means an attacker could potentially receive an organized report without having to study all the stolen information personally. There's an important point here. Researchers identified these capabilities by analyzing the malware's code. They have not established that criminals have successfully used these AI-generated rankings to select real-world victims for additional attacks.
AI-POWERED CYBERATTACKS FUEL 'BLACK OCTOBER' FEARS
New AI-powered malware can steal saved passwords and other sensitive information from a computer, then assess how valuable that data could be to hackers. (Felix Zahn/Photothek via Getty Images)
The malware can delete itself after stealing your data

Another concerning capability is VOLTA-AUTODOXER's ability to remove its main executable after completing its work. That could make an infection harder to investigate. However, Cisco Talos found that the malware may leave behind a diagnostic file called volta_debug.txt. That file can contain a record of what the malware collected and whether the AI analysis succeeded. For security investigators, it could provide valuable clues about what happened.

There's another detail worth knowing. The malware uses the infected computer's own internet connection to contact the AI service. Researchers also found that its observed network destinations belong to third-party services rather than infrastructure owned by the attacker. That could make suspicious activity less obvious, although it does not guarantee the malware will escape detection.

Researchers also found evidence suggesting the malware was designed as a customizable product. Its developer appears to have created a system where different criminals could supply their own settings and receive a customized version. Cisco Talos believes this could make AI-powered victim profiling available to criminals who lack advanced technical skills. However, researchers have not confirmed that the malware is being sold.
What researchers still don't know

There are some important unanswered questions. Cisco Talos first observed the analyzed sample on October 11, 2026, but researchers have not established how many computers VOLTA-AUTODOXER has infected or how widely it has spread. They also have not confirmed a specific campaign distributing this malware.

That means there's no evidence in the published findings that this malware is currently infecting large numbers of everyday computer users. Still, its capabilities show how criminals could use AI to get more value from information they already know how to steal. And for now, there's no confirmed method of distribution for VOLTA-AUTODOXER. That's why it's important to focus on protecting your computer against information-stealing malware in general rather than assuming this particular threat arrives through a specific type of message or download.
How to protect yourself from AI-powered malware

You don't need to understand how AI works to reduce your risk. VOLTA-AUTODOXER still needs access to your computer before it can collect sensitive information. That means many of the same precautions that protect against traditional malware can help here, too. Here are some practical steps worth taking.

One of the best ways to protect yourself is to have strong antivirus software running on your devices. Good security software can help detect malicious downloads, suspicious programs and other threats before they steal your information. Keep your protection updated and run regular scans. Look for software that monitors suspicious behavior in addition to scanning for known threats. That's especially helpful when dealing with malware designed to hide its activity or delete itself after an attack. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

VOLTA-AUTODOXER specifically targets credentials stored in web browsers. Consider using a reputable password manager that protects your passwords in an encrypted vault instead. Create a strong, unique password for every important account. That way, one stolen password won't automatically give criminals access to other services. However, a password manager alone cannot guarantee protection if your computer has already been compromised. Some malware can steal active login sessions or capture sensitive information while you're using it.

Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) for your email, financial accounts and other important services. Whenever possible, use passkeys or a hardware security key. However, remember that some information-stealing malware can steal active login sessions. That means 2FA alone may not stop every account takeover. If you suspect an infection, sign out of existing sessions after securing your device.

Install Windows security updates and keep your browser current. Updates can close vulnerabilities that attackers exploit to install malware. Also, avoid downloading software from unfamiliar websites. Be especially cautious about unexpected attachments or messages urging you to install something immediately. And never copy commands into Windows PowerShell, Command Prompt or the Run dialog because a random website tells you to fix a problem. Criminals have used these tactics to trick people into installing other information-stealing malware.
HACKERS HIDE DANGEROUS FAKE AI DOWNLOADS BEHIND GOOGLE ADS
Cisco Talos researchers uncovered malware that can steal passwords, payment information and login sessions before using AI to build a profile of its victim. (Pornyot Palilai via Getty Images)

VOLTA-AUTODOXER shows how seemingly unrelated personal details can help criminals build a profile of you. Consider using a personal data removal service to reduce the information that data brokers publish about you. These services cannot erase information already stolen from your computer. However, they can help reduce the amount of personal information available through public data broker listings. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Because this malware collects financial and identifying information, consider using an identity theft protection service. Such services can monitor for certain signs of misuse and alert you to suspicious activity. You should also review your financial statements and credit reports regularly. If criminals gain access to your information, early detection could help limit the damage. You can also place a free credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. That can help prevent criminals from opening new credit accounts in your name, even if they've stolen personal information. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.

VOLTA-AUTODOXER can also target information connected to your workplace. That includes certain Microsoft account tokens, cloud credentials and Slack workspace details. If you use your computer for work, avoid storing sensitive access keys in unprotected files. Follow your company's security policies and report suspicious activity to your IT department immediately. Cisco Talos also identified a technique that attempts to bypass Chrome's App-Bound Encryption protection. Organizations can reduce that risk by controlling which programs can launch Chrome in headless mode. That is a more technical safeguard your IT or security team can evaluate.
What to do if you think your computer has been infected
If you suspect malware has stolen your information, act quickly.

Disconnect the affected computer from the internet to help stop additional unauthorized activity. Avoid signing into sensitive accounts from that computer until it has been checked.Use a trusted antivirus or security tool to investigate. If you cannot confirm the infection has been removed, consider getting professional help. In some cases, reinstalling Windows from trusted installation media may be the safest recovery option.Change your important passwords from a separate, trusted device, starting with your email and financial accounts. Revoke suspicious login sessions and replace any compromised security tokens or API keys.Contact your employer's IT or security team if your work accounts may have been exposed. Let your bank or credit card company know if you see suspicious transactions or believe your payment information has been stolen.Protect your cryptocurrency holdings. If you store cryptocurrency wallet recovery phrases on your computer, treat them as compromised. Move funds to a new wallet with a freshly generated recovery phrase using a trusted, secure device. For particularly sensitive holdings, Cisco Talos recommends generating the new recovery phrase on an offline device.Preserve potential evidence. Cisco Talos recommends preserving the volta_debug.txt file if investigators find it. That file could help establish what information the malware collected. Avoid deleting potential evidence before a security professional has examined it.
Disconnect the affected computer from the internet to help stop additional unauthorized activity. Avoid signing into sensitive accounts from that computer until it has been checked.

Use a trusted antivirus or security tool to investigate. If you cannot confirm the infection has been removed, consider getting professional help. In some cases, reinstalling Windows from trusted installation media may be the safest recovery option.

Change your important passwords from a separate, trusted device, starting with your email and financial accounts. Revoke suspicious login sessions and replace any compromised security tokens or API keys.

Contact your employer's IT or security team if your work accounts may have been exposed. Let your bank or credit card company know if you see suspicious transactions or believe your payment information has been stolen.

Protect your cryptocurrency holdings. If you store cryptocurrency wallet recovery phrases on your computer, treat them as compromised. Move funds to a new wallet with a freshly generated recovery phrase using a trusted, secure device. For particularly sensitive holdings, Cisco Talos recommends generating the new recovery phrase on an offline device.

Preserve potential evidence. Cisco Talos recommends preserving the volta_debug.txt file if investigators find it. That file could help establish what information the malware collected. Avoid deleting potential evidence before a security professional has examined it.

Most importantly, don't assume you're safe because the suspicious program has disappeared. This malware can delete itself after stealing your information, and the stolen credentials may still be usable by criminals.
Kurt's key takeaways

What concerns me most about VOLTA-AUTODOXER is how much someone could learn about you just by getting into your computer. Think about what's sitting on your device right now. Maybe you've saved a few passwords in your browser. Your email probably contains years of receipts, including orders delivered right to your front door. Now, consider what happens when a criminal feeds all that information into AI and asks one simple question: How much is this person worth? That's what caught my attention about this research. The malware is designed to do the homework for the criminal and help identify which stolen information deserves the most attention. We still don't know how widely VOLTA-AUTODOXER has spread, so there's no reason to assume your computer has been targeted. But I do think this gives us a pretty good idea of where cybercrime could be heading. The less work criminals have to do themselves, the easier it could become for them to target more people. And that's one more reason to take your personal information seriously before someone gets hold of it.

How would you feel knowing that hackers could use AI to put a dollar value on your personal information? And do you think AI companies should do more to prevent criminals from using their technology this way? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: New big rig safety tech could save your life
summary: Daimler Truck's Oregon demos show how a Freightliner Cascadia's automatic emergency braking responds when dummy cars suddenly cross a moving truck's path.
story: Daimler Truck's advanced safety systems use radar and cameras to monitor surrounding vehicles and help prevent dangerous collisions. (Joe Raedle/Newsmakers via Getty Images)

Ever find yourself driving next to a massive 18-wheeler and wondering if the driver can actually see your car? It's a reasonable concern. Big rigs have enormous blind spots, and stopping one takes a lot more time and distance than stopping your car. Now, new big rig safety tech from Daimler Truck could help prevent some of the most dangerous crashes on our roads.

The company behind Freightliner is upgrading its trucks with technology that can recognize potential collisions and automatically hit the brakes. We're talking about situations where another driver suddenly cuts across a truck's path or a pedestrian gets dangerously close during a turn. And demonstrations at Daimler's Oregon proving grounds offer a revealing look at what happens when this technology faces situations that could turn deadly on public roads.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
100 KODIAK DRIVERLESS TRUCKS ARE HEADED FOR PUBLIC ROADS
What happens when a car suddenly cuts in front of a big rig?

At Daimler Truck's testing facility in Oregon, engineers recreated situations that could easily turn deadly on a public road. They used dummy cars mounted on remote-controlled platforms to simulate vehicles suddenly crossing in front of a moving Freightliner Cascadia. In one demonstration, the truck successfully avoided a collision. In another, it clipped the dummy car after braking. That second test may sound like a failure, but consider what could have happened if the truck had continued at full speed. Slowing down before impact can make an enormous difference when a passenger car comes face-to-face with a fully loaded truck.

The demonstrations generally took place at speeds between 40 and 55 mph. Daimler said the truck's trailer carried approximately 30,000 pounds during the tests. That's a lot of weight pushing forward when the brakes suddenly engage. And here's what caught my attention. The technology was designed to recognize these developing dangers and respond even when the driver had little time to react. That's especially important because a few seconds can determine how serious a collision becomes.
How big rig safety tech spots trouble before a crash

The technology comes from Detroit Assurance, Daimler Truck North America's collection of advanced driver assistance systems. At the center is Active Brake Assist 6, also known as ABA6. It uses five radar sensors and a camera to monitor what's happening around the truck. Together, they provide approximately 270 degrees of coverage, including areas alongside a standard 53-foot trailer.

Think of it as another set of electronic eyes helping the driver keep track of nearby traffic. The system can identify certain vehicles that have stopped unexpectedly, including cars sitting at unusual angles after an accident. For example, a truck approaching a crash scene might encounter a disabled vehicle partly blocking the roadway. Active Brake Assist 6 is designed to recognize these situations and warn the driver. If necessary, it can also apply the brakes.

The technology can recognize pedestrians and cyclists in certain scenarios, too. That's particularly useful when a large truck travels through busy areas where people may be difficult to see from the cab. And Daimler is now expanding those capabilities to address another dangerous situation.
WHAT HAPPENS IF THE WAYMO COMPUTER FAILS?
Freightliner’s latest safety systems use radar and cameras to monitor traffic around big rigs and respond when a collision threat develops. (Stock Photos)
New Freightliner safety systems can brake at intersections

Intersections can be especially challenging for truck drivers. They have to maneuver a massive vehicle while watching traffic that may approach from several directions. All it takes is one person making an unexpected move. That's where a new feature called Cross Traffic Assist comes in. The system uses radar to detect vehicles crossing the truck's path at intersections. If it recognizes a potential collision, it can alert the driver with audible and visual warnings. When the danger becomes more serious, it can also apply partial or full braking. Now, think about what that could mean if someone accidentally pulls out in front of an approaching truck. The system may give the driver extra time to respond or help reduce the force of a collision.

Another improvement involves Active Side Guard Assist 2. The enhanced system adds protection when the truck makes a left turn across oncoming traffic. With the left turn signal activated, it can recognize certain approaching vehicles and warn the driver. If necessary, it can also apply the brakes. The new left-turn protection builds on existing safety technology that monitors the passenger-side blind spot during right turns. That system can detect pedestrians and cyclists and apply braking when necessary.

These improvements are scheduled to become standard on Freightliner Cascadias built beginning in 2027, with production planned for January. Active Brake Assist 6 itself is already standard on the fifth-generation Cascadia. According to Daimler Truck North America, the goal is to give professional drivers additional support when visibility or reaction time becomes limited.
What if a truck driver suddenly stops responding?

There's another feature that deserves attention because it addresses a frightening possibility. What happens if someone behind the wheel of a big rig suddenly becomes unresponsive? Freightliner's optional Active Lane Assist 2 can help keep the truck centered in its lane and correct unintended drifting. It can also provide steering assistance during certain challenging driving conditions, such as strong crosswinds.

But the feature I find particularly interesting is called Attentive Driver Protection. When the lane-keeping system is active, Attentive Driver Protection monitors whether the driver continues responding. If the driver fails to respond to escalating warnings, the technology can slow the truck to a stop while helping keep it centered in its lane. It can also activate the hazard lights to warn surrounding traffic.

Consider the potential consequences of a driver becoming unresponsive while operating a massive truck on a busy highway. Having an additional safety system that can help bring the vehicle to a controlled stop could make a significant difference. However, the feature doesn't diagnose medical emergencies or determine why a driver has stopped responding. It reacts to a lack of driver response under specific conditions. And like the other safety systems, it still depends on factors such as road conditions and sensor performance.
HUMANLESS BIG RIG COMPLETES FIRST US FREIGHT RUN
Freightliner’s Attentive Driver Protection can slow a truck to a stop if the driver stops responding to escalating warnings. (Noah Berger, File/AP Photo)
What this means to you

You may never drive a Freightliner, but chances are you share the road with big rigs regularly. And that's why these improvements should interest you. If a truck can recognize a dangerous situation and begin braking before the driver has time to react, the people in nearby vehicles could have a better chance of avoiding serious injuries. Even reducing the speed of an unavoidable collision could make a significant difference.

But don't assume every truck you encounter has these features. Many older trucks won't have the newest technology, and even equipped vehicles have limitations. Sensors can struggle in poor weather or when visibility becomes limited. Automatic braking also cannot guarantee that every collision will be avoided.

So, continue giving big rigs plenty of room. Avoid lingering beside a truck where the driver might have trouble seeing you. And when passing, make sure there's sufficient space before moving back into its lane. Remember that even the smartest technology cannot change the physics of a massive truck traveling at highway speed. The safest approach is to stay alert and avoid putting yourself in a situation where a truck driver has to make a sudden move.
Kurt's key takeaways

Here's what I find encouraging about Daimler's latest safety technology. It recognizes something we all know about driving. People make mistakes. Someone misjudges an intersection or pulls out without realizing how quickly a truck is approaching. Those split-second decisions can have terrible consequences, especially when a massive vehicle has little room to stop. The demonstrations in Oregon showed why this technology has potential. In one scenario, the truck avoided a collision. In another, contact still occurred, but the braking reduced the impact. That second result is an important reminder that a safety system can still provide protection even when it cannot prevent every accident. I also think we're seeing an interesting shift in how truck manufacturers approach safety. There's been plenty of attention on trucks that can drive themselves. Yet here we have technology designed to help professional drivers do their jobs more safely. And when you consider how many trucks share our highways, even modest improvements in collision prevention could have an enormous impact. Of course, controlled demonstrations are one thing. Everyday traffic brings unexpected challenges that are much harder to predict. I'll be interested to see how these systems perform as more equipped trucks reach the road. If the technology can prevent serious crashes, that's something we can all appreciate.

Would you feel safer knowing an 18-wheeler could automatically brake to avoid hitting your car, or would you still be nervous driving alongside a massive truck that relies on software to react? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Facebook recovery scams use fake FBI profiles
summary: Facebook ads promising to recover stolen funds are targeting scam victims again, and Meta confirmed removing flagged accounts after investigation.
story: From voice cloning to fake arrests, cyber expert Morgan Wright breaks down how scammers use high-tech tools to exploit basic human fears.

You've already lost money to a scam. You're frustrated and probably wondering whether you'll ever see that money again. Then, while scrolling through Facebook, an advertisement appears promising to recover your stolen funds. Suddenly, there's a little hope. Maybe someone out there can actually help. Unfortunately, that moment of hope is exactly what scammers are trying to exploit.

One of our loyal CyberGuy followers, Patrick K, recently tipped us off to suspicious fraud recovery advertisements and profiles appearing on Facebook. He shared screenshots of what he was seeing and urged us to warn others.

His tip caught our attention, so we decided to dig deeper and contacted Meta about the suspicious accounts and advertisements. After reviewing the examples we provided, Meta confirmed to CyberGuy that it removed the flagged accounts and ads for violating its impersonation policies. The screenshots Patrick shared are especially concerning. One promotes stolen-asset recovery services. Another uses FBI-related imagery and claims to help people navigate the Internet Crime Complaint Center, better known as IC3. Together, they show how convincing these offers can appear.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

WHY IDENTITY THEFT COMES BACK FOR THE SAME PEOPLE
Scammers are using Facebook pages and advertisements as fronts to exploit previous scam victims. (Gabby Jones/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Facebook recovery ads promise to get your money back

The first screenshot Patrick shared shows a Facebook advertisement displayed under the name Adam Molina. The promotional image features a smiling man in a business suit against a purple background. The graphic bears the name "DARKTRACER" and asks whether you've lost assets or funds to scammers. Below that message, the ad promotes services like recovering stolen assets and retrieving hacked cryptocurrency wallets. At the bottom, there's a Facebook Messenger button inviting people to send a message.

That's what concerns me. Someone who just lost thousands of dollars could see this advertisement and believe they've finally found a solution. After all, it looks like a company offering specialized assistance. And because it appears as a paid Facebook advertisement, some people may assume the advertiser has been thoroughly vetted.
Fake FBI investigator profiles create another trap

The second screenshot Patrick sent us is even more troubling. It shows a Facebook page displaying the title "Director of Fraud Investigations" and the name Grace K. The cover image features the White House, the FBI's J. Edgar Hoover Building and cryptocurrency graphics. It also displays references to IC3 and the U.S. Department of Justice. The page description claims to help fraud victims navigate the IC3 reporting process. It even suggests that people who lost more than $4,000 may qualify for federal review. That claim appears on the page, but we found no support for such a dollar threshold in the FBI's published guidance.

It's a convincing presentation for someone desperately searching for help. The American flags and official-looking graphics create the impression that a federal agency may be involved. But here's what you need to know. The FBI says IC3 has no official social media presence. It never investigates crimes or recovers stolen money through Facebook Messenger or Telegram. That means any Facebook page claiming to represent IC3 should immediately raise suspicion, regardless of how official it looks. Meta's subsequent removal of the flagged accounts and advertisements reinforces those concerns.
Meta removes Facebook recovery scam accounts after CyberGuy inquiry

After CyberGuy shared Patrick's screenshots with Meta, the company investigated and confirmed that it removed the flagged accounts and advertisements for violating its impersonation policies. Meta also provided broader details about its efforts to combat these schemes. According to the company, it removed more than 179 million accounts, Pages and Groups for misrepresenting identity during the first half of 2026. Most were removed before anyone reported them. Since 2025, Meta says it has also removed more than 17.3 million Facebook and Instagram accounts linked to criminal scam centers.

This problem isn't new to Meta. The company previously worked with cybersecurity researchers at Graphika to identify fraudulent websites impersonating the FBI's IC3 complaint center. The scammers promised to help victims recover stolen money, including cryptocurrency. Meta says it blocked the fraudulent websites and removed accounts connected to those operations. However, the examples Patrick discovered show how these impersonation schemes continue to reach Facebook users.
FBI warns about fake IC3 recovery investigators

On July 20, 2026, the FBI issued an updated public warning about scammers impersonating IC3 investigators. According to the agency, criminals create fraudulent social media profiles that appear connected to the FBI. They then approach people who have already reported losing money to online scams. In one documented scheme, a victim realizes they've been defrauded and threatens to report the crime to the FBI. Later, someone pretending to be an FBI agent contacts the victim through Facebook Messenger. The conversation may move to Telegram, where the impersonator provides a link supposedly connected to the victim's IC3 complaint. That link may contain malicious code or collect additional financial information. Either way, the victim faces another potential loss.

The FBI also warns about AI-generated videos impersonating federal officials. Some of these videos direct victims to fraudulent websites designed to resemble the real IC3 complaint center. Once there, visitors may be asked to submit personal information under the impression they're dealing with federal investigators. And this type of impersonation extends well beyond Facebook. In a separate September 17, 2026, warning, the FBI reported nearly 61,000 complaints involving law enforcement or government impersonation scams between January 2025 and July 2026. Reported losses exceeded $1.6 billion. Those figures cover a broad range of government impersonation schemes, not Facebook recovery scams specifically. However, they show how costly impersonating official authorities has become.
SCAMMERS ARE COMING FOR YOUR MONEY. HERE’S THE ONE THING YOU MUST NEVER DO
Scammers increasingly target previous fraud victims with online offers promising to recover stolen money. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why scammers target people who already lost money

There's a particularly cruel element to recovery fraud. The criminals approach people who may already be dealing with serious financial hardship. Some have lost retirement savings, while others have been tricked into sending cryptocurrency to someone they trusted. When an offer arrives promising to recover those funds, it's understandable why someone might want to believe it.

In August 2026, the Federal Trade Commission warned that recovery scammers sometimes purchase lists of people who previously lost money to fraud. They use those details to make their offers appear credible. For example, someone may contact you claiming they've located your stolen funds. They might even know approximately how much you lost. That information can make the person sound legitimate, especially when they claim to represent a government agency or law firm.

Eventually, the supposed recovery agent introduces a fee. They might call it a processing charge or claim the payment will release your recovered funds. But after you pay, the promised refund never arrives. In some cases, the scammer also collects enough personal information to attempt identity theft. How to spot Facebook recovery scams before losing more money

A convincing advertisement or official-looking Facebook profile can fool someone who's searching for answers. Fortunately, there are warning signs you can look for before responding. Here's how to protect yourself.

Anyone claiming they can definitely retrieve stolen cryptocurrency or recover all your lost money deserves close scrutiny. Recovery depends on the circumstances, and no legitimate service can guarantee success. Be especially cautious when someone promises fast results.

The FTC warns that scammers often demand processing fees before supposedly releasing recovered funds. These payments may be described as taxes or administrative charges. However, the FBI says IC3 never charges victims to recover stolen money.

If someone on Facebook claims to work for IC3, don't engage. The FBI says IC3 has no official social media presence. Instead, type IC3.gov directly into your browser to verify information or submit a complaint.

Scammers may begin contacting you through Facebook Messenger before asking to continue on Telegram. The FBI specifically identified this behavior in IC3 impersonation cases. Be cautious when an unexpected contact pressures you to switch platforms.

Never share banking passwords or cryptocurrency wallet recovery phrases with someone advertising recovery services. Also, don't install remote-access software at the request of an unexpected contact. Doing so could give scammers access to your accounts or device.

Search for the company's name alongside terms such as "scam" or "complaint." Look for independently verifiable business information and a legitimate track record. Keep in mind that scammers can create fake testimonials and misleading websites to appear trustworthy.

What to do if you already contacted a recovery scammer

title: Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck production after sales slump
summary: Tesla Cybertruck production is winding down at Gigafactory Texas to make room for Cybercab robotaxi manufacturing, but key questions remain for owners.
story: Elon Musk takes aim at Waymo over animal collisions and touts a Tesla robotaxi update to detect pets at night during a Tesla Owners of Silicon Valley livestream. Credit: Tesla Owners of Silicon Valley

You have to give Tesla credit for one thing. The Cybertruck certainly got people talking. With its sharp angles and stainless steel body, it looked unlike anything else pulling into a supermarket parking lot. Some people loved it. Others couldn't understand why anyone would want one. Either way, you couldn't miss it. Now, the truck that Elon Musk once promoted as the future of pickup trucks appears to be heading toward an early retirement.

On November 6, 2026, Musk announced plans to wind down Tesla Cybertruck production at its Texas factory around the middle of 2027. The reason? Tesla wants to make more Cybercabs, its self-driving taxis. For a vehicle that arrived with enormous expectations, that's quite a turnaround. And if you already own a Cybertruck, you may be wondering what this means for your investment.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
TESLA ROADSTER FLIES, FLIPS AND HITS 60 MPH IN A FLASH
Tesla's Cybertruck made a bold entrance with its stainless steel body and angular design, but disappointing sales are now threatening its future. (Reginald Mathalone/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Why Tesla Cybertruck production is winding down

Musk made the announcement in a post on X, explaining that Tesla plans to use more of its Texas factory for Cybercab production. The move signals a major change in direction for a company that once expected the Cybertruck to become a significant part of its vehicle lineup. However, there's an important detail worth pointing out. Musk specifically discussed winding down production at Gigafactory Texas. Tesla has not confirmed whether it will move Cybertruck manufacturing elsewhere or discontinue the vehicle entirely. Texas is currently the only known Tesla factory equipped to manufacture its specialized stainless steel body components.

Still, the announcement raises an obvious question. Why would Tesla scale back one of its most recognizable vehicles so soon after introducing it? The sales numbers offer a pretty convincing explanation.
We reached out to Tesla for clarification on its Cybertruck production plans and what they mean for current owners, but did not hear back before our publication deadline.
Cybertruck sales never lived up to the hype

When Tesla unveiled the Cybertruck in November 2019, enthusiasm seemed enormous. Musk reported approximately 250,000 reservations within five days. At one point, he suggested demand could support annual sales of 250,000 vehicles. There was plenty of excitement. But those early reservations required relatively small refundable deposits, and many never became actual vehicle purchases. According to Kelley Blue Book estimates, Tesla reportedly sold 38,965 Cybertrucks in the United States during 2024. That number dropped to just 20,237 in 2025, a decline of 48%. Things didn't improve much in 2026. Kelley Blue Book data indicates that Tesla sold 11,586 Cybertrucks during the first nine months of the year, down 28% compared with the same period in 2025.

Those figures tell a very different story from the excitement surrounding the original launch. And then there's the price. Tesla originally promised a single-motor Cybertruck starting at $39,900 when it unveiled the truck in 2019. That model never reached customers at the advertised price. On November 5, 2026, Tesla raised Cybertruck prices again. The Dual-Motor AWD version climbed to $82,490, although Tesla paused new orders for that model. That left the Premium AWD as the least expensive version available to order, starting at $92,490 before additional fees. Of course, the Cybertruck offers impressive technology, including powerful electric motors and the ability to supply electricity to external equipment. But at those prices, buyers have plenty of other vehicles to consider.
ELON MUSK REVEALS PRICE OF TESLA'S CYBERCAB
Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck production in Texas by mid-2027 as Elon Musk shifts the company's focus toward self-driving vehicles. (Getty Images)
Cybertruck recalls added to its problems

Sales were only part of the Cybertruck's difficult journey. The vehicle also developed a reputation for recalls and manufacturing concerns. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, Tesla has issued 11 Cybertruck recalls since customer deliveries began in late 2023. Some involved software problems that Tesla could fix remotely. Others required owners to have their vehicles physically repaired. One of the most concerning recalls came in April 2024, when Tesla recalled 3,878 Cybertrucks because an accelerator pedal pad could come loose. In certain circumstances, the pad could become trapped by interior trim and leave the accelerator pressed down, increasing the risk of a crash. Then, in March 2025, Tesla recalled 46,096 Cybertrucks because a stainless steel exterior trim panel could detach while driving. That created a potential hazard for other motorists.

The problems continued in 2026. An April recall affected 173 Cybertrucks equipped with certain 18-inch steel wheels. Tesla warned that cracks could develop around brake rotor stud holes, potentially allowing a wheel stud to separate from the hub. That could increase the risk of losing vehicle control. Importantly, Tesla reported no known crashes, injuries or fatalities related to that particular defect when it issued the recall. To be fair, these recalls varied significantly in severity and the number of vehicles affected. A recall alone doesn't establish that every Cybertruck has a safety problem. However, repeated headlines about repairs hardly helped a vehicle already struggling to attract buyers. And remember the famous Cybertruck unveiling? During the 2019 demonstration, two windows cracked when Tesla attempted to demonstrate the strength of the glass. That moment went viral before the first customer ever drove one home.
Tesla is betting its future on Cybercab

Tesla is making room for a car you may never actually drive. It's called Cybercab, and Musk believes these two-seat, self-driving taxis could become a huge part of Tesla's future. There's no steering wheel or traditional pedals. You get in, tell it where you want to go and let the technology do the driving. At least, that's the idea.

Tesla began carrying paying Cybercab passengers in Austin, Texas, in September 2026. We've already covered some of the restrictions Tesla has placed on younger passengers. And while the technology sounds promising, there are still some important questions about safety. Federal regulators are examining how Tesla certified that Cybercab meets vehicle safety standards. That review has yet to establish any safety violations, but Tesla still has questions to answer.

What I find especially interesting is how much Musk is willing to bet on this technology. He's scaling back a pickup truck people waited years to buy so Tesla can build more vehicles that drive themselves. That's a pretty big gamble, especially when self-driving technology still has plenty to prove. And I wonder how many people are actually ready to climb into a car with no steering wheel and trust it to get them home safely.
TESLA TO WIND DOWN CYBERTRUCK PRODUCTION AT TEXAS FACTORY NEXT YEAR TO MAKE ROOM FOR CYBERCAB
Tesla is betting on its driverless two-seater, scaling back production of the Cybertruck to increase its output of Cybercabs. (Photo by Jacek Boczarski/Anadolu via Getty Images)
What this means to you

If you already own a Cybertruck, there's no reason to panic or rush out and sell it because of this announcement. Tesla has not announced that existing owners will lose warranty coverage or access to service. Tesla currently lists a basic vehicle warranty of four years or 50,000 miles for new Cybertrucks, whichever comes first. Its battery and drive unit warranty runs eight years or 150,000 miles, subject to the applicable terms. You can review the details on Tesla's official warranty page. However, the long-term availability of replacement parts deserves attention, especially given the truck's specialized body panels. Tesla has not provided a detailed public explanation of how its production plans will affect future parts supplies.

If you're thinking about buying a Cybertruck, consider how long you intend to keep it. Ask Tesla about service support and any outstanding recalls before making a purchase. You can check whether a specific vehicle has an open safety recall by entering its VIN at NHTSA's recall website. Resale value is another consideration. Limited production sometimes makes a vehicle more desirable to collectors. However, weaker demand can push prices in the opposite direction. Nobody can say with certainty where Cybertruck values will go. And if you're shopping for any expensive new vehicle, the Cybertruck offers a useful reminder. Exciting technology can attract attention, but long-term ownership costs deserve just as much consideration.
Kurt's key takeaways

Here's what gets me about the Cybertruck. Tesla spent years building up excitement around this vehicle. People put down deposits, waited for deliveries and ended up paying a lot more than the original advertised price. Now, roughly three years after the first trucks reached customers, Tesla is preparing to move on. I understand why Musk is excited about Cybercab. The idea of getting into a car and having it drive you home is pretty remarkable. But if I owned a Cybertruck, I'd want some reassurance that Tesla will continue supporting it for years to come. These owners spent serious money believing in Tesla's vision. I think they deserve some straight answers about what happens next.

A serial rapist from Mexico who murdered an American woman more than two decades ago and terrorized other women in the United States has finally been brought to justice.

Sharon Van Gilder, 39, was murdered by convicted killer and serial rapist Miguel Urbano-Vazquez, 50. (Pierce County Prosecutor's Office)

title: NYC woman allegedly struck by LGBTQ+ activist after questioning trans youth treatments: 'Never have answers'
summary: LGBTQ+ activist Jay Walker allegedly elbowed a counter-protester outside Mount Sinai Hospital in New York City as she questioned his support for youth transgender procedures.
story: A New York City woman, Christiane Torello, says she was elbowed in the chest by queer activist Jay Walker during a rally outside Mount Sinai Hospital in Manhattan as she was questioning his support for transgender treatment for minors.

A woman says she was assaulted by a prominent LGBTQ+ activist at a recent New York City protest as she was questioning his push for transgender medical procedures for children, according to video of the incident provided by the alleged victim.

Christiane Torello was a counter-protester at the rally outside Mount Sinai Hospital in Manhattan on Nov. 5 when she was allegedly elbowed in the chest by Jay Walker, the president of Gays Against Guns who also served as a 2026 NYC Pride Grand Marshal.

Walker was part of a group rallying against the hospital's decision in September to end transgender treatments for minors to resolve a Department of Justice investigation into youth gender transition procedures.

"The hospital is no longer providing any type of gender-affirming care for minors, including surgeries, puberty blockers and hormones," Torello told Fox News Digital. "There’s always a group of individuals who go to these protests to show their discomfort and displeasure with the hospital stopping these procedures because they want the children to transition. I usually go there in opposition to them. I support the hospital’s decision to stop providing that care. I always go by myself and ask questions."
MAJOR BLUE STATE HOSPITAL PULLS PLUG ON CONTROVERSIAL CHILD TRANSGENDER TREATMENTS AFTER DOJ INTERVENTION
A man identified as Jay Walker was part of a group rallying against Mount Sinai Hospital's decision in September to end transgender treatments for minors. (Erik McGregor/LightRocket via Getty Images)

In the video she captured of the incident, Torello questioned Walker why he wanted to "have penises in the locker room" as he was yelling and walking away from her on a sidewalk. Walker then stopped, wound his elbow up and allegedly struck her in the chest before repeatedly shouting at her to "get away from me."
She said demonstrators often attempt to obstruct her path and shove their signs in her face, but that this incident was more violent than most of the rallies she has been to.

"I'm usually followed around the protest by two or three people. They block me and put signs in my face, which is fine because they’re allowed to do that. But this time, it became particularly violent," Torello said.

"When I asked the organizer of the protest, Jay Walker, what size dongs he’d like in the girls’ locker room, he didn’t have an answer. They never have answers to those questions. They don’t like to talk about it," she continued.
Torello said Walker was shouting slurs at her as he was walking away from the protest and she followed him to question him more about what he was saying.
She then accused Walker of hitting her in the chest with his elbow, adding that she thinks he intended to strike her in the face but had "pretty bad aim."

"As we were walking, he stopped in front of me, wound up his elbow and blasted me in the chest," she said. "He’s about 6'5" and I’m 5'5", so I’m pretty sure he intended to hit me in the face but had pretty bad aim and hit me in the chest."
After the alleged assault, Torello continued following Walker down the street.
UTAH STUDENT CITED AFTER PHYSICAL ALTERCATION WITH COLLEGE REPUBLICAN CAUGHT ON CAMERA
Christiane Torello accused Jay Walker of hitting her in the chest with his elbow as he was leaving the protest. (Erik McGregor/LightRocket via Getty Images)
The video shows both Torello and Walker yelling and cursing at one another as they were walking.

Walker was heard calling her "psychotic," "scumbag," a "garbage person" and a "stalker," while she accused him of being a "woman abuser." At one point, he was allegedly seen lunging at Torello, to which she dared him to "do it again" and said she would post the video on social media.
"I'm so glad I got it on camera," she shouted at Walker.
Torello told Fox News Digital that she reported the incident to the New York City Police Department, but she is not confident any charges will be filed.

"I want to press charges because I feel like New York doesn’t do anything when it comes to a lot of violence," she said. "But this is a different type of violence. I have a First Amendment right to be there and peacefully protest. I wasn’t hitting anybody. Do I ask questions that may be annoying or triggering? Sure. But that’s the extent of what I do. That doesn’t warrant me getting hit, elbowed or punched."
Mount Sinai Hospital in New York City moved to end transgender treatments for minors in September to resolve a Department of Justice investigation. (Bryan Bedder/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"This is actually the second time a man has put his hands on me at a protest," she continued. "The first happened about a month and a half ago. There were two NYPD detectives in front of that other protest who watched me get hit, and they didn’t even talk to me. I asked them if they could direct me somewhere, and they wouldn’t say one word to me. I had to figure it out on my own. I filed a report, and nothing happened to that man either."
It is unclear if police plan to make any arrests in connection with the alleged assault.
The NYPD and Walker's group, Gays Against Guns NY, did not respond to Fox News Digital's multiple requests for comment.
"I just really hope this brings some awareness and puts pressure on the NYPD to do something, because they don’t do anything at all," Torello said.

title: New Orleans boat crash called ‘miracle on the Mississippi’ as everyone is accounted for, officials say
summary: Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry called it "a literal miracle on the Mississippi" after a tanker capsized the American Heritage cruiser in New Orleans.
story: Travelers aboard the American Heritage share their experiences after a tanker struck the docked river cruiser in New Orleans, causing it to capsize and triggering a rescue operation. Credit: Kat Ramirez for Fox News Digital

Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry called it "a literal miracle on the Mississippi" Friday after officials said everyone was accounted for following a tanker collision that capsized a docked New Orleans river cruiser and sent 32 passengers to hospitals.
"This is a miracle," Landry said at a news conference. "The Mississippi River is not some quiet pond, right? I mean, there were challenges out there."
Mayor Helena Moreno said none of the hospitalized passengers had critical injuries. Two Harbor Police officers were also hospitalized and were in good condition, officials said.
CRUISE PASSENGER HAILED AS HERO AFTER JUMPING INTO WATER TO SAVE 84-YEAR-OLD MAN

The Atlantic Asphalt tanker and American Heritage river cruiser after a collision on the Mississippi River in New Orleans Nov. 13, 2026. The cruiser was docked with about 129 passengers, plus crew members, aboard, port officials said. (Facebook/Tarzan Duran)
"We have zero people unaccounted for, which is a miracle," Moreno said, crediting local, state and federal responders who jumped into the water to help.
Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham confirmed the search and rescue operation had ended.
"We got everybody," Landry added.
TEEN BOATER FOUND CLINGING TO CAPSIZED VESSEL AFTER 3 GO MISSING; 2 BODIES RECOVERED
Tugboats surround the Atlantic Asphalt tanker in New Orleans following its collision with the docked American Heritage river cruiser on Nov. 13, 2026. (Kat Ramirez for Fox News Digital)

Officials said the tanker lost control before striking the American Heritage. Passengers were evacuating when the cruiser began taking on water and capsized, leaving some people in the river and others on a portion of the vessel still above water.

Harbor Police responded first, firefighters lowered ladders over the dock and nearby vessels helped pull people from the water. New Orleans Police Superintendent Anne Kirkpatrick said a police drone already airborne for an unrelated theft call was redirected to the crash within moments.
Landry said the incident remains under active investigation. Burnham said investigators were examining an apparent loss of steering, but the exact cause was not yet known.
MOM LOSES GRIP ON DAUGHTER AS PASSENGER FERRY CAPSIZES WITH 20 PEOPLE STILL MISSING
A map shows the site of the tanker collision at the Port of New Orleans. (Fox News)
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) initially announced that it was dispatching a Go Team to investigate the collision, with investigators expected to arrive on Saturday morning.
However, the agency later said that lingering flight disruptions from Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop had forced a change in plans.

"Due to the residual delays from the nationwide ground stop, the NTSB will no longer send a board member and will instead send a team of investigators by ground to the scene of the vessel collision in New Orleans," the agency wrote on X.
11-NIGHT CARIBBEAN CRUISE ABRUPTLY CANCELED AFTER COAST GUARD DETAINS SHIP

The Atlantic Asphalt tanker struck American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage around 12:30 p.m. on the Mississippi River, the Port of New Orleans said in a statement shared with Fox News. Port officials initially reported about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, aboard. Moreno later estimated roughly 180 to 190 people were on the ship.

University Medical Center New Orleans and other LCMC Health hospitals had earlier received an estimated two dozen patients following the incident, LCMC Health said in a statement. Medical teams were evaluating patients and providing care while coordinating with emergency responders. Moreno subsequently announced the updated total of 32 hospitalized passengers.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the Coast Guard was supporting state and local responders near mile marker 96 on the Mississippi River.

"We are throwing every asset we have to help rescue missing passengers," Mullin wrote on X, adding that DHS was coordinating closely with Louisiana officials. "Our prayers are with all those impacted by this terrible tragedy."
TWO DEAD, INCLUDING INFANT, AFTER BOAT CAPSIZES IN NEW YORK HARBOR; 12 RESCUED

American Cruise Lines confirmed that guests and crew were evacuated. In an updated statement, the company thanked the Coast Guard, its crew and local first responders for their rescue efforts and said it was helping everyone aboard find accommodations.

"We are getting everyone who was aboard the ship settled into hotels and making sure they have everything they need," the company said. "We are also in close contact with the U.S. Coast Guard, New Orleans Police, and other agencies, and will continue to coordinate with them."
The United Cajun Navy said on X that it was on standby at the port.
The New Orleans Fire Department and NOLA Ready said in an earlier Facebook update that multiple people had been rescued and search and rescue operations were ongoing at the time of the post.

Acadian Ambulance said in an earlier update on X that it had transported eight patients and had 15 units and two sprint trucks on scene to assist New Orleans EMS and other first responders. The ambulance service said it was prepared to send additional units if needed.

Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department, the U.S. Coast Guard and emergency medical personnel were on scene conducting rescue and response operations.
AT LEAST 40 RESCUED, 2 DEAD AS BOAT CAPSIZES AFTER MACHETE FIGHT NEAR PUERTO RICO

Passengers were brought inside the Port of New Orleans Administration Building for triage and assistance, officials said. Moreno said crews conducted roll calls and checked hospital lists to account for everyone.

New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno, center, stands beside Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry during a news conference about the American Heritage river cruiser’s capsizing on Nov. 13, 2026. (Kat Ramirez/Fox News Digital )

Officials were arranging hotel rooms, transportation, replacement prescriptions and ways for passengers to contact relatives after losing phones, identification and other belongings. The Red Cross and medical partners were helping, Moreno said. She said no children were aboard, and no injuries were reported on the tanker.
The American Heritage had been docked about two hours before the collision to begin letting passengers off.

According to a news release, skies were clear with no precipitation around the time of the collision, with temperatures in the upper 60s and north winds of 8 to 12 mph, gusting to 15 to 17 mph. The release listed the current water temperature at around 66 degrees.

At the news conference, Landry said Moreno called him in Baton Rouge to request resources. He contacted Mullin before President Donald Trump called to offer whatever assistance Louisiana needed. Landry said the state would continue helping until passengers were able to return home.
In a follow-up post on X, Landry credited first responders with saving "countless lives" and reiterated that all passengers had been accounted for.
"Because of the heroic work of our first responders ALL PASSENGERS have been accounted for. This is nothing short of a miracle," he wrote.
Trump also praised the rescue effort in a statement shared by the White House on X.

"Thank you to the United States Coast Guard for doing such an incredible job of rescue, and other work, having to do with the crash of the two ships in Louisiana," Trump said. "Likewise, all of Law Enforcement and First Responders were fantastic."

House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said on X that the NTSB chair called to brief him on the collision. In a post describing rescues as ongoing, before officials announced everyone was accounted for, Johnson said he was monitoring the situation and praying for passengers and crew to be recovered safely.
"So grateful for this update," Johnson wrote in a follow-up post, quoting Landry’s announcement that all passengers had been accounted for and calling the rescue "nothing short of a miracle."
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., also thanked first responders.

"Becky and I are praying for everyone involved in the terrible ship collision in New Orleans," Kennedy wrote on X. "We’re grateful for the brave first responders working to rescue those in danger and praying everyone makes it home safely."
Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., said he was closely monitoring the response.

"I am devastated to hear about the ships crashing near the Port of New Orleans," Carter wrote on X. "I am monitoring the situation closely and praying for the swift rescue of survivors and for all emergency crews responding to the situation."

title: Animal rights activist attacks NYC horse carriage driver with skateboard during tirade, union says
summary: Abigail Holbrook allegedly punched two Central Park horse carriage drivers and struck one with a skateboard after screaming about animal abuse.
story: Abigail Holbrook, 27, is facing charges after police confirmed to Fox News Digital she used her skateboard to assault a horse carriage driver in New York City's Central Park. The Transport Workers Union is condemning the alleged attack.

An angry animal rights activist armed with a skateboard allegedly assaulted two horse-drawn carriage drivers in Central Park on Tuesday after launching an expletive-laden tirade in front of visiting families, union representatives said.
Abigail Holbrook, 27, of Philadelphia, was arrested after screaming at drivers and accusing them of "animal abuse" near a carriage stand, according to police and video of the incident.

"You’re animal abusers! Horses do not do well in New York City. They are very sensitive to light and noise," Holbrook shouted, according to video of the confrontation. "The people that are f------ using these horses are animal abusers. I’m Squid the Kid, bro. Y’all will know my f------ name."
MAMDANI ACCUSED OF BETRAYING NYC WORKERS AS UNION BOSS BLASTS 'ANTI-LABOR' HORSE CARRIAGE BAN
Abigail Holbrook, 27, is facing charges after police say she assaulted horse carriage drivers in NYC's Central Park. (Ali Yildirim)
During the altercation, Holbrook punched two 45-year-old drivers and struck one of them in the head with her skateboard, the Transport Workers Union of America (TWU) told Fox News Digital.
Both victims suffered minor injuries and declined medical treatment at the scene. Holbrook was taken into custody by the New York City Police Department and is charged with two counts of assault.
VIGIL PLANNED FOR 18-YEAR-OLD TOURIST KILLED IN CENTRAL PARK HORSE-DRAWN CARRIAGE INCIDENT
Holbrook allegedly hit the victim with her skateboard during the violent incident. (Ali Yildirim)

"This is outrageous and unacceptable," TWU Local 100 Administrative Vice President Alexander Kemp said in a statement. "We need a more visible police presence for our members at horse-carriage stands in the park to protect against these wackos. This is their place of work and people are coming just to harass and attack them. All workers deserve to be safe at work."
Christina Hansen, a union shop steward who witnessed the assault and alerted police, placed the blame on rhetoric from city leadership and advocacy groups.
MAN KILLED AFTER HORSE-DRAWN CARRIAGE BOLTS AND FLIPS NEAR POPULAR NEW YORK CITY TOURIST DESTINATION

"The problem is that a lot of people, you know, don't know anything about horses, and they get misled by these animal rights groups who liken it to slavery, and say that the horses are being tortured by being forced to drag heavy carriages around as if carriages don't have wheels," Hansen told Fox News Digital.
Hansen noted that the financial livelihoods of carriage drivers depend on whether their horses are well taken care of.

"Let's face it, these organizations ... make money by getting donations and there's no money to be made by telling people that our horses are well taken care of," she said. "I only make money if my horse is well taken care of because I can't go to work if he can't pull the carriage, if he doesn't enjoy his job ... so my monetary interest is that my horse is taken care of. Their monetary interest is that the horses are being abused or exploited or whatever."
The violence erupted amid ongoing legal and political battles surrounding the city's historic carriage industry.
CLASH IN THE CASTLE: MEDIEVAL TIMES DINNER THEATER INSIDERS ALLEGE ANIMAL CRUELTY, SEXUAL HARASSMENT
Last month, the city council voted 40 to 7 to pass Romanch's Law, named in memory of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, who died in June after being thrown from a runaway carriage in Central Park.
The legislation would phase out horse-drawn carriages entirely by June 1, 2028, while directing the city to establish a transition program for more than 150 drivers and industry workers.
In a statement to Fox News Digital, People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) pushed back against the union's accusations.
Horse-drawn carriages offer trips through through Central Park, Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Yuki Iwamura)
"If the horse-drawn carriage trade is suddenly concerned about hostility and violence, it might start by looking in the mirror," the group said.

Horse-drawn carriages have been a staple of Central Park and Fifth Avenue for generations, providing iconic rides for tourists visiting the city.

"Carriage horses have been pulling carriages in Central Park since the day the park opened in December 1858," said Hansen. "They've been living on Manhattan since 1625. The city would not be the city that it is, and Central Park would not be the park that it is, except for horses."

title: Mom who plowed into soccer field and killed 2 will not face charges, DA says

story: The driver whose pickup truck plowed into a youth soccer field and killed two and wounded ten others will not face any charges prosecutors announced. The incident that occurred on Oct. 17.

A driver who was asleep at the wheel when her pickup truck plowed onto a youth soccer field, killing a young boy and a father, will not face criminal charges following an investigation, prosecutors announced.

Last month, the driver, who has not been identified by authorities, drove into players and spectators at the Stryker Sports Complex in Wichita, Kansas. Cole Adrian, 6, and Nicholas Schafer, 35, were both killed and several others were injured in the Oct. 17 incident.

On Thursday, a 28-page report released by Sedgwick County District Attorney Marc Bennett said investigators did not find enough evidence to charge the driver, concluding the crash was the result of "negligence" rather than a criminal act.

title: SEE IT: Door-kicking pranksters target California homes as police warn trend can end badly
summary: Irvine Police Department shared surveillance videos of the door kick challenge, warning the viral prank is vandalism that can lead to criminal charges.
story: Irvine police released video showing people kicking front doors as hard as they can before running away, warning the social media challenge can damage property and lead to dangerous encounters.

A viral social media challenge that sends people running up to strangers' homes and kicking their front doors is making the rounds again, prompting California police to warn the stunt can lead to more than property damage.

The Irvine Police Department released surveillance videos on social media showing people taking part in the "Door Kick Challenge," which involves kicking someone's front door as hard as possible, recording it and running away before anyone answers.
"This isn't a prank. It's vandalism, and it can end badly," the department said.
TWO TEENS ARRESTED AFTER CARRYING WHAT LOOKED LIKE RIFLES TO DELAWARE HOMES IN LATE-NIGHT PRANK: POLICE

The videos show groups approaching homes before running away. In one clip, a group of boys gathers outside a front door as one repeatedly knocks. As they run away, one of the boys turns and kicks the door.
A group approaches the front door of an Irvine, California, home in surveillance video released by police as authorities warn about the "Door Kick Challenge." (Credit: Irvine Police Department)
The department warned that the challenge could leave behind damaged property and frightened homeowners while creating the risk of a dangerous confrontation.
COPS FLUSH HOMECOMING PRANK PLANS AFTER SEIZING 650 TOILET PAPER ROLLS IN ‘OPERATION CLEAN SWEEP’
"A damaged door, a scared homeowner, a dangerous confrontation, criminal charges or someone getting seriously hurt can all be part of the outcome," the department said.

Irvine police have received more than 20 calls related to the Door Kick Challenge since October, including reports from residents whose homes were targeted and witnesses who saw it happen, Officer Ziggy Azarcon told Fox News Digital.
Seven incidents have resulted in vandalism reports, and the department's Youth Services Unit is investigating them.
"We have seen an increase in this last month, even though this has been an ongoing trend for the last couple of years," Azarcon said.
Police are urging parents to talk to their children about the dangers of taking part.

A person is captured on a doorbell camera during a previous "ding-dong ditch" incident, a similar door-knocking prank to the "Door Kick Challenge" now drawing warnings from California police. (Bradenton Police Department)
"These residents don't know who's on the other side kicking their door," Azarcon said. "It may scare them and cause them to take action, and the last thing we want is to see someone get hurt."
The warning comes less than a week after a similar door-knocking prank ended in gunfire in Boise, Idaho.

A group of boys had been playing "ding-dong ditch" at a home Nov. 7 when they returned to the property and the resident chased them and opened fire, Boise police said. A 15-year-old boy was struck and suffered injuries initially considered serious or critical, though they were not believed to be life-threatening.

title: New York City building collapse probe raises questions about neighboring property owner’s violation history
summary: N Tech Design of America defied a New York City stop-work order months before the deadly Brooklyn building collapse that killed eight people.
story: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said at an on-site news conference Thursday that an investigation is underway after a three-story building collapse on Flatbush Avenue left eight people dead. The Department of Buildings is launching sweeps of related construction sites,

The owner of a property next to the site of Wednesday’s deadly building collapse in New York City is facing scrutiny over past construction violations, including a contractor’s decision to defy a city stop-work order in March, according to public records.

Wednesday afternoon's collapse of a three-story building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. in Brooklyn resulted in the deaths of at least eight people and triggered a massive emergency response. The building collapse has raised questions about construction activity next door, where city records show prior violations and a stop-work order that was issued months beforehand.
A stop-work order was issued at the adjacent property, 2621 Bedford Ave., in March by New York City's Department of Buildings, according to public records obtained by Fox News Digital.

The agency determined that the contractors, N Tech Design of America, had failed to install proper safety precautions, which included netting and sheds, Department of Buildings spokesperson Andrew Rudansky told The Gothamist.
NYC BUILDING COLLAPSE: EIGHT BODIES RECOVERED AS FIRST RESPONDERS SEARCH FOR SURVIVORS
First responders work the scene after a building collapsed in the Brooklyn borough of New York, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Ryan Murphy)
One month later, an inspector with the Department of Buildings found that the demolition work had proceeded and issued a $10,000 penalty. The order was lifted on May 8.
NYC Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani said during a news conference on Wednesday that excavation work was ongoing at the Bedford Avenue site when the building collapsed.

"The type of work they were conducting was excavation work on that job site. And so, that was what they were working on today. They have a plan approved for a three-story building, but they have current plans looking for a nine-story building, which has not yet been approved for. At this point, all we have at this time is excavation work in that section of the construction site," Tigani said.
Tigani said the construction workers were "digging down."
First responders work the scene after a building collapsed in the Brooklyn borough of New York, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Ryan Murphy)
Agency records show the Bedford Avenue building's owner, Robert Fischman, sent a letter to landlords neighboring the property in June to inform them of the excavation.
A representative for N Tech Design of America told WABC that the company performed the demolition but left the site by late April or early May, months before Wednesday's collapse.
Read the notice of construction:

Engineering plans for the neighboring construction site also addressed the potential for accumulated water to damage nearby foundations. A drainage note states that construction operations accounted for preventing water accumulation, which "could cause damage to nearby building foundations on the subject property or on adjacent properties."
It was not immediately clear whether the precautions outlined in the engineering plans had been implemented or whether any structural concerns were documented before the collapse.

"We have immediately launched a full investigation into how exactly this happened with our law enforcement partners, and we will be looking into all aspects of the building and the neighboring construction site," Tigani said.
First responders tend to a collapsed building in Brooklyn on Nov. 11, 2026. (kena betancur/AFP via Getty Images)

The New York Police Department said the first 911 call on the building collapse at 1321 Flatbush Ave. came in at 4:01 p.m. The property, a three-story mixed-use building, collapsed into an excavation pit at a neighboring construction site. The collapse also tore away a wall of 1323 Flatbush Ave., leaving apartments and stairwells exposed.

Firefighters with the New York City Fire Department reached the scene within a minute after the building collapsed, as there were already some in the area. The building contained a store at street level and apartments above it.
