title: MICHAEL RUIZ: JonBenet Ramsey investigators are retesting evidence with newer technology, police chief says
summary: Boulder investigators are retesting decades-old DNA evidence in the JonBenet Ramsey cold case using advanced technology that didn't exist in 1997.
story: Boulder Police Chief Steve Redfearn and District Attorney Michael Dougherty say old evidence is being retested with state-of-the-art technology as JonBenet Ramsey's unsolved murder nears the 30-year mark.
Investigators in Boulder are retesting decades-old evidence in the murder of JonBenet Ramsey as her family nears 30 years since the unsolved slaying in their former Colorado home.

"Chief [Steve] Redfearn and I are more hopeful now than we have been in the past because of the advances in the investigation and the advances in technology," Boulder County District Attorney Michael Dougherty told reporters in a news briefing this week. "And I say that based on just how DNA has progressed over time."

Her father, John Ramsey, had spent years begging authorities to attempt to solve the case through investigative genetic genealogy, a relatively new technique for ginning up DNA leads that involves combining genetic testing results with genealogy research to identify potential persons of interest. IGG itself is rapidly evolving as state-of-the-art DNA testing also improves.
And her brother, John Andrew Ramsey, told Fox News Digital he believes the samples in police possession do contain the DNA of JonBenet's killer.
JONBENET RAMSEY'S FATHER ASKS TRUMP FOR HELP IN DAUGHTER'S UNSOLVED MURDER CASE

JonBenet Patricia Ramsey, 4, lies on a white seamless backdrop wearing white lace gloves during a studio session for a commercial ad and actress portfolio in Boulder, Colo., on May 1, 1994. (ZUMAPRESS.com)

"The testing available in the late 1990s was far less sensitive than today’s, yet it still detected this male DNA in the same spot as her blood," he said. "In 2008, touch DNA testing found the same unknown male’s DNA on both the left and right sides of the waistband of her long johns. It is the killer’s DNA."

A cold case review panel was convened in Boulder as local police, state and federal investigators continue to dig into what happened on Dec. 26, 1996, when JonBenet was found strangled and with head trauma in the basement of her home. Although investigators have pursued a number of potential suspects, persons of interest and theories about how she died over the years, no one has been convicted, and her death remains one of America's most prominent unsolved cases.

"It's no secret," Boulder Police Chief Steve Redfearn told reporters in a sit-down interview earlier this week. "We're also going back, based on that cold case review, and retesting things that were tested 30 years ago with newer technology."
MICHAEL RUIZ: JONBENÉT RAMSEY'S FATHER CHALLENGES DA AFTER REPORT SAYS FAMILY SHOULDN'T HAVE BEEN CLEARED

Boulder Police Chief Steve Redfearn and District Attorney Michael Dougherty speak with reporters at a news briefing on the JonBenet Ramsey case in November 2026. The Colorado 6-year-old's 1996 murder remains unsolved. (City of Boulder)
Redfearn appeared to confirm a recent revelation John Andrew Ramsey, who told Fox News Digital previously that the family had learned this year that new testing had begun in the fall of 2025.

"Maybe something comes of that," Redfearn said. "Not that it was missed, but maybe the technology just improved enough that we look at, hey, this item was tested in '97, we're testing it again, and hey, look, we found something that was missed in '97."
Dougherty gave an example of a recent trial that he said involved the testimony of four different DNA experts because testing had been done on multiple occasions as the technology improved.
Among the benefits of rapidly improving technology is an increasingly successful ability to identify DNA profiles contained in mixed samples, Dougherty added.
"To me, it's quantity, quality, and location of the DNA," he said.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Traditionally, testing a sample left behind by a single donor is straightforward, he explained.

"When it's a single source in DNA, just generally speaking, it's much easier assuming you have enough to test, particularly if it's blood or semen," he said. "But if it's touch, and it's a single source, that's different than if it's touch or saliva, and it is a mixture."

JonBenet Ramsey pictured in an undated portrait. The 6-year-old was found dead in her home on Dec. 26, 1996, in one of America's most high-profile unsolved cases. (Splash News)
When two or more people leave DNA on the same surface, it must first be untangled in a lab.

The process can be destructive to the evidence, especially when there isn't much left, he said, and that complicates things under evidence rules that must be validated and stand up in court.
SEND US A TIP

"We're not gonna do it recklessly, to use Chief Redfearn's word," Dougherty said. "We're also not gonna hesitate. We recognize the clock's ticking. None of us are gonna be here forever. We wanna see this case solved for everyone involved and everyone impacted by it. And we're absolutely committed to doing that."

John Ramsey speaks with Fox News Digital in Las Vegas in April 2022. He is the father of JonBenet Ramsey, the 6-year-old whose murder on Dec. 26, 1996, remains unsolved nearly 30 years later. (Michael Ruiz/Fox News Digital)
John Andrew Ramsey questioned how much of the sample is available for testing by investigators now and whether there's enough to be re-tested by a potential criminal defense team in the future.
"Do we really only have one shot at this?" he asked.
JONBENET RAMSEY CASE: FATHER REMEMBERS 'DADDY'S GIRL' ON WHAT WOULD BE HER 32ND BIRTHDAY

Separately, Redfearn told reporters that if the new DNA testing fails to yield results, investigators have additional previously unreleased evidence they could make public in the hope that someone comes forward.

"There’s still plenty of things that are not out there that we have," he told reporters.
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
While tips continue to come in regularly almost three decades after JonBenet's slaying, investigators are still asking anyone who may have information to come forward.

"There is more than one someone out there that knows something," Redfearn said.

title: Couple accused of killing registered sex offender in pre-planned stabbing in Arizona desert
summary: A couple allegedly planned the stabbing of a registered sex offender in a desert area in Arizona and now face first-degree homicide charges, police say.
story: An Arizona couple faces first-degree homicide charges after police said they planned and carried out the stabbing death of a registered sex offender, then left his body in a remote desert area.
An Arizona couple was arrested after allegedly stabbing a registered sex offender to death in a desert area of the state, according to authorities.

Jacob Middlebrook, 35, and his girlfriend, Layne McIntosh, 36, were initially taken into custody for second-degree homicide in the death of 29-year-old Arron Christopher Warren, Bullhead City Police said on social media.

Police began investigating after a motorist found a dead man on the side of the road in the 3100 block of Silver Creek Road on Saturday. The circumstances surrounding the man’s death appeared suspicious, so detectives were called to the scene to conduct a homicide investigation.
MICHIGAN DECISION FORCES REMOVAL OF DISGRACED SPORTS DOCTOR LARRY NASSAR FROM SEX OFFENDER REGISTRY
Jacob Middlebrook and his girlfriend, Layne McIntosh, are facing homicide charges. (Bullhead City Police)
Detectives later identified the man as Warren, a Bullhead City "transient." Detectives also identified a possible suspect and discovered that the victim’s vehicle was missing.
Hours later, Las Vegas Metro Police assisted Bullhead City investigators and located the victim’s vehicle parked at a casino in Laughlin, Nevada.

Middlebrook and McIntosh were taken into custody by Las Vegas Metro Police and booked into the Clark County Detention Center in Las Vegas, where they will be held until they can be extradited to Mohave County, Arizona.
On Monday, the pair's charges were upgraded to first-degree homicide.
CALIFORNIA SHERIFF FIGHTS PLAN TO HOUSE CONVICTED SEX PREDATOR NEAR GIRL SCOUT CAMP
Investigators determined that the two were also "local transients" who had known the victim for the past few months.
"Detectives discovered that the couple had expressed distaste for registered sex offenders and had planned the homicide in advance," Bullhead City police said.

"The couple reportedly pre-determined the desert location where they intended to leave Warren’s body. They also reportedly measured furniture/beds that could be large enough to cover the victim’s body along the side of the road. Warren was a registered Level 2 sex offender," the post added.
Police in Bullhead City, Arizona, say a couple allegedly stabbed a registered sex offender to death and planned the homicide in advance. (Bullhead City Police)

Bullhead City Police Chief Paul George said the department updates the community when certain registered sex offenders move in or change addresses but that he "will not tolerate anyone using this information as a reason to threaten, intimidate, harass or harm another person."

"When a Level 2 or Level 3 sex offender moves into our area or, more commonly, changes addresses, the Bullhead City Police Department shares that information as a public service to help keep residents informed," he said in a statement. "While required notifications are mailed to residents living within an approximate 1,000 feet radius of an offender’s registered address, we go a step further by sharing these notifications on social media to reach a broader audience. Our goal is to provide information, not create fear or alarm. We believe an informed community is a safer community."

"Our Bureau of Criminal Investigations conducts monthly address verification checks to help ensure registered sex offenders are complying with registration requirements. Our responsibility is to protect our community, keep residents informed and to enforce the law. We take all three of these seriously," George continued.

title: DHS touts highest ICE deportations in history, as Mullin says agency has been ‘unleashed’
summary: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin announced record ICE arrests and deportations in fiscal 2026, with arrests exceeding three Biden fiscal years combined.
story: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin discusses the future of the Trump administration’s immigration policy and the viability of working with Democrats on ‘The Ingraham Angle.’

Immigration officials on Thursday announced a historic milestone, saying arrests and deportations this year reached the highest levels in the agency’s history, with arrests surpassing the combined totals of the Biden administration’s final three years and deportations nearly matching them.
"Fiscal year 2026 saw the highest number of ICE deportations and arrests for any year in ICE’s history," Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Department of Homeland Security (DHS), said.

"The total number of ICE arrests in Fiscal Year 2026 was more than all three full fiscal years under Biden combined, as the patriots of ICE work around the clock to make America safe again. Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, ICE has been unleashed to target and remove illegal aliens so that we can save American lives."
Officials made more than 491,000 arrests, including nearly 475,000 administrative arrests, the highest administrative total in agency history.
MULLIN VOWS ‘ZERO CHANGE’ ON IMMIGRATION AFTER REPUBLICANS SUFFER CRUSHING MIDTERM LOSSES
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin credited Trump’s leadership for record ICE arrests and deportations, saying the agency has been "unleashed." (Cliff Owen)
ICE also carried out 483,200 deportations this fiscal year, surpassing the previous agency record of 442,640 set the year before.
Total arrests exceeded the combined figures for fiscal years 2022, 2023 and 2024 under the Biden administration by nearly 65,000, DHS said.
Meanwhile, deportations this fiscal year nearly matched the combined total for all three full fiscal years under Biden, falling short by fewer than 3,000, according to the department.
WHITE HOUSE DOUBLES DOWN AFTER TRUMP ANGERS BASE BY FLOATING ILLEGAL ALIEN DEAL WITH DEMS
Trump’s immigration crackdown drove ICE arrests and deportations to historic highs in fiscal 2026, according to DHS. (Christian Torres/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images)
Specifically, this year's arrests were more than six times higher than those recorded during former President Joe Biden's first fiscal year in office.
Deportations were also more than eight times higher for the same time period.
August 2026 also set a new record for arrests, with 50,925, marking the highest number for any single month in ICE history, Mullin said.
That pace continued into September, which logged over 48,000 arrests, representing a more than 300% increase over the average September under the previous administration.

ICE deported 483,200 people in fiscal 2026, nearly matching the combined total from Biden’s final three full fiscal years, DHS said. (REUTERS/Carielle Doe)
Under Trump's leadership, more than 3 million migrants have left the U.S., DHS said.
As of October, the administration had deported nearly 1.2 million illegal aliens and arrested more than 1.25 million, according to the department.
"I couldn’t be prouder of the brave men and women of ICE, who just broke more historic records," Mullin said.

title: Texas man executed for beheading 3 children: 'Going to be with my kids'
summary: John Allen Rubio thanked loved ones and said he would soon be with the three children he killed before receiving a lethal injection in Texas.
story: Three states carried out executions on the same day, while California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced plans to commute all 548 of his state’s death sentences.
A South Texas man convicted of murdering three young children he helped raise was executed Thursday evening, nearly 23 years after the killings.
John Allen Rubio, 46, of Brownsville, received a lethal injection at a state prison in Huntsville, according to The Associated Press (AP).

Rubio was convicted of stabbing and beheading his children, Julissa Quezada, 3, John Esteban Rubio, 1, and Mary Jane Rubio, 2 months old. He was prosecuted alongside his common-law wife, Angela Camacho.
Rubio was pronounced dead at 6:47 p.m., 21 minutes after the lethal injection began, The AP said.
OKLAHOMA MAN, 73, EXECUTED FOR PLOTTING MURDER OF LOVER'S HUSBAND, OFFERS NO LAST WORDS

A fence, barbed wire and a guard are visible at a Texas prison on Jan. 22, 2025. John Allen Rubio was executed in Texas Nov. 12, 2026.  (Cecile Clocheret/AFP via Getty Images; Texas Department of Criminal Justice via AP)
The execution, scheduled for 6 p.m., proceeded without incident.

In his final statement, Rubio thanked his friends and family for their "love and understanding," acknowledged that he was "not the same person I once was" and expressed his love for his wife, according to the AP.
"I want to say I’m sorry to my wife’s family," he said. "I can’t change the past, but I can tell you my life is going to be over. But that’s not going to make you happy.
"I’m going to be with my kids in a little bit," he added. "I’m ready to go to heaven to be with my lord and savior."
ALABAMA GOVERNOR COMMUTES DEATH SENTENCE AS DOUBTS EMERGE ABOUT EVIDENCE IN MURDER CONVICTION
John Allen Rubio was convicted of murdering three young children in 2003 and sentenced to death. (Texas Department of Criminal Justice )
The execution brought an end to a case dating back to March 11, 2003, when Rubio and Camacho killed their three children inside a windowless apartment.
According to court records, Rubio was not the biological father of the two older children but had nevertheless taken on a parental role in their lives, the outlet reported.
In the lead-up to the killings, Rubio reportedly claimed the children were possessed and cast himself as the "chosen one" destined to save the world.
Rubio at one point pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity. Defense experts reportedly diagnosed him with paranoid schizophrenia, but prosecution experts ultimately disputed the findings.
His defense team also painted a picture of a deeply troubled childhood, citing violence, toxic parents, drug use and prostitution as factors that stunted his development, the AP said.
Camacho pleaded guilty and is serving a life sentence for her role in the murders, according to reports.
The apartment building where the children were killed has since been demolished, and the property was transformed into a community park and garden, according to the AP.

This photo provided by the Oklahoma Department of Corrections shows James Pavatt in February 2023. Pavatt was executed just hours before Rubio was administered lethal injection.  (Bryan Terry/The Oklahoman/USA Today Network; Oklahoma Department of Corrections via AP)

Rubio's death marked the second of two executions scheduled in the U.S. for Thursday.
Just hours earlier, James Pavatt, 73, was put to death by lethal injection in Oklahoma. Pavatt was convicted of plotting and carrying out the 2001 killing of his partner's estranged husband.

She and her husband of four years, Mark Longo, were planning to attend a TikTok event when officers approached them, according to the New York Post.

Longo said his wife's detention stemmed from what he described as a minor paperwork issue, The AP said. The couple reportedly made an error on one of her immigration forms and failed to catch it while dealing with the seizure and euthanasia of Peanut.
OWNERS OF BELOVED PEANUT THE SQUIRREL PLAN TO SUE NEW YORK STATE OVER SEIZURE AND KILLING BY AUTHORITIES

Mark Longo, center, and his wife Daniela Bittner, left, speak during a news conference on April 8, 2025, in Albany, N.Y. Bittner’s husband says her ICE detention stems from a paperwork error. (AP Photo/Michael Hill)
"She came into this country legally on a visa. We filed the paperwork and stuff and apparently the government is saying we filed the wrong piece of paper," Longo told The Post.

"They had asked for additional information, which we provided, and then apparently they sent a letter stating that it was denied because we filed the wrong paperwork, which we never received," he said.
"This is a minor paperwork issue and it’s being treated as if my wife literally crawled out a hole to get into this country," he added.
PEANUT THE PET SQUIRREL TAKEN AWAY BY NEW YORK STATE OFFICIALS FROM ADOPTED HOME, MAY BE EUTHANIZED
Peanut was rescued at 5 weeks old by his adoptive human parents after his mother was run over by a car. (peanut_the_squirrel12 via Instagram)
Longo said Bittner has no criminal history and was hit with the maximum penalty, potentially facing deportation without a hearing, according to The Post.
The couple reportedly married in 2022, shortly after Bittner returned to Germany to resolve a visa situation.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) told the outlet that Bittner lawfully entered the U.S. multiple times between May 2021 and November 2022, each time receiving permission to stay for a temporary period.
However, DHS said she was arrested because she "chose to overstay her welcome in defiance of our nation's laws."
"To be clear, a pending application does not confer legal status in the United States," DHS told the Post.
Bittner has reportedly been transferred between several detention centers, from Syracuse to Buffalo, Louisiana and eventually Texas.
Longo described the conditions his wife has faced in federal custody as "deplorable," The AP said.
Her arrest has also cast uncertainty over the couple's nonprofit animal rescue operation, where Bittner reportedly cares for 600 animals rescued from neglect.

"If my wife gets deported for a paperwork issue, we will lose EVERYTHING we worked for. Our Nonprofit Animal Sanctuary will close and 600 animals will have to find another home. All we wanted was to be left alone. We finally moved on from the tragic murder of P'Nut, now to this," he said.
Peanut the squirrel enjoys some peanuts in this photo shared on Instagram. (peanut_the_squirrel12 via Instagram)

Longo had rescued Peanut when he was just 5 weeks old after the squirrel's mother was reportedly struck and killed by a car. The animal later became a viral social media sensation, amassing a large following online.

title: Oklahoma man, 73, executed for plotting murder of lover's husband, offers no last words
summary: James Pavatt was pronounced dead after lethal injection for plotting the 2001 murder of Rob Andrew, who was gunned down in his garage just before Thanksgiving.
story: This photo provided by the Oklahoma Department of Corrections shows James Pavatt in Feb. 2023. (BRYAN TERRY/THE OKLAHOMAN / USA TODAY NETWORK; Oklahoma Department of Corrections via AP)
An Oklahoma man convicted of plotting with his lover to kill her estranged husband 25 years ago was executed Thursday without uttering any final words.

James Pavatt, 73, was put to death by lethal injection at the Oklahoma State Penitentiary in McAlester for the 2001 murder of Rob Andrew, a 39-year-old advertising executive who was gunned down in his garage while picking up his two young children just before Thanksgiving.

Pavatt was pronounced dead at 10:12 a.m. local time, according to the Oklahoma Department of Corrections. Prison officials described the execution as "uneventful," adding that Pavatt had no last words, according to local news station KOKH.
FLORIDA DEATH ROW INMATE USES LAST WORDS TO MAINTAIN INNOCENCE BEFORE EXECUTION
This photo provided by the Oklahoma Department of Corrections shows James Pavatt in February 2023. (Oklahoma Department of Corrections via AP)
For his last meal, Pavatt requested a strawberry milkshake and a barbecue dinner of smoked chicken, brisket, pulled pork, fried okra, baked beans and pickles, KOCO reported.

Pavatt was convicted of first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit murder. He had been having an affair with Rob Andrew's wife, Brenda Andrew, who was convicted in a separate trial and also sentenced to death.
Weeks before the killing, Rob Andrew told police someone was trying to kill him after the brake lines on his car were cut.
The Oklahoma State Penitentiary in McAlester, Okla., Nov. 17, 2021. (Bryan Terry/The Oklahoman/USA Today Network)

Brenda Andrew later claimed masked intruders shot her in the arm and fatally shot her husband at the Oklahoma City home the couple previously shared. Prosecutors, however, said she and Pavatt plotted the murder.
The pair fled to Mexico with Brenda Andrew's two children after the shooting but were arrested three months later while re-entering the United States.
At a clemency hearing last month, Pavatt maintained his innocence and claimed Brenda Andrew had manipulated him.
ALABAMA GOVERNOR COMMUTES DEATH SENTENCE AS DOUBTS EMERGE ABOUT EVIDENCE IN MURDER CONVICTION
"It was not until my trial that I began to see the extent to which I had been manipulated by Brenda," he told the board. "I can see why the jury believed that we were both involved in Rob's murder."
An entrance sign and guard tower at Oklahoma State Penitentiary. (Shepard Sherbell/Corbis Saba/Corbis via Getty Images)
Prosecutors maintained that both were equally responsible for the killing, regardless of who fired the fatal shots.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Pavatt's execution was the first of two scheduled in the United States on Thursday. In Texas, John Allen Rubio, 46, was set to be executed that evening for the 2003 stabbing and beheading of three young children he was raising in Brownsville. The victims were 3 years old, 14 months old and 2 months old.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

story: A legal challenge heading to the Supreme Court on Monday targets the California governor's death penalty decisions. Critics argue the administration's sweeping commutations ignore voter intent and fail to evaluate cases individually.

A California prosecutor said Thursday he plans to challenge a new statewide death row clemency push in court after highlighting the twisted impact of nearly 50 death row inmates in his county expected to benefit from Gov. "When we go to court, and we file on Monday, we're going to make unequivocally clear to the Supreme Court that they are being asked by the governor to overturn the decisions they made affirming these death cases," Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer said Thursday, alongside a group of victims' families and advocates.
He said the court is in a "legal quagmire" after reviewing hundreds of cases and confirming the convictions and death sentences — only to now be asked to reverse their own decisions.
"I'm praying, and I think we may have to actually get down on our knees on this one, that those justices understand," he said.

title: Mysterious object moving through space could be lost Soviet probe as NASA weighs in on theory
summary: Near-Earth asteroid 1998 KY26 shows nongravitational acceleration, and Harvard researchers say it closely matches lost Soviet spacecraft Phobos 1.
story: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman discusses the U.S. space race with China and the importance of NASA's partnership with SpaceX amid potential Democratic investigations into Elon Musk.
A mysterious object speeding through the solar system is accelerating in a way gravity alone cannot explain, fueling a theory that it could be a Soviet spacecraft lost nearly four decades ago.

Known as 1998 KY26, the roughly 36-foot-wide object is believed to be a near-Earth asteroid, but something other than gravity appears to be affecting its path. New research has now cast doubt on one explanation for what is pushing it through space.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman weighed in on the growing speculation Thursday morning on "Fox & Friends," saying some in the UAP community believe the object is making unusual movements, but he has seen no evidence KY26 is anything other than an asteroid.
NASA CHIEF CONFIRMS AGENCY HAS UNEXPLAINED UFO IMAGERY: 'WE DON'T KNOW WHAT IT IS'
"First of all, nothing is about to hit us, to be very clear on this," Isaacman said. "I've not seen any evidence to suggest this is a threat to our planet or anything other than an asteroid."
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman speaks during a Senate hearing in Washington, D.C. (REUTERS)
METEORITE THAT CRASHED INTO NJ HOME HOLDS BUILDING BLOCKS OF LIFE, SCIENTISTS SAY
Scientists refer to KY26's unusual movement as "nongravitational acceleration," meaning something besides the pull of the sun and planets is affecting its path.

One theory has been that KY26 is a "dark comet" containing buried water that turns to gas and gives the object a push through space, even though astronomers have not detected the cloud or tail normally associated with a comet.
But a new peer-reviewed study by Georgia Institute of Technology researchers Korbin Hansen and Masatoshi Hirabayashi casts doubt on that explanation.
Their study, published in the journal Icarus, found KY26 is likely too warm for buried water ice to survive long enough to account for the unusual movement.
Two shape models show scientists' estimates of the form of near-Earth object 1998 KY26. (Credit: NASA)
The researchers concluded that calculated water-loss rates "preclude 1998 KY26 being a dark comet at present."
There are other possible explanations. Previous research found that sunlight hitting KY26 and heat escaping from its surface could produce the extra push without buried water.
HARVARD ASTRONOMER TAPPED TO LEAD WHITE HOUSE UFO COUNCIL SAYS US GOVERNMENT 'BAFFLED BY WHAT THEY ARE SEEING'
Another group of researchers, however, has explored a far more unusual possibility.

Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb and researchers Adam Hibberd and Adam Crowl have examined whether KY26 could actually be Phobos 1, an unmanned Soviet spacecraft that stopped communicating while traveling to Mars in 1988.
NASA SHUTS OFF VOYAGER 1 INSTRUMENT TO SAVE POWER 15B MILES FROM EARTH
An illustration shows the Soviet Phobos 1 spacecraft, which was launched toward Mars in July 1988 but lost after a faulty command caused it to shut down. (Credit: NASA)
KY26 is about 36 feet across, reflects roughly 52% of the sunlight that hits it and completes a full rotation every 5.35 minutes.

The researchers built a simplified model of Phobos 1 and compared the way it would reflect sunlight as it spun with observations of KY26. They found the spacecraft model closely matched eight sets of observations of the object.
GIANT ROBOTIC CLAWS WILL GRAB DEAD SATELLITES IN SPACE
They also tested whether sunlight pushing against a cylinder or solar panels could help explain KY26's movement and found the model better matched hundreds of telescope and radar observations.
"Although an investigation of this kind cannot be conclusive," the researchers wrote, the findings "add strong weight to the Phobos 1 hypothesis."
NASA CHIEF PULLS BACK CURTAIN ON TRUMP UFO FILES AFTER BIZARRE FINDS SURFACE IN BURIED FED RECORDS
The researchers stressed, though, that their model does not prove KY26 is the missing spacecraft, describing the theory as "strongly plausible but presently unproven."
Other research points to a more conventional answer.

A separate study published this year in Astronomy & Astrophysics examined the light reflected by KY26 and found its makeup appears consistent with a type of rocky asteroid. Researchers concluded it likely came from the inner part of the asteroid belt.
Isaacman said NASA continues to monitor KY26 but sees no reason for alarm.
An illustration shows an asteroid passing near Earth as scientists study the unusual movement of near-Earth object 1998 KY26 and whether it could be a long-lost Soviet spacecraft. (istock)
SEND US A TIP
"I have no reason to believe this is in any way remotely a threat to our planet or anything other than just an asteroid," he said.
GOT A TIP?
Scientists may eventually get a definitive answer.
The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's Hayabusa2 spacecraft is scheduled to rendezvous with KY26 in July 2031, according to a 2025 study published in Nature Communications.

For Loeb, that encounter could provide the ultimate test of the Phobos 1 theory.

"Our prediction is that instead of an iceberg, Hayabusa 2’s cameras will reveal the label 'Made in the U.S.S.R.,'" Loeb wrote.

story: Rescuers search for survivors after a building collapse in Brooklyn, New York, leaves at least eight people dead. Fox News' Alexis McAdams reports the latest on the deadly incident.
A three-story building in New York City collapsed into a construction site Wednesday afternoon, leaving at least eight people dead and triggering a massive rescue operation that is ongoing.
A timeline of the disaster shows how the building collapse unfolded in Brooklyn's Flatbush neighborhood, from the first 911 call and subsequent frantic search for survivors to a mounting death toll.
The collapse raised questions about previous construction violations at a nearby worksite.
NYC BUILDING COLLAPSE: EIGHT BODIES RECOVERED AS FIRST RESPONDERS SEARCH FOR SURVIVORS
First responders respond to a collapsed building in the Brooklyn borough of New York City on Nov. 11, 2026. (kena betancur/AFP via Getty Images)

title: Iran's shadow operations stretch across Europe as chilling spy convictions expose Tehran's reach
summary: Two Iranian men convicted of spying in Britain as France accuses the IRGC of cyberattacks and UAE officials warn of Iranian sleeper cells abroad.
story: Lisa Daftari says years of hacking, surveillance and threats have changed how she lives, warning that Iran’s intimidation tactics are designed to silence critics abroad.

Two Iranian men were convicted in Britain on Thursday of spying on journalists and critics of Tehran, the latest case raising alarm over Iranian operations beyond the Middle East, as France accuses the IRGC of unprecedented cyberattacks and a senior UAE official warns of Iranian sleeper cells abroad.

The developments come as the Trump administration continues its campaign of economic pressure against Tehran while leaving the door open to diplomatic negotiations, raising questions about how Iran's overseas intelligence networks and alleged covert activities might factor into any future agreement.

A jury at Woolwich Crown Court in London found Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, guilty of engaging in conduct likely to assist a foreign intelligence service after prosecutors said they carried out surveillance of journalists and other individuals critical of the Iranian government, according to Reuters.
IRAN TURNS CITIZENS INTO INFORMANTS AS CHILLING CRACKDOWN SPREADS BEYOND ITS BORDERS

EU designates Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a terrorist organization as Ursula von der Leyen pledges rapid implementation following a violent crackdown. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
The targets included journalists working for Iran International, a London-based Persian-language news outlet critical of Tehran, and a prominent figure associated with UK Lawyers for Israel.

According to prosecutors, the surveillance operation took place between August 2024 and March 2025 and involved visits to locations associated with the targets, photographs, videos and online research.

Sepahvand was also convicted of engaging in preparatory conduct with the intention of committing serious violence against a person in Britain, while Manesh was acquitted of that charge and a third defendant was cleared of all charges.

British authorities described the case as the first convictions of Iranian nationals under the National Security Act of 2023, warning that the verdicts underscored an ongoing threat from Iranian intelligence operations. Iran has denied involvement.

Similar concerns have emerged in the United States. Just two days before the British verdicts, the U.S. Justice Department announced terrorism charges against three alleged Iranian-backed operatives accused of involvement in nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks across Europe and the United States.

The three men allegedly supported Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and Kata'ib Hezbollah, targeting Jewish communities and plotting an attack on RAF Fairford, a British air base housing American military personnel, according to the Nov. 10 indictment. Prosecutors allege that one defendant, Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, continued coordinating terrorist activities through coded messages while imprisoned in New York. The network was also allegedly involved in planning an attack on a Manhattan synagogue.
FRENCH SUPERMARKETS FACE MILLIONS IN LOSSES AFTER CYBERATTACK HITS REFRIGERATORS NATIONWIDE
Mohammad Ali Al-Hassani, left, and Mohsen Mohajeri appear in an April 2026 video that prosecutors say shows them planning terrorist attacks. (Department of Justice)
In France, authorities on Monday accused Iran's IRGC of orchestrating a major cyberattack against the country's food supply infrastructure.

According to a Nov. 9 report by France's Cyber Crisis Coordination Centre, Iranian-linked hackers targeted refrigeration controllers at approximately 700 retail locations across France on Oct. 11 and 12.

Investigators said the attackers remotely altered defrost settings, causing refrigeration equipment to reach abnormally high temperatures, spoiling significant quantities of food and triggering at least 15 reported fire outbreaks.
The operation affected major supermarket chains, including Carrefour, Leclerc and Intermarché, as well as other businesses in the food industry.
French investigators attributed the operation to Shahid Kaveh, a cyber-offensive unit operating under the IRGC's electronic and cyber command.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot described the attack as unprecedented in its scale and aggression, while authorities announced plans to pursue European sanctions against those responsible.

Iran's Foreign Ministry rejected what it described as baseless and malicious allegations in a statement issued Tuesday strongly condemning the "persistent practice" of directing accusations toward Tehran.
'KEEP A LOW PROFILE': STATE DEPARTMENT WARNS AMERICANS OVERSEAS THEY COULD BE TARGETED

A woman walks past empty fresh-food refrigerators at an Intermarché supermarket in Névez, western France, on Oct. 12, 2026, following a cyberattack that caused supermarket refrigerators to defrost. Some 150 to 200 Intermarché stores were targeted, along with nearly 100 Coopérative U outlets. (Fred Tanneau/AFP via Getty Images)
The European cases echo warnings from the Gulf, where officials have raised concerns that Iran's regional operations extend beyond missiles, drones and armed proxy groups.

Dr. Ali Rashid Al Nuaimi, chairman of the Defense, Interior and Foreign Affairs Committee of the UAE's Federal National Council, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview that Iranian-linked sleeper cells were operating both within the region and elsewhere.

"They created these sleeping cells in the region and also in other places," Al Nuaimi said. "We were fortunate to find out about these cells, to act and to implement the law, our law, the UAE law, against them."

Al Nuaimi previously disclosed during an Oct. 15 briefing that hundreds of suspected Iranian sleeper-cell members had been arrested in the UAE, including individuals he said helped direct Iranian missile and drone attacks against the country.

Speaking separately to Fox News Digital, Al Nuaimi argued that negotiations with Tehran should address not only its nuclear program and regional proxies, but also covert networks operating in other countries.
"This is where it should be part of the negotiation with the Iranians: you have to stop not only the proxies that we know, but also using these sleeping cells in other countries," he said.

Beyond the criminal investigations, Iranian-American journalist and foreign policy analyst Lisa Daftari described the personal toll of what she believes to be Iranian intelligence operations on U.S. soil. In an earlier interview with Fox News Digital, Daftari said she had been followed in Los Angeles and New York, repeatedly hacked and approached in person. She said the FBI informed her that she was on a list of potential Iranian regime targets after hackers gained access to her accounts. "The message they want to send is very clear, that we know where you are, we can reach you," she said.
TRUMP'S FIRST IRAN WAR ESCALATION POST-MIDTERM LOSSES SEEKS TO CHOKE OFF TEHRAN’S TRADE
A 2024 photo released by the Justice Department shows Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi in a conference room with weapons and a map of the United States. (Department of Justice)

In a joint declaration issued Wednesday following a meeting in Paris, G7 foreign ministers expressed grave concern about Iranian involvement in violent plots targeting people and territory in their countries.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking to reporters following the G7 meeting on Tuesday, accused Tehran of being responsible for much of the instability across the Middle East.

"They are behind all the instability in the region; they are the source of instability in the region," Rubio said, referring to Iran's support for armed groups, including Hezbollah, Hamas and the Houthis.

Rubio argued that the Trump administration's economic pressure campaign was significantly weakening the Iranian government and reducing its ability to finance activities abroad, including terrorism and cyber operations.
He said Washington remained open to diplomacy but would not accept what he described as unrealistic Iranian demands.
The G7 declaration also pledged to continue coordinating economic and political measures designed to constrain Tehran's ability to destabilize countries both inside and outside the Middle East.

The British convictions, French cyberattack findings and UAE allegations involve different types of activity, and no evidence has been presented establishing that they formed part of a single coordinated operation.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

G7 foreign ministers and officials pose for a photograph at the start of their summit in Paris, where they are gathered to discuss support for Ukraine and stabilization efforts in the Middle East, on Nov. 9, 2026. (Christophe Petit Tesson/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)

Taken together, however, they illustrate the range of threats Western and Gulf authorities are attributing to Iran — from surveillance of dissidents and alleged sleeper networks to attacks on civilian infrastructure — even as diplomatic efforts seek to prevent another round of military escalation.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. title: El Salvador-backed air assault destroys Haiti gang headquarters amid search for missing troops

story: El Salvador’s president said the operation destroyed a major Haiti gang’s headquarters believed to be used for kidnappings, weapons trafficking and extortion. (@nayibbukele/X)

El Salvador's president on Tuesday said the country's military helped deliver a devastating air assault against the headquarters of one of Haiti's most powerful criminal gangs, which has been linked to mass kidnappings, weapons trafficking and extortion.
Airstrikes targeted strongholds belonging to 400 Mawozo and the home of its leader, Lanmò San Jou, Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele said.
The attack took place Sunday near Port-au-Prince and was carried out by a Haitian police task force backed by Salvadoran troops, The Miami Herald reported.

El Salvador’s president said the operation destroyed a major Haiti gang’s headquarters used for kidnappings, weapons trafficking and extortion. (@nayibbukele/X)

Videos showed several helicopters launching airstrikes against multiple compounds inside sprawling complexes. Dozens of people were also seen fleeing the properties on foot and motorbikes after the strikes.
"Most of them ran away without even trying to fight. What cowards!" Bukele said.
As many as 20 people are believed to have been killed in the operation, according to The Miami Herald, citing anonymous sources.

"Hats off to President Nayib Bukele @nayibbukele for your support and commitment to the national fight against gangs. Haiti, El Salvador, GSF: same fight, same determination! The collaboration will continue. THE GANGS WILL GET NO SLEEP!"
Black smoke rises across a field after a helicopter strike targeting a major gang’s headquarters in Haiti. (@nayibbukele/X)

title: Iran escalates in Hormuz, claims strike on Omani island it says 'enemy' uses for US military ops
summary: Iran claims its Revolutionary Guard struck navigation equipment on Oman's Didamar Island in the Strait of Hormuz, but Omani officials dispute damage.
story: The IRGC reported a strike against ‘enemy navigation aid systems,’ radar and communications equipment located on Didamar Island in Hormuz (Credit: Reuters).

Iran claims it struck a small Omani island in the Strait of Hormuz, targeting oil tanker navigation infrastructure as CENTCOM maintains its blockade of Iranian ports and protects commercial shipping from Iranian attacks along the southern route.

Three sources also confirmed to Reuters Wednesday that navigation systems and communications equipment on Didamar Island, also known as Little Quoin Island, had been attacked, raising concerns about the vulnerability of maritime infrastructure used to maintain oil shipments through the Gulf.

Iran's semiofficial Fars News Agency reported that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) navy targeted the island, alleging the systems were being used to help vessels transit the strait without Tehran's authorization.
WHITE HOUSE SILENT ON IRAN-OMAN HORMUZ PLAN TEHRAN SAYS WOULD BAN US WARSHIPS
A satellite image shows Didamar Island, Oman (Google/Airbus/Handout via Reuters)

Iranian state television also claimed that personnel and equipment on the island "were helping the flow of oil smuggling by the enemy," with the IRGC maintaining it had carried out the strikes, Reuters reported.
Video published by Reuters showed smoke rising near the rocky outcrop.
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said it identified the attack as occurring Nov. 8, before Iranian state media claimed responsibility on Nov. 10.
ISW also questioned the extent of the reported damage, noting that commercial vessels continued using the southern route after the attack.
"The extent of the damage to these systems and the systems struck remains unclear at the time of this writing," ISW said in its assessment.
Satellite imagery from the European Union's Copernicus Sentinel-2 program, cited by Reuters and dated Nov. 8, also showed apparent scorch marks near radar and radio equipment on the island.
TRADE VESSEL STRUCK BY PROJECTILE IN STRAIT OF HORMUZ AMID US-IRAN TALKS
A ship passes through the Strait of Hormuz during a two-week temporary ceasefire between the United States and Iran April 8, 2026. (Shady Alassar/Anadolu/Getty Images)
The strike comes as U.S. forces carry out missions to escort ships through the Strait of Hormuz, which connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea.

The U.S. Navy imposed its blockade of Iranian ports in April after Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in February amid escalating tensions. The U.S. lifted the blockade in June following a temporary ceasefire agreement, but then reinstated it in July.
Commercial and allied shipping through the waterway is advised to use a southern route through Omani territorial waters, located outside of Tehran’s direct military control and overseen by CENTCOM.
The latest incident on Didamar Island comes as Gulf oil exporters work to restore shipments disrupted by the conflict.
TRUMP MEETS KEY IRAN WAR MEDIATOR AS UAE REVEALS MAJOR OIL EXPORT SURGE DESPITE CONFLICT

An Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps speedboat sails in the Persian Gulf during an IRGC marine parade marking Persian Gulf National Day near the Bushehr nuclear power plant in Bushehr, Iran, April 29, 2024. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
According to Reuters, regional oil exports recovered to more than 80% of prewar levels in September and October, aided by CENTCOM and increased Saudi exports through the Red Sea.
Shipping companies have also relied on offshore tanker-to-tanker transfers near Oman and the United Arab Emirates to maintain flows.

Didamar, meanwhile, belongs to Oman, making the reported attack particularly sensitive as Tehran seeks to disrupt maritime operations in the region. It is a small, uninhabited rocky island roughly 10 nautical miles north of the tip of Oman's Musandam Peninsula, near one of the principal commercial shipping routes through the strait.
The island has long served as a navigational landmark for vessels traveling along the waterway, including through a lighthouse established in 1914.
Its maritime infrastructure reportedly includes a radar system mounted on a roughly 25-meter tower and radio communications equipment used to assist vessels navigating the narrow passage.
The island has also been associated with the Hormuz Control Centre, which coordinates maritime traffic in the area.
OIL SQUEEZE TIGHTENS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS CRIPPLE HORMUZ ESCAPE ROUTES
A satellite image shows the Strait of Hormuz, a key maritime passage connecting the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman, vital for global energy supply. (Amanda Macias/Fox News Digital)
Arabian Maritime and Navigation Aids Services (AMMAS) has been identified as a provider of navigational support infrastructure in the region, including maritime lights, buoys and other equipment.
The reported Didamar attack also follows U.S. military operations against Iranian targets elsewhere in the waterway.
U.S. forces struck targets on Iran's Qeshm Island Nov. 2, and officials described the strikes as "defensive" actions targeting Iranian surface-to-air missile threats.
Qeshm Island, located near the Strait of Hormuz, is home to Iranian naval facilities and military infrastructure associated with the Revolutionary Guard.
President Donald Trump also acknowledged Nov. 6 that American forces continue to conduct limited strikes against Iranian targets.

Asked by a reporter about the strikes near Qeshm Island, Trump said, "I don't want to talk about it. We do minor strikes. They built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device, and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five."

title: Fiery chaos erupts across Spain as protesters clash with police during massive nationwide strike

story: Clashes broke out during a general strike in Madrid, with riot police detaining demonstrators in the Spanish capital. (Credit: Reuters)

Unruly protesters set fires, smashed storefronts and launched fireworks at riot police across parts of Spain on Wednesday as a massive nationwide strike over soaring housing costs disrupted transportation and businesses.

Violent scenes unfolded in Barcelona, where some demonstrators vandalized stores along the city's popular Paseo de Gracia shopping boulevard, set small bonfires and launched fireworks at officers arriving in riot gear and armored vehicles, according to The Associated Press.
The violence erupted after a largely peaceful march as Spain experienced its first general strike in 14 years, with workers demanding relief from skyrocketing rents and the rising cost of living.
TRAVELERS MAY FACE MAJOR DISRUPTIONS AS STRIKES THREATEN AIRPORTS AND POPULAR ATTRACTIONS
A protestor holds up a poster as objects burn in the background during a demonstration over the housing crisis Wednesday in Barcelona, Spain. (David Ramos/Getty Images)

Housing activists claimed 400,000 people marched through Barcelona, while city officials estimated attendance at 55,000. Government officials reported another 120,000 demonstrators gathered in Madrid despite heavy rain, the AP reported.

The nationwide walkout disrupted public transportation, forced some businesses to close and blocked major roads. Police made arrests across the country, while officers used pepper spray against demonstrators in Madrid, according to the AP.
ANGRY LOCALS BLOCK FAMOUS BEACH AS MASS TOURISM PROTESTS ESCALATE AT VACATION HOT SPOT

Rioters burn trash cans Wednesday in Spain during a nationwide general strike over the country's housing crisis, with workers also demanding greater purchasing power ahead of a snap general election at the end of the month, near Catalunya square in Barcelona. (Josep Lago/AFP via Getty Images)

The unrest comes amid growing frustration over Spain's housing crisis, fueled in part by the eviction of an 87-year-old Madrid woman who had lived in her apartment for seven decades before reportedly facing a tripling of her rent. She died weeks later, according to the BBC.

The housing crisis has become a major political flashpoint ahead of Spain's Nov. 29 parliamentary elections, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez reportedly encouraging workers to exercise their right to strike.
SPANISH OPPOSITION LEADER CALLS PRIME MINISTER A ‘TRAITOR’ OVER CEUTA MIGRANT CRISIS
Rioters light fires and throw objects during unrest Wednesday over the housing crisis in Barcelona, Spain. (David Ramos/Getty Images)
But the demonstrations have also sparked a political clash, with conservative opposition leaders accusing Sánchez's government of exploiting the unrest for electoral gain, according to the BBC.

Meanwhile, Spain's largest labor unions declared the ongoing strike a success despite business groups disputing claims of widespread participation.
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: DNA links 4 grizzly bears to deadly attack on mother and daughter in Canada, officials say
summary: DNA evidence linked four grizzly bears to the deaths of Jennifer Balcarras and Selah Reed near Bella Coola, British Columbia, officials said.
story: Canadian wildlife officials say DNA testing linked an adult female grizzly and her three offspring to the deaths of a mother and daughter near Bella Coola, British Columbia. Investigators say the attack likely involved predatory behavior.

Four grizzly bears have been linked through DNA evidence to a deadly attack on a mother and daughter in British Columbia, prompting Canadian wildlife officers to kill all four animals, officials announced Tuesday.

The British Columbia Conservation Officer Service said forensic testing conclusively linked an adult female grizzly and her three offspring to the deaths of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter, Selah Reed, 20, near Bella Coola.

The bears were captured over the weekend and killed in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines to protect public safety, according to a Nov. 10 statement from the agency.
BODY OF MISSING HIKER DISCOVERED OFF TRAIL AS INVESTIGATORS PROBE RARE DEADLY BEAR ENCOUNTER
An image showing a photo of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her 20-year-old daughter Selah Reed, who were killed in a grizzly bear attack. (Facebook/Josh Kara Balcarras)
Investigators determined that the encounter likely involved predatory behavior, although officials did not elaborate on how the attack unfolded.

"This was a heartbreaking event for the families, the Nuxalk Nation and the Bella Coola community. We hope the efforts of everyone who responded, along with these findings, bring some measure of closure," said Insp. Jeff Tyre in a news briefing.
More than a dozen conservation officers participated in the response, helping recover the victims, collect evidence and locate the bears while working in difficult terrain and weather conditions.
GRIZZLY BEAR MAULS HIKER, DRAGS HIM DOZENS OF FEET ON GLACIER NATIONAL PARK TRAIL
FILE – Grizzly bear in Jasper National Park, Canada. (Getty Images/iStockphoto)
Balcarras, an art therapist, and Reed went missing after taking a walk on the Snooka West Trail near their home.

Family members contacted the Royal Canadian Mounted Police after Balcarras missed a scheduled online meet-up. Investigators found her vehicle at the trailhead before recovering her body on Nov. 2 and Reed's body on Nov. 3.

The agency said DNA testing also confirmed the four bears were not involved in a separate 2025 grizzly bear attack on a school group near Bella Coola that injured 11 people, including students and teachers.
The investigation has concluded, although officials said further analysis will examine the response and circumstances surrounding the attack.
Royal Canadian Mounted Police board, on April 10, 2024, in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada. (Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The conservation service said fatal grizzly bear attacks involving predatory behavior are rare and encouraged people traveling in bear country to leash pets, travel in groups and learn how to reduce the risk of wildlife encounters.Fox News Digital's Louis Casiano contributed to this report.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Russian Ambassador to US Alexander Darchiev dies suddenly at 66
summary: Russia's ambassador to the United States Alexander Darchiev, 66, had been appointed by Putin to lead a rapprochement with the Trump administration.
story: Fox News' Gillian Turner reports on the arrest of a senior U.S. Army officer in Britain on suspicion of spying for Russia following a joint U.S.-U.K. investigation.
Russia's Ambassador to the United States Alexander Darchiev, 66, died suddenly Wednesday, the Russian Foreign Ministry announced.

"The leadership and staff of the Russian Foreign Ministry report with deep sorrow that on Nov. 11, at the age of 66, the Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Russian Federation to the United States of America, Alexander Nikitich Darchiev, passed away suddenly," Russia's statement, as translated to English, said. "A distinguished diplomat, experienced leader, kind colleague, and mentor has departed this life. A consummate professional and brilliant Americanist, A.N. Darchiev served on one of the most critical and demanding fronts of Russian foreign policy."

"We express our deepest and most sincere condolences to the family and loved ones of Alexander Nikitich Darchiev," the statement added. "The cherished memory of our untimely departed colleague will forever remain in our hearts."
Fox News confirmed the death came in Russia and not the U.S.
MELANIA TRUMP HAILS OLESHKY CEASEFIRE AS POTENTIAL ‘SPARK’ FOR PROGRESS AMID UKRAINE-RUSSIA WAR

Alexander Darchiyev, head of the Russian Foreign Ministry's North America Department and a candidate for the position of ambassador to the United States, poses for a picture before a session of the Federation Council's committee on foreign affairs in Moscow, Russia, on Nov. 25, 2024. (Kommersant Photo/Dmitry Dukhanin via Reuters)

Russia's Vladimir Putin appointed Darchiev, a veteran diplomat known in the past for his public denunciations of the West, as ambassador to Washington in March 2025 to lead a rapprochement with the Trump administration that has rattled Ukraine, the European Union and NATO.
His death comes less than a week after a White House news conference hailing a temporary ceasefire in Ukrainian territory occupied by Russia.
First lady Melania Trump and envoys from both Russia and Ukraine hailed the ceasefire in the Oleshky region.

"We have chosen humanity over war," the first lady said. "Undeniably, the lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace. Every significant transformation begins with a small spark."
KUSHNER ENTERS UKRAINE PEACE TALKS AS TRUMP EYES SECURING SAFEGUARDS AGAINST ANOTHER RUSSIAN INVASION
Shortly after being tapped as ambassador, Darchiev met with Trump administration officials and delivered a message of hope for peace.

"Russia and the United States are destined, as great powers, to have non-confrontational peaceful existence," Darchiev said during a June 10, 2025, Russia Day reception at the Russian Embassy in Washington after delivering his credentials to the White House, adding, "our discussion was very constructive."

Before taking the helm of the Russian Embassy in Washington, Darchiev played a role as the Kremlin’s point man for high-stakes bilateral negotiations, most notably during the delicate discussions that led to prisoner swaps involving imprisoned arms dealer Viktor Bout and detained Americans Brittney Griner and Paul Whelan.
EVAN GERSHKOVICH DETAILS RUSSIAN ARREST, REVEALS MOMENT THAT NEARLY BROKE HIM DURING WRONGFUL DETENTION

In August 2022, while serving as the director of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s North American Department, Darchiev provided the first on-the-record Russian confirmation that Moscow and Washington were actively discussing those situations.

"This quite sensitive issue of the swap of convicted Russian and U.S. citizens is being pursued along the channels designated by our presidents," Darchiev told the Russian state news agency TASS. "The individuals are, indeed, being discussed. The Russian side has long been seeking the release of Viktor Bout. The negotiations are bearing fruit."

An empty table for the Russian Ambassador to the United States Alexander Darchiev is visible during a Senate Appropriations Subcommittee hearing on "The Abduction of Ukrainian Children by the Russian Federation" on Capitol Hill on December 3, 2025 in Washington, DC. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

His comments marked a breakthrough moment in months of backchannel diplomacy, which ultimately culminated in December 2022 when the U.S. and Russia completed a one-for-one swap of Griner for Bout at an airport in Abu Dhabi.
Fox News' Gillian Turner, The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

title: Israel's political shake-up enters new phase as former PM plays kingmaker — and deadline looms
summary: Benjamin Netanyahu called for unity, but Gadi Eisenkot canceled Likud talks after calling the outgoing prime minister's speech "delusional."
story: With final election results leaving both major blocs short of a majority, Fox News Digital reporter Efrat Lachter reports from Israel on the negotiations that could determine the country's next government.

Israel's newly elected parliament was sworn in Tuesday, marking the beginning of a political transition that could end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's long tenure in power. Despite the opposition's parliamentary gains, the country remains without a new government, and negotiations to form one face significant obstacles.

At the center of those negotiations is former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who was tasked by President Isaac Herzog on Sunday with assembling Israel's next governing coalition after 67 lawmakers recommended him for the position, compared with 46 who supported Netanyahu.

Although Eisenkot's Yashar party won 21 seats in the Oct. 27 election, he is working closely with former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, whose B'Yachad party, formed with former Prime Minister Yair Lapid, secured another 12 seats.
NETANYAHU FACES COALITION SHOWDOWN AS RIVALS MANEUVER TO FORM ISRAEL'S NEXT GOVERNMENT

Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Israeli President Isaac Herzog and other Israeli officials pose for a photo on the day of the inauguration of Israel's 26th parliament, at the Knesset in Jerusalem, Nov. 10, 2026. (Ronen Zvulun/Reuters)

The two parties have not merged, but their cooperation effectively gives Eisenkot the negotiating backing of 33 lawmakers — more than Netanyahu's Likud, which remains the largest individual party in the Knesset with 27 seats.

A source with knowledge of discussions within the bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu told Fox News Digital that Bennett has decided to act as a political kingmaker, supporting Eisenkot's leadership bid rather than seeking the premiership himself.
Bennett intends to coordinate closely with Eisenkot throughout the negotiations while preserving his party's independent leadership and parliamentary identity, according to the source.
Parliament members attend an opening ceremony on the day of the inauguration of Israel's 26th parliament, at the Knesset in Jerusalem, Nov. 10, 2026. (Ronen Zvulun/Reuters)

The arrangement does not create a new 33-seat party or guarantee that the two leaders will agree on every coalition arrangement. But it places Eisenkot in a stronger negotiating position than his party's 21 seats alone would suggest.

During Tuesday's swearing-in of the new Knesset, Netanyahu called for a national unity government, citing Israel's security challenges, but also sharply attacked the Arab parties, accusing them of supporting terrorism and warning against forming a government dependent on their votes.
Bennett, normally an outspoken political figure who has largely avoided the spotlight during the coalition negotiations, broke his relative silence to repeatedly confront Netanyahu during the speech.
FORMER ISRAELI PM EMERGES AS WILD CARD IN HIGH-STAKES ELECTION WITH MIDDLE EAST'S FUTURE AT STAKE
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu delivers remarks during a toast by heads of Israel's political factions, at the Knesset in Jerusalem, Nov. 10, 2026. (Ronen Zvulun/Reuters)

"What about your Qatari advisors?" Bennett shouted, referring to the investigation into allegations that members of Netanyahu's inner circle had financial ties to Qatar while working for the prime minister. Bennett also demanded to know why Netanyahu had not established a state commission of inquiry into the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks and challenged him to declare Qatar an enemy state.
The confrontation disrupted Netanyahu's address, with other lawmakers joining the shouting as the prime minister continued warning against a government supported by Arab parties.

Eisenkot responded with an unusually forceful condemnation. "I sat and listened to the outgoing prime minister’s delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful speech," Eisenkot said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital on Nov. 10. "I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute."
Eisenkot subsequently instructed his negotiating team to cancel a meeting scheduled with Likud representatives for Wednesday.

In a separate statement, Yashar said the canceled meeting had been intended to explore coalition possibilities based on Eisenkot's four governing principles, but Netanyahu's speech made the planned discussions untenable.
FORMER ISRAELI ARMY CHIEF GADI EISENKOT EMERGES AS NETANYAHU’S LEADING ELECTION CHALLENGER

Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar ("Straight") party, waves an Israeli flag onstage following the release of the first exit poll results in Israel's general election in Tel Aviv, Oct. 28, 2026. (Ariel Schalit/AP Photo)

Netanyahu, however, continued advocating for a unity government on Wednesday, arguing that Israel's security challenges demanded cooperation across political divisions, according to The Times of Israel.

Despite the public confrontation, a national unity government remains one of the most tangible scenarios under consideration, according to a source with knowledge of negotiations within the bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu.

The source told Fox News Digital that such an arrangement would depend on Netanyahu agreeing not to serve as prime minister first, potentially allowing Eisenkot to lead the government under a rotation agreement while Netanyahu assumes the position of alternate prime minister.

Eisenkot's allies are keeping several options open, according to the source, including agreements with ultra-Orthodox or Arab parties, partly to strengthen their negotiating position and increase pressure on Netanyahu to accept a power-sharing arrangement.
But whether Netanyahu would agree to relinquish the premiership, even temporarily, remains unclear. The source emphasized that negotiations are fluid and that no agreement has been reached.
NETANYAHU GAINS OVERNIGHT AS ISRAEL ELECTION HEADS TOWARD POLITICAL DEADLOCK
Naftali Bennett, former prime minister and head of the Together party, speaks at a press conference at the Israeli parliament on May 20, 2026, in Jerusalem. (Amir Levy/Getty Images)

The official election results left Netanyahu's bloc with 53 seats, while the four parties seeking to replace him secured 48. The remaining 19 seats went to two Arab-led parties: the Joint List, with 11, and Ra'am, led by Mansour Abbas, with eight.
While 67 lawmakers supported Eisenkot receiving the mandate to form a government, that support does not automatically translate into a workable governing coalition.
Herzog acknowledged the challenge during consultations with parliamentary leaders, citing disagreements and mutual political vetoes that could prevent either side from forming a stable government.

Eisenkot's principal partners are Bennett, Lapid, Yair Golan of the Democrats and Avigdor Liberman of Yisrael Beytenu. Together, their parties hold 48 seats, 13 short of the 61 generally needed for a parliamentary majority.

Eisenkot has outlined four principles for potential coalition partners: recognizing Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accepting the values of the Declaration of Independence, supporting military or civilian national service for all, and recognizing Hamas as a terrorist organization whose military and governing capabilities must be dismantled.
But those conditions have created a difficult political equation.
The ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, collectively hold 13 seats — precisely the number Eisenkot's existing four-party bloc would need to reach 61.
However, both parties have historically opposed broadening military conscription to include ultra-Orthodox religious students, directly conflicting with Eisenkot's demand for national service.
At a Nov. 10 faction meeting, Eisenkot reiterated that he would not abandon the principle of universal military, national or civilian service, according to The Times of Israel.

The disagreement became even more visible Wednesday, when Bennett's party submitted legislation proposing expanded benefits for soldiers and reservists, while United Torah Judaism introduced bills seeking to preserve military draft exemptions for religious students, The Times of Israel reported Tuesday.
The Arab parties present a different challenge.

While Ra'am's eight lawmakers could help Eisenkot establish a government, Liberman has rejected relying on Arab parties, and the political acceptability of such an arrangement remains disputed within the bloc.
A source within Eisenkot's party told Fox News Digital that the party has not categorically ruled out cooperation with Ra'am, provided its leadership accepts the four governing principles.
The source acknowledged that negotiations remain difficult and that multiple coalition arrangements are still under consideration.

One option involves securing the support of ultra-Orthodox parties. Another would require cooperation with Arab lawmakers, potentially including support from outside the government. A broader national unity arrangement involving Likud has also been discussed.

Each scenario presents political obstacles, leaving Eisenkot facing the difficult task of assembling a coalition among parties with sharply different views on religion, national identity and security policy.
NETANYAHU DEFIES EXIT POLLS AS VOTE SHIFTS IN HIS FAVOR, BUT MAJORITY REMAINS ELUSIVE
Mansour Abbas, leader of the Ra'am party, speaks at the plenum at the Knesset, Israel's parliament, in Jerusalem, July 13, 2026. (Ronen Zvulun/Reuters)
Even without a new government, Eisenkot and his allies have begun exercising their influence in the newly sworn-in parliament.

In a Monday statement provided to Fox News Digital, Yashar announced that it had submitted legislation to establish a state commission of inquiry into the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks and introduce term limits for the prime minister.

The party also submitted proposals to repeal legislation associated with Netanyahu's judicial overhaul, including changes to the judiciary, the attorney general's authority, the police and the circumstances under which a prime minister can be declared unable to serve.
A vote to replace current Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally, is scheduled for Nov. 17.
The appointments could give Eisenkot's allies considerable influence over Israel's legislative agenda before they secure control of the government.
Beyond the domestic political negotiations, Eisenkot has also sought to reassure American leaders about the future of U.S.-Israel relations.

In a Nov. 4 public statement addressed to Americans and the international community, Eisenkot pledged to restore bipartisan cooperation with Washington and deepen Israel's relationship with the United States.

"The bond between Israel and the United States is more than an alliance between governments," Eisenkot wrote. "It is a partnership between peoples, built over generations, sustained by shared democratic values, and strengthened by the conviction that our nations are more secure and more prosperous when we stand together."
He also directly addressed his willingness to work with President Donald Trump.
"I look forward to working closely and constructively with President Trump and his administration, whose friendship and commitment to Israel we deeply value," Eisenkot said.
The message comes amid heightened debate in Washington over the future of U.S. support for Israel, following the American midterm elections and disagreements over the country's regional policies.

A source within Eisenkot's party told Fox News Digital that rebuilding relations with the United States, including with both major American political parties, would be among the priorities of a new government.
Eisenkot has also emphasized his intention to pursue regional cooperation and diplomatic opportunities while maintaining Israel's security commitments.
ISRAEL HEADS INTO DEEPLY DIVIDED ELECTION AS OCT. 7 RECKONING LOOMS: WHAT TO KNOW

Yair Golan of the Democrats party speaks during a rally to demand the establishment of an independent state commission of inquiry into the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks and the events leading up to them, in Tel Aviv, Israel Oct. 24, 2026. (Kevin Coombs/Reuters)

Under Israeli law, Eisenkot has 28 days from Nov. 8 to form a government, giving him until Dec. 6 to reach an agreement. Herzog can grant an extension of up to 14 additional days, potentially pushing the deadline to Dec. 20.

If Eisenkot fails, the president may give another lawmaker the opportunity to form a government. Additional parliamentary procedures would follow if a second attempt also fails, potentially culminating in another national election.

The outcome could determine not only who becomes Israel's next prime minister, but also the country's direction on military conscription, judicial reform, accountability for October 7 and its relations with Washington.

For now, Israel is experiencing an unusual political transition: a newly elected parliament is beginning to challenge the outgoing government's agenda, while the leader tasked with forming its replacement is still negotiating over who will join him.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
A road sign stands in front of a billboard featuring Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot, in Ramat Gan on Oct. 20, 2026. (Jack Guez/AFP via Getty Images)

Eisenkot has the presidential mandate, Bennett's backing and the support of a parliamentary majority willing to recommend him. What he does not yet have is an agreement among those parties on how to govern together.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition.
